articles.title: Rubio Trip Highlights US Push For Deeper Ties With Central Asia
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio departed Uzbekistan on October 20 for India after meetings with all five Central Asian countries, wrapping up a visit aimed at expanding Washington’s economic and diplomatic engagement with a region increasingly intent on shaping its own international partnerships.

articles.title: 'We're Never Going To Be The Major Player': Former Diplomat's Reality Check On US Ambitions In Central Asia
articles.summary: Marco Rubio has brought nearly 300 American business representatives to Uzbekistan for a meeting with representatives of the five states of Central Asia. But Daniel N. Rosenblum, a former US ambassador to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, cautions that investment faces major obstacles.

articles.title: Rubio Travels To Central Asia As US Seeks Deeper Trade And Security Ties In Region
articles.summary: As Secretary of State Marco Rubio heads to Uzbekistan, Washington is hoping the high-level diplomatic engagement translates into concrete economic and security cooperation.

articles.title: Rubio Heads To Central Asia As US Seeks Bigger Role In Region Dominated By Russia, China
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio heads to Uzbekistan this weekend for talks with five Central Asian countries as the Trump administration seeks to strengthen commercial ties and expand Washington's strategic presence in the region.

articles.title: As Russian Arms Exports Slide, Central Asia Shops Elsewhere
articles.summary: Central Asian nations are increasingly turning to India, China, Turkey, and Europe for military equipment to reduce their dependence on Russia. Analysts note that this diversification offers greater political flexibility but could create long-term logistical and operational challenges.

articles.summary: The deportation of several Tajik opposition figures from Germany and other European countries, and their subsequent imprisonment, have heightened fears among Tajik oppositionists in exile. Some say they fear not only being sent home but also losing the Western support they once counted on.

articles.summary: The Soviet-era Roghun Dam project has endured decades of uncertainty and opposition. Now major funding tranches appear to have the project on track to transform Central Asia's energy landscape -- and displace tens of thousands of Tajik villagers.

articles.title: Russia Strikes Kyiv's Energy Infrastructure, Northern Bridge Ahead Of Abu Dhabi Talks
articles.summary: Kyiv faced widespread damage and disruptions to essential services on November 7 after Russia launched 172 attack drones and 36 ballistic missiles at the Ukrainian capital and other regions, striking energy infrastructure, residential housing, and a major bridge over the Dnipro River.

articles.title: The Coverup: Russia's Air Bases Transformed Amid Ukrainian Drone Threat
articles.summary: Recent satellite imagery captures the reshaping of air bases throughout Russia and Crimea as the threat from Ukrainian strikes changes how Moscow houses and protects its military aircraft.

articles.title: IRGC Says Iran Expanding Range Of Missiles
articles.summary: President Donald Trump repeated his assertion that the United States is winning the war with Iran and said that Tehran wants a deal, adding: “It could happen.”

articles.title: Ukraine Hopes Oleshky Can Serve As Model For Wider Truce, Delegation Says In DC
articles.summary: Ukraine hopes a temporary cease-fire that enabled humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky could serve as a model for wider de-escalation efforts, Ukrainian officials said on November 6.

articles.title: Exclusive: How Ukraine's Security Service Sought Access To The Anti-Corruption Court's Restricted Database
articles.summary: The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) has long been at odds with the law enforcement network tasked with tackling corruption. The investigative unit of RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service, Schemes, reveals how the SBU sought unfettered access to the entire internal database of the High Anti-Corruption Court.

articles.title: What Is Male State, The Group Reportedly Linked To Airline Bomb Threats?
articles.summary: Multiple bomb threats have affected flights across Europe on November 6, after a series of hoaxes disrupted air traffic across the continent this week. So far, the only lead is an email claiming responsibility signed by “Fighters of the Male State,” a shadowy Russian group.

articles.title: US-China-Russia Hypersonic Weapons Race Accelerates
articles.summary: American defense contractor Lockheed Martin’s recent announcement that it had been awarded a $694 million contract by the US Air Force to produce a new air-launched hypersonic missile is the latest sign of an accelerating tripartite arms race involving the US, China, and Russia.

articles.title: White House Outlines Broader European Security Plan Ahead Of Ukraine Peace Talks
articles.summary: The White House has outlined a proposed European security framework alongside security guarantees for Ukraine, as the Trump administration prepares for trilateral peace talks with Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi next week.

articles.title: 'Carthage' Investigation: Ukrainian Security Officials Accused Of Involvement In Criminal Activities
articles.summary: Three senior Ukrainian officials have been accused by the country's anti-graft agencies of taking part in a criminal organization uncovered in a major investigation, as Kyiv seeks to tackle corruption amid its bid to join the European Union.

articles.title: Serbia's New Government Will Face Old Economic Dilemmas With Russia And China
articles.summary: As Serbia’s new parliamentary majority plots a new path for the country, its hands may be tied by old economic dependencies on Russian energy resources and Chinese investments.

articles.title: War, Deal, Or Stalemate? What The Midterms Mean For Trump's Iran War
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump, with roughly two months before a Democratic Congress takes control, faces a set of less-than-ideal options with the Iran war: negotiate, escalate, or sit tight.

articles.title: How Russia's War Recruitment Machine Became Big Business
articles.summary: An increasing number of cases point to the human cost of a recruitment system in Russia that increasingly relies on private companies and intermediaries who often work on the fringes to bolster the ranks of a military depleted by the war against Ukraine.

articles.title: The Week In Russia: A Political Killing, A Seismic Shift, And A 'Vile' Attack
articles.summary: Twenty years after investigative journalist Anna Politikovskaya was shot dead, the paper she worked for is crushed under pressure from the Russian state. A small cease-fire in Ukraine is followed by a massive attack, while a seismic political shift in the US precedes new trilateral peace talks.

articles.title: US Court Temporarily Blocks Deportation Of Afghan Nationals Over Safety Concerns
articles.summary: A reported plan to deport dozens of Afghan nationals has been temporarily halted by a New York-based federal judge following a warning from several US lawmakers and rights groups that sending them home or to neighboring Pakistan could put their lives at risk.

articles.title: Iran Watching For Trump's Next Move After Stunning Midterm Elections Blow
articles.summary: The landslide victory by Democrats in US midterm elections is expected to bring change to Congress and foreign policy in Washington. But inside Iran, many officials said they expect the country will remain in the crosshairs of President Donald Trump, even if the vote has left him weaker.

articles.title: Cold Play: Nations Line Up To Boycott Ice Hockey Games Against Russia
articles.summary: A growing list of countries are lining up against a court decision allowing Russia to rejoin international ice hockey events, saying they will boycott any team Moscow sends, putting the World Championships next year in jeopardy.

articles.title: Ukraine Monitoring 8 Tankers Carrying Russian Diesel Potentially Bound For US
articles.summary: Ukrainian authorities are monitoring eight tankers carrying more than 300,000 tons of Russian diesel fuel that could be bound for the United States, Ukrainian government sources told RFE/RL on November 3.

articles.title: Following Oleshky Truce, Melania Trump To Host Russia-Ukraine Talks
articles.summary: US first lady Melania Trump will host Russian and Ukrainian representatives at the White House on November 5 for a meeting following a localized cease-fire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, as a new round of US-mediated peace talks is set to take place next week.

articles.title: Clashes Near Kyiv Highlight Tension Over Military Manpower Challenges
articles.summary: Crowds clashed with Ukrainian riot police and national guardsmen in a Kyiv suburb on November 2 in the latest tensions over military efforts to catch alleged deserters and enlist men -- sometimes forcibly -- to fight in the war against Russia.

articles.source: Human Rights Foundation — Europe & Asie centrale
articles.title: Blog Post Oct 28, 2026 Dispatches from Detention: Ulviyya Ali On May 6, 2025, seven police officers stormed the Baku home of Azerbaijani journalist Ulviyya Ali at midnight, searched it, and arrested her. articles.title: Op-Ed Oct 16, 2026 To Secretary Rubio: Demand Freedom for Uzbekistan’s Political Prisoners U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will lead a delegation of executives from more than 200 American businesses to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, for a meeting with Central Asia’s five foreign ministers on October 17. This C5+1 visit gives Washington a rare opportunity to press the region, and more specifically Uzbekistan, for long-awaited institutional reforms and the release of political prisoners in exchange for American investment––an opportunity that may only come once.

The Human Rights Foundation (HRF) marks this anniversary by calling for the immediate release of Kobzev and Liptser, who remain imprisoned in harsh conditions in Russian penal colonies solely for doing their jobs as lawyers.

https://hrf.org/latest/rwanda-transnatio.body: @HRF View post It has been nearly three weeks since the headless body of Rwandan dissident Robert Kabera was found in Uganda. Local police have neither recovered the rest of Kabera’s remains nor made arrests, raising suspicion of transnational repression by the Kagame regime. HRF condemns the gruesome killing and calls for a credible international investigation. Ugandan police announced the discovery of Kabera’s body on Oct. 17 in Luwala village, roughly 45 km southwest of Kampala, where he was constructing a house. He was 50. His brother told reporters he had no enemies in Uganda, and that any threats or problems he faced came from Rwanda. Kabera, a former Rwanda Defence Forces sergeant major and soloist in the Army Jazz Band, fled to Uganda in 2020, citing fears for his safety. The Rwandan military later opened a criminal case against him that his family says was politically motivated. While in exile, Kabera became an outspoken critic of Paul Kagame and his regime, building a following of more than 144,000 subscribers on his YouTube channel, “Major Robert TV.” In October 2023, he survived an attack by three unidentified assaillants. Rwandan authorities have not commented on Kabera’s murder , but his death follows a pattern of suspicious assassinations and attempted assassinations of exiled critics of Kagame. Kabera was killed just days after Kagame’s regime secured a controversial 10-year deal with Formula 1. View post

https://www.rfa.org/english/uyghur/2026/.body: Read a version of this story in Uyghur Chinese authorities in 2018 lied to the family of a Uyghur bus driver who died in their custody, an investigation by Radio Free Asia has revealed. Authorities told the family of Yasinjan Toxti, who had been detained in a “re-education” facility on suspicion of “religious radicalism,” that he had died in a car accident. Yasinjan’s sister Reyhangul told RFA that the details did not add up. A resident of Belgium, Reyhangul discussed the moment in 2018 when her younger sister in the Uyghur region told her of her brother’s death. “How could someone held in ‘re-education’ die in a traffic accident?” she recalled asking. She said her sister replied, “That is what the police told us. We have to accept that explanation. Under the current circumstances, we cannot ask any further questions about it.” 2018 was the height of China’s Uyghur internment campaign aimed at “curbing terrorism” where an estimated 1.8 million Uyghurs were put in detainment facilities claimed by authorities to be vocational training centers. The U.S. in 2020 classified Beijing’s actions in the Uyghur region as a genocide. Inconsistencies uncovered In an attempt to gain more clarity on the circumstances of Yasinjan’s death, RFA this month telephoned the Qartal Bazaar police station in Aksu, an oasis city in the Uyghur region, where Yasinjan lived and worked. Two separate police personnel shared information that conflicted with what authorities told Reyhangul’s family in 2018. The chief of the police station was the first to answer RFA’s questions. yasinjan-toxti-uyghur RFA spoke to the chief of police in Aksu, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region. (RFA Illustration) A police officer on duty provided further details. yasinjan-toxti-uyghur RFA spoke to a police officer in Aksu, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region. (RFA Illustration) In assessing that Yasinjan had been in detention for “five or six months,” the police chief may have been referring to his cumulative time in re-education across multiple sentences, and the police officer who said he was taken to the hospital after “nine or 10 days” may have been referring to the length of time into his latest sentence. RFA was unable to confirm what either expression of time meant exactly. Educational pursuits Yasinjan was born in 1980 in Aksu and lived there his entire life. Having received only a primary school education himself, Yasinjan saw the importance of education and sent his five-year-old son, Hebibulla Yasin, to study in Egypt. His sister was already living in Egypt overseeing her own children’s education, and agreed to be Hebibulla’s caretaker there. Sending children abroad for educational purposes was at the time common for many Uyghur families, because China had been expanding its policy of “bilingual education,” – which in practice was replacing the Uyghur language with Mandarin Chinese for most classes. Many Uyghur parents viewed this as accelerating assimilation, and feared their children would lose their Uyghur cultural and religious identity. Egypt, which had a strong reputation for Islamic education, and relatively low living costs, was a natural choice for families wishing to preserve their culture. Before 2017, more than 5,000 Uyghurs were living in Egypt, but mass arrests by the Chinese government under the “Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism” intensified the next year . Arrests often targeted Uyghurs with family members abroad, especially in “sensitive” Muslim majority countries like Turkey and Egypt. Arousing suspicion Because his son was in Egypt, Yasinjan was detained several times between 2016 and 2018 on suspicion of “religious radicalism” and subjected to short periods of “re-education,” according to Reyhangul. Authorities were able to compel Yasinjan to bring Hebibulla home, but even after his son returned, Yasinjan remained under suspicion. Yasinjan was in custody four separate times between 2016 and 2018. His latest detention was for stopping the bus in the middle of his route to allow Muslim passengers to observe the call to prayer. It was during this latest detention that he died – not of a traffic accident as Reyhangul said authorities previously claimed – but after arriving in a “re-education camp” as confirmed by police in RFA’s investigation. Years after Yasinjan’s death, while Reyhangul was searching for more information, she learned that other members of her family had been detained – her sister, who had told her about their brother’s death, for “leaking state secrets,” and her mother, who had traveled to Turkey, for “visiting a sensitive country.” Still, Reyhangul does not know where they are detained, nor the length of their sentences, she said. Edited by Eugene Whong and Charlie Dharapak.

Uyghur advocates have urged U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to seek commitments not to deport Uyghurs to China and to protect them from Beijing’s transnational repression during his upcoming meetings with Central Asian officials, the leader of a prominent Uyghur rights organization told Radio Free Asia. Rubio is leading a U.S. delegation of more than 200 business representatives and will arrive in Uzbekistan on Saturday for the first leg of a six-day trip that also includes two stops in India. While in Samarkand, he will attend the C5+1 ministerial meetings – with officials from the five Central Asian countries of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. marco-rubio U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio boards a plane, Oct. 8, 2026, in Lisbon. (Mark Schiefelbein/AP) According to the Washington-based Uyghur Human Rights Project, more than 400,000 Uyghurs live in these Central Asian countries and combined they form the “vast majority” of the Uyghur diaspora outside of East Turkestan, which is the name by which Uyghurs call their homeland, currently under the control of the People’s Republic of China. As a U.S. senator, Rubio was a champion of Uyghur issues and now as Washington’s top diplomat, he is expected to discuss the safety and rights of Uyghurs with the C5 leaders, Abdureshit Abdulhamit, vice president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress, told RFA. uyghur-central-asia Abdureshit Abdulhamit, vice president of the World Uyghur Congress. (RFA Illustration) “We urge him to seek clear commitments that no Uyghur will be forcibly returned to China, where they could face persecution, imprisonment or torture,” said Abdureshit. “Uyghurs seeking protection should have access to fair asylum procedures.” He also urged Rubio to address intimidation and surveillance targeting Uyghur communities, saying people should be able to preserve their culture, discuss detained relatives and communicate abroad without fear. Communities at risk Compared to Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, Uyghurs in Uzbekistan face more challenges to their social and cultural rights, Zumretay Erkin, another vice president of the organization, told RFA. “Uzbekistan is also complicit in deporting Uyghurs to China at the explicit request of the Chinese government,” she said. “Uyghurs are subjected to tight surveillance and transnational repression.” uyghur-central-asia Zumretay Erkin, vice president of the World Uyghur Congress. (RFA Illustration) Zumretay said Rubio’s diplomatic visit is a “unique opportunity to raise Uyghur human rights, even in a trade and investment context,” noting that the U.S. government was among the first to take action to address the Uyghur genocide. Washington classified China’s treatment of Uyghurs in the Uyghur region as genocide in 2021. Moral leadership Rubio can show the world that the United States’ moral leadership still matters, Omer Kanat, executive director of the Washington-based Uyghur Human Rights Project, wrote in an opinion piece in The Diplomat. Kanat cited former U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo’s public calls against returning Uyghurs to China as a precedent. He also pointed to Thailand’s February 2025 deportation of 40 Uyghurs as a warning of the consequences when diplomatic efforts fail. uyghur-central-asia Omer Kanat, executive director of the Uyghur Human Rights Project. (RFA Illustration) “This upcoming trip to Central Asia gives Rubio a chance to show that the United States won’t countenance a repeat of that tragedy,” he wrote. “With the right messaging, the trip can fortify China’s neighbors to stand firm against Beijing’s pressure to return Uyghurs to China.” The WUC also called on Rubio to hear directly from Uyghur representatives and establish follow-up mechanisms for individual cases. “We would judge the visit by concrete results: stronger protection against deportation, action on cases of harassment and a clear American commitment to follow through after the meetings end,” said Abdureshit. Edited by Eugene Whong.

https://www.rfa.org/english/uyghur/2024/.body: WASHINGTON - A campaign by China’s government to rewrite the cultural identity and history of the country’s minority ethnic groups and political dissidents is increasingly being waged on American shores, activists told a U.S. congressional hearing on Thursday. The Tibetan, Uyghur, Mongolian and Chinese activists said that while the United States once stood as a bastion of free speech and a redoubt of cultural preservation for groups targeted by the Chinese Communist Party, many now feared Beijing’s extensive reach. Rishat Abbas, the president of the U.S.-based Uyghur Academy, told the hearing of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China that his sister Gulshan had been jailed in China on a 20-year sentence due to his and other family member’s anti-government activism abroad. RELATED STORIES Students banned from speaking Tibetan in Sichuan schools Hong Kongers self-censor out of fear, says sacked Tiananmen scholar US officials call for release of detained retired Uyghur doctor The U.S. government says China’s government is carrying out a “genocide” against the mostly Muslium Uyghur minority in the country’s far-west. Many Uyghurs abroad actively campaign to end the genocide and to do what they can to preserve their language and culture. But many look to the treatment of the family members, still trapped in China, of those Uyghurs who choose to speak out, and decide it’s safer not to provoke the Chinese Communist Party, even from abroad. “My sister’s imprisonment is a clear action of retaliation,” he said. “Her detention exposes the CCP’s aggressive policies that target Uyghurs simply for their identity and for the activism of their relatives abroad.” “She has never engaged in any form of advocacy in her life,” he said. Abbas said he was nonetheless not deterred, and hoped to one day bring a Uyghur-language textbook developed in the United States back to China’s Xinjiang region, where Uyghurs live under surveillance. Lawfare It’s not only Uyghur immigrants who have been targeted. In years gone by, American higher education institutions like Stanford University fearlessly curated U.S.-based historical archives about events censored by the Chinese government, said Julian Ku, a constitutional law professor at New York’s Hofstra University. But things have changed. Ku pointed to a lawsuit brought in the United States by the Beijing-based widow of the late Li Rui – a former secretary to Mao Zedong and later dissident who donated diaries to Stanford. Stanford says Li Rui donated the diaries through his daughter, fearing that they would be destroyed by Chinese officials if left in China. But Li Rui’s widow says they are rightfully hers and wants them returned. The widow, Ku explained, was inexplicably being represented by “some of the most expensive law firms in the United States,” and had likely already racked up legal fees in the “hundreds of thousands of dollars – and probably more – on a widow’s Chinese state pension.” Describing the tactic as “lawfare,” he suggested that the widow had powerful backers funding the battle, who may not even care if the litigation is ultimately successful. The nearly four years of costly legal battles sent a message to other U.S. universities, museums or nonprofits to avoid any contentious documents that might attract the attention of Beijing, Ku said. “They might think, ‘Well, maybe I don’t want to acquire that one, because it might subject me to litigation in China and maybe litigation here in the United States,” he said. “It serves as a deterrence for universities, museums and other institutions in the United States.” Living in fear Like Uyghurs, many ethnically Han Chinese in America also fear speaking out against Beijing even while in the United States, said Rowena He, a historian of the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre in Beijing who was last year banned from entering Hong Kong . “It’s very difficult to not to be emotional being in this room again because I remember 5-10 years ago, when I was first invited to testify to Congress,” He recalled. “I was extremely hesitant, because I was so concerned about my family members, and I was so worried.” “I lived with fear ever since the day I started teaching and researching the topic of Tiananmen,” she explained, citing the “taboo” around the topic in China, where the massacre is not openly acknowledged. She said increased funding for curriculums with alternate Chinese histories to the one put forward by Beijing could be one way to counter the “monopoly on historiography” held by China’s government. “If you go to Chinatown, many people are still supporting the CCP, even though they’re physically in the United States,” He said, noting that figures like herself were denigrated as anti-government. “Sometimes people call us ‘underground historians,’ but I do not like the term ‘underground,’” she said. “We are the historians.” Government funding Geshe Lobsang Monlam, a Tibetan monk who authored a 223-volume Tibetan dictionary and helps lead efforts to preserve Tibetan language outside of China, said one of the main obstacles for Tibetans outside China outside of pressure from Beijing was finding needed funds. “Inside Tibet, the young Tibetans have appeared powerless in their ability to preserve and promote their language,” the monk said, pointing to concerted efforts to erase use of the Tibetan language as young Tibetans grow proficient in using Mandarin through smartphones. “If there can be assistance by the United States to help procure technological equipment that can enable those of us in exile to continue our work on preservation of Tibetan culture and language and way of life ... that would be very useful for us,” he explained. Temulun Togochog, a 17-year-old U.S.-born Southern Mongolian activist, similarly appealed for more funding for cultural preservation. uyghur-preserving-history-hearing-02 Temulun Togochog,17, U.S.-born Southern Mongolian activist testifies before the Congressional-Executive Commission on China, Dec. 5, 2024. (Image from Congressional-Executive Commission on China video) Togochog said while the decreased global focus on the plight of Mongolians in China had allowed her family in the United States to openly teach her about Mongolian culture and their native language with little fear of reprisal, resources were few and far between. Mongolians living in China’s Inner Mongolia were increasingly facing a similar treatment to Tibetans and Uyghurs, she said, with a “systematic oppression and erasure of Mongolian language” taking place in favor of what is called “patriotic education” lionizing the communist party. In September 2020, many Southern Mongolians protested the policies through coordinated school boycotts and strikes, but there was little news coverage of the ensuing mass arrests, she explained. “Approximately 300,000 southern Mongolian students joined the movement,” she said. “The Chinese government responded harshly, detaining and placing under house arrest 8-10,000 people.” The young activist called on Congress to fund Mongolian-language programs on Voice of America, which currently do not exist. She said that would help the “minority within a minority” to more actively “preserve their language, culture and identity” from erasure. Edited by Malcolm Foster.

https://www.rfa.org/english/myanmar/2026.body: Updated at 11:30 a.m. ET on Nov. 4, 2026. Read a version of this story in Burmese Armed ethnic groups and members of Myanmar’s shadow government are hoping that a recently made public U.S. strategy for their country decrease fighting and bring about peace with the military-backed government, the organizations told Radio Free Asia. The U.S. State Department recently released an Integrated Country Strategy document for Myanmar that outlines Washington’s aims to use diplomacy to promote peace in the volatile Southeast Asian country, potentially providing access to rare earth deposits dominated by China. The policy document lays out four mission goals, which include protecting U.S. citizens, addressing trade deficits, promoting peace, and increasing U.S. regional influence through engagement. us-myanmar-strategy-rare-earths Lwe River network, Mekong Tributary, with clusters of rare earth mines in Shan State, Myanmar, Nov. 11, 2025. (Planet Labs via Reuters) To achieve these goals, dealing with Myanmar’s military-backed government – headed by the same people who ousted the previous government in a coup in 2021 – cannot be avoided. Washington initially shunned engagement with the military after the coup and imposed sanctions on its most senior leaders, but has since softened its stance, rolling back some sanctions and even holding high level talks in September 2026. A U.S. State Department spokesperson on Tuesday explained the shift to RFA. “The Administration has been evaluating how to calibrate Washington’s policy towards Burma to achieve regional stability, and also make progress on key U.S. priorities and has determined that wholesale disengagement with the authorities in Naypyidaw countered U.S. strategic interests in Burma and the region. We are pursuing a policy that welcomes dialogue with all stakeholders involved in the conflict as we encourage Burma to make progress on key U.S. priorities, including addressing scam centers, improving the domestic operating environment for U.S. businesses, and building towards a genuine peace process that stabilizes the country.” myanmar-coup-2021-photo-gallery Riot police man a barrier in front of the Yangon City Hall on Feb. 6, 2021, in Yangon, Myanmar. (Getty Images) David Gum Awng, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs for the National Unity Government, or NUG, a shadow government made up of former government officials who were ousted in the 2021 coup, told RFA he understood the realities of the situation. “The NUG respects and acknowledges that the U.S. government is actively engaging in Myanmar affairs and formulating a strategy aimed at peace, economy, and regional stability. The NUG will continue to engage in discussions with the U.S. government, Congress, and the international community including relevant partner nations. We will also continue to urge that the U.S. government’s policies and practical actions towards Myanmar support the democratic and federal aspirations of the Myanmar people, address the root causes of the conflict, and lead toward an inclusive political resolution. International engagement in Myanmar affairs should not prolong the military dictatorship, but should aim to bring about genuine political change based on the will and rights of the people after escaping from this bad system.” Kyaw Ni, Deputy Minister of Home Affairs and Immigration for the NUG, shared his opinion that amidst the policies of superpower nations, one must strive to achieve benefits for one’s own country. “In this policy shift of a superpower nation, small countries suffer a lot, so a country undergoing revolution like Burma suffers even more. It is likely to be affected. Since these are superpower nations, they write policies based on their own interests. So our public also has to struggle among these policies to reach our desired revolutionary goal without harming the interests of our country, our people, and our revolution.” The Chin National Front (CNF) soldiers in an undated photo. (Chin Information Center) Salai Htet Ni, spokesperson for the Chin National Front, an armed ethnic rebel group, said the U.S. government needs to understand the underlying problems in Myanmar politics and get deeply involved. “The U.S. government needs to understand the military junta’s unjust violence and killing of the people. They need to consider that. On our part, if they can perform first-stage actions like humanitarian aid for war refugees and addressing violent attacks and killings, we would welcome the U.S. involvement even more.” Another ethnic armed group, — the Karen National Union — said U.S. involvement might reduce the amount of internal fighting, spokesperson Saw Kler Say told RFA on Wednesday. “The new U.S. strategy could bring about changes or have a specific impact on our country from a military perspective. Firstly, it might lead to a situation where the military junta is compelled to stop its attacks targeting the civilian population. Secondly, the U.S. might take steps — or offer recommendations — aimed at halting the ongoing internal conflicts. Politically, we also believe they are likely envisioning a political landscape that is acceptable to all parties—one that would include both the detained opposition leaders and the revolutionary forces. To achieve sustainable peace in Myanmar by 2030, the first step must be to cease attacks targeting the civilian population. The next step involves reaching a consensus on a dialogue process aimed at ending internal conflicts; only through such a mutually agreed-upon framework can a ceasefire be attained. In addition to these measures, all detained opposition leaders and political prisoners must be released. Without these actions, I believe that any dialogue will be extremely difficult. If detained political prisoners are excluded, meaning the process fails to be truly all inclusive, then a successful outcome may well be entirely impossible. Regarding the emergence of a federal democracy in Myanmar, the new U.S. strategy presents both positive opportunities and concerning risks. On one hand, it could potentially lead to a genuine transition toward a federal democracy—for instance, by facilitating the abolition of the 2008 Constitution and the drafting and adoption of a new federal constitution. On the other hand, there is a risk that if the discourse is driven solely by U.S. interests, the path toward the federal democracy we envision could be diverted, creating significant challenges." Representatives of the Kachin Independence Army and the Arakan Army responded that they were not ready to comment. myanmar-arakan-army-conscription-rakhine_03272025_0 Arakan Army soldiers in an undated photo. (Arakan Army) The Arakan Army’s Khaing Thukha asked that questions be channeled through official emails. Hla Thein, spokesperson for the Union Solidarity and Development Party – formed by former military officers – told RFA that the U.S. strategy document is constructive for mutual interest and should be welcomed. “Big nations becoming interested in our country, interested from a positive and beneficial perspective, should be welcomed no matter what. We have no permanent friends and no permanent enemies. If they come to cooperate fairly for our country’s interest, our people’s interest, and national interest, we will warmly welcome them.” RFA attempted to contact Khaing Khaing Soe, spokesperson for the military government’s presidential office, but received no reply. Col. Saw Kyaw Nyunt, spokesperson for the 7 EAO Alliance of ethnic armed organizations that have individually signed a Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement with the military, said the shift in U.S. attitude might be due to an understanding of Myanmar’s needs. “In attempting to restart the peace process, international support and assistance are needed. The shift in attitude by the U.S. toward the peace process is likely because they realized that peace is urgently needed due to Myanmar’s reality. By 2030, which is in three or fo

https://www.rfa.org/english/tibet/2026/1.body: The U.S. government Thursday urged China to stop interfering with Tibetan religious freedom after sources in eastern Tibet told Radio Free Asia that Chinese authorities began demolishing monks’ quarters at a monastery there. Authorities on Oct. 25 and 26 began demolishing about 200 monks’ residences at Dza Sershul Thekchen Dargyeling Monastery in Sershul County in the Kardze (Ganzi in Chinese) Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, sources there told RFA, speaking on the condition of anonymity for security reasons. “Everything is over now,” the source said. “We are losing everything.” A U.S. State Department spokesperson told RFA on Thursday that the demolitions in Sershul reflect broader Chinese government efforts to bring spiritual institutions, religious education, and monastic life under government control. “We call on Beijing to end its interference in Tibetan religious life,” the spokesperson said. “Tibetan Buddhists should have the right to practice their faith freely, educate their clergy and choose their religious leaders, including the Dalai Lama and the Panchen Lama, without government interference,” the spokesperson said, referring to Beijing’s past and likely future interference with the established succession customs of the two most important figures in Tibetan Buddhism. The demolition in Sershul is not isolated, but part of a larger campaign to reduce monk populations at Tibetan religious institutions. RFA reported in August that authorities resumed demolition of the Larung Gar Buddhist Academy. Activists noted the timing – China’s new Ethnic Unity and Progress Law – had just come into effect the previous month. The law focuses on reshaping ethnic identity, changing the legal framework around language, expanding state oversight of religion, and extending the law’s reach beyond China’s border. tibet-china-monastery-demolition Dza Sershul Thekchen Dargyeling Monastery in an undated photo. (Citizen photo) The source in Tibet said that authorities are planning further restrictions that would prevent monks from staying at the monastery after the demolitions. “Tibetan religion and culture are being destroyed,” the source told RFA, adding that there is little recourse for those opposed to the demolitions. “No matter how much local people speak out, the authorities do not listen,” the source said. “They do not remember, they ignore us. We have no solutions and we don’t know what will happen.” RFA contacted the relevant county-level officials in Sershul for comment, but the official who answered the phone did not respond to RFA’s questions and hung up. Promoting “ethnic unity” The demolitions and reductions of the monk population are clearly intended to assimilate Tibetans so that they accept Chinese identity, Tenzin Lekshay, spokesperson for the Central Tibetan Administration, or CTA, the Tibetan government-in-exile based in Dharamsala, India, told RFA. “This is a mask used by the Chinese government under the recently enacted Ethnic Unity Law to assimilate Tibetans and destroy Tibetan religion, culture, and language,” he said. “This is not the first time. We have also seen young monks forcibly expelled from monasteries and sent to China’s colonial boarding schools .” Though Beijing claims the boarding schools are aimed at providing education to a scattered population, critics have noted that their actual goal is assimilation. “We strongly condemn the Chinese government’s continued attempts to shut down monasteries and schools established by Tibetans while claiming its authority over Tibet and seeking to eradicate Tibetan national identity,” Tenzin Lekshay said. “It is time for the Chinese government to acknowledge and trust that Tibetan religion and culture are beneficial to China and the world and that the destruction of Tibetan religion and culture will have negative consequences for both China and the world.” He said that the Chinese government’s actions, which violate international law, would undermine Beijing’s ambition to establish itself as a global leader. tibet-china-monastery-demolition The entrance to Dza Sershul Thekchen Dargyeling Monastery in an undated photo. (Citizen photo) Tibetan monasteries are central to preserving Tibetan culture and religious identity, Sangay Kyab, Chinese liaison officer at the Tibet Bureau, the CTA’s representative office in Geneva, Switzerland, told RFA. “Tibetan culture and religion are central to the identity of the Tibetan people. China’s policy and goal is to destroy everything that keeps Tibet alive,” he said. “Since China invaded Tibet, there have been successive campaigns against Tibetan monasteries, often under the pretext of reforming them.” He explained how monks and nuns are subjected to political education aimed at making monasteries conform to the Chinese Communist Party’s ideology. “The main goal is to restrict the study and practice of Tibetan Buddhism and undermine the Tibetan people’s ability to unite,” he said. “The incident at the monastery is connected to the Chinese government’s broader policies toward Tibet, and there is a risk that similar incidents could occur elsewhere,” he said. Restrictions in Tibet threaten Tibetan Buddhist heritage, warned the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, an independent, bipartisan U.S. government commission that monitors religious freedom abroad and makes policy recommendations to the U.S. government. “Demolition of Tibetan monasteries is just one tactic in a wider effort by Chinese authorities to sever the people of Tibet from their Tibetan Buddhist heritage, including the forced assimilation of ethnic minorities through the draconian ‘Ethnic Unity’ law that came into effect in July,” commission chair Asif Mahmood told RFA. He cited the resumption of demolition at Larung Gar in Sichuan province in July as another example of restrictions on Tibetan Buddhist religious freedom. “Buddhist monks in these circumstances have faced persistent threats of harassment, expulsion from their monasteries, imprisonment, and worse,” he said. China is trying to destroy Tibetan Buddhism at its roots, Bhuchung K. Tsering, head of the Research and Monitoring Unit at the Washington-based International Campaign for Tibet, told RFA. “Monasteries across Tibet are required to follow the orders of the Chinese Communist Party and serve its objectives,” he said. “The Chinese government claims that Tibetans enjoy freedom of religion, but the reality is the opposite of its claims that it is promoting Tibetan Buddhism,” he added. Translation and additional reporting by Tenzin Dickyi, edited by Tawang for RFA Tibetan. Edited by Eugene Whong for RFA English.

https://www.rfa.org/english/uyghur/2026/.body: Read a version of this story in Uyghur In 1986, a Uyghur kebab vendor found a Chinese baby in a cardboard box on his way home from work. Now Abdulla Tomur is willing to do anything to get Zohregul – the abandoned girl he raised as his daughter – released from a Chinese prison. Abdulla hasn’t been back to the Uyghur region since a year before Chinese authorities began their large-scale “anti-terrorism” Uyghur internment campaign in 2017, during which Zohregul was arrested. From Istanbul, Turkey, where he currently resides, Abdulla tells Radio Free Asia the story of his first encounter with Zohregul, and how he now feels powerless to help his imprisoned daughter. Cries from a cardboard box At the time when he found Zohregul, Abdulla had been operating a market stall in Guizhou province, far away from Kucha (in Chinese, Kuche), Aksu prefecture (Akesu), his hometown in the Uyghur region. The family had relocated to southern China due to economic hardship. One day, after packing up his kebab equipment, he started to return home, but stopped when he heard a baby crying. The sound came from a cardboard box left in front of a hospital. He hurried toward it, finding what appeared to be an abandoned Han Chinese baby girl. At first he was hesitant. He thought about what his wife might say. They were already struggling to support their two young sons. He imagined her asking how they could possibly feed a third child when poverty had driven them to move so far away. He started toward home again, but the thought of the crying baby tugged at his heartstrings. Though the baby was left in front of the hospital, Abdulla said he had reason to believe those inside already knew she had been abandoned, and because he did not speak Chinese, communicating with them would have been difficult. So, he decided it would be easier to take the baby and hand her over to the authorities later. He lifted her from the box, wrapped her in the cloth he used to cover his kebab meat, and carried her home. His wife’s response was nothing like the one he had feared. Instead of scolding him, she condemned the people who had abandoned the infant. “How could anyone leave an innocent baby like this?” she asked. She began breastfeeding the girl. The crying subsided, and the baby fell asleep. The couple planned to care for her for three days before taking her to the authorities. By the fourth day, they had changed their minds. Their sons, aged three and five, were already attached to their new companion. Abdulla recalled that they put aside their toys and gathered around her. The parents decided to keep her until she was about a year old, then hand her over to the authorities when they returned to their hometown in the Aksu area. But by her first birthday, she was their daughter, and a sister to their sons. “How could we hand over a child who called us ‘Dad’ and ‘Mom’?” Abdulla said. The family secret Eventually the family returned to the Uyghur region. Zohregul grew up in Kucha, in a Uyghur household, as a native speaker of the Uyghur language, and a follower of the Muslim religion – an upbringing firmly anchored in Uyghur culture. They did not disclose Zohregul’s background to the authorities at the time because they wanted to keep it secret. Birth certificates were not required or routinely issued then, so they could register her as their own child unless someone else came forward to claim her. Late registration was also possible by paying a fine. People suspected that his daughter was not Uyghur, but most avoided asking out of respect. Only a few close relatives asked. Abdulla told them, “She might have been switched at the hospital, but at this point, I have no way to investigate.” Zohregul also repeatedly asked, “Why don’t I look like my two brothers?” He would reply, “You look like my grandmother.” The family’s remaining concern was how people in their community might react if they learned Zohregul was Han Chinese. Abdulla feared that his neighbors, who considered the Chinese presence in the Uyghur homeland to be an occupation , would be bothered by his family raising a Chinese child. He had already formulated a response – rooted in his Muslim faith – should anyone confront the family over their decision. “Our religion teaches that every child is born innocent,” he said. “This child is pure and innocent. Her blood relationship to those who oppress us was not her choice. She is one of God’s servants.” Still, he doubted that this explanation would satisfy everyone, so he and his wife decided to keep Zohregul’s origins a family secret. A family divided In 2016, Abdulla traveled to Turkey to visit his eldest son, who was studying in Istanbul. When the mass arrests by the Chinese government under the “Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism” intensified the next year in the Uyghur region, he wanted to return home. Abdulla had already been sent to a camp the year before for “illegal gathering.” He said that while incarcerated , he was deprived of sleep and forced to confess to alleged illegal activities by himself or his neighbors. But Abdulla’s son urged him to stay, fearing that his father too would be detained again. From Istanbul, Abdulla worried constantly about his children at home, especially Zohregul. He had nightmares of seeing her in handcuffs. Eventually, an acquaintance told Abdulla that both Zohregul and his younger son Rehim were in prison. As with many other detentions by Chinese authorities at the time, no official reason was given. Upon hearing this, a father’s first impulse was to return home immediately. But Abdulla realized he would be unable to help either child if he returned and became imprisoned himself. At first, he convinced himself that the detentions could not continue indefinitely. “How could they keep so many people for so long?” he recalled thinking. “Surely they would release them.” Revealing the truth In 2020, three years after learning about his children’s detentions, Abdulla – still in Turkey – began trying to secure their release. He participated in demonstrations outside the Chinese Consulate in Istanbul, appearing in media interviews, and trying to find more information. When six years of those efforts yielded no results, he took to social media and made a direct appeal to Chinese authorities. “I am an uneducated farmer,” he said. “I have not participated in political activities here. Please give me information about my children. If they are in prison, release them.” He offered to return to the Uyghur region to resume farming, or submit to imprisonment himself. “At least release my innocent daughter, Zohregul,” he pleaded. Abdulla said the appeal circulated on Facebook and then on Douyin – the Chinese version of TikTok – where it received more than 50,000 views. Four people contacted him, claiming to be consular personnel, customs officers, or police. They said they would help, but the conversations soon turned to requests for information about Uyghurs in Syria and Afghanistan. Abdulla said he knew nothing and could not provide them with any information. During one conversation, out of desperation, he disclosed that Zohregul was an adopted Han Chinese child and asked the caller to relay that information to officials in Aksu. It was the first time Abdulla had publicly revealed his daughter’s Chinese origin, in the hope of getting help to secure her release from prison. Abdulla hoped her ancestry might make a difference. During his years in Kucha, he had seen officials pay particular attention to Chinese settlers’ safety. He also recalled authorities rewarding Uyghur families who adopted Chinese children as part of “ethnic unity” campaigns. One Chinese officer showed interest after learning the family secret, Abdulla said. But the officer only told him that Zohregul had received a 12-year sentence and had three years remaining. The officer also told him to return to China and “repent” before they could discuss his daughter’s situation further. An RFA

https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2.body: In response to the Israeli military’s arrest of Palestinian farmer and land defender Ghassan Najjar during a pre-dawn raid on the village of Burin south of Nablus in the northern occupied West Bank, on 27 October, Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty International’s Senior Director for Research, Policy, Advocacy and Campaigns, said: “Israeli authorities must immediately release Ghassan Najjar who was arrested solely because of his peaceful activism to protect the olive harvest season in Burin. Israeli intelligence agents had explicitly threatened Ghassan Najjar, co-founder of Burin’s Land and Farming Agricultural Cooperative, that he would be arrested if he did not stop his activism. His activism includes community organizing, supporting mutual aid among farmers through the cooperative, organizing an annual Kite Festival in the village and leading numerous cultural initiatives. Ghassan Najjar had been facing repeated threats since the start of the olive harvest season and their frequency intensified during the week prior to his arrest. “Ghassan Najjar’s arrest illustrates the devastating twin threat facing Palestinian farmers and land defenders: Israeli military restrictions and state-driven settler violence prevent them from accessing their land and harvesting their olives while the Israeli authorities intensify their crackdown through arbitrary arrests, threats, and intimidation for trying to protect what is left of their land. “A military interrogator informed Ghassan Najjar’s lawyer that he is likely to be placed under administrative detention, a tactic systematically used by Israeli authorities to punish and persecute Palestinians by holding them indefinitely without charges or trial based on secret evidence they cannot access. As of October 2026, Israeli authorities had been holding 3,101 Palestinians under administrative detention. Ghassan Najjar had already spent nearly a decade in Israeli jails, mostly under administrative detention. His first arrest came when he was just 15 years old. “Like Palestinian human rights defender Ayman Bani Owda and countless other Palestinians, Ghassan Najjar is being hounded by a discriminatory justice system that has played a key role in legitimizing and maintaining Israel’s system of apartheid and unlawful occupation. States with influence on Israel must use their leverage to pressure Israeli authorities into releasing all arbitrarily detained Palestinians, including Ghassan Najjar, and finally end their use of administrative detention.” Background Burin is a Palestinian village located south of Nablus, in the occupied West Bank. For over two decades, the village has been subjected to frequent attacks by Israeli settlers and repeated military raids by Israeli forces, significantly affecting the daily lives and livelihoods of its residents. These incidents include assaults on Palestinian residents and their property, damage to agricultural land, and restrictions on farmers’ access to their lands, particularly during the olive harvest season. In addition to his role in Burin’s Land and Farming Agricultural Cooperative, Ghassan Najjar, 36, is the coordinator for the Sumoud network supporting farmers and shepherds, including during the olive harvest season. He is currently held in the Huwara military detention facility.

Responding to reports that two Uyghur men recently moved to an Immigration Detention Centre in Thailand face imminent forcible deportation to China, Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard said: “Thai authorities must immediately halt any plans to forcibly return these two Uyghur men to China, where they face a real risk of torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. Thailand must not repeat last year’s unlawful deportation of 40 Uyghurs, who were forced back to danger in China. “These two men fled persecution only to spend more than a decade detained in Thailand. Amnesty International has documented crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang. Returning them would expose them to the abuses they sought to escape. “Both men have previously made clear to their legal representatives that they fear for their lives if returned to China and do not consent to being sent back. Thai authorities must now allow them access to a lawyer of their choice and, together with the international community, urgently find a safe and voluntary third-country solution for them and the other Uyghurs still detained in Thailand. “No amount of diplomatic assurance from China can override Thailand’s obligations not to return anyone to a real risk of torture or other serious human rights violations. After more than a decade in detention, these men must be released and given the chance to rebuild their lives in safety and freedom “ Background The two men are among five Uyghurs remaining in Thailand from a group of over 300 who were apprehended without charge by the Thai authorities on 13 March 2014 after they had fled persecution and discrimination in China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region. On 21 October 2026, two of the five men were released from prison under a royal pardon and transferred to the Immigration Detention Centre in Bangkok. Since then, Thai authorities have denied the two men access to their lawyers, as well as blocked access to the men by civil society organizations and the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand. The two men have spent more than 12 years in Thai detention. In June 2015, Thailand allowed 173 women and children from the group to travel to Türkiye but unlawfully deported at least 109 people to China. A document obtained by Amnesty International shows that, on 7 January 2025, the Chinese embassy in Thailand sent a letter to Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs requesting the “repatriation” of 45 Uyghur men who remained in the country. In February 2025, Thailand forcibly deported 40 of them, in breach international law . Five remained in a Thai prison to serve sentences related to an attempt to escape the Immigration Detention Centre. Following the deportations, Thai authorities made two visits to Xinjiang in February and March 2025 at China’s invitation, as part of its efforts to provide diplomatic assurances. NGOs monitoring the case reported that Thai authorities were able to meet fewer than 10 deportees and that no subsequent updates have established that all are alive and safe; their whereabouts and wellbeing remain unknown. Amnesty International previously called on both governments to disclose the whereabouts of all 40 men. Amnesty International opposes any use of diplomatic assurances that a person transferred would not be subjected to torture or other ill-treatment as it undermines the universality of the prohibition of torture and cannot be considered reliable. Thailand is bound by the Convention against Torture, and the principle of non-refoulement under international law, which prohibits States from returning or transferring anyone to a place where they would be at real risk of persecution or other human rights violations. Article 13 of Thailand’s Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act, in force since 2023, prohibits deportation where there are substantial grounds to believe a person would face torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, or enforced disappearance. Amnesty International issued a groundbreaking report in 2021 documenting crimes against humanity of imprisonment, torture and persecution against Uyghurs, Kazakhs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang. Despite similar UN findings released in an assessment report in August 2022 , China has taken no steps to implement recommendations, remedy documented violations or investigate and hold accountable perpetrators. Instead, the government continues to silence criticism from those within and beyond its borders, issue counternarratives denying abuse and maintains its discriminatory and assimilationist policies. *Update: Amnesty International received information that, a few hours after the publication of this statement on 4 November, the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand was able to visit the two men at the detention centre. However, their lawyers remained unable to visit them.

Responding to the 10-year sentence handed to Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong for “colluding with foreign forces”, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks said: “The Hong Kong authorities’ persecution of Joshua Wong continues with this latest national security conviction, which cruelly – and perhaps deliberately – comes mere months before he would have been eligible for release under his previous conviction. “Joshua Wong’s bravery in speaking truth to power should be commended, but instead in Hong Kong it makes him a criminal. Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s National Security Law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security. “The international community should not accept the continued criminalization of legitimate activism as the new normal in Hong Kong. Governments must continue to press for the protection of human rights and the release of those imprisoned solely for exercising their rights. “Amnesty International reiterates its call on the Hong Kong authorities to overturn Joshua Wong’s national security convictions and to repeal all legislation that violates Hong Kong’s international human rights obligations.” Background Joshua Wong was today sentenced to 10 years in prison after pleading guilty to conspiring to collude with foreign forces under Hong Kong’s Beijing-imposed National Security Law (NSL). Under his second national security conviction, Wong was accused of conspiring with self-exiled activist Nathan Law and “other persons unknown” between July 2020 and November 2020 to request foreign countries or organizations to impose sanctions, blockades or engage in other hostile activities against Hong Kong or China. The prominent activist had been sentenced in 2024, in the largest mass prosecution under the NSL to date, to four years and eight months for “conspiracy to commit subversion”. He was one of 45 opposition figures jailed due to their participation in unofficial “primaries” in 2020, on charges which UN experts considered to relate to activities protected under international human rights law. This previous sentence is scheduled to end in January 2027. Hong Kong’s human rights situation has deteriorated dramatically since 2020, with more than 300 people arrested for violating the NSL or a colonial-era “sedition” law. In addition, the so-called Article 23 legislation introduced by the local authorities in 2024 has further deepened repression and silenced opposition voices in the city.

Amnesty International condemns the decision by Peru’s Public Prosecutor’s Office to close the investigation into the forced sterilisation of 4,172 Peruvian women during the 1990s. This decision was taken pursuant to Law 32107, passed in 2024, which allows statutes of limitations to be applied to war crimes and crimes against humanity committed before 1 July 2002. “Closing an investigation that the Public Prosecutor’s Office itself recognises as involving crimes against humanity is an affront to the victims, who have waited almost 30 years for justice. The Peruvian state cannot use a law that contravenes international law to block their path to truth, justice and reparation. This decision must be reversed and Law 32107 repealed to prevent it from continuing to be used as a tool of impunity,” said Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International. Closing an investigation that the Public Prosecutor’s Office itself recognises as involving crimes against humanity is an affront to the victims, who have waited almost 30 years for justice.” Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International. During the 1990s, at least 200,000 people; most of them Indigenous women and women from rural communities; were sterilised, many without their full and informed consent and through deception, threats, pressure and other forms of coercion. This took place under the National Reproductive Health and Family Planning Programme, a state population-control policy targeting people living in poverty in Peru. Amnesty International considers that the widespread forced sterilisation of women in Peru during the 1990s amounts to crimes against humanity, which are not subject to statutes of limitations under the international standards and obligations binding on the Peruvian state. “For decades, victims have faced obstacles, delays and decisions that have denied them justice. Forced sterilisations violated their rights to personal integrity, health, reproductive autonomy and privacy and, in some cases, resulted in their deaths. The Peruvian state must place victims at the centre of its response and ensure that all those responsible are held to account. It is outrageous that a law promoting impunity is being used in an attempt to deny victims their rights to truth, justice and reparation,” said Jennie Dador Tozzini, Director of Amnesty International Peru. In March 2026, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found the Peruvian state responsible for the forced sterilisation and death of Celia Ramos Durand in 1997, as well as for the lack of due diligence and the unjustified delay in investigating the case. The Court found that the policy was discriminatory and ordered measures of reparation, guarantees of non-recurrence and a public acknowledgement of the state’s international responsibility. This ruling represented an act of justice for Celia Ramos’s family and, symbolically, for thousands of victims. This latest attempt to close the case, more than 20 years after the first prosecutorial investigation began, sends a clear message of impunity and contravenes the Peruvian state’s international obligations to investigate, prosecute and punish these grave human rights violations. “Every year of delay compounds the harm caused and reinforces an impunity that the Peruvian state has an obligation to combat. There is still time to reverse this decision. Civil society organisations will pursue every available avenue to ensure that the authorities fulfil their duty to listen to victims and guarantee their right to access justice,” added Jennie Dador Tozzini. “Every year of delay compounds the harm caused and reinforces an impunity that the Peruvian state has an obligation to combat. There is still time to reverse this decision.” Jennie Dador Tozzini, Director of Amnesty International Peru. Amnesty International calls on the Peruvian state to reverse the closure of the investigation and repeal Law 32107, as well as any other legislation that contravenes international human rights law. The authorities must also guarantee the continuation of the investigation and ensure that victims and their families have access to truth, justice, full reparation and effective guarantees of non-recurrence. Judges must ensure that no domestic law overrides the human rights protected by Peru’s Constitution and the international treaties ratified by the Peruvian state. Peruvian society has the right to know the full truth about these crimes, and victims have the right to obtain justice. Further information: Peru: Another step towards consolidating impunity Peru: Amicus curiae brief submitted by Amnesty International to the Criminal Court in Peru on forced sterilisations committed by the Peruvian State during the 1990s [Spanish] Peru: The right to justice of victims of forced sterilisation is not subject to statutes of limitations For more information or to schedule an interview, please contact [email protected]

Ahead of the vote in Belgian Federal Parliament on Thursday 5 November on whether to allow police raids on people’s homes for migration control purposes, including homes of people who may be hosting undocumented migrants, Dinushika Dissanayake the Deputy Regional Director of Amnesty International said: “These proposals which allow for home raids are bound to sow fear and division. The bill before Belgium’s parliament gives police vast powers to enter people’s homes for migration control purposes, between the hours of 5am and 9pm and irrespective of whether children are present. “This would not only cause a serious intrusion into people’s private and family life but also the bill fails to provide effective ways to appeal or challenge these decisions. “Belgium has a strong tradition of showing solidarity towards migrant communities, with many people opening their doors and homes to offer beds, food and support – as is their prerogative. This will discourage people from doing so in future. “These disproportionate powers are another cruel and coercive tool to create an increasingly hostile environment for migrants in Europe and for those showing solidarity with them. “The Belgian proposals are very much in line with the EU’s return regulation and its dogged and misguided insistence on ramping up deportations, raids, and detention at any cost, with disproportionate impacts on racialized people. “These punitive proposals will tear communities apart and make everyday life more dangerous, complicated and frightening for ordinary people. The Belgian Parliament must reject them, along with any attempt to scapegoat migrants “At a time when the cost of living is soaring and economic insecurity is gripping millions across the country, politicians must not deflect attention by targeting one of the most marginalized groups in society.” Background On 5 November, the Belgian Federal Parliament will vote on an amendment to the law on the access, residence, settlement, and removal of foreign nationals, that introduces the possibility of ‘home inspections’. The bill stipulates that police officers can “enter the residence of a foreign national, even if it is the home or place of residence of a third party,” provided that they obtain authorization for a home inspection from an investigative judge who wouldn’t have full investigative powers . They would decide on the basis of a series of criteria, including that the targeted individual is under a deportation order and that they are considered to pose a risk to public order or national security; a criterion that is not defined in the text. The bill also fails to provide affected people and those who live with them or host them with an effective avenue to appeal the decision ordering the home visit or challenge its proportionality. Police will be able to force open peoples’ doors from 5am until 9pm and will have powers to search the home for identity documents. They are allowed to enter people’s homes even if children are present, under certain conditions. Amnesty International Belgium together with 36 Belgian organizations are organizing a demonstration in front of the Palace of Justice in Brussels at 5pm, 4 November. More than 50 decentralized actions are also organized in the country. More details here .

https://www.azattyq.org/a/almaty-soty-ba.body: ЖАҢАЛЫҚТАР Алматы соты Бажкенованы бұрынғы министр туралы жазғандарын терістеуге міндеттеді 7 қараша 2026 жыл, 14:45 Алматы соты Бажкенованы бұрынғы министр туралы жазғандарын терістеуге міндеттеді Бөлісу Сілтемесін көшіру Facebook X (Twitter) WhatsApp Email Бөлісу Бөлісу Сілтемесін көшіру Facebook X (Twitter) WhatsApp Email Бөлісу PDF VPN-сіз оқу Сайт бұғатталып тұрса да, материалды осы сілтемемен кіріп оқуға болады Google-да басымдық бер Гүлнар Бажкенова. Астана, шілде айы, 2025 жылы. Алматы қаласының Бостандық аудандық соты 5 қарашада бұрынғы оқу-ағарту министрі Ғани Бейсембаевтың Orda.kz басылымының бұрынғы бас редакторы Гүлнар Бажкеноваға қарсы азаматтық ісі бойынша шешім шығарды. Бейсембаев соттан 2025 жылы қазанда Бажкенованың әлеуметтік желідегі парақшаларында жарияланған өзі мен бұрынғы сыртқы істер министрі Мұрат Нұртілеудің туыстығы туралы ақпаратты жалған әрі абырой мен іскерлік беделіне нұқсан келтіреді деп тануды талап еткен. Талапкер осы іс бойынша 2026 жылы 30 маусымда Алматының әкімшілік соты шығарған шешімге сүйенген. Ол кезде Бажкенова жала жабу ісі бойынша кінәлі деп танылып, 778 мың теңге айыппұл төлеуге міндеттелген еді. Азаматтық іс 7 қазанда қарала бастады. Бейсембаев Бажкеновадан материалды өшіруді, бес жұмыс күні ішінде терістеуді және моральдық өтемақы ретінде 20 миллион теңге төлеуді талап еткен. Алғашқы сот отырысына дейін жауапкер тарап миллион теңге көлеміндегі өтемақыны бөліп төлеуді ұсынып, медиациялық келісім жасауды ұсынған. 7 қазандағы алғашқы отырыста талапкердің өкілі бұрынғы министрдің кәсібилігі туралы материал жазуды да талап еткен. Алайда 5 қарашадағы сот шешімінде ол жөнінде ештеңе айтылмаған. Бажкенова талап арызбен келіспеді. Оның пікірінше, әкімшілік соттың қаулысы моральдық өтемақының мөлшерін және 20 миллион теңге талап етуге қаншалықты негіз бар дегенді анықтамайды. Оның сөзінше, талапта көрсетілген зардап объективті дәлелдермен расталмаған. Ол соттан талапты қанағаттандырмауды немесе өтемақы көлемін негізді мөлшерде белгілеуді сұрады. Судья Айдар Өтебеков талапты ішінара қанағаттандырды. Сот Бажкенованың 2025 жылғы 7 қазанда Facebook, Instagram және Telegram-дағы Bazhkenova vs. арнасында жариялаған мәліметтерінің мына бөлігін шындыққа сәйкес келмейді әрі Бейсембаевтың ар-намысына, қадір-қасиеті мен іскерлік беделіне нұқсан келтіреді деп таныды: Ғани Бейсембаев пен Мұрат Нұртілеудің туыстық немесе құдандалық байланысы бар деген мәлімет; Бейсембаев осы байланыстың арқасында қызметте жоғарылады деген тұжырым. Сот Бажкеноваға шешім заңды күшіне енгеннен кейін бес жұмыс күні ішінде 2025 жылғы 7 қазандағы материалдарды өшіруді және сол әлеуметтік желілердегі аккаунттарда теріске шығаруды міндеттеді. Сонымен қатар сот Бажкеновадан Бейсембаевтың пайдасына 500 мың теңге моральдық өтемақы және 7 162 теңге мемлекеттік баж өндіріп алу туралы шешім шығарды. Талаптың қалған бөлігі қанағаттандырылған жоқ. Азаттық Азияның сот шешіміне қатысты сұрағына Бажкенованың адвокаты Эльдар Мұсаев оның азаматтық талаппен келіспейтінін жеткізді. Қорғаушының айтуынша, талап әкімшілік соттың шешіміне негізделген. «Алғашқы әкімшілік сот отырысына ол қатысқан жоқ, өйткені процесс туралы оған бір күн бұрын ғана хабарлаған. Ол кезде адвокаты да болмаған, сондықтан өзін қорғауға мүмкіндігі болмады. Оның үстіне сол уақытта қылмыстық іс бойынша сотқа дайындалып жүрген еді. Істің мән-жайын ескерсек, сот бұрын жарияланған ақпараттың шын-өтірігін анықтау мәселесін шешкен жоқ. Сондықтан азаматтық іс бойынша соттың шешімін жеткілікті дәрежеде әділ деп санаймын. Өйткені талапкер негізсіз үлкен сома талап етті» деді адвокат. Тамыз айында Гүлнар Бажкенова қылмыстық іс бойынша кінәлі деп танылып, сегіз жылға бас бостандығынан айырылған. Алайда кәмелетке толмаған баласы бар болғандықтан, жаза екі жылға кейінге қалдырылған. Оған журналистикамен айналысуына тыйым салынған. Бажкеноваға Қылмыстық кодекстің үш бабы бойынша айып тағылған: 189-бап — «Бөтеннің мүлкін иемдену немесе талан-таражға салу», 214-бап — «Заңсыз кәсіпкерлік» және 274-бап — «Көрінеу жалған ақпарат тарату». Ол айыптарды мойындамады. Журналист редакцияның тәуелсіздігі мен кәсіби ұстанымдарын қорғағаны үшін сот алдында жауап беріп отырғанын айтты. Гүлнар Бажкенова — қазақстандық журналист және медиаменеджер. Ол әр жылдары бірнеше ірі медиа жобаны басқарған. Қылмыстық қудалауға дейін Orda.kz интернет-басылымының бас редакторы болған. Бажкеноваға үкім шыққаннан кейін басылым жұмысын тоқтатты. Ғани Бейсембаев 2023 жылғы 4 қаңтардан 2025 жылғы 29 қыркүйекке дейін оқу-ағарту министрі болды. Мұрат Нұртілеу 2024 жылғы сәуірден 2025 жылғы қыркүйекке дейін сыртқы істер министрі қызметін атқарды. 2025 жылдың күзінен бері ол президенттің халықаралық инвестициялық және сауда ынтымақтастығы жөніндегі көмекшісі. Астана, 7 қараша 2026 жыл. 7 қарашада Астанада Тәжікстан басшысы Эмомали Рахмонды Ақордада салтанатты түрде қарсы алды. Ақорданың жазуынша, президент резиденциясы алдында Қазақстан әуе қорғанысы күштерінің тікұшақтары Қазақстан мен Тәжікстанның мемлекеттік туларын желбіретіп ұшырды. Бұдан соң Қазақстан басшысы Қасым-Жомарт Тоқаев пен Тәжікстан басшысы Эмомали Рахмон бір-біріне ресми делегация мүшелерін таныстырды. Екі жақ арасындағы келіссөз кезінде Тоқаев екі ел арасында тасымалданатын тауар түрлері көбейіп, түрлі өнім көлемі артқанын жеткізді. Теміржолмен жеткізілетін экспорт-импорт жүгі де ұлғайып келеді деді. "Бұл ретте елдеріміздің жыл сайынғы тауар айналымы тұрақты түрде 1 миллиард доллардан асады. Осының есебінен Қазақстан ұдайы Тәжікстанның ең ірі сауда серіктестерінің үштігіне еніп отыр" деді Қазақстан басшысы. Тоқаев сонымен бірге екі елдің мәдени-гуманитарлық байланыстары да кеңейгенін айтты. 7 қарашада екі ел басшылары Астана қаласында Тәжікстан елшілігінің жаңа ғимаратының ашылуына қатыспақ. Өз кезегінде Тәжікстан басшысы Қазақстан Тәжікстанның алдыңғы қатарлы сауда және экономикалық серіктестерінің санатына кіретінін атап өтті. "Биыл тоғыз айдың қорытындысы бойынша елдеріміз арасындағы тауар айналымының көлемі 1 миллиард доллардан асты. Бұл өткен жылдың осы кезеңімен салыстырғанда шамамен 26 пайызға жоғары. Инвестициялық ықпалдастық дәйекті түрде дамып келеді. Бүгінде Тәжікстанда Қазақстан капиталының қатысуымен 130-дан аса кәсіпорын тіркелген. Ал Қазақстанда тәжік тарапының 580-нен астам кәсіпорны жұмыс істейді. Олардың 500-і толығымен тәжік капиталының қатысуы арқылы еңбек етеді. Бұл – өте жақсы көрсеткіш" деді Эмомали Рахмон. Ақорданың жазуынша, Тоқаев тәжік әріптесін Qoja Ahmet Yasaui орденімен марапаттады. Марапаттау кезінде Тоқаев Эмомали Рахмонның "Қазақстан мен Тәжікстан арасындағы сан қырлы байланыстарды тереңдетуде айрықша рөл атқарғанына" назар аударды. Рахмон Тоқаевқа алғыс айтты. Келіссөздің соңына қарай Тоқаев пен Рахмон Қазақстан мен Тәжікстан арасындағы ынтымақтастықты одан әрі дамытудың басым бағыттарын айқындайтын бірлескен мәлімдеме қабылдады. Ақорданың жазуынша, екі елдің ресми делегация мүшелері үкіметаралық және ведомствоаралық құжаттар алмасты. Арасында Қазақстан мен Тәжікстан арасында "Ұлттық қауіпсіздік мемлекеттік комитетінің Шекара әскерлері үшін кадр даярлау саласындағы келісім", электр энергетикасы саласындағы ынтымақтастық туралы келісім, тау-кен өндіру және тау-кен металлургиясы салаларындағы жобаларды дамыту мақсатында ұзақмерзімді ынтымақтастықты одан әрі дамыту және тереңдету туралы келісім бар. БАҚ өкілдеріне арналған брифинг кезінде Тоқаев Қазақстан мен Тәжікстан арасында "қандай да бір шешілмеген немесе түйіні тарқамайтын мәселе жоқ" екенін айтты. Ресми ақпаратқа қарағанда, былтыр екі ел арасындағы ауыл шаруашылығы өнімдерінің жеткізілімі 11 пайызға өсіп, шамамен 600 миллион долларды құраған. Бұл – бүкіл тауар айналымының тең жартысы. Екі жақ тауар айналымы 2 миллиард долларлық межеге таяп қалғаны айтылды. Авто және теміржолмен жүк транзиті көлемі сәйкесінше 8 және 15 пайызға ұлғайып, шамамен 7 миллион тоннаны құрады. Қазақстан мен Тәжікстанның қарым-қатынасы соңғы жылдары стратегиялық әріптестіктен одақтастық деңгейіне көтерілді. Әсіресе 2024–2026 жылдары екі ел арасындағы жоғары деңгейдегі кездесулер жиілеп, Орталық Азиядағы өңірлік ынтымақтастыққа басымдық берілді. Қазақстан мен Тәжікстан Орталық Азиядағы бірнеше маңызды мәселе бойынша ортақ мүддеге ие. Мысалы, екі ел Еуропа, Кавказ және Оңтүстік Азия нарықтарына шығатын көлік дәліздерін дамытуға мүдделі. ОҚИ ОТЫРЫҢЫЗ Әуелі мақтайды, кейін даттайды. Орталық Азия басшыларынан культ жасау қалай жүріп жатыр? "Сонша мұнайды қайдан алады?" Жаңа жанармай зауыттары Орталық Азиядағы тапшылықты жоя ма?
