https://www.azattyq.org/a/reseidin-sogys.body: УКРАИНАДАҒЫ СОҒЫС Қазақстандықтар Ресей пропагандасының ықпалына қалай ұшырайды? Бағдат АСЫЛБЕК 7 қараша 2026 жыл, 12:05 Қазақстандықтар Ресей пропагандасының ықпалына қалай ұшырайды? Бөлісу Сілтемесін көшіру Facebook X (Twitter) WhatsApp Email Бөлісу Бөлісу Сілтемесін көшіру Facebook X (Twitter) WhatsApp Email Бөлісу PDF VPN-сіз оқу Сайт бұғатталып тұрса да, материалды осы сілтемемен кіріп оқуға болады Google-да басымдық бер Ресейдің көрші елге басып кіруін ақтайтын пропаганда қалай жұмыс істейді? Кремльдің нарративтері Қазақстан аудиториясының бір бөлігіне неге әсер етеді және оған кімдер көбірек бейім? Азаттық Азия бұл жөнінде қазақстандықтардың Ресейдің Украинаға қарсы соғысына көзқарасын зерттеп жүрген Medianet халықаралық журналистика орталығының өкілі Снежана Цойдан сұхбат алды. Снежана Цой — Medianet халықаралық журналистика орталығының зерттеу бағдарламаларының жетекшісі, Орталық Азиядағы алғашқы фактчекинг ресурсы Factcheck.kz үйлестірушісі және Demoscope қоғамдық пікірді бақылау бюросының жобаларына жетекшілік етеді. 2022 жылдан бері Demoscope Ресейдің Украинаға басып кіруіне қатысты сауалнамалар жүргізіп, ресейлік насихаттың қазақстандық аудиторияға әсерін зерттеп келеді. Снежана Цой РЕСЕЙ НАСИХАТЫ ҚАЗАҚСТАНДА ҚАЛАЙ ТАРАЛАДЫ? Азаттық Азия: Ресей пропагандасы деп нені айтамыз? Снежана Цой: Ресей пропагандасы да, жалпы пропаганданың өзі де — анықтау оңай емес күрделі құбылыс. Қарапайым тілмен айтқанда, пропаганда дегеніміз — қоғамдық пікірге жүйелі әрі мақсатты түрде әсер етіп, белгілі бір көзқарас пен құндылықтарды қалыптастыру, адамдардың қоғамда өзін ұстауына ықпал ету. Украинадағы соғыс және оның Қазақстанның ақпараттық кеңістігіне әсері туралы айтсақ, ресейлік насихат — өте зиянды құбылыс. Оның негізгі қаупі — ақпараттық ықпалында. Ресей насихаты қоғамдық пікірді манипуляциялау және өзгерту арқылы жұмыс істейді. Азаттық Азия: Журналистика, пропаганда және ресейшіл көзқарастың ара-жігін қалай ажыратуға болады? Снежана Цой: Журналистика бейтарап болуы керек. Ақпаратты объективті түрде, жауапкершілікпен және бейтарап жеткізуі тиіс. Ал пропаганда керісінше әрекет етеді. Бірақ оның ерекшелігі — жасырын сипатында. Ол өзін насихат ретінде көрсетпейді. «Қазір миыңызды улаймыз» деген белгі жоқ. Керісінше, журналистік форматтарды пайдаланады, фактчекинг пен кәсіби медианың кейпіне енеді. Алайда түпкі мақсаты — қоғамдық пікірді манипуляциялау. Қауіптілігі де осында. Азаттық Азия: Қарапайым оқырманға түсінікті болу үшін бірнеше мысал келтіре аласыз ба? Снежана Цой: Көп қолданылатын эмоциялық ұғымдардың бірі — «русофобия». Украинадағы соғыс кезінде бұл сөз «орыс әлемін» және Украинадағы орыс тілін қорғау қажеттігін ақтау үшін жиі қолданылады. Қазақстанда да осындай жағдай кездеседі. Мысалы, бір топ адам отарсыздандыру, қазақ тілін дамыту және оның маңызын арттыру мәселесін көтерсе, оларды бірден «жау жақтың өкілдері» деп көрсетуі мүмкін. Олардың мақсаты орыстілді азаматтарды кемсіту дегендей пікір қалыптастырады. Ресей пропагандасындағы ең белгілі әрі зиянды ұстанымдардың бірі — «құлдырап бара жатқан Батыс» туралы түсінік. Бұл ұғым патшалық Ресей кезінде пайда болып, кейін советтік идеологияға енді. Қазір ол шартты түрде «ұжымдық Батыстың» беделін түсіру үшін белсенді қолданылады. Мысалы, Ресей НАТО және Батыс елдерімен соғысып жатыр деген уәж айтылады. «Құлдырап бара жатқан Батыс» туралы әңгіме қуғын-сүргінді ақтауға және назарды басқа жаққа аударуға көмектеседі. Адамдар бағаның өсіп, тұрмыс сапасының төмендегенін көріп отыр делік. Бірақ пропагандалық сюжеттерде Еуропада адамдар суық пәтерлерде тоңып, тіпті үй жануарларын жеуге мәжбүр болып жатқаны айтылады. Яғни, «олардың жағдайы бізден де нашар» деген ой қалыптастырылады. Азаттық Азия: Манипуляция мен насихат элементтері бар ресейлік ақпарат Қазақстанға қандай арналар арқылы тарайды? Снежана Цой: Қазақстанның ақпараттық кеңістігі салыстырмалы түрде ашық. Бір жағынан, бұл жақсы. Екінші жағынан, сыртқы ақпараттық ықпалдың, соның ішінде Ресей пропагандасының елге енуіне мүмкіндік береді. Ресей ақпараттық соғысты қазір тек телеарналар арқылы жүргізіп отырған жоқ. Әртүрлі мультимедиалық форматтар мен әлеуметтік желілерді де тиімді пайдаланады. Жастарға арналған қысқа видеолар жасайды. Өкінішке қарай, Қазақстанда ресейлік телеарналар әлі де еркін көрсетіледі. Кабельдік желілерде ресейлік күн тәртібін белсенді насихаттайтын Sputnik Қазақстан да жұмыс істейді. Азаттық Азия: 2022 жылы Қазақстандағы шағын жергілікті провайдер ресейлік телеарналарды көрсетуден бас тартқан еді. Бұл оқиға немен аяқталды? Снежана Цой: Менің білуімше, бұл шешім көп ұзамай кері қайтарылды. Бірақ мәселе бір ғана жергілікті арнаның шешімінде емес. Біздің ұйым, басқа да құқық қорғау және тәуелсіз медиа ұйымдары, жалпы азаматтық қоғам ресейлік телеарналардың хабар таратуын шектеу қажеттігін бірнеше рет көтерді. Біз бұл талапты әлі де айтып келеміз. Қазақстанда соғысты, өшпенділікті, кемсітуді насихаттауға және адамдарды қудалауға шақыруға тыйым салынған. Азаматтық және саяси құқықтар туралы халықаралық пактінің 20-бабы да соғысты насихаттауға және өшпенділік тіліне жол бермейді. Өкінішке қарай, қазір қоғамымызда насихаттық әрі зиянды контентке еркін, ешқандай шектеусіз қол жеткізуге болады. ОҚИ ОТЫРЫҢЫЗ "Қостанай – Ресейдің жері" деген азаматтың ісі тоқтады. Сараптама "қылмыс құрамы жоқ" дейді ПРОПАГАНДА КІМДЕРГЕ КӨБІРЕК ӘСЕР ЕТЕДІ? Азаттық Азия: Мемлекеттік органдар мұндай манипуляциялық ақпаратты бақылап, анықтап отыр ма? Снежана Цой: Ресей пропагандасының қоғамдық пікірге әсерін өлшейтін қандай да бір сауалнама немесе зерттеу жүргізіліп жатыр ма десеңіз, ондай зерттеулерді көрген жоқпыз. Мүмкін, ішкі талдаулар жасалатын шығар. Бірақ бұл туралы ашық ақпарат та, қоғамдық талқылау да жоқ. Бұл өте өкінішті. Меніңше, ең алдымен мемлекет деңгейінде реформалар жүргізіп, заңнаманы және мұндай құбылыстарға жауап беру тәсілдерін өзгерту қажет. Бір кездері ақпарат министрі болған Аида Балаева ресейлік «Звезда» телеарнасының әскери бағдарламасын қазақстандық «ОҢ ТВ» арнасының қайталап көрсеткеніне пікір білдірген еді. Бағдарламада әскери техника мен ғылымның жетістіктері туралы айтылғанымен, онда соғысты және адам өлтіруді ақтайтын өрескел насихат болды. Қазақстан билігі отандық медианы контент таңдауда жауапкершілік танытуға шақырды. Тағы бір маңызды қауіп факторы бар. Қазақстанда орыс тіліндегі контентті тұтынатын адамдар көп. Оның ішінде соғысты насихаттайтын зиянды ақпарат та бар. Demoscope сауалнамалары ақпаратты тұтынатын тіл мен ресейлік пропагандаға бейімділік арасында айқын байланыс бар екенін көрсетті. Өкінішке қарай, орыстілді азаматтар ресейлік насихатқа көбірек ұшырайды. Себебі ақпаратты негізінен орыс тілінде алады. Мысалы, 2025 жылғы сауалнамада «арнайы әскери операция» деген атауды респонденттердің 21 пайызы таңдаған. Ал қазақтілді азаматтар арасында бұл көрсеткіш небәрі 6 пайыз болды. Сауалнамалар Кремльдің Украинадағы жағдайға қатысты ұстанымдарын қайталайтындардың арасында егде жастағы орыстілді адамдардың үлесі жоғары екенін де көрсетті. Азаттық Азия: Пропаганда адамдардың көзқарасын қалай қалыптастырады? Снежана Цой: Пропаганда «біз жақсымыз, олар жаман» деген қарапайым тәсілді қолданады. Осылайша қоғамды екіге бөліп, қорқыныш, ашу-ыза мен агрессия тудырады. Қарсы тарапты адам ретінде қабылдамауға итермелейді. Пропагандада эмоциялық бояуы қанық сөздер қолданылады. Бір тарапты «қасиетті жауынгерлер» деп дәріптесе, екінші тарапты «жау», «фашист» деп көрсетеді. Адамдарға ақпараттың дайын, жеңілдетілген нұсқасы ұсынылады. Күрделі геосаяси жағдайды немесе үлкен соғысты қарапайым түсініктерге бөліп береді. Сосын: «Біз қасиетті соғыс жүргізіп жатырмыз, орыстарды қорғаймыз, оларды сол жақта кемсітіп жатыр» деген дайын түсінік қалыптастырады. Азаттық Азия: Ресейшіл көзқарастағы адамдар сіздерді Украинаны жақтайсыздар, Ресейге қарсысыздар деп айыптауы мүмкін ғой. Снежана Цой: Ресейшіл көзқарас пен Ресей пропагандасы, журналистиканың айырмашылығына тоқталайын. Бұл жерде мәселе біржақты емес. Ресейшіл деп Ресейдегі диссиденттерді

Ақтөбе әкімдігі мүгедектігі бар азаматтардың әлеуметтік құқығы мәселелеріне арналған митингке рұқсат беру туралы шешімнің күшін жойды. Бұл жөнінде құқық қорғаушы Мұсағали Дауылов желіде хабарлады. Бұған дейін Ақтөбе әкімдігі белсенділерге 3 желтоқсанда Ақтөбенің Астана ауданындағы "Авиатор саябағында" сағат 10:00-ден 11:55 аралығында митинг өткізуге рұқсат берген еді. Ақтөбе қаласы әкімінің орынбасары Әсет Оралбаевтың хатында "Aqtobe Su-Energy Group АҚ апаттық қалпына келтіру жұмыстарын жүргізіп жатқандықтан, көрсетілген аумақта бейбіт жиын өткізу мүмкін емес" екені жазылған. "Қазіргі жағдайға байланысты Ақтөбе қаласының әкімдігі 14 қазандағы No762 қаулының күшін жою туралы қаулы шығарды" деп жазылған әкімдіктің хатында. Әкімдік хатта "жоспарланған шараларға байланысты" бейбіт жиынды басқа орында, басқа уақытта өткізу мүмкін емес екенін де жазған. Бұған дейін 3 желтоқсанда өтеді делінген шарада қатысушылар азаматтардың әлеуметтік-экономикалық құқықтарын қорғауды, мүгедектігі бар азаматтарды қолдау мәселесін, сонымен бірге демократиялық реформаны жүргізуді қозғайтынын айтқан еді. Олар мүгедектігі бар адамдарға кедергісіз орта құру, инклюзивті білім, сапалы медициналық көмек, реабилитация және әділетті әлеуметтік жәрдемақы тағайындау, тең еңбек жағдайымен қамтамасыз ету, лайықты жалақы, баспана мәселесін көтеретінін жеткізген. Олар сонымен бірге мемлекет пен азаматтық қоғам арасындағы ашық диалог орнату мәселесін де айтпақ болған. "Біздің мақсатымыз - еліміздегі адами қадір-қасиет пен әлеуметтік әділеттілікті анықтайтын мәселелерді ашық, заңды және өркениетті түрде қозғау" деп жазған еді Дауылов. Қазақстан билігі елде "бейбіт жиын өткізу үшін азаматтардың рұқсат сұрауы міндетті емес" деп биік мінберлерде мәлімдегенмен іс жүзінде "рұқсат етілмеген митингілерге" барған азаматтар ұсталып, көп жағдайда әкімшілік жазаға тартылады. Халықаралық ұйымдар азаматтардың бейбіт жиналу құқығы бұзылып жатқандығын жиі айтады. Human Rights Watch 2026 жылға әлемдік есебінде "Қазақстан билігі сөз бостандығын, бірлесу және бейбіт жиналу еркіндігін қатаң шектеп отыр" деп жазған. Елде билік орындарының жауаптылығы, сот төрелігі, пікір айту, бейбіт жиналу еркіндігі бойынша мәселелер бар, билікке сын айтатындар мен құқық қорғаушыларды қудалау жалғасып жатыр деп жазған. https://www.rferl.org/a/us-china-russia-.body: China US-China-Russia Hypersonic Weapons Race Accelerates By Matthew Fulco November 06, 2026 14:38 CET US-China-Russia Hypersonic Weapons Race Accelerates Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google China parades its first operational hypersonic cruise missile in Beijing in September 2025. American defense contractor Lockheed Martin’s recent announcement that it had been awarded a $694 million contract by the US Air Force to produce a new air-launched hypersonic missile is the latest sign of an accelerating tripartite arms race involving the US, China, and Russia. A hypersonic missile is a weapon able to move at speeds exceeding Mach 5 -- more than five times the speed of sound or roughly 6,100 kilometers per hour -- while maintaining the ability to perform sharp, sustained maneuvers within the Earth's atmosphere. “What makes certain newer hypersonic weapons particularly challenging is the combination of speed, maneuverability, and flight trajectory, which can complicate detection, continuous tracking and the prediction of where the weapon will be at the point of interception,” Eva Sula, a senior fellow for defense and security at the London-headquartered Baltic International Security Center (BISC), said in an interview. Lockheed said the missile’s -- known as the ARRW -- “production readiness makes it an essential asset for the military, providing a critical capability to counter emerging threats.” China and Russia, which have had a “no limits partnership” since early 2022, are foremost among those threats. Beijing has the world’s leading hypersonic arsenal, driven by a high-volume manufacturing strategy. Russia leads the US in operational fielding of hypersonic weapons, having used them in combat during its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Analysts say that if current production trends hold, by 2035 China and Russia will field a joint hypersonic weapons arsenal of 5,000 -- with Beijing accounting for 4,000. “It's one piece of the puzzle as the US scrambles -- with some success -- to rapidly build up its hypersonic capabilities, both defensive and offensive,” Grant Newsham, a senior fellow at the Center for Security Policy in Washington and retired Marines colonel, told RFE/RL. Washington “is making surprisingly rapid progress, particularly on the offensive end -- and that includes the Air Force, Navy, and Army,” he added. The Pentagon plans to spend $37.9 billion on hypersonic weapons programs from the 2027 to 2031 fiscal years in a push to catch up with China and Russia. That includes $10.1 billion for the Army to field 4,500 intermediate-range hypersonic weapons, $2.1 billion for the Navy to procure 59 missiles, and broad funding for the Air Force to acquire the ARRW and the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM). China’s Advantages In the hypersonic weapons race, China leads for several reasons. First, it has an early mover’s advantage. In 2020, it deployed the world’s first operational hypersonic weapon system, which is composed of the DF-17 medium-range ballistic missile and DF-ZF hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV). “China’s development of its conventional missiles, not bound by INF [the arms control agreement signed by the US and Soviet Union in 1987], gave them a leg up in the medium-range ballistic missiles that can be used as hypersonic boosters,” John Van Oudenaren, a research analyst for the technology consultancy BluePath Labs in Washington, told RFE/RL. Beijing further benefits from a testing infrastructure for hypersonic weapons that is more varied and expansive than the US’s, he adds. China is the only country to have successfully integrated an HGV with a Fractional Orbital Bombardment System (FOBS), a warhead delivery system that places a weapon into low-Earth orbit (LEO) before de-orbiting it toward a target. Beijing carried out two tests in 2021 that demonstrated this integration. SEE ALSO: China, Russia Deepen Arctic Cooperation In Challenge To US Though the HGV in the first test missed its target by 39 kilometers, it successfully fired a separate projectile mid-flight. The Pentagon was stunned. No country had ever released a payload from a vehicle moving at hypersonic speeds without destroying the craft or destabilizing its flight path. General Mark Milley, then-chairman of the US Joint Chiefs of Staff, called it a "Sputnik moment.” At the same time, China’s hypersonic tests highlighted US vulnerability to an attack from the south. That’s because US missile defense is designed with the assumption that a Russian nuclear attack on the American homeland would travel across the shortest distance -- the North Pole and Arctic. But in China’s hypersonic tests, the weapons moved in low-Earth orbit over Antarctica, where US radar coverage is limited. A FOBS can approach from unexpected trajectories because it does not fly on high, predictable parabolic arcs like a traditional intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM). Beijing denied that it tested hypersonic weapons. Its Foreign Ministry said that the tests involved verifying reusable space vehicle technologies to help lower the cost of spacecraft operations. “They are lying. It's part and parcel of Chinese strategy,” the Center for Security Policy’s Newsham says, adding that Beijing vastly understates its military spending. The Pentagon estimates that China spends 40-90 percent more on defense than in its stated budget. Another advantage China has in the hypersonic competition is its manufacturing prowess, compounded by its de facto alliance with Russia. “Russia is in a wartime economy and China is a manufacturing powerhouse. They are able to build these missiles very quickly compared to the US,” Ali Javaheri, a senior emerging technology analyst at private markets data firm PitchBook in New York, told RFE/RL. Russia and China respectively produce an estimated 80 and 370 hypersonic weapons annually, while the US manufactures them in the single digits. “The US is great at making exquisite defense systems -- like the F-35 fighter jet -- but not so good at making the mid-tier stuff” like hypersonics, says Javaheri. He notes that after the Cold War ended, the American defense industrial base atrophied, with dramatic consolidation and decoupling from the commercial economy. Defense contractors focused on producing advanced, low-volume, and expensive platforms for the Pentagon. The US military ultimately acquired some world-leading defense systems, but at the expense of mass production and surge capacity. Increased Threat To Taiwan American military planners worry that China’s burgeoning hypersonic arsenal could complicate US efforts to intervene in a Taiwan crisis, the most likely scenario that could thrust the two superpowers into armed conflict. While China already boasts the world’s largest conventional missile force, hypersonic weapons present unique challenges because of their speed, low-altitude atmospheric flight and real-time maneuverability. The Pentagon’s Overmatch brief, a classified assessment of US military preparedness that was first brought to light by The New York Times in December 2025, found in war-game simulations of a Taiwan conflict that Beijing used hypersonic weapons as part of a devastating campaign that disabled or destroyed the US Navy’s advanced Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carriers. https://www.rferl.org/a/ukraine-sbu-anti.body: Schemes: Investigating Ukraine Exclusive: How Ukraine's Security Service Sought Access To The Anti-Corruption Court's Restricted Database By Valeriya Yegoshyna , Olya Ivleva and Schemes November 06, 2026 21:34 CET Exclusive: How Ukraine's Security Service Sought Access To The Anti-Corruption Court's Restricted Database Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google An illustrative collage depicting the High Anti-Corruption Court of Ukraine Earlier this year, investigators from the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) sought full access to the internal document-management system of the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC), a key part of Ukraine's anti-corruption infrastructure that completes the chain from investigation and prosecution to conviction or exoneration. Several civil-society organizations monitoring government transparency and corruption risks among officials and law enforcement agencies would later call the move part of a series of attacks on anti-corruption bodies in Ukraine, where citizens and activists say high-level graft undermines the country's defense against the full-scale Russian invasion, now in its fifth year. The hearings on the access request at Kyiv's Shevchenkivskiy District Court were held behind closed doors at the insistence of an SBU officer, who cited the confidentiality of the investigation. He also objected to the presence of civic activists, asserting they could harm the investigation. The judge granted the motion for closed hearings but ultimately rejected the request. While extensive access was denied, activists said the attempt exposed a possible means of undermining the independence of Ukraine's main anti-corruption system: the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU), the Special Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), and the HACC. SEE ALSO: Zelenskyy’s Anti-Corruption Climbdown: What It Means For Ukraine It came a year after large street protests in cities nationwide prompted President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to retract a law he had signed two days earlier that critics in Ukraine and the West said robbed NABU and SAPO of their independence and set back years of progress on justice and the rule of law. A new chapter in the confrontation between the SBU and the anti-corruption bodies has unfolded this week with the release of NABU recordings concerning suspected criminal activity by SBU officials, among others, as part of an investigation dubbed Operation Carthage. On November 5, NABU said it had served notices of suspicion on a senior SBU official and two National Police officials, as well as other suspects. Schemes, the investigative unit of RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service , was given the opportunity to review the full text of the Shevchenkivskiy court's confidential August 26 ruling. Reporters established how SBU representatives justified their request for temporary total access to the HACC database, what might have provided formal grounds for such a step, why the request may have been so sweeping, and who argued for it in court. The timing of the request raises questions about the motive for an attempt to gain such broad access to the court's document-management system. The background of the request is complex. In late August 2026, SBU investigators were in the throes of a probe into possible interference by HACC employees in the anti-corruption court's database during the automated assignment of a case to a judge. The case concerns an alleged corruption scheme involving the sale, at below-market prices, of seized property entrusted to the Asset Recovery and Management Agency (ARMA). NABU and SAPO, which have handled the case since 2019, said they established losses exceeding 440 million hryvnyas ($9.7 million). Anton Yanchuk (left), Viktor Vyshnyov (center), and Andriy Dovbenko The 11 defendants included former ARMA head Anton Yanchuk and Viktor Vyshnyov, a former director of SETAM, a state enterprise established by the Justice Ministry to organize transparent online auctions of seized property. Investigators allege the property was sold to "controlled companies at reduced prices on a controlled trading platform" and have identified lawyer Andriy Dovbenko as the alleged organizer. Controlled, in this case, means controlled by the defendants or their associates. According to recordings quoted at hearings in the case, participants in the alleged scheme referred to the assets involved as "shashlik" -- skewered grilled meat -- and to the auctions as "grilling shashlik." In May 2025, the indictment was sent to the HACC, whose automated document-management system selected the presiding judge on the second attempt. This set in motion what followed: a new investigation, expert examinations, court hearings, and what activists would later call an attack by the SBU on the anti-corruption system. Almost a year later, in April 2026, SBU investigators opened an investigation into possible interference with the HACC system. They requested the software and temporary full access to a copy of the court's database. The software, called D-3, stores documents submitted to the anti-corruption court by NABU detectives and SAPO prosecutors, among other things. It includes material that must remain unknown to anyone other than the investigators until the last possible moment, such as applications for search warrants and authorization for other investigative measures. Why did the SBU suddenly take an interest in the HACC's automated judicial assignment in the so-called Shashlik case, many months after it took place? That question was raised by Vyshnyov, the defendant and former SETAM director. In late February of this year, Vyshnyov's lawyer complained to the SBU about what he claimed was possible interference with the automated assignment system by HACC administrative staff, including their head. Schemes examined records in the public register of court decisions in an effort to determine whether HACC staff had in fact manipulated the system and whether the SBU was within its rights to investigate the case. 'Insufficient Grounds' An April 1 ruling by the Shevchenkivskiy court shows that after Vyshnyov complained to the SBU, the agency promptly decided the matter was outside its investigative jurisdiction and forwarded it to the State Bureau of Investigation (SBI). The SBI also declined to register a case based on Vyshnyov's complaint, citing "insufficient grounds" for a pretrial investigation. Almost 10 months after the assignment of the case in May 2025, Vyshnyov took the matter to court, where the investigating judge, Vadym Kovtunenko, determined the fate of the prospective investigation. In his ruling, Kovtunenko effectively compelled the SBU to open a case, the register indicates. The judge did not examine which agency had jurisdiction over the alleged offense by HACC employees. He ruled that because the complaint had originally been filed with the SBU, it was the SBU that had to make a procedural decision within 24 hours of receiving the decision. Was there anything in the anti-corruption court employees' actions for SBU investigators to investigate? The HACC's own May 14 ruling on the recusal of the judge initially assigned to the ARMA/SETAM case sheds some light on that issue, pointing to alleged problems with the automated case-assignment system. The judge recused himself because of previous involvement in a related case. "In effect, several successive attempts to assign this indictment automatically took place on a single day, May 1, 2025, some of which were erroneous," says the 11-page recusal ruling, which details all the assignment attempts and shows that the case was indeed registered several times in the system. The court described these as "technical errors corrected in accordance with procedure" -- an explanation provided by court staff that the judge found "entirely logical." https://www.rferl.org/a/ukraine-oleshky-.body: News Ukraine Hopes Oleshky Can Serve As Model For Wider Truce, Delegation Says In DC By Alex Raufoglu November 06, 2026 22:15 CET Ukraine Hopes Oleshky Can Serve As Model For Wider Truce, Delegation Says In DC Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US first lady Melania Trump meets with Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, while David Arakhamia looks on. Listen to this article 10 min This audio is automated Learn more WASHINGTON -- Ukraine hopes a temporary cease-fire that enabled humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky could serve as a model for wider de-escalation efforts, top officials said. Top Ukrainian officials, speaking at a news conference at the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington on November 6, described the operation as a practical test of mechanisms that could eventually help monitor a broader truce. Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and David Arakhamia, head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's parliamentary faction, said the six-day humanitarian initiative had demonstrated that even amid the ongoing war, the two sides could agree on and implement a localized cease-fire with international involvement. SEE ALSO: White House Outlines Broader European Security Plan Ahead Of Ukraine Peace Talks The operation, facilitated by US first lady Melania Trump, involved a temporary halt in fighting around Oleshky in Ukraine's occupied Kherson region, allowing roads to be cleared of mines, humanitarian supplies to reach residents, and civilians wishing to leave to be evacuated. "We have chosen humanity over war," Melania Trump said at a White House event on November 5 recognizing the initiative. Lubinets said the cease-fire, which began at 3 a.m. Kyiv time on October 27 and ended late on November 1, was the longest such arrangement since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. He described the operation as a breakthrough not only because of the humanitarian assistance delivered but also because it established a new mechanism for negotiating, monitoring and verifying a cease-fire. The Oleshky Model The operation unfolded in several stages, Lubinets said. After the cease-fire took effect, Russian forces began demining roads leading to Oleshky, a process that continued through October 29. Humanitarian supplies, including food, medicine, drinking water, and specialized hospital equipment, were then delivered. Lubinets and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, accompanied by their teams and journalists from Ukraine, the US, and Russia, subsequently entered the occupied city to oversee the distribution of aid and assist residents seeking evacuation. SEE ALSO: What Is Male State, The Group Reportedly Linked To Airline Bomb Threats? Residents were given three options: remain in Oleshky and receive humanitarian assistance, leave for Ukrainian-controlled territory, or travel to Russia or territory under Russian control. "All people who wanted to be evacuated from Oleshky to Ukraine are now in Ukraine," Lubinets said. He said he had personally overseen the evacuation process and spoken with residents to establish whether their decisions were voluntary. Some chose to remain despite the lack of electricity and heating, while others initially stayed because they doubted the humanitarian mission would succeed. Lubinets said his office had since received additional requests from residents seeking evacuation and expressed hope that another operation could be organized. SEE ALSO: War, Deal, Or Stalemate? What The Midterms Mean For Trump's Iran War Arakhamia said the Ukrainian delegation was considering extending the approach to other difficult areas, although he declined to identify potential locations, saying publicizing them could jeopardize negotiations with Moscow. The humanitarian track would focus on two priorities, he said: returning people whose cases have remained unresolved, including civilians separated from their families, and replicating the Oleshky operation in other occupied or otherwise difficult-to-access areas. He said the two sides were also considering keeping humanitarian negotiations separate from the broader political process, so that disagreements over a peace settlement would not derail efforts to help civilians. 'A Pilot' For Monitoring Broader Cease-Fire Beyond its immediate humanitarian impact, Arakhamia said, the Oleshky initiative offered a real-world test of truce-monitoring arrangements previously developed during earlier rounds of trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia, and the US. Those discussions had produced a comprehensive document outlining how a cease-fire could be monitored if a wider peace agreement were reached, he said. The Oleshky operation allowed the sides to test some of those principles on a smaller scale, including the use of drones to monitor the area and verify potential violations. "One thing is doing a theoretical exercise, another thing is seeing in practice how it's going to work on a smaller scale," Arakhamia said. Lubinets said the operation was particularly significant because he was the first Ukrainian official since 2022 to enter Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory as part of an official humanitarian mission. SEE ALSO: 'Carthage' Investigation: Ukrainian Security Officials Accused Of Involvement In Criminal Activities The delegation also experimented with drone surveillance and direct communication between Ukrainian and Russian military representatives to monitor compliance. Arakhamia said the experience had helped demonstrate how localized cease-fires could be verified rather than relying solely on competing military intelligence claims. The Ukrainian delegation seeks to use the lessons from Oleshky in the next round of negotiations in Abu Dhabi, scheduled for next week. Arakhamia also said Kyiv would favor involving European representatives in future monitoring arrangements, arguing that Europe should have a central role in any postwar security architecture. Kyiv Rejects Equivalence Over Deported Children The Ukrainian officials also addressed President Donald Trump's meeting with Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House on November 5, which took place without a corresponding meeting with the Ukrainian delegation. Arakhamia said the Ukrainian side had not expected or requested a meeting with Trump as part of the Oleshky mission and regarded the encounter with Dmitriev as a separate diplomatic track. He said he did not believe the meeting necessarily concerned Ukraine directly, adding that Kyiv remained in regular contact with US and European national security officials. Asked whether the encounter amounted to negotiations about Ukraine without Ukraine, Arakhamia reiterated that the principle remained valid. He said Washington had generally kept Kyiv informed when discussions with European or Russian representatives touched on Ukrainian issues. Arakhamia suggested that US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were trying to broaden the diplomatic conversation beyond the most intractable territorial questions in Donbas and toward a wider European security arrangement. The idea, he said, was to encourage Russia to consider compromises within a broader framework, although he cautioned that it remained unclear whether the approach would succeed. Asked about references to the return of both Ukrainian and Russian children, Lubinets said Ukraine had never prevented Russian citizens, including children, from leaving Ukrainian territory. He said Kyiv welcomed Melania Trump's assistance in bringing Ukrainian children back from Russia but questioned the use of language suggesting that Ukrainian and Russian children were being returned under equivalent circumstances. https://www.rferl.org/a/what-is-male-sta.body: News Analysis What Is Male State, The Group Reportedly Linked To Airline Bomb Threats? By Ray Furlong November 06, 2026 15:41 CET What Is Male State, The Group Reportedly Linked To Airline Bomb Threats? Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Aircraft at Vaclav Havel Airport, Prague, after Czech police registered bomb threats against flights on November 6. Multiple bomb threats affected flights in Europe on November 6, after a series of hoaxes disrupted air traffic across the continent on November 3 and November 5. So far, the cause of the ongoing chaos is unknown -- with the only lead being an email claiming responsibility signed by “Fighters of the Male State,” apparently linking it to a shadowy Russian group dubbed both Male State and Male Legion. The group itself does not appear to have been very active in recent years. RFE/RL has reported extensively on its activities in the past, most recently in 2022 when it targeted a bar in Tbilisi that was frequented by anti-Kremlin Russians. It was founded in 2016 by Vladislav Pozdnyakov, a fitness coach, who fled Russia two years later after receiving a suspended sentence on charges of "inciting hatred toward women." The reported link to the airline threats has not been confirmed -- and denials have been made. The BBC cited a Telegram channel linked to it, while Reuters cited Pozdnyakov himself, with both saying the group no longer existed and was not involved. Male State, which was banned in Russia in 2021, was noted for extreme right-wing views, racism, misogyny, and anti-LGBT statements. Members had even celebrated Adolf Hitler’s birthday. SEE ALSO: 'We Are Coming For You': Russian Feminists Face Intimidation Campaign Online The movement first came to notice when it began campaigning against the introduction in Russia of a law on domestic violence. A feminist activist told RFE/RL at the time that she had been targeted with insults and death threats, and that others had had their addresses published online. Male State also gained notoriety for targeting women in relationships with black men, and was reportedly involved in targeting a sushi chain that used a black man in an advert. A Faked Death In Indonesia Pozdnyakov’s current whereabouts are unknown. His Telegram channel, which has some 5,400 subscribers, is still running and is a platform that promotes Russia’s war on Ukraine. There was no immediate comment on the channel on the reported email relating to the airline threats. On November 6, it posted on subjects including a Russian regional court banning a pornographic video featuring Muslim women, the US midterm elections, and pay rises for Russian soldiers. Pozdnyakov made news again in October last year by faking his own death in Indonesia. There was even a pixelated photo of a man with similar physical appearance, lying on the ground with his shirt covered in blood. Two days later, Pozdnyakov reappeared and admitted that it was a publicity stunt. Russian authorities have often aggressively pursued political exiles but do not appear to have gone after Pozdnyakov. This has fed speculation, fueled by Pozdnyakov himself, that he might have ties to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). Some Russian rights activists have also suggested that Pozdnyakov began cooperating with the FSB after his arrest. 'Hybrid Aggression' Officials in European countries affected by the bomb threats have not voiced any direct suspicions about who is behind them but have indicated that they appear to be coordinated. "The most reasonable assumption is that we are facing an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare," Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said. The threats come amid increasing warnings from Western officials about a Russian shadow campaign of drone incursions, sabotage, and assassination attempts in European NATO countries. SEE ALSO: Interview: Russia's Shadow War On NATO Is 'Bound To Intensify' This week has also seen a series of cyberattacks on supermarket freezers across Europe. “The refrigeration attacks and airline bomb threats may ultimately prove unrelated to Russia -- or to one another. Both nevertheless demonstrate how relatively modest actions can disrupt ordinary life, impose economic costs, and test public confidence in essential services,” wrote David Cattler , former NATO Assistant Secretary General for Intelligence and Security, on November 5. “Europe cannot wait for Russian fingerprints before protecting the systems its citizens depend on,” he added. The Kremlin has dismissed any suggestion of Russian involvement in the freezer attacks. "These are absurd claims. As always, they are backed up by absolutely no reasoning, no evidence whatsoever, and yet here we have such baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything," spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on November 5. There was no immediate comment on the airline threats. What Is Male State, The Group Reportedly Linked To Airline Bomb Threats? Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Follow us Facebook X (Twitter) Youtube Instagram Follow us Print Ray Furlong Ray Furlong is a Senior International Correspondent for RFE/RL. He has reported for RFE/RL from the Balkans, Kazakhstan, Georgia, and elsewhere since joining the company in 2014. He previously worked for 17 years for the BBC as a foreign correspondent in Prague and Berlin, and as a roving international reporter across Europe and the former Soviet Union. This item is part of Russia News Analysis

https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-strikes-k.body: News Russia Strikes Kyiv's Energy Infrastructure, Northern Bridge Ahead Of Abu Dhabi Talks By RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service and RFE/RL's Russian Service November 07, 2026 11:10 CET Russia Strikes Kyiv's Energy Infrastructure, Northern Bridge Ahead Of Abu Dhabi Talks Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google A man stands next to an blast crater outside a residential building following an overnight Russian missile strike on Kyiv on November 7. Kyiv faced widespread damage and disruptions to essential services on November 7 after Russia launched 172 attack drones and 36 ballistic missiles at the Ukrainian capital and other regions, striking energy infrastructure, residential housing, and a major bridge over the Dnipro River. According to Ukraine's Air Force, the strikes damaged energy facilities, residential buildings, and key transport infrastructure, leaving parts of the capital without electricity, heating, and water supplies. Mayor Vitali Klitschko described the situation with the city's energy supply as "extremely difficult" following strikes on infrastructure in the Kyiv and Zhytomyr regions. Several apartment buildings, a kindergarten, and a nonresidential building were also damaged. Five people were injured in Kyiv, including a 14-year-old. The Northern Bridge -- a major bridge in the capital -- over the Dnipro River was also struck and temporarily closed in both directions. Klitschko said the attack damaged the road surface, overhead trolleybus power lines, and electricity transmission lines. The blast wave also damaged five trucks parked nearby. The mayor published a video showing damage the bridge's roadway and safety barriers and said repair work had begun. Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed the strike, claiming the bridge was used to transport weapons and military equipment for the Ukrainian Armed Forces. Elsewhere in the country, Russian strikes on four districts of the Dnipropetrovsk region overnight killed one person and injured four others, including an 11-year-old girl, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service. Zelenskyy: 'Ukraine Must Not be Left Alone' In a November 7 Telegram post accompanied by photos showing extensive damage from the overnight strikes, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles, all targeting Kyiv and other regions. He said substations connecting the Rivne and Khmelnytskiy nuclear power plants to Kyiv and Ukraine's central regions were targeted and that additional substations were reportedly damaged in the Vinnytsya, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv, and Dnipropetrovsk regions. Zelenskyy called on Washington to maintain and increase support for Ukraine, urging greater Congressional unity on security issues, condemnation of Russian aggression, and stronger sanctions pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin. SEE ALSO: Ukraine Hopes Oleshky Can Serve As Model For Wider Truce, Delegation Says In DC "When Russia is trying to plunge Kyiv -- a city of millions -- and the entire country into a blackout, Ukraine must not be left alone," Zelenskyy wrote. "America's determination and consistency in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer," he added. Russia has resisted calls for a partial or total cease-fire, saying fighting would stop when a comprehensive peace deal is reached. It has stepped up strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, along with attacks on civilian sites, as the potentially brutal winter months approach. Meanwhile, the death toll from a massive November 2 Russian air strike on an aid center in Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhya region, rose 55 after rescuers recovered nine more bodies from the rubble in the past 24 hours. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said search operations were continuing for a sixth consecutive day despite the threat of further strikes. Zelenskyy said on November 2 that Russian forces had dropped nine aerial bombs on the settlement, striking a humanitarian aid distribution point and subsequently hitting rescuers and police who arrived at the scene. Ukraine Strikes Targets Inside Russia Ukraine has continued its campaign against Russian energy infrastructure and military-industrial facilities, targeting sites Kyiv says help sustain Moscow's war effort. Overnight on November 6-7, Ukraine carried out strikes on several Russian facilities linked to the oil industry and military production. Ukraine's General Staff confirmed that its missile forces used Neptune coastal missile systems to strike JSC Proton-Electrotex in Oryol, a Russian military-industrial enterprise producing electronic and optoelectronic components. SEE ALSO: The Coverup: Russia's Air Bases Transformed Amid Ukrainian Drone Threat The Ukrainian military says the company produces components used in Russia's Iskander-M ballistic missiles and cruise missile systems. Kyiv said the strike could complicate Russian production of weapons used against Ukrainian cities. Oryol regional authorities reported damage to warehouses and production facilities belonging to commercial enterprises, as well as three private houses. In Russia's Saratov region, a fire broke out at the Saratov Oil Refinery following a Ukrainian drone attack, according to the independent Russian outlet ASTRA and Ukrainian monitoring channels. Several residential buildings were also reportedly damaged. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its air defense systems shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight. The figure has not been independently verified. Trilateral Talks In Abu Dhabi The latest escalation comes just days before planned trilateral negotiations between Ukraine, Russia, and the United States in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11. Ukraine's delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service and a former defense minister, according to Ukrainian media reports. It will also include Presidential Office chief Kyrylo Budanov; David Arakhamia, head of the Servant of the People parliamentary faction; presidential communications adviser Dmytro Lytvyn; and Serhiy Kyslytsia, first deputy head of the Presidential Office. Онҳоеро, ки худсарона боздошт шудаанд, билофосила озод ва саркӯбҳои фаромиллии тоҷикистониёнро дар хориҷа бас кунанд. Лийке Бренд Ӯ омода шудани тарҳи нави Кодекси ҷиноии Тоҷикистон; то 15 сол сангинтар шудани ҷазо барои шиканҷа; ҷорӣ кардани ҷазо барои хушунати хонаводагӣ; татбиқи афв нисбат ба беш аз 18 ҳазор нафар; бекор шудани ҷазо барои “лайк” дар шабакаҳои иҷтимоиро намунаҳои иҷрои машваратҳои пешина номид. “Бар асоси қонун, ҳар нафар дар кишвар ҳақ дорад, ки назарашро озод баён кунад... Дар кишвар корҳо дар самти такмили қонун дар мавриди кори расонаҳо идома дорад,” – афзуд вазири адлияи Тоҷикистон. Музаффар Ашӯриён аз фаъолияти беш аз дусад нашрияву телевизион ва хабаргузориҳои давлатию мустақил чун намунаи кори озоди журналистон мисол овард. Онҳоеро, ки худсарона боздошт шудаанд, билофосила озод ва саркӯбҳои фаромиллии тоҷикистониёнро дар хориҷа бас кунанд. Ба бастани созмонҳои иҷтимоӣ бо ангезаҳои сиёсӣ хотима дода, ниҳодҳои ҷамъиятии басташударо аз нав ба қайд гиранд, то фаъолияти худро ба роҳ монанд”. Ба бовари ин узви кумита, аз нигарониҳо дар бахши амнияти миллӣ ва экстремизм набояд барои саркӯби эътирозҳои сулҳомез суистифода шавад ва Тоҷикистон бояд барои решакан шудани шиканҷа ва ҷазо додани омилони азияту озор ва бадрафторӣ кори ҷиддӣ кунад. Намояндаи Белгия Ҷино Брунсвик машварат дод, ки Тоҷикистон ҳама ташаббусҳоро дар мавриди берун шудан аз Оинномаи Руми Додгоҳи байнулмилалии ҷиноӣ бозбинӣ кунад. Нишасти Шӯрои ҳуқуқи башари Созмони Милал Яке аз машваратҳои дигар ба издивоҷи барвақтии духтарон рабт дошт ва ба бовари, масалан, намояндаи Бритониё, ҳама гуна истисноҳо дар иҷозаи арӯсии кӯдакон бояд бекор карда шавад. Дар Тоҷикистон ташкили оила аз 18-солагӣ иҷоза аст ва дар ҳолатҳои истисноӣ додгоҳ метавонад ба духтар арӯсиро як сол пеш аз ин син иҷоза диҳад. Аммо ахиран чунин истисноҳо ба маротиб афзудаанд. Дар миёни дигар машваратҳо эҷоди шароити пурра барои афроди камтавон (маълул) ва солманд, таъмини аҳолӣ бо оби ошомиданӣ ва мусоидат ба бахши хусусӣ, ба вижа занони соҳибкор садо дод. https://uhrp.org/statement/uhrp-condemns.body: UHRP Condemns Cruel 10-Year Sentence for Hong Kong Democracy Activist Joshua Wong, Calls for Immediate Release - Uyghur Human Rights Project Skip to content UHRP Condemns Cruel 10-Year Sentence for Hong Kong Democracy Activist Joshua Wong, Calls for Immediate Release For immediate release November 6, 2026 | 4:00 p.m. EST Contact: Omer Kanat, +1 (202) 790-1795 The Uyghur Human Rights Project (UHRP) strongly condemns the sentencing of Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong to 10 years in prison under Beijing’s draconian national security law, and calls for his immediate and unconditional release. Wong, who came to prominence as a student leader during Hong Kong’s 2014 Umbrella Movement and as a cofounder of pro-democracy party Demosistō, has been imprisoned since 2020. Wong was due to be released in January 2027, but was instead sentenced on November 5, 2026 to another 10 years on baseless charges of conspiring to collude with foreign forces. Now aged 30, Wong faces imprisonment until age 40. “The cruel sentencing of Joshua Wong is a horrific reminder of the Chinese government’s complete intolerance of dissent,” said UHRP Executive Director Omer Kanat . “The Chinese government has weaponized ‘national security’ to silence those advocating for democracy in Hong Kong, just as it has used the same pretext to justify the arbitrary arrest, detention, imprisonment, and enforced disappearance of countless Uyghurs.” Since imposing its national security law on Hong Kong in 2020, the Chinese government has silenced protest movements, forced activists into exile, and systematically dismantled fundamental freedoms of speech and assembly in Hong Kong. Wong’s sentencing, his second prosecution under the law, is a further violation of the rights and freedoms guaranteed by both the Sino-British Joint Declaration and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. UHRP welcomes statements condemning the sentence from the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, and other governments and urges them to continue pressing for Wong’s release. President Trump must make his release, and the release of all political prisoners, a priority in his upcoming meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping. In a recent letter from prison, Wong told a friend, “The only thing I worry about is that people will forget Hong Kong.” The international community must ensure that Joshua Wong, the people of Hong Kong, and all those imprisoned for exercising fundamental freedoms are not forgotten. https://www.amnesty.org/fr/latest/news/2.body: En réaction à l’arrestation par l’armée israélienne de Ghassan Najjar, agriculteur palestinien et défenseur des terres, lors d’un raid mené avant l’aube le 27 octobre 2026 dans le village de Burin, au sud de Naplouse, dans le nord de la Cisjordanie occupée, Erika Guevara Rosas, directrice générale des recherches, de l’élaboration des lignes de conduite, du travail de plaidoyer et des campagnes à Amnesty International, a déclaré : « Les autorités israéliennes doivent libérer Ghassan Najjar, arrêté uniquement en raison de son engagement pacifique pour protéger la saison de récolte des olives à Burin. Des agents des services de renseignement israéliens avaient explicitement menacé d’arrêter Ghassan Najjar, cofondateur de la Coopérative agricole de la terre et de l’élevage de Burin, s’il poursuivait ses activités militantes. Il organise entre autres des actions de mobilisation locale, un réseau d’entraide entre agriculteurs par le biais de la coopérative, un festival annuel de cerfs-volants dans le village et de nombreuses initiatives culturelles. Ghassan Najjar faisait l’objet de menaces répétées depuis le début des récoltes d’olives, menaces devenues de plus en plus fréquentes au cours de la semaine précédant son interpellation. « L’arrestation de Ghassan Najjar illustre la double menace à laquelle sont confrontés les agriculteurs palestiniens et les défenseurs des terres : les restrictions militaires israéliennes et les violences perpétrées par les colons avec l’aval de l’État les empêchent de se rendre sur leurs terres et de récolter les olives, tandis que les autorités israéliennes durcissent la répression sous forme d’arrestations arbitraires, de menaces et d’actes d’intimidation à l’encontre de ceux qui tentent de protéger ce qui reste de leurs terres. « Un chargé d’interrogatoire de l’armée israélienne a informé l’avocat de Ghassan Najjar que son client risquait d’être placé en détention administrative, une tactique systématiquement utilisée pour sanctionner et persécuter les Palestinien·ne·s en les détenant pour une durée indéfinie, sans inculpation ni procès, sur la base de preuves secrètes auxquelles ils n’ont pas accès. En octobre 2026, on recensait 3 101 Palestinien·ne·s placés en détention administrative. Ghassan Najjar a déjà passé près de 10 ans dans les prisons israéliennes, principalement en détention administrative. Lorsqu’il a été arrêté pour la première fois, il n’avait que 15 ans. « À l’instar du défenseur palestinien des droits humains Ayman Bani Owda et de nombreux autres Palestinien·ne·s, Ghassan Najjar est harcelé par un système judiciaire discriminatoire qui joue un rôle clé s’agissant de légitimer et maintenir le système d’apartheid et l’occupation illégale. Les États ayant de l’influence sur Israël doivent faire pression afin que tous les Palestinien·ne·s détenus arbitrairement, dont Ghassan Najjar, soient libérés et que le recours à la détention administrative soit abandonné. » Contexte Burin est un village palestinien situé au sud de Naplouse, en Cisjordanie occupée. Depuis plus de 20 ans, il subit des attaques fréquentes de colons israéliens et des raids militaires répétés menés par les forces israéliennes, ce qui affecte considérablement la vie quotidienne et les moyens de subsistance de ses habitant·e·s. Parmi ces agissements, citons les agressions visant les habitant·e·s palestiniens et leurs biens, les dommages causés aux terres agricoles et l’accès restreint des agriculteurs à leurs terres, en particulier pendant la saison de récolte des olives. Outre son rôle au sein de la Coopérative agricole de la terre et de l’élevage de Burin, Ghassan Najjar, 36 ans, est coordinateur du réseau Sumud, qui soutient les agriculteurs et les bergers, notamment pendant la récolte des olives. Il est actuellement enfermé au centre de détention militaire de Huwara.

À la veille du vote prévu le 5 novembre 2026 au Parlement fédéral belge sur la question de savoir s’il convient d’autoriser les descentes de police aux domiciles de particuliers à des fins de contrôle de l’immigration, notamment chez des gens pouvant héberger des personnes migrantes en situation irrégulière, Dinushika Dissanayake, directrice régionale adjointe d’Amnesty International pour l’Europe, a déclaré : « Ces propositions, qui autorisent les visites domiciliaires, ne manqueront pas de semer la peur et la division. Le projet de loi soumis au Parlement belge confère à la police des pouvoirs étendus lui permettant de pénétrer dans des logements privés à des fins de contrôle de l’immigration, entre 5 heures du matin et 21 heures, que des enfants soient présents ou non. « Ces visites constitueraient une grave atteinte à la vie privée et familiale, et le projet de loi ne prévoit pas de recours efficaces pour faire appel de ces décisions ou les contester. « La Belgique a une forte tradition de solidarité envers les personnes migrantes : nombreux sont ceux qui ouvrent leurs portes et leurs foyers pour offrir un lit, de la nourriture et du soutien – ce qui est leur droit. Or, cette loi les dissuadera de le faire à l’avenir. « Ces pouvoirs disproportionnés sont un nouvel outil cruel et coercitif visant à créer un environnement de plus en plus hostile pour les personnes migrantes en Europe et pour ceux qui leur témoignent de la solidarité. « Les propositions de la Belgique s’inscrivent tout à fait dans le sillage du Règlement de l’UE en matière de retour et de sa volonté obstinée et malavisée d’intensifier à tout prix les expulsions, les descentes et la détention, ce qui a des conséquences disproportionnées pour les personnes racisées. « Ces mesures punitives vont séparer les communautés et rendre la vie quotidienne plus dangereuse, compliquée et angoissante pour les gens ordinaires. Le Parlement belge doit les rejeter, ainsi que toute manœuvre visant à désigner les migrant·e·s comme boucs émissaires. « À l’heure où le coût de la vie grimpe en flèche et où l’insécurité économique enserre des millions de citoyennes et citoyens à travers le pays, les responsables politiques doivent éviter de détourner l’attention en ciblant l’un des groupes les plus marginalisés de la société. » Contexte Le 5 novembre, le Parlement fédéral de Belgique se prononcera sur une modification de la loi relative à l’accès au territoire, au séjour, à l’établissement et à l’éloignement des étrangers, qui introduit la possibilité de « visites domiciliaires ». Aux termes de ce projet de loi, les fonctionnaires de police peuvent « entrer dans un lieu de résidence d’un étranger, même s’il s’agit du domicile ou du lieu de résidence d’un tiers » à condition de disposer de l’autorisation de visite domiciliaire délivrée par un juge d’instruction sans mettre en œuvre ses pleins pouvoirs d’enquête . Ils prendraient leur décision sur la base de différents critères, notamment si la personne étrangère visée fait l’objet d’une mesure d’expulsion et est considérée comme un danger pour l’ordre public ou la sécurité nationale – un critère qui n’est pas défini dans le texte. Par ailleurs, le projet de loi ne prévoit pas de recours effectif permettant aux personnes concernées, ainsi qu’à celles qui vivent avec elles ou les hébergent, de faire appel de la décision ordonnant la visite domiciliaire ou d’en contester la proportionnalité. La police pourra forcer la porte d’un domicile entre 5 heures du matin et 21 heures et sera habilitée à fouiller le logement à la recherche de documents d’identité. Elle sera autorisée à pénétrer dans le domicile même si des enfants sont présents, sous certaines conditions. Amnesty International Belgique se joint à 36 organisations belges pour manifester devant le Palais de Justice de Bruxelles le 4 novembre à 17 h. Plus de 50 actions décentralisées sont également organisées à travers le pays. Pour en savoir plus, veuillez cliquer ici .

Réagissant à la peine de 10 ans d’emprisonnement prononcée contre le militant hongkongais Joshua Wong pour « collusion avec des forces étrangères », Sarah Brooks, directrice régionale adjointe à Amnesty International, a déclaré : « La persécution de Joshua Wong par les autorités de Hong Kong se poursuit avec cette nouvelle condamnation prononcée au titre de la Loi sur la sécurité nationale, qui intervient impitoyablement – et peut-être délibérément – quelques mois seulement avant qu’il ne soit éligible à une libération pour sa précédente condamnation. « Le courage dont fait preuve Joshua Wong en disant la vérité au pouvoir devrait être salué, mais à Hong Kong, cela fait de lui un criminel. La condamnation prononcée aujourd’hui rappelle tristement, une fois de plus, qu’à Hong Kong, la Loi sur la sécurité nationale est devenue un outil utilisé pour punir la dissidence alors qu’elle devrait servir à réellement protéger la sécurité nationale. « La communauté internationale ne doit pas accepter de voir la criminalisation persistante du militantisme légitime devenir la nouvelle norme à Hong Kong. Les gouvernements doivent continuer de faire pression en faveur de la protection des droits humains et de la libération des personnes emprisonnées uniquement pour avoir exercé leurs droits. « Amnesty International réitère son appel adressé aux autorités de Hong Kong pour qu’elles annulent les condamnations prononcées contre Joshua Wong au titre de la Loi sur la sécurité nationale, et pour qu’elles abrogent toutes les lois qui violent les obligations internationales de Hong Kong en matière de droits humains. » Contexte Joshua Wong a été condamné aujourd’hui, au titre de la Loi sur la sécurité nationale imposée à Hong Kong par Pékin, à 10 ans d’emprisonnement après avoir plaidé coupable de collusion avec des forces étrangères. Dans le cadre de ce deuxième procès pour atteinte à la sécurité nationale, Joshua Wong était accusé d’avoir conspiré avec le militant en exil Nathan Law et « d’autres personnes non identifiées » entre juillet 2020 et novembre 2020 en vue de demander à des pays ou à des organisations étrangers d’imposer des sanctions ou des blocus ou de mener d’autres activités hostiles contre Hong Kong et la Chine. Ce militant de premier plan avait été condamné en 2024, dans le cadre du plus grand procès collectif jamais mené jusqu’à présent au titre de la Loi sur la sécurité nationale, à quatre ans et huit mois d’emprisonnement pour « complot en vue de commettre un acte de subversion ». Il faisait partie des 45 figures de l’opposition emprisonnées pour avoir participé à des « primaires » non officielles en 2020, sur la base d’accusations que des expert·e·s des Nations unies ont jugées liées à des activités pourtant protégées par le droit international relatif aux droits humains. Il allait, en principe, avoir fini de purger cette première peine en janvier 2027. La situation des droits humains à Hong Kong s’est considérablement détériorée depuis 2020 : Amnesty International a recensé plus de 300 arrestations de personnes accusées d’avoir enfreint la Loi sur la sécurité nationale ou une loi sur la « sédition » datant de l’époque coloniale. De plus, les dispositions relatives à l’Article 23 adoptées par les autorités locales en 2024 ont davantage encore aggravé la répression et réduit au silence les voix de l’opposition dans la ville.

Réagissant aux informations indiquant que le Pôle crimes contre l’humanité, crimes et délits de guerre du Tribunal judiciaire de Paris a ouvert, à la suite d’une plainte déposée par l’artiste et cinéaste franco-libanais Ali Cherri et la Fédération internationale pour les droits humains (FIDH), une information judiciaire sur une frappe israélienne meurtrière menée contre un immeuble civil du centre de Beyrouth en novembre 2024, Heba Morayef, directrice régionale pour le Moyen-Orient et l’Afrique du Nord à Amnesty International, a déclaré : L’ouverture de cette information judiciaire par le Pôle crimes contre l’humanité est une étape décisive qui n’a que trop tardé en vue de fissurer le mur d’impunité généralisée dont bénéficient les forces israéliennes pour les crimes de guerre commis au Liban Heba Morayef, Amnesty International « L’ouverture de cette information judiciaire par le Pôle crimes contre l’humanité est une étape décisive qui n’a que trop tardé en vue de fissurer le mur d’impunité généralisée dont bénéficient les forces israéliennes pour les crimes de guerre commis au Liban. « Pour les victimes et leurs familles, cette affaire offre une voie rare et essentielle pour obtenir la vérité, la justice et la reddition de comptes tant attendue par le biais d’une juridiction européenne. « Les recherches d’Amnesty International sur cette frappe ont révélé qu’aucun avertissement préalable efficace n’avait été donné et n’ont identifié aucun élément attestant de la présence d’un objectif militaire à proximité de l’immeuble touché, ce qui permet de conclure que l’attaque doit faire l’objet d’une enquête pour crime de guerre. Depuis octobre 2023, Amnesty International a recueilli des informations sur des attaques illégales répétées des forces israéliennes au Liban, et pourtant, les victimes sont toujours privées de justice, de vérité et de réparations. « Alors que les opérations militaires israéliennes dans le sud du Liban se poursuivent et que des civil·e·s continuent de subir les conséquences du déplacement et de la destruction de biens de caractère civil, les États doivent user de toutes les voies juridiques disponibles, y compris la compétence extraterritoriale, pour veiller à ce que toutes les personnes soupçonnées de porter une responsabilité pénale soient traduites en justice dans le cadre de procès équitables et mettre fin à l’impunité. » Complément d’information La plainte avec constitution de partie civile a été déposée le 1 er avril 2026 devant le Pôle crimes contre l’humanité, crimes et délits de guerre par le cinéaste franco-libanais Ali Cherri, aux côtés de la Fédération internationale pour les droits humains (FIDH), après la frappe du 26 novembre 2024 contre l’immeuble de la famille Cherri dans le quartier de Nouweiri à Beyrouth. L’attaque a tué sept civil·e·s, dont les parents d’Ali Cherri, Nadira Hayek (78 ans) et Mahmoud Naim Cherri (88 ans), et leur aide à domicile Birki Negesa, qui vivait avec eux. L’ enquête de février 2025 d’Amnesty International a démontré que, à 17 h 30 le 26 novembre 2024, soit dix heures et demie avant l’entrée en vigueur d’un cessez-le-feu, une frappe aérienne israélienne avait touché un immeuble d’habitation de 12 étages dans le quartier de Nouweiri, à Beyrouth, tuant au moins sept civil·e·s, qui habitaient tous dans l’immeuble, et avait causé l’effondrement de trois étages de l’immeuble et gravement endommagé un quatrième étage. L’organisation a conclu qu’aucun avertissement préalable efficace n’avait été diffusé et n’a identifié aucun objectif militaire dans les environs de l’immeuble, ce qui fournit des motifs raisonnables de conclure que cette attaque a enfreint le droit international humanitaire et doit faire l’objet d’une enquête en tant que crime de guerre. Ali Cherri a pu déposer plainte devant le Pôle crimes contre l’humanité, crimes et délits de guerre au titre de sa double nationalité franco-libanaise. Compte tenu de cette compétence, les juges d’instruction nommés enquêteront donc sur le bombardement de son appartement à Beyrouth pour des accusations de « lancement d’une attaque délibérée contre un bien civil, constitutif de crime de guerre » d’après le dossier. Au 30 octobre 2026, le ministère de la Santé publique libanais faisait état de 8 956 personnes tuées et 30 664 personnes blessées dans des attaques israéliennes au Liban depuis octobre 2023.

https://skopje.osce.org/news/mission-sko.body: News News Item Essay writing contest Issued on: 7 November 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Skopje The Future of Corruption 2036: Integrity, Good Governance and Accountability Open to: Students attending Bachelor’s and Master’s studies at Ss. Cyril and Methodius University in Skopje, Goce Delcev University – Shtip, University St. Kliment Ohridski Bitola, South East European University, and University American College Skopje. Employees, consultants, or interns of the OSCE and their immediate family members, are not eligible to participate. Submission deadline: 25 November 2026 Awards: The authors of the three best essays will each receive a prize (IT equipment). Background and purpose The OSCE Mission to Skopje aims to advance the rule of law and human rights by implementing applicable international standards and OSCE commitments in the areas of the judiciary and fundamental rights, in line with North Macedonia’s strategic priorities. The Mission addresses challenges related to judicial independence and impartiality, criminal justice, anti-corruption, anti-discrimination, gender equality and fundamental rights, as identified in governmental policy documents and international expert assessments. In parallel with the anti-corruption masterclass series, organized in co-operation with five national universities (University American College Skopje, Ss. Cyril and Methodius University in Skopje, Goce Delcev University – Shtip, University St. Kliment Ohridski Bitola, and South East European University), the OSCE Mission to Skopje has welcomed the strong interest and engagement shown by students. Building on this enthusiasm, the Mission is pleased to announce an essay writing competition that invites students to explore the future of corruption, integrity, good governance and accountability. The competition aims to encourage young people to look beyond current challenges and critically examine how corruption risks, transparency, public trust and governance may evolve over the next decade, under the influence of technological, political, economic and social changes. By introducing a future-oriented perspective, the competition will encourage participants to consider not only how corruption may change by 2036, but also what governments, institutions and citizens can do today to strengthen integrity, accountability and democratic resilience. It will also promote civic awareness, ethical reflection and the active participation of young people in building a more transparent and accountable society. Essay requirements and suggested approach Essays should demonstrate a well-informed understanding of corruption and integrity challenges, combining critical analysis of current developments with a forward-looking perspective. Authors are encouraged to explore plausible future developments, identify emerging risks and opportunities, and propose realistic and evidence-based measures to prevent and address corruption. The central question guiding the competition is: “How might corruption evolve in the future and what can societies do today to build a stronger culture of integrity and accountability?” Participants are encouraged to develop their own arguments and perspectives, supported by credible academic, legal or policy sources. Essays should demonstrate independent thinking, originality and an ability to connect present-day challenges with possible future developments. Authors should ensure that their arguments are convincing, their recommendations are practical, and their essays are written in a clear and well-structured manner. To encourage creativity and innovation, participants may approach the topic through different formats and perspectives, including: Future scenarios: Exploring plausible scenarios for corruption, integrity and accountability in 2036. Narrative essays set in 2036: Imagining how corruption risks and anti-corruption efforts might affect institutions and society in the future. A letter from the future: Writing a letter from 2036 reflecting on the choices made today and their consequences for integrity and accountability. Policy recommendations from a future perspective: Proposing measures that governments, institutions and citizens should adopt today to prevent future corruption. Fictitious newspaper articles or diary entries from the future: Using creative storytelling to examine future governance challenges and possible responses. These formats are suggestions intended to encourage diverse approaches. Regardless of the chosen format, submissions should demonstrate critical thinking, a sound understanding of corruption and integrity issues, and a credible connection between present-day developments and possible futures. Evaluation criteria An evaluation committee consisting of four professors will assess the anonymously submitted essays according to the following criteria: Originality and creativity (maximum 25 points) Understanding of corruption and integrity issues (maximum 25 points) Critical and future-oriented thinking, including the credibility of scenarios and arguments (maximum 25 points) Quality of recommendations and reflections (maximum 25 points) Format and length Essays shall be written in English, using Times New Roman font, size 12, with 1.15 line spacing. The total length should be between 1,400 and 1,600 words (approximately three pages). Essays that exceed this word count will not be considered. Originality and use of AI tools All essays must be the original work of the authors and reflect their own ideas, critical thinking and analysis. Participants may use AI tools to support research, brainstorming, proofreading or language editing, provided that such use does not replace their own intellectual contribution or the independent development of their arguments, scenarios and recommendations. The use of AI tools to generate substantial parts of an essay, or to produce the analysis, arguments or recommendations presented as the author’s own work, is not permitted. Participants must ensure that all factual claims and references are accurate and verifiable, and that all sources are properly acknowledged. Participants must disclose any use of AI tools in a brief statement at the end of their submission, specifying the tools used and the purpose for which they were used. Failure to comply with these requirements, as well as plagiarism or misrepresentation of authorship, may result in disqualification from the competition. Info session For interested students, the OSCE Mission to Skopje will organize an online information session with more precise guidelines on how to prepare a competitive essay, one week before the essay submission deadline. To obtain information on the exact date and time of the session and a Zoom link, please send an email to arben.ajrulai@osce.org and provide your contact information. Application process Instructions for the essay writing competition will also be available in Macedonian and Albanian. Authors shall submit their essays as PDF files to arben.ajrulai@osce.org by 25 November 2026. To support the process of anonymous evaluation, authors should include their full name, surname and the name of their university in the body of the email. Authors must ensure that their names do not appear in the essay document itself. Nothing in or related to this contest shall be construed as a waiver, express or implied, of any of the privileges and immunities of the OSCE.
