https://www.trend.az/azerbaijan/4244032..body: Home Azerbaijan President Ilham Aliyev attends inauguration of Emergency Department of Garabagh University Clinic (PHOTO) Azerbaijan News 7 November 2026 11:06 (UTC +04:00) Photo: Press Service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Nijat Ismiyev Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 7. President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev attended the inauguration of the Emergency Department of Garabagh University Clinic on November 7. The information was confirmed in an official statement released by the Press Service of the President of Azerbaijan. Rector of Garabagh University Shahin Bayramov and General Director of the University Clinic Samir Babayev briefed the head of state on the facilities created at the clinic. In accordance with approved architectural and planning designs, the existing engineering and communication systems were fully reconstructed, enabling the department to operate in accordance with modern standards. Functional zones meeting high medical standards have been established in the emergency department to ensure the efficient reception, examination and treatment of patients. The facility features resuscitation and pediatric units, patient wards, medicine storage areas, and service rooms for supporting daily operations and medical care. Equipping the department with state-of-the-art medical equipment and advanced engineering infrastructure enhances its functional capabilities and operational efficiency. Ambulances equipped for resuscitation and intensive care are also available to transfer patients to other specialized institutions when medically indicated. The clinic currently has 70 inpatient beds, including five intensive care beds. Additionally, 19 beds and five operating rooms are provided in the Emergency Department. Thus, the facility can accommodate 70 inpatients and 19 emergency patients simultaneously. Under the development plan for 2027, between 230 and 250 staff members are expected to be employed at the medical institution. The core mission of the University Clinic is not only to provide medical services but also to develop into a leading medical center integrating modern medical education, clinical practice and scientific research. https://thediplomat.com/2026/10/why-chin.body: Subscribe for ads-free reading China has a huge problem: Chinese people aren’t spending enough money. China today has the lowest consumption rate of any major economy in the world – in fact, its consumption rate is lower than any major economy in the past 100 years. Consumption makes up just about 56 percent of China’s GDP. In most economies, it’s 70 percent or more. To put this in perspective, China’s consumption as a share of GDP is about 10 percentage points lower that Japan’s was in the 1990s, at the worst point in its economic stagnation. Why does low consumption matter? Because it’s a flashing warning sign that China’s economic model is fundamentally broken. That’s why GDP growth is coming to a screeching halt, dropping from highs of 10 percent or more in the early 2000s to under 5 percent today. It’s also why China’s debt is growing to alarming levels. And this is not just a problem for China. Low consumption in China means its people aren’t buying all that much – but China can’t scale back production without mass layoffs. So what does China do with all the extra stuff? It exports more and more abroad, at lower and lower prices. The technical term for that is “dumping” – and countries from Europe to Asia are starting to complain about it. China’s huge excess production is killing manufacturing industries around the world. And all of these problems have the same root cause. Already have an account? Log in . You have reached the limit of 3 free articles this month. https://thediplomat.com/2026/10/will-isl.body: Credit: Depositphotos Subscribe for ads-free reading On October 23, the Central Bank of Uzbekistan (CBU) issued its first license granting official permission to provide Islamic banking services to Open Bank Joint-Stock Company, marking a new page in the country’s attempt to expand financial inclusion. Uzbekistan has been trying to expand access to financial services and bring more money into the formal banking system for years. In 2019, Uzbekistan became a member of the International Islamic Trade and Finance Corporation and the Investment and Export Credit Insurance Islamic Corporation. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, in his 2020 address to the parliament, highlighted the need to introduce Islamic financing. “The time has come to create a legal framework for the introduction of Islamic financial services in our country,” Mirziyoyev said. “Experts from the Islamic Development Bank and other international financial organizations will be involved in this regard.” In a 2023 pre-election meeting with potential voters in Namangan, one of the most populated areas of Uzbekistan historically following a stricter form of Islam, Mirziyoyev even promised to have Islamic financing system operating in Namangan. Although Uzbekistan allowed microfinance organizations to provide Islamic financing from 2022, the CBU only approved regulations governing such services in 2024. That year, the CBU joined the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB). In 2025, Tashkent hosted the 20th International Shariah Scholars Forum in Islamic Finance (ISSF) – the first time the event was held outside Malaysia. Also in 2024, the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis adopted a draft law on introducing Islamic banking activities. In 2026, progress accelerated. In March, Mirziyoyev signed a law that established the legal framework for organizing Islamic banking, including establishing licensing, regulating, and taxing requirements. By mid-July, the CBU established a Islamic Finance Council of five people, including members from the Muslim Board of Uzbekistan. While Tashkent’s ambitions are clear, the economic case rests on two expectations: that people use Islamic financing and savers will place their savings in Islamic investment accounts. Uzbekistan is a Muslim-majority country with a total population exceeding 39 million . The exact number of Muslims is hard to gauge – while both the U.S. Department of State and Human Rights Watch estimate that over 80 percent of the population follow Islam, the Committee on Religious Affairs of Uzbekistan reported that figure to be 94 percent as of 2015. Neither, however, estimates how many Uzbek citizens would prefer Islamic financing, regardless of their faith. In 2023, Bakhrom Nomonov, then chairman of the board of Apex Bank , noted that 20 percent of Uzbek citizens do not take out traditional loans from banks due to their religious beliefs. Therefore, he argued, Islamic financing could attract up to $10 billion a year to the country. A 2020 survey conducted within the framework of the United Nations Development Program on “Analysis of Islamic financial products in Uzbekistan” also indicated religious beliefs as one of the main reasons many Uzbek people not to take out traditional bank loans. The Muslim Board of Uzbekistan , as well as popular imams , all interpret riba – taking an interest-based loan from a bank (locally known as taking a credit) – as a sinful act, while other forms of Islamic financing – such as leasing, and murabaha –are deemed permissible. This, however, does not mean a nationwide strict observation of Islam, including in finance. Many Uzbeks consider Islam a part of their culture. It is something that they are born into and many people simply do not follow every single fatwa or recommendation from an imam. (Uzbekistan is a secular state and the fatwas issued by imams are not binding by law.) The existence of some strict observers is matched by those with more lax approaches. The latest report from the Central Bank shows that as of 2025, 20 percent of adults in the country have an active bank credit account with almost one-third of them having taken 1.7 loans on average. Whether Uzbek citizens take out bank loans or put their savings into investment accounts is not entirely – or even predominantly – a religious question. The availability of halal loans might create more chances, but if Islamic financing costs more than conventional bank loans – when a new product is launched, it usually competes with other similar products in the market – there is no guarantee that the Muslims of Uzbekistan will choose a more expensive halal one. Another obstacle lies with reputation. Inclusion of members from the Muslim Board of Uzbekistan into the CBU’s Islamic Finance Council will increase its credibility among the public as the majority of Muslims in Uzbekistan trust official religious endorsements. However, this also raises the question of who checks these systems for compliance and conducts audits. IMAN invest, a company that offers Islamic investment products, is currently embroiled in a huge scandal. The Islamic Finance Consulting Board (IFCB) terminated its cooperation with the company, with board member Mahmud Usmon alleging misuse of investor funds in violation of Islamic finance principles and a deficit of $20 million in its investment portfolio. The company has disputed the allegation and is trying to restore public trust. This one dispute does not mean that licensed Islamic banks will face the same difficulties or allegations, but the risks remain. It just takes one respected scholar questioning a product’s Islamic compliance to undermine public trust, and without public trust even the devout might shy away from Islamic financing options. Reportedly , more than 10 commercial banks in Uzbekistan are preparing to introduce Islamic finance products. Their success with previously underserved populations is to be seen in the coming years and is subject to competing services and credibility. The number of licenses is an initial indicator of interest, not a guarantee of success. This research was supported by a Marie Curie Staff Exchange within the Horizon Europe Programme (CARSI, no: 101086415) Already have an account? Log in . https://thediplomat.com/2026/11/kazakhst.body: Credit: Pixabay Subscribe for ads-free reading Kazakhstan announced in June 2025 that it would build its first nuclear power plant in partnership with a consortium led by Russia’s Rosatom . Almost immediately afterward, Astana announced that it would build its second with China. As the shape of that project begins to take form, the country’s authorities have set 2035 as the target date for both to be completed. Kazakhstan’s first nuclear power plant is planned for a site near the village of Ulken, in Almaty Region on the shore of Lake Balkhash. The second plant will also be near Balkhash. It’s name, Moyynkum , was revealed earlier this year. Meanwhile, Kazakhstan is considering two locations – either in the east or west of the country – for a third nuclear power plant. This week , Kazakh Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said during a government briefing that “[t]he first Balkhash NPP [nuclear power plant] will be built with the Russian consortium Rosatom, and the second NPP, Moyynkum, is currently being developed with the China National Nuclear Corporation [CNNC].” In late October, during his annual state of the nation speech , Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev iterated his proposal to turn the country into a “big construction site.” This endeavor includes Astana’s nuclear power ambitions. He referred to nuclear power as being of “fundamental importance,” and praised as the “correct decision” the approval of a referendum on the topic in 2024 . That referendum took place under heavy government pressure on critics of nuclear power. Tokayev went on to note that Kazakhstan needs more than just nuclear power plants; it needs to develop a whole host of facilities and human capital. “It is important to engage foreign partners involved in the construction of nuclear power plants, the creation of high-tech production facilities in Kazakhstan, the transfer of nuclear energy expertise, and the training of domestic nuclear specialists,” he said. “Such proposals are being received from Russian and Chinese companies.” Tokayev then said that it was possible, “perhaps necessary,” to begin construction of the Balkhash NPP in 2027 and also to “sign a comprehensive cooperation agreement with the goal of promptly commencing construction of the Moyynkum NPP.” In June, Russian President Vladimir Putin visited the Kazakh capital to plant an oak tree in the “Alley of Eternal Friendship between Kazakhstan and Russia,” and oversee the signing of a dozen agreements , including several related to the nuclear power plant project. Among those agreements was one on the provision of a state export loan from Russia to Kazakhstan to finance the project. While the exact details of Russia’s export loan to Kazakhstan have not been revealed, it was reported that Moscow was furnishing as much as 85 percent of the project’s financing. The Balkhash NPP includes pair of VVER-1200 III+ reactors with a combined capacity of 2.4 GWe. In August 2025 survey work began on the project, the pricetag on which was stated as $14-15 billion at the time. As of June 2026, that figure has grown to around $16.4 billion . Akkenzhenov, the energy minister, said that the details of the second nuclear power plant project are currently under discussion with China’s CNNC. “The parameters of the project are currently being discussed, including the terms of the deal and the timeline. We believe that the projects should be completed by 2035,” he said. That is the timeline Kazakh authorities have cited previously for the Balkhash nuclear power plant – construction starting in 2027 and operations beginning by 2035. For Moyynkum, it seems more of a stretch since there isn’t even a deal settled. Earlier, when Kazakh authorities were considering offers to lead the consortium for the first plant, CNNC had proposed its HPR-1000. Also known as a Hualong One, the HPR-1000 is a generation III+ pressurized water reactor like Rosatom’s VVER-1200 III+ with a similar electrical output. Presumably that’s what’s on offer. Tengrinews reported in April, when the second plant’s name was revealed, “It is expected that the new NPP will consist of two power units with a capacity of 1,200 megawatts each.” As for Kazakhstan’s third nuclear power plant, the chairman of the country’s Atomic Energy Agency, lmassadam Satkaliyev, said on November 2 that Astana is considering a medium-capacity plant of 300 to 600 MW – considerably smaller than the Balkhash plant as announced or the presumable design of the Moyynkum plant. The options for location include the city of Kurchatov in eastern Kazakhstan’s Abai Region or somewhere in western Kazakhstan, which encompasses the regions of Aktobe, Atyrau, Mangystau, and West Kazakhstan. https://thediplomat.com/2026/10/tokayev-.body: Credit: Akorda Subscribe for ads-free reading “Kazakhstan must turn into one big construction site,” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proclaimed in his October 28 national address , proposing that the government dip into the National Fund, to the tune of 6.5 trillion tenge (approximately $14.4 billion at the current exchange rate) to fund projects through 2029. That represents more than 21 percent of the National Fund, a sovereign wealth fund created in 2000 and supplied by tax revenues from oil and gas companies. RFE/RL reported that the fund currently holds around $66.7 billion. Tokayev’s new ambition scraps a previous goal, stated in 2022 in the wake of the Qandy Qantar events as part of his “Fair Kazakhstan” pitch, to increase the National Fund’s assets to $100 billion by 2030. From 2026 through the first two months of 2027, Tokayev said in his recent speech, 1.5 trillion tenge ($3.3 billion) would be allocated for social projects. “I am confident that no one will object if we call this initiative a ‘People’s Construction Project,’” Tokayev said. In his subsequent remarks, he wandered through a smorgasbord of initiatives, mentioning a handful of specific efforts already underway, and spoke more generally about a huge range of ambitions. “Particular focus should be placed on developing logistics infrastructure,” he said. Here Tokayev spoke at length about the importance of logistics – from roads to rail to air transport – in furthering Kazakhstan’s development. Tokayev mentioned the Bakhty-Ayagoz rail line , which runs from Ayagoz in eastern Kazakhstan to the Chinese border and is expected to be completed by the end of 2027. He noted the start of construction in August of the the Aral-Caspian Highway , which “will shorten the route along the Trans-Caspian Corridor by approximately 1,000 kilometers, reducing cargo delivery time to three days.” Tokayev took time to put special emphasis on the quality of roads – a perennial complaint in Kazakhstan – and criticize “executive bodies at the center and locally” who have treated the issue like a football. “They kicked the issue around and did everything possible to drown the problem in an impassable swamp,” Tokayev, who has been president of Kazakhstan since 2019, said. After discussing the importance of developing air corridors – “huge profits are literally flying past our country” – Tokayev shifted to energy. He stated the ambition for Kazakhstan to achieve a “sustainable energy surplus” by 2029, on the back of a full range of energy sources, from “clean coal” to renewables like solar. Nuclear power, he said, is of “fundamental importance,” praising as the “correct decision” the approval of a referendum on the topic in 2024 . That referendum took place under heavy government pressure on critics of nuclear power. Closely related is the hot topic of critical minerals. On that, Tokayev cautioned that “new businesses should not create obstacles for existing businesses in the local area.” He specifically referenced Qarmet, which until 2023 was known as ArcelorMittal Temirtau. That year it was acquired by the the Qazaqstan Investment Corporation. Tokayev obliqued referenced similar production facilities to those operated by Qarmet as being planned in three other regions with the help of presumably foreign investors. “It is obvious that the benefits of such inappropriate decisions are questionable,” he said, without clarifying. “It is obvious that the role of the government in this matter needs to be significantly strengthened.” That may raise red flags for potential investors, as it suggests a heavy government hand in managing the pathways investments take. A 2025 report from the U.S. Department of State on Kazakhstan’s investment climate noted “significant progress,” but also pointed to ongoing restrictions on foreign ownership in certain sectors – notably “a 20 percent ceiling on foreign ownership of media outlets and a 49 percent limit on domestic and international air transportation services” – while also stating that “foreign companies sometimes experience difficulties with licensing, taxation, and legal disputes due to bureaucratic hurdles and inconsistent regulatory enforcement.” Later in his speech, Tokayev pontificated on the necessity of attracting global and domestic companies, once again criticizing “individual departments and individuals” for taking “chaotic and uncoordinated” actions. “Therefore, investment policy management should be concentrated in a single center,” Tokayev said. Centralization has its benefits, but it also concentrates both wealth and risk. The speech went on to touch on subjects as varied as tax policy and education, ending with orders to reform the public administration system. “Civil servants must serve as models of competence,” Tokayev said. “Unfortunately, we are not seeing this yet.” Already have an account? https://thediplomat.com/2026/10/how-woul.body: Credit: Depositphotos Subscribe for ads-free reading On September 12, the University of Hong Kong’s Beijing Center held a low-profile symposium at which Chinese scholars discussed the institutional design and governance arrangements that would follow unification with Taiwan. The participants reached 12 points of consensus on how the “One Country, Two Systems” principle should be implemented in Taiwan. All of Taiwan’s power would derive from authorization by Beijing; Taiwan’s armed forces would be disbanded and People’s Liberation Army (PLA) troops stationed on the island. All this while still upholding the central government’s policy on Taiwan: “peaceful reunification.” The blueprint, however, also accounts for the scenario of achieving “reunification through non-peaceful means,” which would involve a transition period of “quasi-military governance for a duration of three to five years.” The symposium built on Xi Jinping’s 2019 speech marking the 40th anniversary of the “Message to Compatriots in Taiwan,” in which he called for exploring a “Two Systems” solution for Taiwan. The symposium was not an isolated event. Chinese scholars regularly debate and publish on how Beijing should approach unification. This article puts the 12-point consensus in context and compares it with the 2022 white paper “The Taiwan Question and China’s Reunification in the New Era,” to assess how part of China’s scholarly community envisions governing Taiwan after unification, and where that vision departs from the contemporary official line. One Country, Two Systems More than 20 Chinese scholars who participated in the symposium drew on the post-handover experience Beijing has from Hong Kong and Macao, both Special Administrative Regions (SARs) that operate under the principle of “One Country, Two Systems.” Hong Kong was transferred from British to Chinese sovereignty on July 1, 1997, after more than 150 years of British rule following the First Opium War (1839-1842). During the negotiations, Beijing promised Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy and pledged to maintain its capitalist system and way of life unchanged for 50 years. Macao, where Portuguese traders settled in the 1550s, was handed over to Beijing on December 20, 1999, becoming China’s second SAR. The “One Country, Two Systems” principle was initially designed with Taiwan in mind. In September 1981, Ye Jianying, a top military leader and chairman of the National People’s Congress Standing Committee, set out a nine-point proposal for peaceful unification, which became known as “Ye’s Nine Points.” At that point, it was proposed that Taiwan would maintain a “high degree of autonomy” as an SAR. In 1982, Deng Xiaoping, China’s paramount leader after Mao’s death, developed these ideas into the “One Country, Two Systems” formula. The principle was first applied to Hong Kong and later to Macao. The recent symposium attempted to spell out what a Taiwan version would involve. The Symposium Consensus According to the 12-point consensus, the “One Country, Two Systems” principle would be implemented whether the unification came by peacefully or via “non-peaceful means.” In a “non-peaceful” scenario, the scholars envisioned a post-conflict transition period of “quasi-military governance,” which could be implemented for a duration of three to five years, during which the central government would crack down on “Taiwan independence elements,” or (in Beijing’s terminology ) “Taiwan independence separatists.” China uses the term to refer to anyone who advocates or promotes the de jure independence of Taiwan. The symposium’s direct discussion of the use of force against Taiwan – and what would follow – is an outlier. “Peaceful reunification” remains Beijing’s official discursive approach to Taiwan, reflected in many official documents of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Force is left as a last resort aimed at external interference and a “very small number of separatists,” as stated in the 2022 white paper. The possibility of a military conflict across the Taiwan Strait is widely regarded as one of the most serious geopolitical flashpoints today. In the last decade, China has been steadily intensifying military pressure on Taiwan through a combination of large-scale military exercises and gray-zone operations around the island. However, many analysts argue that a large-scale military conflict across the Taiwan Strait – particularly if the United States, Japan, or other regional actors were drawn in – would carry serious risks for the CCP’s primary goal: maintaining its monopoly on political power and ensuring the regime’s survival. As a professor at MIT and China researcher M. Taylor Fravel argued , China is even more aware of such a risk since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Following the “reunification,” all existing Taiwanese armed forces would be disbanded, their weapons “collected and turned over” to the central government, and the island’s defense would become Beijing’s responsibility. The central government would station troops in Taiwan, following the practice in Hong Kong and Macao, where PLA garrisons have been present since 1997 and 1999, respectively. The 2022 white paper did not mention anything about the future of Taiwan’s military, but the 1993 white paper on “reunification” stated that Taiwan would keep its own military and the mainland would not send troops or administrative personnel to Taiwan. According to the symposium’s 12-point plan, Taiwanese people would also be allowed to voluntarily enlist in the PLA. The PLA is the armed force of the CCP, which commands it through the Central Military Commission, chaired by Xi Jinping, following the principle that “the party commands the gun.” Taiwan’s armed forces, by contrast, are constitutionally required to stand above party affiliation, as stated in Article 138 of the Constitution of the Republic of China (ROC). Matters of security, defense, and foreign affairs involving Taiwan are expected to be the sole responsibility of the central government in Beijing following unification. In terms of law, the Chinese scholars proposed a “de-nationalization” and “de-centralization” of the old legal system, transferring the whole body of law to the SAR regulations. They called for ensuring that “patriots govern Taiwan,” while the existing political parties could be retained under the new constitution. This diverges from the 2022 white paper, which was silent on this topic. Taiwan is a fully functioning democracy with a pluralistic, multiparty electoral system. Since the democratization in the 1990s, the two dominant parties at the national level have been the Kuomintang (KMT) and the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), both holding the presidency and controlling parliament at different times. The KMT generally favors closer cross-strait relations and engagement with China, while the DPP generally emphasizes Taiwan’s distinct identity and supports maintaining Taiwan’s de facto independence and autonomy, while officially calling for the preservation of the status quo in the Taiwan Strait. China, on the other hand, is a one-party state with the leadership of the Communist Party embedded in the PRC Constitution . Alongside the CCP, however, exist eight other legally recognized political parties, all of which accept the CCP’s leadership. While China holds no elections these parties can contest, they participate in the state advisory body, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference. The 12-point consensus also covers a complete reorganization of Taiwan’s administrative divisions and electoral system. The scholars also called for a thorough reform of Taiwanese textbooks to align with the “patriotic and national” education of China. Post-unification, Taiwan and the mainland are expected to undergo deeper economic integration. Commerce and cultural ties would continue as usual. Credit: Oliver Fisk Subscribe for ads-free reading Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang had an unmistakable air of confidence about him on October 23 as he took to the stage in Astana, Kazakhstan, before an eager audience of business executives, tech workers, political figures, and journalists. In a nearly hour-long fireside chat with Kazakhstan’s Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev, Huang waxed effusive about the “incredibly visionary” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, praising his foresight in declaring AI development to be a “national priority.” After Madiyev announced that Nvidia had invested an undisclosed sum in Higgsfield, an AI video-generation company that became Kazakhstan’s first unicorn in September 2025, Huang also heaped praise on the startup and its founders. But above all, the microchip engineer-turned-billionaire executive was most bullish in describing the upward trajectory of the global AI industry and Kazakhstan’s potential to position itself at its center. “Kazakhstan has a fundamental advantage because you have so many natural resources already. Instead of just exporting energy in the future, you could transform this energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” Huang said. “You’re going to be a hub, a computing hub, an AI factory hub for all of Europe.” On one level, Huang’s visit to Kazakhstan was just the latest stop on the barnstorming world tour the Nvidia boss first began in 2024 to sell the idea of “sovereign AI” to national leaders and statesmen. But at another, it marked a meeting of minds and ambitions. The venerable chipmaker seeking to extend the global reach of its technology by powering next-generation data centers meets a resource-rich country hoping to turn its energy reserves into a competitive advantage in the AI economy. It’s a match made in heaven – or so it would seem. Beyond this storybook partnership, however, lie significant challenges. Kazakhstan’s far-reaching AI plans call for billions of dollars in investment, expanded computing infrastructure, and a shift from supplying raw materials to producing higher-value digital services. But experts say building and operating energy-intensive data centers will require not just abundant natural resources, but also a reliable electricity supply, the infrastructure to deliver it, and customers willing to pay for faraway computing capacity. Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at a crowded alem.ai, Kazakhstan’s new “artificial intelligence center.” Photo by Oliver Fisk. Coded in the Stars For Nvidia, Kazakhstan is in some ways the ideal case study for its “Sovereign AI” strategy , which encourages governments to build domestic AI ecosystems around data centers, homegrown LLMs and local AI entrepreneurs, all powered by Nvidia chips. Thanks in part to pitches like the one delivered by Huang in Astana, the strategy is quietly flourishing. In February, Nvidia’s chief financial officer said sovereign AI revenue had more than tripled to over $30 billion, and industry estimates suggest the company’s hardware underpins the overwhelming majority of sovereign AI language models. But few countries have embraced Nvidia’s vision as fully as Kazakhstan. Since Tokayev pledged in 2025 to make the country a “fully digital nation” within three years, Astana has created an AI ministry, enrolled more than 650,000 students in AI training, and passed a comprehensive AI law, which entered force in 2026 amid the government’s “Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence.” This convergence was on full display in Astana last week, as Huang approvingly noted that Kazakhstan was “the first country that I’ve been to where the president declared the country to be an AI nation.” Madiyev, for his part, framed the government’s strategy in Nvidia’s terms, calling Huang’s “five-layer cake” AI economic model “the main pillar” of Kazakhstan’s digital strategy, and pitching the country’s mines and factories as a testing ground for Nvidia’s advancements in “physical AI.” The more substantive partnership between the two, however, centers around the planned Data Center Valley in Ekibastuz, in northeastern Kazakhstan. There, beside the coal-fired Ekibastuz GRES-1, the country’s largest power plant, the government broke ground in January on Data Center Valley, a campus it hopes will eventually reach one gigawatt worth of computing capacity. (It was this project Huang had in mind when he called Kazakhstan a future “AI factory hub for all of Europe.”) In June, Astana announced a $10 billion package of agreements with Firebird, a U.S. cloud operator, and state-owned Kazakhtelecom to develop the site using Nvidia technology. Under the arrangement, Kazakhtelecom will provide power, cooling, and telecommunications infrastructure, while Firebird is set to finance the computing hardware. More details about this investment became public last week, when Firebird signed an investment agreement with the government at the Akorda presidential palace, according to which the Data Center Valley site will be primarily used to generate computing power for international clients, with 10 percent of Firebird’s total GPU capacity to be allocated to Kazakhstani companies and government agencies. Under the agreement, the site will be powered by 45,000 high-end Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs, for which U.S. export licenses were announced last week. For some experts, like Dr. Rustem Bigari, an AI and digital governance expert, this collaboration’s mutual appeal is apparent. According to Bigari, Kazakhstan can offer globally competitive electricity prices, while data centers across the country are running low on capacity, meaning additional computing power is needed to fulfill the country’s AI ambitions, including developing Kazakh-language language models. “We are offering the basic foundations that Nvidia needs,” Bigari told The Diplomat, adding that further investment in computing power would help Kazakhstan “become the main AI and cloud computing hub in the whole region.” Similarly, Asad Bokhari, an assistant professor at Nazarbayev University’s Graduate School of Public Policy, sees Nvidia’s arrival as vindication of the government’s broader digitalization campaign , and a signal that Amazon, Microsoft or Google “may also follow in its footsteps” by investing in the country. “If the government of Kazakhstan was not prepared, all of the country’s resources would be useless for Nvidia’s data center plans,” Bokhari said, crediting the government’s institutional readiness. “But it is, so it’s a win-win for both sides.” Critical Error! But not everyone in the expert community was so impressed by Astana’s Nvidia-themed festivities last weekend. “We looked at Jensen’s visit as basically just PR and marketing,” said Marat Beksultanov, a New York-based geospatial consultant who has studied the Data Center Valley project. “We weren’t expecting any breakthrough announcements.” An attempt by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to take an impromptu selfie led to event attendees rushing the stage in an excited frenzy. Photo by Oliver Fisk. This is significant because, according to Beksultanov, the most important questions about the Data Center Valley remain unanswered. “There’s actually two extremely big issues,” Beksultanov told The Diplomat. “One is power, and then the other one is customers.” Since 2023, Kazakhstan has consumed more electricity than it generated each year, typically making up the shortfall by importing power from Russia. Last winter, during a record peak, national grid operator KEGOC reported that the country had no spare generating capacity, leading to nearly 1,000 megawatts having to be imported on December 27. The government had previously expected to achieve a modest power surplus by 2027. But the Data Center Valley’s first phase alone would see it consume more electricity at full capacity than that entire increased figure

https://thediplomat.com/2026/10/what-tok.body: Credit: Facebook / Aqorda Subscribe for ads-free reading For Kazakhstan, a country linking China and Europe while sharing a long border with Russia, infrastructure is never entirely a domestic matter. Railways determine how goods move across Eurasia, electricity supplies shape industrial investment, and the ability to process minerals affects the country’s place in international supply chains. These connections offer a useful way to read President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s October 28 State of the Nation address , which was mostly about economic development but had also important implications for foreign relations. Tokayev began by warning of deepening mistrust among major powers and a more unpredictable international environment. Rather than proposing a new diplomatic alignment, he emphasized a stronger economy, modern infrastructure, technology, and effective institutions. For Kazakhstan’s longstanding balanced and multivector foreign policy, the underlying logic is that domestic capacity can widen the scope for cooperation with different partners at the same time. The most visible proposal was the nationwide “People’s Construction” program, backed by 6.5 trillion tenge (approximately $14 billion) from the National Fund through 2029, including 1.5 trillion tenge earmarked for early social projects. Roads, utilities, housing, and public facilities are central to the plan. Tokayev also proposed a higher minimum wage and new healthcare facilities. These measures principally address domestic needs, but more reliable services and regional infrastructure can also reduce costs for investors and make industrial projects more viable outside the largest cities. The president’s insistence that public spending mobilize private capital, rather than substitute for it, gives the initiative an international dimension. The clearest connection between domestic investment and foreign relations is transport. Tokayev said the Bakhty-Ayagoz railway should enter service in 2027, adding 20 million tons of capacity on routes toward China. Construction has also begun on an Aral-Caspian corridor intended to shorten the Trans-Caspian route by roughly 1,000 kilometers. Both projects respond to an established demand for more dependable links between Asian production centers and European markets. In February, the World Bank approved an $846 million guarantee designed to mobilize $1.41 billion in commercial financing for Kazakhstan’s rail network along the Middle Corridor. The geopolitical value of these routes lies in their usefulness to multiple economies. China gains additional westward capacity, European businesses gain another option for moving goods, and Kazakhstan can expand its role in services surrounding that trade. Tokayev’s call for freight consolidation centers, logistics operators, and factories near transport junctions suggests an ambition to capture value beyond transit fees. Yet the route’s performance will depend not only on Kazakh construction but also on ports, customs procedures and coordination with Azerbaijan, Georgia, and other corridor partners. Greater connectivity is a regional undertaking, not simply a national project. The same logic applies to data. On October 15, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan inaugurated a 380-kilometer fiber-optic link beneath the Caspian Sea, designed to carry information between Central Asia and Europe. Mentioned again in the address, the cable shows how physical and digital connectivity can reinforce one another. Reliable cross-border data links matter to cloud services, financial transactions, and the data centers Kazakhstan wants to attract. China’s role is notable in other spheres too. At a September China-Kazakhstan investment forum, Tokayev described a portfolio of 260 joint industrial projects valued at more than $62 billion, spanning manufacturing, metallurgy, agriculture, and energy storage. Its composition indicates how the relationship is developing from commodity trade and transport toward local production and technology. The address’s emphasis on manufacturing capacity and domestic suppliers is consistent with this direction. Energy provides a second intersection between internal requirements and external partnerships. Kazakhstan generates about 123 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually but still faces shortages. Tokayev set a goal of achieving a sustained surplus by 2029 through new generation, modernized grids and a broader mix of energy sources. Russia is an established partner in this sector. During President Vladimir Putin’s May visit, the two countries signed a nuclear power agreement and arrangements for Russian export-credit financing. Chinese companies have also proposed nuclear cooperation, including technology transfer and specialist training, as Tokayev noted in the address. These projects are significant because a nuclear partnership can encompass engineering, fuel services, training and maintenance over decades. They should not, however, be mistaken for an immediate solution to the 2029 electricity target: the first planned reactor is not expected to begin operating before the following decade. In the nearer term, grid upgrades and other generation projects will remain decisive. For Kazakhstan’s partners, a more dependable power system would also improve the prospects for energy-intensive manufacturing, mineral processing and computing infrastructure. Critical minerals offer another area in which domestic reforms can produce international effects. Tokayev called for modern geological exploration, better access to geological data, long-term financing and offtake arrangements, alongside consideration of a dedicated mechanism for nonferrous and rare-earth metals. The objective is to develop processing and other parts of industrial value chains. This meets interests expressed by both Western and Asian partners, although turning resource potential into competitive production will require technology, investment and skills. During Tokayev’s June visit to Brussels , EU leaders identified critical raw materials, energy, transport and digitalization as priorities for expanded cooperation. As Kazakhstan’s largest trading and investment partner, the EU has a particularly strong interest in the development of these sectors. The United States and Kazakhstan have also agreed to cooperate on mineral supply chains, including a proposed American-backed tungsten mining and processing project. These relationships have distinct commercial purposes, but each could support Kazakhstan’s stated goal of producing more value domestically. They complement its established energy and industrial ties with Russia and China rather than necessarily displacing them. Technology is becoming a further point of international engagement. The address highlighted two operating supercomputers, another planned before year’s end, and efforts to apply artificial intelligence to agriculture, industry and public services. In June, Kazakhstan joined the U.S.-backed Pax Silica initiative and signed an AI Opportunity Partnership statement, connecting cooperation on computing, semiconductors, energy, critical minerals and research. On October 23, Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang visited Astana and met Tokayev. Nvidia’s own account of the visit described planned computing investments and potential applications in mining, agriculture and industrial automation. These developments give the digital agenda a tangible international dimension, although the economic benefits will depend on adoption by ordinary businesses as much as high-profile infrastructure. The final link is institutional. Tokayev acknowledged weaknesses in investment coordination and proposed a larger role for the Baiterek development holding, a new civil code, adjustments to tax rules and an English common law-based investment court in Alatau. Credit: Shutterstock Subscribe for ads-free reading What would Japanese youngsters respond when asked about Chinese culture? Chances are that they will point to the neon-lit streets of Yokohama Chinatown, the culinary tradition that invented gyoza and mapo tofu, and perhaps something they overheard from friends, classmates, and coworkers who are part of the 900,000 -strong Chinese diaspora in Japan. But what about Genshin Impact, the role-playing video game created by Shanghai-based miHoYo ? It certainly is wildly popular. After launching in 2020, it earned $10 billion in revenue by the end of 2025, becoming the fastest mobile game ever to reach that milestone. In Japan, it was ranked first in popularity as late as 2024, and remains within the top 20 for new downloads, more than six years after launch. While created by a Chinese firm, Genshin Impact draws heavily from Japanese pop culture. Its graphics use the typical nijigen visuals perfected through the country’s anime and manga industries, while the gameplay features gacha mechanics of obtaining mystery items, so culturally rooted in Japan’s gachapon capsule toy vending machines. MiHoYo, branded internationally as Cognosphere, had been publishing games for China’s otaku community since its founding in 2011. The co-founders stated that their inspiration for creating games came from personal love for Japanese anime and technology. However, their business has expanded far beyond those roots. Only 5 percent of Genshin’s total downloads come from Japan despite the game’s popularity in the country. And as miHoYo increasingly expands globally, its games now mix Japanese, Chinese, and Western elements to attract a more diverse audience, as the transnational visuals of its successful Honkai series attest. Translating Japanese cultural vocabulary for the global audience has become a source of success for other Chinese firms too. Toymaker PopMart manufactured a global fad for its Labubu dolls by applying that same gacha mechanics to its blind boxes, compelling fans to buy more to chase those rare varieties. Consumer goods retailer Miniso – much derided in Japan as “(Daiso + Muji) / 2” – has become an international promoter of Japanese characters such as Chiikawa and Hello Kitty through licensing agreements. Notably, Miniso has more than 8,000 stores in 110 countries. With Japanese firms largely absent from large swathes of Africa and South America, Chinese firms have become the first point of contact local consumers have with Japanese aesthetics. Now, these Chinese firms are ready to sell Japanese culture back to Japan. If miHoYo’s success in Japan through Genshin was accidental, the next wave of Japanified Chinese products will be anything but. Following PopMart’s entry into the Japanese market in 2022 , Miniso-owned toymaker TopToy entered Japan in 2025 using the same formula. Mellojoy, leveraging Japan’s love for punipuni , engineered a craze among young Japanese women for its own handmade squishies. Even Miniso itself is making a return to Japan through a pop-up shop in collaboration with renowned idol Lisa. Japanese firms will now be in an unusual situation of competing for Japanese consumers in products they have long believed to be idiosyncratically Japanese. The case of the BYD Racco is illustrative. The Chinese electric vehicle giant became the first foreign company to ever launch a dedicated Japanese kei car, a class of ultra-compact cars found only in Japan. Japanese carmakers long considered the kei class to have a technological, cultural, and regulatory moat deep enough to deter foreigners. After the Racco sold more than 1,000 two weeks after its launch, domestic rivals were driven out of their complacency and compelled to respond. Suzuki’s recent launch of the e SKY, an electric kei car using BYD-made batteries, will surely ignite more competition in the previously insular market. As that competition heats up, Japanese firms may come to discover that consumers no longer really care what it means for a product to be culturally Japanese. A coordinated effort to promote the country abroad through the Cool Japan Fund’s investments in media and retail proved a costly failure , while Miniso plans 900-1,000 new stores every year and BYD is readying the Racco for the international market. As Genshin Impact showed us, people are interested in a Japanese aesthetic that anyone can access affordably. Credit: Russian Presidential Press and Information Service Subscribe for ads-free reading North Korean support for Russia’s war against Ukraine has not materialized in the way Kyiv had originally predicted this past summer. In August, Ukrainian intelligence assessed that the Kremlin had requested upwards of 30,000 more troops to support an autumn offensive. Kyiv also announced that Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong Un would meet sometime in September . It is now November, but no Russia-North Korea summit has taken place, and while there have been reports of additional North Korean troop deployments to Russia, there is no indication that tens of thousands more combat troops have moved from the Korean Peninsula to the front lines in Eastern Europe. So, what happened, and where does North Korea’s involvement in the war stand today? Answering these questions requires revisiting the successive phases of North Korean support to understand how its role has evolved and where it might be headed. Recapping North Korea’s Wartime Support The Russia-North Korea relationship has a checkered past. Although the two countries’ trajectories have been intertwined since the end of World War II, their relationship has not always been cooperative. Thus, when the Kremlin launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the level of North Korean support that has emerged over the past four-and-a-half years was not a given. In fact, North Korea’s response to Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014 was one of quiet diplomatic backing. Pyongyang avoided publicized statements of support, but still accepted the Kremlin’s territorial ambitions. Russian media reported that North Korea’s ambassador to Moscow conveyed his government’s backing on March 15, 2014. The following week, North Korea voted against United Nations General Assembly Resolution 68/262 , which affirmed Ukraine’s territorial integrity and rejected the legitimacy of Russia’s annexation. Since then, North Korea has published atlases displaying Crimea as part of Russian territory. At the outset of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Pyongyang’s response appeared to follow the same pattern of diplomatic support. In March 2022, North Korea was one of only five countries to vote against U.N. General Assembly Resolution ES-11/1 , which condemned Russia’s invasion. It subsequently aligned its voting with Moscow on a series of related resolutions. In July 2022, Pyongyang recognized the independence of the Russian-backed “People’s Republic of Donetsk” and the “People’s Republic of Lugansk,” and expressed support for Russia’s annexation of the occupied Ukrainian territories that October. North Korean support, however, took an important turn in the autumn of 2022. Russian forces were running short of munitions , leaving their positions vulnerable as Ukraine mounted a series of successful counteroffensives . This created an opportunity for North Korea to contribute to the war beyond diplomatic backing. Pyongyang’s extensive stockpiles of Soviet-era munitions offered Moscow a solution to its ammunition shortages. In November 2022, the U.S. National Security Council released the first concrete intelligence indicating that North Korea was supplying military materiel to Russia. This marked the first instance during the war in which Pyongyang’s increased support played an indispensable role in extending the conflict. By providing critical munitions, North Korea enabled Russian forces to blunt the Ukrainian counteroffensive that had up to that point been proving successful. Materiel support continued throughout 2023 as the Kim regime took steps to deepen its relationship with the Kremlin. The September 2023 summit between Putin and Kim at the Vostochny Cosmodrome accelerated these efforts, eventually setting the stage for the signing of their Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership during Putin’s reciprocal visit to Pyongyang in June 2024. The formalization of their revitalized alliance arrangements provided the foundation for the next major evolution of North Korean support: direct military involvement in the campaign to retake Kursk. In August 2024, Ukrainian forces crossed the Russian border into Kursk Oblast , advancing toward Sudzha and Korenovo. By October, the Ukrainian government had publicly disclosed intelligence that Russia was preparing to employ North Korean military personnel. Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate, part of the Ministry of Defense, assessed that North Korea was preparing to send as many as 12,000 personnel to Russia’s Kursk region. The U.S. Department of Defense subsequently confirmed that at least 10,000 North Korean soldiers were present to participate in the campaign. This marked the second instance in which the escalation of North Korean support helped the Kremlin extend its war effort. By helping Russia expel Ukrainian forces from Kursk, Pyongyang enabled the Kremlin to eliminate an important bargaining chip for Kyiv in ceasefire negotiations. Ukrainian control of Russian territory could have provided leverage in negotiations over reciprocal withdrawals, where the tradeoff would have been Russian forces leaving occupied parts of the Donbas region in exchange for Ukrainian withdrawal from Kursk. Following the expulsion of Ukrainian forces, North Korea continued providing materiel, labor, and other forms of assistance, with both Pyongyang and Moscow lauding the strength of their alliance. The question, however, was what might come next as the Kremlin sought to consolidate its gains and push Ukrainian forces completely out of their remaining footholds in the Donbas region. Where Things Stand Today Heading into autumn 2026, Kyiv assessed that the Kremlin had once again requested a surge of North Korean soldiers to support a forthcoming offensive. However, troop deployments of that magnitude have not occurred, and neither the Kremlin nor Pyongyang has given clear indications of their current or future designs for North Korean participation in Russia’s war effort. There are four potential explanations here. First, Ukraine’s assessment may have been based on faulty intelligence. The indications and warnings suggesting that the Kremlin was seeking so many additional North Korean forces may have been inaccurate or exaggerated, potentially reflecting shortcomings in human intelligence sources. Second, Kyiv may have assessed the most dangerous course of action as the most likely one. In other words, there may have been more indicators suggesting that Pyongyang would not surge forces, but Ukraine focused on the comparatively fewer signs pointing to a major new deployment. Whether deliberate or unintentional, such an assessment was more likely to draw attention to the potential scale of North Korean involvement and the risks it posed. Third, the Kremlin may have withdrawn its request. Putin could have reconsidered the merits of a major autumn offensive, whether because of political calculations involving the White House and the U.S. midterm elections or because Russia lacked the capacity to mobilize enough domestic forces to make a North Korean surge consequential on the battlefield. Finally, Pyongyang may have declined the Kremlin’s request. While the Kim regime was comfortable overtly deploying troops in support of Russia’s campaign to retake Kursk within Russia’s prewar borders, it has not committed North Korean combat forces en masse to the front lines in occupied Ukrainian territories. This may represent a political red line, meaning that if the Kremlin asked for North Korean soldiers to participate in forward operations aimed at capturing the remainder of Donetsk, Pyongyang may simply have refused. Rather than a mass deployment of troops, Ukraine has reported other forms of North Korean military involvement. Thes

https://thediplomat.com/2026/11/the-taip.body: Credit: Depositphotos Subscribe for ads-free reading In October, well-known Taiwanese television host Kevin Tsai, popular on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, was spotted by the media attending a campaign event for Puma Shen, a legislator running for mayor of Taipei. Given Tsai’s popularity in China, his appearance quickly sparked criticism. The incumbent Taipei mayor, Chiang Wan-an, helped defuse the controversy by inviting Tsai to the opening of his own campaign headquarters. Three weeks after attending Shen’s campaign event, Tsai publicly stated that he had never supported Taiwanese independence and that his work required him to interact with people holding a range of political views. The following day, he attended Chiang’s campaign event. If attending a rally is tantamount to declaring one’s support for Taiwan’s future, imagine what will be made of the November 28 vote. Shen, the candidate of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), has spent years studying Chinese influence operations and promoting civilian preparedness in Taiwan. Chinese authorities have opened an investigation into him on allegations of secession. Chiang, the Kuomintang (KMT) incumbent, has maintained an open channel of communication between officials in Taipei and Shanghai. Beijing and Washington may be tempted to interpret a Shen victory as a vote for independence or a Chiang victory as a turn toward China. Either interpretation, however, would link a municipal election to an issue that Taipei’s voters have not been asked to vote on. Consider an exchange during the October 31 debate between Shen and Chiang. Chiang challenged Shen to explain why two redevelopment projects, one in Datong and the other in Neihu, had stalled. Chiang attributed the delays to restrictions on building heights near Taipei’s Songshan Airport. Shen fired back with a question of his own: If city officials knew about these restrictions, why hadn’t they explained them to residents from the outset? Chiang used the exchange to question his challenger’s command of city affairs. Shen, in turn, used it to ask what good that expertise did residents if they learned about an obstacle too late to do anything about it. The most important takeaway from their heated exchanges, however, is not what the candidates said, but what they left unsaid. China, the elephant in the room when it comes to cross-strait relations, was not raised even once as a key issue during the two-hour debate. That encapsulates the kind of local issues Taipei voters will actually base their decision on. Some might vote for Chiang, crediting him with moving other difficult projects forward, including one at Nanjichang Night Market. Others might favor Shen’s proposal to screen older buildings for earthquake risks and to help residents arrange repairs. Two homeowners could vote for different candidates – while holding precisely the same views about China. The election night count offers no way to tell. Taipei’s recent electoral history illustrates the limits of interpreting local elections through the lens of national politics – and vice versa. In 2022, the city elected Chiang as mayor. Just over a year later, in the presidential election, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te carried Taipei, edging out the KMT’s Hou Yu-ih by just 641 votes. Chiang’s mayoral victory would therefore have been a poor guide to the city’s presidential preferences. There is even less reason to interpret a vote in the capital as evidence of a broader change of heart across Taiwan for or against a political party – or that party’s approach to China. True, the result will shape national politics. Winning Taipei would give Shen a larger audience for his work on civilian defense. A second term would give Chiang greater standing within the KMT to make the case for engagement with Shanghai, and possibly Beijing. Plus, the Taipei mayorship has in the past served as a launching pad for presidential ambitions. Winning office gives a politician the chance to advance causes that may have had little to do with why voters chose him. The election’s outcome could certainly also influence cross-strait relations. During Chiang’s tenure, the Taipei–Shanghai Twin-City Forum has kept officials from the two cities in contact. A Chiang victory would give him another term to pursue those exchanges. A Shen victory would test the conditions under which they can continue. Although Shen has criticized the forum’s value, he has said he would attend if it offered practical benefits and came without political preconditions. On October 14, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office dismissed his offer, citing his alleged support for independence. Suppose Shen wins, repeats his offer, and finds Shanghai unwilling to meet with him. Concluding that Taipei voters chose to sever contact would erase Beijing’s role in the decision. The reverse inference – that vote for Chiang implies approval of his engagement with Chinese officials – would be equally questionable. A Taipei resident might value Chiang’s ability to keep municipal officials talking while still opposing closer political ties. Wanting the conversation with Shanghai to continue is entirely compatible with wanting Beijing to have less say in Taiwan’s affairs. Local governance is undoubtedly important for the stability of the Taiwan Strait. Taipei’s city government, for example, helps residents prepare for an air raid, down to practicing how to reach shelter when the sirens sound. How well the city carries out that work matters regardless of which party holds power. Still, it’s not going to be an issue that is top of mind when Taipei residents fill out their ballots. On November 28, Taipei’s voters will choose who takes responsibility for the safety of their homes, the city’s readiness for an emergency, and its dealings with Shanghai. Beijing and Washington have good reason to pay close attention to what the next mayor does with that authority. But anyone claiming a mandate for independence or unification is looking for evidence the mayoral count cannot provide. Already have an account? Log in . https://novastan.org/fr/kazakhstan/kazak.body: 29 octobre 2026 Rédigé par : La rédaction Traduit par : scombaret Vlast Tags Almaty Janvier 2022 Justice Manifestation Procès Société Traduction Le procès d'un militaire ayant tué par balle deux civils lors des événements de Janvier 2022 au Kazakhstan. Photo : Vlast. Dans la nuit du 6 au 7 janvier 2022, lors des évènements de Janvier à Almaty, Erlan Jaguiparov meurt des suites d’une blessure par balle. Lui et Aouèz Kaspalanov ont été abattus par un militaire. Le média kazakh Vlast raconte trois mois de processus judiciaire. Erlan Jaguiparov, ouvrier du bâtiment, a toujours rêvé de devenir archéologue. Mais ce n’est que quelques années avant sa mort qu’il a commencé à partir en expédition avec l’association « Les chasseurs de pétroglyphes « . L’expérience d’Erlan Jaguiparov dans le secteur de la construction aide l’équipe d’archéologues à relever des défis complexes en matière de recherche et de conservation du patrimoine culturel ancien. C’est lui notamment qui a permis d’extraire une statue en pierre de guerrier turc de 800 kilos, aujourd’hui conservée au musée historique et culturel d’Etat Ecik. Au moment des évènements de Janvier 2022 , les « chasseurs » essaient de conserver le lien entre eux. Chacun prévient les autres de l’endroit où il se trouve. Les membres s’inquiétaient surtout pour ceux qui vivaient dans le centre d’Almaty, où se déroulaient les évènements les plus terribles. Soutenez Novastan, le média associatif d’Asie centrale En vous abonnant à Novastan, vous soutenez le seul média européen spécialisé sur l’Asie centrale. Nous sommes indépendants et pour le rester, nous avons besoin de votre aide ! A partir de 3 € / mois Toute l’actualité d’Asie centrale Abonnez-vous Le 5 janvier, l’état d’urgence est déclaré à Almaty. Depuis la soirée du 4 janvier, des manifestations de soutien à la ville de Janaozen et contre l’élévation du prix du gaz ont lieu. Pendant ce temps, Erlan Jaguiparov se trouve dans sa datcha à Kamenké. Ce n’est que le 6 janvier qu’il se rend en ville, autour de 16 heures, pour se diriger vers la maison de son ami Askar Ouvaliev, qui vivait dans la partie Sud d’Almaty, avant de rendre visite à sa mère malade, qui vivait dans un petit quartier adjacent à la place de la République. Autour de 19 heures, Erlan Jaguiparov part de chez son ami. Plus d’une heure plus tard, c’est un militaire qui répond à son téléphone ; les cris derrière lui laissent penser qu’un homme est en train d’être battu. Puis plus personne ne répond. Dans les jours suivants, il est recherché par ses proches sur les réseaux sociaux, et ce n’est que le 12 janvier que son corps est découvert à la morgue , des menottes à une main. Le début du procès Le 18 décembre 2024, près de trois ans après la mort d’Erlan Jaguiparov, 39 ans, et d’Aouèz Kapsalanov, 35 ans, des suites de blessures par balle, commençait le procès de l’affaire au tribunal militaire de la garnison d’Almaty. Sur le banc des accusés, Aïtchan Aoubakirov, 42 ans, commandant-adjoint des activités éducatives et socio-juridiques de l’unité militaire 5 571 de la Garde nationale, accusé d‘abus de pouvoir en vertu de l’article 451 alinéa 2 du code pénal. L’affaire a été traitée avec lenteur et n’a pas pu être remise au tribunal pendant longtemps, jusqu’à ce que les efforts des proches des victimes ne paient, bien qu’ils ne soient pas d’accord avec la qualification retenue. L’avocate de la famille estime que le meurtre aurait dû être retenu. Askar Ouvaliev, ami d’Erlan Jaguiparov. Photo : Vlast. Ce procès devait être l’un des rares en lien avec des militaires accusés de tirs sur des citoyens qui serait ouvert au public. D’autres procès analogues se sont déroulés à huis clos, et dans beaucoup d’autres cas, les procès ont même été interrompus . Mais au bout de trois auditions, le tribunal a refusé de donner accès à la salle aux journalistes. L’arrestation Selon l’accusation, le 6 janvier, Aïtchan Aoubakirov, avec le deuxième bataillon opérationnel, se trouvait sur le côté Nord-Ouest de la place de la République. Selon le procureur Yeljan Kobeï, de 19h30 à 20h00, sur la place de la République, « des agents non identifiés des forces spéciales du Comité national de la sécurité (KNB) ont arrêté les victimes Jaguiparov et Kapsalanov » . Jusqu’à ce que les détenus soient remis aux policiers, ils ont été gardés par le commandant du premier bataillon opérationnel et un sergent du peloton de véhicules de la troupe 5 571 de la Garde nationale. Almaty, 5 janvier 2022. Photo : Almas Kaïsar / Vlast. Erlan Jaguiparov et Aouèz Kapsalanov ont été détenus près de cinq heures dans le froid près du Monument de l’indépendance, menottés. Ensuite, on les a frappés, avec les poings, les pieds, puis avec une kalachnikov automatique 74. Il s’est avéré par la suite que des affaires pénales distinctes étaient en cours d’instruction pour les faits de torture et de coups, et qu’elles faisaient l’objet d’une enquête par le département d’enquête militaire de la région Sud. L’enquête n’a pas permis de déterminer qui avait battu les hommes, ni quand. De quoi est accusé Aïtchan Aoubakirov ? « Plus tard, approximativement entre 23h00 le 6 janvier et 00h30 le 7 janvier, Aoubakirov, ayant reçu l’ordre du commandant de l’unité militaire 5 571, le colonel Ospanbekov, de libérer les détenus Jaguiparov et Kapsalanov, a appelé les militaires contractuels et leur a ordonné d’emmener les victimes derrière la barricade et de leur enlever les menottes » , a déclaré le procureur lors du procès. Le capitaine désigné a commencé par enlever les menottes à Aouèz Kapsalanov. Quand il a enlevé les menottes à Erlan Jaguiparov, ce dernier, craignant une nouvelle flopée de coups, a brusquement repoussé le militaire et a tenté de s’enfuir du côté de la rue Jeltoksan. Lire aussi sur Novastan : Evénements de janvier au Kazakhstan : des cadres des services de renseignement mis en cause A ce moment, Aïtchan Aoubakirov, ayant vu Erlan Jaguiparov et Aouèz Kapsalanov essayer de s’enfuir, leur tira dessus avec un AK 74 depuis une distance de plus de dix mètres. L’expertise balistique a démontré que toutes les balles ayant atteint les victimes venaient de l’arme d’Aïtchan Aoubakirov. En lisant l’acte d’accusation, le procureur a rappelé qu’Aïtchan Aoubakirov avait conscience que les victimes n’avaient pas molesté de citoyens, n’avaient pas commis d’attentats et ne représentaient pas une menace pour les militaires. Les arguments de la défense Pendant le procès, Aïtchan Aoubakirov n’a parlé qu’avec ses avocats. Il n’a pas reconnu sa culpabilité. Selon sa version, il a vu les détenus pour la première fois à 23:00 et le commandant Ospanbekov ne lui a pas expliqué sous l’ordre de quel militaire ni pourquoi ils étaient retenus. Il lui a seulement ordonné de les laisser partir parce qu’il ne pouvait pas appeler une patrouille pour les transporter. Selon Aïtchan Aoubakirov, au moment d’enlever les menottes, une attaque visant les militaires était survenue, et tous s’étaient dispersés. Lire aussi sur Novastan : Kazakhstan : les oubliés de janvier « Environ une heure et demie plus tard, une voiture s’est approchée de nous et j’ai crié : « bélier ». Au même moment, nous avons été attaqués sur le côté droit, j’ai vu un éclair de coups de feu, je me suis mis en garde et j’ai ouvert le feu. (...) Puis la voiture a fait demi-tour à vive allure, les éclairs se sont arrêtés. Comme il faisait nuit, je ne pouvais pas voir le nombre de personnes – il y avait quelques silhouettes. Les tirs se sont arrêtés, les silhouettes sont tombées » , a-t-il déclaré. Selon lui, ces « éclairs » provenaient de la direction vers laquelle avaient couru Erlan Jaguiparov et Aouèz Kapsalanov auparavant. Selon ses dires, c’était de leur côté que venaient les tirs. Une version mise en doute Mais au cours de l’enquête judiciaire, puis au tribunal, il a été prouvé que les victimes n’étaient pas armées et que leur mort était survenue juste après leur libération. Selon Aïtchan Aoubakirov, il a dix fois tiré en l’a

Support Novastan Blending crime drama, psychological suspense and Kyrgyz mythology, Mergen explores corruption, environmental exploitation and the struggle for justice in contemporary Kyrgyzstan. Director Chingiz Narynov speaks to Novastan about the legends that inspired his film, the challenges of casting its characters, and why audiences at home and abroad have interpreted it differently. Watch here the trailer of Mergen . Kyrgyz cinema has increasingly attracted international attention, with filmmakers exploring contemporary social issues through a variety of cinematic forms. In Mergen, director Chingiz Narynov draws on the country’s rich mythological traditions to tell a dark story about corruption, greed, environmental destruction and the limits of individual morality. Read more on Novastan : Through roads, markets and silence: Tolomush Zhanybekov films Kyrgyzstan’s unseen lives Set in a fictional town, the film follows Nurtai, a police officer confronting a world where powerful interests often prevail over justice. Combining elements of a detective story and psychological thriller with references to Kyrgyz folklore, Mergen raises questions about humanity’s relationship with nature and the moral compromises imposed by an unequal society. The film is featured in the programme of the 2026 Asian Film Festival Barcelona. Novastan Editor-in-Chief Mathieu Lemoine spoke with Narynov about the making of Mergen, the importance of local mythology, and his plans for future projects. Read more on Novastan : New voices: Central Asian short films at the GoEast Festival 2024 Novastan: Mergen combines elements of crime drama, psychological thriller and Kyrgyz mythology, while presenting a rather dark vision of contemporary society. What inspired you to tell this story, and what message did you hope to convey? Chingiz Narynov: The starting point was Kyrgyz mythology. One day, screenwriter Aikyz Gaparova and I were discussing the ancient legend of Karagul-Botom, particularly how relevant it remains today and how it resonates with contemporary problems in Kyrgyz society. That conversation gradually developed into the idea for the film. Read more on Novastan : “Manastchy”: the Kyrgyz soul in all its poetry At the same time, we wanted to tell a contemporary story, which led us towards genre cinema. The problems facing Kyrgyzstan largely shaped the film’s mood and atmosphere. Ultimately, ancient legends and present-day realities came together in Mergen. Chingiz Narynov, director of the Kyrgyz thriller Mergen . Photo: Courtesy of Citylab Films. The characters are particularly convincing, and the casting is one of the film’s strengths. How did you select the actors playing Nurtai, Kerim and the young girl, Anara? Were any of these roles cinematic debuts? The casting process was lengthy. We spent a long time looking for the right actor to play Nurtai, but when Omurbek Israilov came in, I immediately felt that we had found our protagonist. Kerim was more complicated. We held more than eighteen auditions with different actors. Nazym Mendebairov was among our first candidates, but I wanted to move away from the familiar criminal roles that audiences associated with this well-known actor. After a long search, however, we returned to him. Ultimately, he was the most convincing person for the part. Regina Talantbekova, who played Anara, had already had some acting experience, as far as I remember, but Mergen was her feature-film debut. I think she did a wonderful job. Another remarkable debut was the role of Turdukul, played by Tilektesh Usenakunov, who had previously worked primarily as a stunt performer. The role of Jacob also has an interesting story behind it. He was played by Toon Cavens, a mathematics teacher at a private school in Bishkek, making his film debut in Mergen . I think he did a wonderful job. Nurtai is a police officer trying to uphold justice in a world dominated by corruption, violence and powerful interests. He seems torn between his professional duty, his conscience and a system he can do little to change. How did you develop this character, and what did you want to say through him about justice and personal responsibility? In our circumstances, a police officer who acts strictly according to the law and his conscience can almost seem like a fairytale character. That was precisely the painful issue I wanted to address: the feeling that a person with a conscience is doomed to fail within an imperfect, corrupt system, and that without some kind of intervention from above, they cannot achieve anything. I think the nihilism that is widespread in our society is largely connected to the gap between how things ought to work and how they actually function. For someone with an idealistic view of the world, that discrepancy can create a profound internal fracture. Through Nurtai, I wanted to convey this contradiction. Gold mining, poverty and human greed play important roles in Mergen. In Kyrgyzstan, longstanding controversies surrounding the Kumtor gold mine have raised questions about environmental damage, control over natural resources and the distribution of mining revenues. Did these debates influence your film? How closely does the social inequality portrayed in Mergen reflect contemporary Kyrgyz realities? It wasn’t only Kumtor that influenced us. Kyrgyzstan has experienced numerous conflicts surrounding mineral extraction. The tension between the desire to make money and the desire to protect nature and natural resources keeps resurfacing in public debate. Naturally, all of this found its way into our creative thinking. I see the film as a kind of crystal in which the internal problems of our society and the atmosphere surrounding us have come together. We wanted to talk about ourselves, about the things we know and the things that hurt us. That is how the film took shape. Kyrgyz mythology is central to the film. Mergen draws on the legend of Kozhozhash, a hunter who violates the laws of nature, but you also mentioned Karagul-Botom as an important inspiration. The film additionally references Umai-Ene, a female mythological figure associated with motherhood and nature. How did you bring these different traditions together, and what relevance do they have for contemporary Kyrgyz society? We drew inspiration from a whole range of Kyrgyz epics and legends. We took a key plot twist from Karagul-Botom. Kozhozhash was also important: it is the story of a hunter who violates the laws of nature and a tale about human greed. For us, one of its most significant messages is that you should never take more than you need. Umai-Ene is a goddess from Tengrism who embodies motherhood and femininity, as well as the connection with the earth and nature. I consider these images and stories highly relevant today. Otherwise, I would not have turned to them. With every passing year, Kyrgyz folklore and our culture become increasingly interesting to me. Anara’s grandmother in a scene from Mergen , a film drawing inspiration from Kyrgyz legends and mythology. Courtesy of Citylab Films. Spoiler warning: The following question discusses the film’s ending. The ending of Mergen is particularly intriguing and open to interpretation. Does Nurtai actually manage to return to the past and save the girl, or are we seeing his imagined version of how events might have unfolded? Why did you decide to leave the ending ambiguous? We always intended to have an open ending, allowing viewers to experience what happened for themselves and draw their own conclu
