https://en.kabar.kg/news/kyrgyzstan-step.body: Kabar Kyrgyzstan's active engagement within the SCO and its upcoming historic mission at the UN Security Council have elevated the country's international responsibility to a new level. In this context, not just the strength of the authorities but the quality of state institutions takes center stage. Baktygul Kalambekova, a diplomat, former Ambassador of Kyrgyzstan to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and candidate of economics shared this perspective in her interview with Kabar. The ambassador noted that contemporary foreign policy and domestic reform cannot be viewed as separate processes. She also characterized the last five or six years as a period of reconfiguration for Kyrgyzstan's state institutions. Emphasizing that it is incorrect to view this period solely through the lens of political changes, she described the current era as a time when the state is re-evaluating its governance model, economic policy, foreign relations, and the relationship between society and the state. - Dear Baktygul, we recognize that in this era of globalization, Kyrgyzstan must operate in close alignment with international norms. How does Kyrgyzstan’s upcoming UN Security Council membership, alongside its roles in the SCO and EAEU, drive its domestic reforms? — In my view, the key challenge for Kyrgyzstan today is not merely to increase the number of international organizations in which it participates, but to transform that participation into a resource for enhancing the quality of the state's domestic institutions. Kyrgyzstan’s election as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council for the 2027–2028 term marks a significant milestone in the country’s diplomatic history. This will be Kyrgyzstan’s first time serving on the Security Council. Consequently, starting in 2027, the country will participate at a much higher level in discussions and decision-making processes regarding international security issues. Such a status imposes new demands not only on the state’s foreign policy but also on the quality of domestic public administration. First and foremost, it is essential to strengthen and develop the professional diplomatic and analytical capabilities of our personnel. Secondly, high-quality state expertise is required in areas such as international law, security, the economy, energy, climate, water resources, and technological development. Thirdly, a mechanism must be in place to effectively incorporate assumed international obligations into domestic legislation and state policy. Kyrgyzstan’s chairmanship of the SCO for 2025–2026 highlighted these very requirements. At the SCO summit held in Bishkek on September 1, 2026, the results of Kyrgyzstan’s chairmanship were highly praised, and its contribution to strengthening the organization’s institutional capacity and practical cooperation was acknowledged. As for the EAEU, it primarily demands economic and institutional preparedness from Kyrgyzstan. Within the framework of integration, the operations of national institutions, spanning customs, taxation, technical regulation, transport logistics, digital systems, the labor market, and the competitive environment must align with the unified integration space. For instance, it was officially recorded that in 2025, Kyrgyzstan’s mutual trade with EAEU member states reached $5.9 billion. Therefore, foreign policy and domestic reform cannot be viewed as two separate processes. The consistency of a state's activity on the international stage is directly linked to how professionally, legally, and effectively its domestic institutions operate. In other words, international standing is reinforced by the quality of domestic institutions. — Over the past five or six years, Kyrgyzstan has undergone major institutional changes, including constitutional revisions and the strengthening of the vertical power structure. Do these changes demonstrate enhanced operational capacity? To what degree has alignment with these global bodies optimized government agility and strategic decision-making in Kyrgyzstan? — It is important here to distinguish between agility and the quality of decisions. The constitution adopted in 2021 redefined the structure of state power and strengthened the role of the presidency. In the years that followed, a series of reforms were implemented to streamline the public administration structure, reduce bureaucracy, and accelerate decision-making mechanisms. As a result, the state system's decision-making capacity has significantly improved, particularly regarding vertical governance and the mobilization of resources toward a unified goal. For instance, in 2025, additional measures were adopted to enhance the efficiency of the civil service system and eliminate bureaucracy. That same year, amendments were made to the mechanisms for training a new generation of personnel for state and municipal service. By the end of 2025, reforms aimed at improving public administration efficiency and reducing bureaucracy continue. Thus, there are grounds to say that there have been changes in the operational efficiency of the state apparatus. The second issue here concerns the quality of decisions and the stability of institutions. For high-quality public administration, factors such as a decision's soundness, expert review, legality, implementation, consideration of public interests, and long-term impact are crucial. Therefore, while a model of "operational governance" has become quite evident in Kyrgyzstan today, I believe the next stage requires complementing it with a model of a professionally competent and institutionally stable state. In other words, if the first stage required restoring the state's capacity to make decisions, the next stage involves transforming that capacity into institutional quality. In this context, while the strengthening of the vertical of power facilitates the coordination of decisions, it simultaneously underscores the need to develop mechanisms that ensure checks and balances, the quality of decisions, and the ability of state institutions to conduct independent professional expert assessments. — How do you assess the changes that have been taking place in Kyrgyzstan over the past five years? — I would call it as a period of reconfiguration for Kyrgyzstan’s state institutions. It would be incorrect to view this period solely through the lens of political change. It is a time when the state is rethinking its governance model, economic policy, foreign relations, and the relationship between society and the state. The 2021 Constitution established the legal foundation for a new governance model. Subsequently, institutional changes continued in areas such as optimizing public administration, reducing bureaucracy, improving the quality of public service, and reforming tax and customs administration. For instance, the structure of tax and customs administration was reorganized in 2025. At the same time, Kyrgyzstan has become more active on the international stage. Holding the SCO chairmanship for 2025–2026 and being elected to the UN Security Council for 2027–2028 have elevated the country's level of international responsibility. I view these changes not as a completed reform, but as the shaping of a new stage in the state's development. For transforming state institutions is one stage, whereas establishing a culture of their stable operation is a far more prolonged process. Kyrgyzstan has enhanced the speed of state decision-making and the capacity to mobilize state resources. The next task is to transform this potential into high-quality institutions, strengthen the professional civil service, reinforce the rule of law, boost analytical and expert capabilities, and ensure the continuity of state policy. Therefore, to summarize the main outcome of the past five years in a single sentence: Kyrgyzstan is transitioning from the stage of creating a new model of public administration to the stage of strengthening its institutio

https://en.kabar.kg/news/ala-too-ski-res.body: www Bishkek, Nov. 6, 2026 /Kabar/. The Ala-Too Resort ski resort is scheduled to open on December 1. By that time, the resort plans to launch 47 kilometers of ski slopes and 6 cable car lines, Askat Cholponbaev, a representative of Ala-Too Resort OJSC, told on Birinchi Radio. "By December 1, we plan to open 47 kilometers of ski slopes. They will be divided into four categories: for beginners, intermediate skiers, professionals, and those who prefer challenging descents in mountainous terrain," he explained. According to Cholponbaev, the resort also plans to launch 6 cable car lines. Lifts B1 and B2 will feature a combined system, incorporating both gondolas and chairlifts, with each line spanning 4 kilometers. "In addition, lift E will be a chairlift, while lifts C and X will be surface (T-bar/platter) lifts," the company representative said. He added that more than 10,000 guests are expected to attend the opening ceremony, which will also feature a concert program for visitors. Bakytbek Narbekov, Chief Financial Officer of Ala-Too Resort OJSC, stated that a rental center operated by the company MRM GmbH has opened at the resort for the convenience of guests. It offers a full range of equipment, including skis, snowboards, specialized apparel, and helmets. Additionally, an IT-based electronic queuing system is being implemented. According to Narbekov, particular attention has been paid to the preparation of the ski slopes. To this end, the resort has acquired six German-made PistenBully snow groomers—specialized machines designed for leveling and preparing snow surfaces. Four of these have already been delivered to Jyrgalan. Furthermore, the resort’s fleet of vehicles is being expanded with the addition of six snowmobiles and all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), half of which have already arrived at the resort. Print

https://en.kabar.kg/news/turkmenistan-co.body: Kabar During the October 27 trading session at SCRMET, three foreign deals in the energy sector were concluded, Trend reported. This was stated in a press release published by the State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan (SCRMET). According to the report, entrepreneurs from Georgia, the UAE and Afghanistan reached agreements with the Turkmennebit State Concern for the purchase of liquefied gas. SCRMET reported that three transactions totaling $644,200 were finalized during the session. The State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan (SCRMET), established in 1994, is the country’s main organized marketplace for trading commodities and one of the key institutions through which Turkmenistan conducts and facilitates foreign trade. The exchange brings together domestic producers, exporters, and foreign buyers through regular trading sessions, where a range of export-oriented goods are offered and transactions are concluded. Its trading portfolio covers petrochemicals, polymers, textiles, cotton products, construction materials, machinery, and chemical goods, among other commodities. SCRMET also plays an administrative and information role in Turkmenistan’s trade system. In addition to organizing trading sessions and registering export-import contracts, the exchange publishes official quotations based on transactions conducted on the platform. These quotations provide information on the commodities traded, their values, and the markets involved, making SCRMET data a useful indicator of the composition and direction of exchange-based trade. Through these quotations, SCRMET provides a snapshot of the value and sectoral composition of goods offered to international buyers during each trading session, reflecting shifts in the country’s export offering and highlighting which industries dominate Turkmenistan’s exchange-based trade. Print

https://en.kabar.kg/news/baku-hosts-firs.body: Kabar The First Azerbaijan Regional Aquaculture Forum was held in Baku, AZERTAG reported. Organized by Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Agriculture, the forum focused on the current state and prospects of fisheries and aquaculture, government support mechanisms, regional cooperation, and the conservation of aquatic bioresources. The event brought together government officials, representatives of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), delegates from Türkiye, Georgia, Kazakhstan, and Turkmenistan, representatives of international organizations, industry experts, and private sector representatives. Addressing the forum, Minister of Agriculture Majnun Mammadov highlighted institutional efforts, development potential, and key priorities for advancing fisheries and aquaculture in Azerbaijan. He stressed the importance of protecting fish stocks, modernizing infrastructure, introducing advanced technologies, and attracting investment. The minister noted that the 2026–2030 State Programme aims to increase annual aquaculture production from 3,400 to 7,700 tons by 2030. He emphasized the need to strengthen cooperation among the public sector, businesses, academia, and regional partners. He also noted that the forum would contribute to ensuring food security, reducing dependence on imports, and creating jobs in the regions. Tahir Rzayev, Chair of the Milli Majlis Committee on Agrarian Policy, highlighted the importance of food security as a key component of national security. He outlined efforts to improve the legal framework governing fisheries and aquaculture, stressing the need to prevent illegal fishing and strengthen oversight. Latif Gasimov, Head of the Agricultural and Environmental Affairs Department at the Office of the Cabinet of Ministers of Azerbaijan, emphasized the role of the State Programme in expanding aquaculture production, introducing modern technologies, and integrating the sector into global value chains. He also highlighted the importance of digital monitoring, protecting local fish species and the Caspian Sea’s aquatic resources, and developing aquaculture clusters in the liberated Garabagh and East Zangezur economic regions. Nabil Gangi, FAO Deputy Regional Representative for Europe and Central Asia, thanked the Ministry of Agriculture for organizing the forum and highlighted aquaculture’s contribution to food security and rural development. He stressed the importance of climate-resilient practices, modern technologies, and data-driven management, reaffirming FAO’s commitment to expanding cooperation with Azerbaijan and supporting the sustainable development of the country’s aquaculture sector. During the forum, outstanding fisheries and aquaculture enterprises were recognized with awards, and a video highlighting the sector’s achievements and future objectives was screened. The forum continued with panel discussions focusing on national priorities, regional cooperation, fish stock conservation, the regulatory framework, and the role of the private sector in aquaculture development. Print

https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/05/ibc-.body: Share Nigora Bukhorizade , asia+ Categories Business Tajikistan Format News Published 05.11.2026 17:03 Translations Eng Рус On November 25, 2026,Dushanbe will host an IBC Global business breakfast focused on developing modern warehouse infrastructure in Tajikistan. Experts, investors and business representatives will discuss the prospects for building the country’s first Class A warehouse complex. Tajikistan’s market for modern warehouse facilities remains underdeveloped. Importers, distributors and agricultural exporters often rely on their own storage facilities, use adapted premises or store goods in neighboring countries. The event will explore the conditions under which a Class A warehouse complex could be built in Tajikistan and become commercially viable. The business breakfast will take place at the Crowne Plaza Dushanbe hotel, located at 1 Nizami Ganjavi Street. What will participants discuss? IBC Global will present market research covering demand for modern warehouses among logistics, trading and manufacturing companies, construction costs and rental rates needed to make such projects financially sustainable. Participants will also discuss potential anchor tenants and development models, including build-to-suit facilities designed for specific customers and speculative developments intended for future leasing. Special attention will be given to multi-temperature warehouses for agricultural exports and pharmaceuticals, sectors that require specialized storage conditions. Financing will be another key topic, including bank loans, development finance institutions, private investment and currency risks associated with borrowing in US dollars while earning revenue in Tajik somoni. Who can attend? The event is intended for developers, investors, landowners, banks, logistics operators, trading and distribution companies, agricultural exporters and pharmaceutical businesses. Following the presentations, participants will have an opportunity to join an open discussion and network with potential business partners. Event details: Date: November 25, 2026 Venue: Crowne Plaza Dushanbe, 1 Nizami Ganjavi Street Registration and welcome coffee: 9:30 am Business program begins: 10:00 am Admission: By prior registration only The meeting aims to identify practical opportunities for investment in modern warehouse infrastructure and assess the potential for launching Tajikistan’s first Class A warehouse project. Grade A warehouses are the gold standard in warehousing infrastructure. These facilities are built according to modern, globally accepted standards and cater to companies with high-volume, high-efficiency logistics needs. IBC Global is an international consulting and brokerage firm specializing in industrial and warehouse real estate. The company is a leading consultant and broker in the warehouse real estate market across Central Asia. Join us on social media! https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/05/at-t.body: Share Sayfiddin Karaev , asia+ Categories Economics Tajikistan Format Details Photo Published 05.11.2026 15:35 Translations Eng Рус How Tajikistan’s largest hydropower plant is being built, what is happening on both banks of the Vakhsh, and how people live next to the construction site. On October 29, Asia-Plus journalists joined a group of reporters on a visit to the Rogun hydropower plant construction site. “60 cubic meters per trip” Construction at the Rogun HPP never stops for a moment. Service vehicles, trucks and enormous quarry dump trucks follow one another along wide dirt roads. Excavators, bulldozers and other machinery are at work across various sections of the site. After an overnight rain, the roads turned soft and muddy in places, with deep ruts left by heavy vehicles. One dump truck driver, noticing the journalists, raised his hand in greeting from the cab high above the ground. — How much do you haul per trip? — we asked. — 60 cubic meters, — he replied briefly. That is roughly the amount of sand and soil that would fill an ordinary room from floor to ceiling. The dump truck delivers that volume to the dam construction site in a single run. The driver did not linger — he had work to get back to. According to engineer Jahongir Sultonzoda, who accompanied the group, dump trucks with load capacities ranging from 40 to 80 cubic meters are used at the site. Construction starts with a hard hat Before setting out to tour the Rogun HPP, the journalists are briefed on safety rules. Heavy machinery operates around the clock, and rockfalls are possible in some areas. Journalists are therefore warned: do not approach operating machinery, do not cross barriers, and do not stray from the group. Everyone is issued a hard hat and a reflective vest. Before the tour, the journalists met with Murod Sa’dulloev, Deputy Technical Director of the station. He described how construction is progressing and when the next generating units are expected to come online. According to him, more than 20,000 people are currently working at Rogun. Construction continues day and night without interruption. Two hydroelectric generating units are already producing electricity. Since they were commissioned, they have generated more than 11 billion kilowatt-hours. This year, the reservoir water level was raised to 1,140 meters above sea level. In 2027, the plan is to bring it to 1,165 meters in order to increase power output. The third generating unit is scheduled to come online in September 2027. The station will ultimately have six hydroelectric generating units of 630 megawatts each. Once construction is complete, the Rogun HPP’s total capacity will be 3,780 megawatts. By design, the station will be able to generate an average of 14.4 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity per year. After the briefing, we board a bus and set off to tour the construction site. Play video: Роғун имрӯз чӣ ҳол дорад? Pasi Muraho — a village inside the construction site On the way to the first observation point, we pass through the small village of Pasi Muraho, which lies within the fenced perimeter of the Rogun HPP. Through the bus windows, rural houses, orchards and outbuildings come into view. People here grow fruit, keep livestock and tend to their households. Getting into the village, however, is not straightforward — a checkpoint controls entry. Security staff know the local residents by sight, but relatives and other visitors coming to the village must present a passport and obtain an entry permit. The proximity of the construction site gives local residents opportunities to earn income. Some have opened shops and canteens; others provide various services to construction workers. — Does everyone here work at the construction site? — we ask one of the passersby. He replies that no, some residents work in the city of Rogun, which is very close by and can be reached on foot. In the future, however, the residents of Pasi Muraho will have to relocate and leave the homes they currently live in. Soon the village was left behind, and our bus continued on between the mountain slopes. How did the machinery get so high up in the mountains? From the first observation point, the view opens onto the Rogun reservoir. Below, a turquoise expanse of water stretches out, flanked on both sides by steep mountains. Clouds hang over the gorge, obscuring the slopes in places, while snow already whitens the distant peaks. Most striking, though, are the roads cut high into the mountains. Heavy machinery stands on slopes that from a distance look almost sheer. Higher still, power transmission line towers rise above them. How did the builders manage to get equipment up there and install those enormous metal structures? In some spots it seems impossible even to climb on foot. Construction has visibly reshaped the mountain terrain. Wide terraces have been cut into some slopes; others have been reinforced with concrete structures. Roads wind between them, carrying trucks back and forth. The slope reinforcement method was particularly interesting. As the builders explain, deep holes are drilled into the rock and metal anchors up to 70 meters long are installed. Rows of these anchors are visible from the observation point. The dam at the heart of the gorge Deep in the gorge, between high mountains, a wide rock-and-earth embankment — part of the Rogun HPP dam under construction — is gradually rising. By design, it will reach a height of 335 meters. Once complete, it is set to become the tallest rock-fill dam in the world. From the outside, the construction might seem straightforward: dump trucks bring rock and soil, which is gradually built up into the embankment. But as the builders explain, the process is far more complex. Material is laid down layer by layer. Each layer is carefully compacted and checked against design specifications. Only after the required inspections are passed does work on the next layer begin. Enormous volumes of rock, soil, concrete, steel and other materials are used in the construction. The reliability of the future dam depends on their quality and on strict adherence to the construction process. After inspecting the first observation point, we head to the opposite bank of the Vakhsh. The bus crosses a section of the dam under construction that has blocked the river channel. Where a fast, roaring river once rushed, a reservoir now spreads out, continuing to fill. Some of the water flows through penstocks bored through the rock to the generating units, where it drives turbines connected to electric generators. This is how the energy of the water flow is converted into electricity. After passing through the turbines, the water returns to the Vakhsh channel below the dam — and it is precisely there, at the point where water exits the HPP’s underground structures, that we are still to make our way. On either side of the road, rock embankments and reinforced slopes rise up. After the overnight rain, the dirt road is dotted with puddles and deep ruts left by heavy vehicles. The second observation deck offers a completely different view. Instead of the calm surface of the reservoir, there is a vast expanse of earthworks. Dump trucks move at different levels while excavators and other machinery operate below. But from the height of the observation deck, even the massive quarry dump trucks look like toys. Rogun is being built not only by Tajik specialists One of the journalists recalled the construction of the Nurek hydropower plant. — Nurek was built by specialists from all 15 republics of the Soviet Union... — And Rogun, Tajikistan is building on its own, — came the reply. In reality, however, the current construction project is also international in character. The bulk of the work is carried out by Tajik specialists, but more than two thousand foreign workers are working alongside them. https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/05/taji.body: Share Sayfiddin Karaev , asia+ Categories Ecology Security Tajikistan Format News Published 05.11.2026 14:43 Translations Eng Рус Tajikistan is considering the development of a monitoring and early warning system for accidents at industrial waste storage facilities. The initiative was discussed at the fifth meeting of the Interagency Working Group on Industrial Waste Safety and the Prevention of Accidental Water Pollution, held in Dushanbe. Representatives of government agencies, industrial enterprises, research institutions and international organizations discussed the use of digital risk maps, accident prevention measures and Tajikistan’s international obligations. Experts from the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) and the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) presented findings on how climate change affects the safety of tailings facilities. Participants also reviewed progress made in 2025–2026 and discussed a draft action plan for the next period. Why are tailings facilities dangerous? Tailings facilities are structures used to store waste generated during mineral processing. They can contain heavy metals, hazardous chemicals and radioactive materials. If their protective structures fail, contaminants can enter the soil, groundwater and rivers, potentially affecting neighboring countries. According to a UNECE and ESCAP report prepared following a workshop in Bishkek in May 2025, climate change is increasing these risks. Heavy rainfall, floods, landslides and melting glaciers can damage dams and other protective structures. Many tailings facilities in Central Asia were built decades ago and were not designed to withstand today’s climate-related hazards. How many hazardous facilities are there in Tajikistan? A UNECE study identified 61 tailings facilities and more than 130 other potentially hazardous industrial sites in the Syr Darya River basin. Of the 61 tailings facilities, 30 are located in Kyrgyzstan, 12 in Uzbekistan, 10 in Tajikistan and nine in Kazakhstan. At least 33 could pose a transboundary threat in the event of an accident. Tajikistan’s major uranium legacy sites include former industrial facilities in Istiqlol (formerly Taboshar), Degmay and Adrasman in Sughd province. The country’s uranium tailings rehabilitation program for 2025–2030 identifies potential water contamination risks associated with the former Taboshar mines and the Degmay tailings facility. Groundwater affected by the Degmay site drains toward the Syr Darya River, highlighting the need for coordinated monitoring of possible transboundary pollution. What has been done so far? Rehabilitation of former uranium production sites in Tajikistan is ongoing. In 2023, reclamation work was completed at four tailings facilities and a uranium ore dump in Taboshar (currently Istiqlol) in Sughd province. In May 2026, Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom announced that project documentation had been approved for the rehabilitation of facilities in Taboshar and Adrasman. The Adrasman tailings facility contains approximately 400,000 tons of waste. In September, rehabilitation work began at Workshop No. 3 of the former uranium production facility in Taboshar. Meanwhile, Central Asian countries are developing a joint response plan for industrial accidents in the Syr Darya basin. It is expected to establish procedures for information sharing, early warning and coordinated action in the event of water contamination. However, UNECE has noted that regional cooperation mechanisms remain limited, while relatively few tailings facilities have emergency response plans that account for climate-related risks. Tajikistan joins international convention on industrial accidents On June 9, 2026, the UN Convention on the Transboundary Effects of Industrial Accidents entered into force for Tajikistan, making it the convention’s 43rd party. The convention requires participating countries to identify and monitor hazardous industrial facilities, implement accident prevention measures and notify neighboring states when an industrial accident could affect their territory. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has previously raised concerns about uranium tailings facilities in Tajikistan and a shortage of funding for their rehabilitation. According to the IAEA figures cited in the report, 10 uranium tailings facilities in Sughd province contain approximately 55 million tons of radioactive waste. Join us on social media!

https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/05/dush.body: Share Shirin Rakhmanova , asia+ Categories Society Tajikistan Format Details Published 05.11.2026 11:19 Translations Eng Рус Tajikistan has secured a €10 million concessional loan from Austria to modernize the Republican Oncological Scientific Center in Dushanbe. The project will provide new diagnostic and cancer treatment equipment, train medical staff and reduce waiting times for patients. The loan agreement was signed on April 21 between Tajikistan and the Export-Import Bank of Austria. Austrian company AME International, which specializes in healthcare infrastructure, will equip the center with advanced medical technology from leading manufacturers, including Varian and Siemens Healthineers. A total of 14 medical equipment complexes will be installed across four specialized departments. What equipment will the center receive? The modernization will cover four key areas: Radiation therapy: A high-precision linear accelerator, a specialized CT simulator, dosimetry and patient positioning systems, and digital treatment planning technology. Brachytherapy: Equipment for delivering radiation directly to tumors, including a high-dose-rate brachytherapy system using iridium-192 and real-time imaging technology. Diagnostics: A modern MRI scanner, digital mammography equipment and an advanced ultrasound system. Nuclear medicine: A hybrid SPECT-CT scanner for detecting diseases and a specialized laboratory for handling radiopharmaceuticals. According to the center, the new equipment will initially allow up to 4,000 patients to receive modern radiation therapy annually, with the possibility of expanding capacity. Treatment waiting times are expected to fall to 7–10 days. The center also expects the new technology to improve treatment accuracy, reduce complications and minimize radiation exposure to healthy tissues. “High precision in positioning and protection of healthy organs will significantly reduce the risk of complications, which is especially important in treating children and severe pathologies,” the center said. Officials also expect the modernization to reduce the need for patients to travel abroad for cancer treatment, helping families save money. Medical staff to undergo training The project includes training for medical and technical personnel working in radiation therapy, brachytherapy, diagnostics and nuclear medicine. Training will take place at the center and will combine theoretical courses with practical instruction by internationally certified specialists. Eight key employees, mainly medical physicists and radiologists, will also undergo internships at leading oncology centers in Austria or elsewhere in Europe. According to the center, training will begin once the loan agreement enters into force, allowing specialists to start treating patients as soon as the new equipment is installed and commissioned. When will the new equipment become available? The Ministry of Finance is working to fulfill the conditions required for the loan agreement to enter into force. Once the agreement takes effect and the necessary facilities are prepared, the Radiation Therapy Department is expected to become operational within six to eight months. The entire modernization project, including the installation and commissioning of all medical equipment, is scheduled for completion within 18 months. The project is being implemented under Tajikistan’s Program for the Prevention and Control of Oncological Diseases for 2025–2029. How will the €10 million be spent? The concessional loan will cover the purchase and delivery of medical equipment, installation, commissioning, warranty services and staff training. According to the center’s management, no additional funding from the state budget will be required for the project. The center said the equipment will be new, energy-efficient and supplied by leading international manufacturers. Warranty servicing and subsequent technical support are also included in the project. Will cancer treatment become more expensive? The center’s management assured Asia-Plus that the modernization will not lead to higher treatment prices. According to officials, the project is part of the government’s healthcare programs, and access to modern cancer diagnosis and treatment will remain under state oversight. Join us on social media!

https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/10/26/tile.body: Share Press release Categories Business Companies News Persona Society Tajikistan Format News Published 26.10.2026 11:18 Translations Eng Рус Wildberries has appointed Tilek Sulaimanov as its director in Tajikistan, where he will oversee business development, the launch of new services and cooperation with local entrepreneurs and partners, the company announced. Wildberries has operated in Tajikistan since April 2025. According to Wildberries’ press release, its online marketplace currently offers millions of products to customers in the country, with several dozen order pick-up points in operation. Tajik entrepreneurs can also register on the platform to sell their products. The company said its strategy in Tajikistan focuses on expanding marketplace infrastructure and introducing tools to help local entrepreneurs develop their businesses. “In Tajikistan, we want to make Wildberries a convenient platform for entrepreneurs where they can find new customers and grow their sales. Working with sellers and helping them understand the marketplace’s tools, we can see that local businesses have great potential for growth. I am confident that we will be able to realize it by developing e-commerce in the country together,” Sulaimanov said. Before joining Wildberries, Sulaimanov reportedly spent several years at Yandex Kyrgyzstan , where he was responsible for developing existing services and launching new ones. He previously worked at Beeline Kyrgyzstan and Beeline Kazakhstan, managing corporate sales and overseeing sales and customer service offices. Denis Pokhaznikov, director of the CIS Countries Development Department, said Sulaimanov’s experience in Central Asia would help the company better understand the local market and the needs of Tajik entrepreneurs. https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/04/parv.body: Share Manzuma Firuz , asia+ Categories Governance Tajikistan Format News Published 04.11.2026 18:13 Translations Eng Рус Parviz Shodmonzoda has been dismissed as director-general of Tajikistan’s national airline, Tajik Air. The government resolution was signed by President Emomali Rahmon on November 4. The resolution states that Shodmonzoda has been relieved of his position as director-general of OJSC Tajik Air but does not specify the reasons for his dismissal. His successor has not yet been announced. What changed at Tajik Air under Shodmonzoda? Parviz Shodmonzoda was appointed head of Tajik Air on September 29, 2022, replacing Dilshod Ismatullozoda , who had led the airline since January 2019. Before taking up the position, Shodmonzoda served as deputy director of Bokhtar International Airport and had previously worked at Tajik Air. He took over the national carrier at a difficult time, when the airline was struggling with financial problems, mounting debts and a sharp reduction in flight operations. During his tenure, Tajik Air made several attempts to restore its services. In November 2024, the airline announced plans to operate charter flights on several domestic routes. In January 2025, it resumed flights between Dushanbe and Kulob. Another significant development was the resolution of a long-running dispute with Lithuanian company SkyRoad Leasing over an outstanding debt of $36.6 million. In January 2025, Shodmonzoda announced that the dispute had been settled. In July 2025, it emerged that two Boeing aircraft previously owned by SkyRoad Leasing had been transferred to Tajik Air. However, both aircraft required repairs before they could return to service. Despite these developments, Shodmonzoda’s tenure did not see a full recovery of the national carrier’s operations. Tajik Air continued to face financial and operational difficulties, while regular international flights remained suspended. Join us on social media! During his visit to Tashkent, he reviewed the master plan for the New Tashkent urban development project and laid a wreath at the Independence Monument. As part of the visit, Emomali laid a wreath at the Independence Monument in New Uzbekistan Park in a gesture of respect for the country’s history and national statehood. New Tashkent is planned as a large-scale city development covering approximately 20,000–25,000 hectares, with a projected population of 2–2.5 million. The project envisions modern residential neighborhoods, business and public spaces, educational and healthcare facilities, transport networks and extensive green areas. Its design also incorporates modern technologies and environmentally sustainable solutions. Investment in the first phase of the project alone is estimated at $50 billion. The development is intended to accommodate Uzbekistan’s growing urban population and support the expansion of economic and social infrastructure in the Tashkent metropolitan area. https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/10/20/bank.body: Share Partnership post Categories Companies News Economics Money Tajikistan Format News Published 20.10.2026 16:56 Translations Eng Рус The Association of Banks of Tajikistan held the “Joizai Rushdi Bonkdori — 2026” ceremony (Award for Contribution to Banking Development), recognising achievements in digital banking. Winners were determined by a special commission, while a public vote ran in parallel — clients chose the banks whose services they found most convenient to use. What the banks were awarded for Transferring money in a matter of seconds, opening a deposit from your phone, applying for a loan online — we have grown so accustomed to these possibilities that we are now surprised if an ordinary transaction requires a trip to a branch. Behind everyday convenience lie years of work: developing applications, installing terminals, building payment systems and training specialists. The award was an occasion to recognise the people and organisations thanks to whom banking services are becoming more accessible. To determine the winners, a special commission and working group examined the results of financial organisations, their statistics and data from the National Bank. Awards were presented in three categories: development of digital infrastructure, development of digital banking services, and education in this field. The public vote covered ten nominations: digital cards, mobile banking, payment infrastructure, financial innovation, digital savings and deposits, digital lending, government payments, digital banking in the regions, and digital education for bank staff and clients. Poetry, music and a conversation about the future The evening opened with rubaiyat by Omar Khayyam in Tajik and Russian. Guests were welcomed by young women in national dress and offered grape juice in piala cups. Poetry about the power of the human mind served as a fitting introduction to a conversation about the knowledge and decisions that are transforming an entire industry. The ceremony was opened by Junaidulo Sharafov, Chairman of the Association of Banks of Tajikistan, and Gulbakhor Naziri, Deputy Chairman of the National Bank of Tajikistan. Guests also flew in from abroad: Olga Rudkovskaya, Director of Consulting Services Development at Mastercard for Central Asian countries, and Elena Skvortsova, General Partner of the ceremony and Vice-President of the Association of Banks of Russia. “Our associations are bound not only by business relations but also by warm friendship, mutual trust and a shared commitment to developing the banking community. We are glad to exchange experience and support each other’s initiatives,” noted Elena Skvortsova. Digital infrastructure: from cards to QR codes Who was recognised for developing digital infrastructure? Dushanbe City Bank received an award for its contribution to the development of digital payments and payment card services. Alif Bank was recognised for the development of mobile banking. Humo Bank won in the category of payment infrastructure development and the expansion of the banking payment agent network, including QR codes, ATMs and POS terminals. Oriyonbank received an award for the use of innovative technologies. Behind each of these categories lie familiar situations: paying by phone in a shop, withdrawing cash near home, or transferring money to loved ones directly from an app. Deposits, loans and services in the regions The second category brought together achievements in the development of specific banking services. International Bank of Tajikistan received an award for the development of digital savings and deposits. Bank Eskhata — for the development of digital lending. Amonatbank — for the development of digital government services. Imon International — for the development of digital banking in the regions. The last category is especially important for clients outside Dushanbe: access to modern financial tools should not depend on proximity to the capital. Who teaches people to use digital capabilities Even the most user-friendly application requires some familiarisation, and new technologies require trained specialists. Separate awards were therefore dedicated to the training of staff and clients. Arvand Bank was recognised for training staff of credit organisations on digitalisation. FINCA received an award for client training and consultation. The ceremony also drew attention to work with women: financial literacy programmes, entrepreneurship training and the activities of a women entrepreneurs’ club. Certificates of appreciation and material incentives in the category “Best Teacher in Digital Banking” were awarded to Sharif Rahimzoda and Bakhrom Sharipov . In the category “Best Book Author in Digital Banking” — to Umed Khikmatov and Salmon Mavlonazarov . Public vote: recognition from clients In addition to the commission, banks were also assessed through a public vote. Clients evaluated what they encounter every day: how intuitive the app is, how easy it is to pay for a service, open a deposit or apply for a loan. Humo Bank received the most votes across the various nominations. The survey results were presented by Lola Salimova , Deputy Chairman of the Association of Banks of Tajikistan. The public vote added an important dimension to the award: behind the figures and technologies always lies the personal experience of a person who entrusts their money to a bank. The next award — for the Association’s 20th anniversary In 2027, the Association of Banks of Tajikistan will mark its 20th anniversary . The next award is planned to focus on three areas: the use of artificial intelligence tools, green economy standards and information security in banking . Join us on social media!

https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/04/migr.body: Share Roza Shaposhnik , asia+ Categories Law-order Russia Society Tajikistan Format Interview Published 04.11.2026 16:46 Updated 17:09 Translations Eng Рус According to statistics , labor migrants from Central Asian countries make up the largest foreign workforce in Russia. Yet foreigners who come here often get confused by the required paperwork: applications, fees, work permits. This is compounded by the fact that Russian authorities change the rules for foreign workers quite frequently, making it necessary to keep track of every new development to avoid fines or even deportation. To provide legal assistance to newcomers, a website called MigraForma appeared online some time ago. It offers detailed information on regulations, downloadable application forms, and more. The founder of the MigraForma service, Gleb Ryvkin, told Fergana about this useful web resource and the latest changes in migration legislation. — What will change in migration legislation starting November 3, and how will it affect foreigners and host parties? — Starting November 3, Federal Law No. 294-FZ of August 4, 2026, comes into force. It amends the Code of Administrative Offenses of the Russian Federation but does not require any new documents from people. What does change, however, is the level of liability. First, the list of offenses for which a foreigner can be expelled from Russia has grown significantly: from 22 to 45 articles. Added to the list are, for example, petty hooliganism, violations of rules governing public gatherings, and the display of prohibited symbols. Second, fines have increased. For violating the terms of stay — Article 18.8 — the fine is now 4,000–7,000 rubles ($49–86) instead of 2,000–5,000 ($25–61), while in Moscow, St. Petersburg, Moscow Oblast, and Leningrad Oblast the penalties will rise to 7,000–9,000 rubles ($86–111). The fine for illegal employment is also 4,000–7,000 rubles. In the cities and regions listed above it will be 7,000–9,000 rubles, and administrative expulsion is mandatory there. “ It has also become more costly for host parties to deal with newcomers. An individual faces a fine of 4,000–7,000 rubles for illegally hiring a foreign worker, an official faces 25,000–50,000 rubles ($309–617), and an organization faces 250,000 ($3,087) to 800,000 rubles ($9,879) or a suspension of operations for up to 90 days. For failing to fulfill migration registration obligations, a host party (such as an apartment owner) may be fined 4,000–6,000 rubles ($49–74), while an organization faces 400,000–500,000 rubles ($4,940–6,174). — Why does the government keep tightening the rules for foreigners, and what is it trying to achieve? “ — It seems to me that the logic here is mainly this: order at the border and during stays, so that it is clear who is where, and so that foreigners work legally — with taxes and proper registration. From that perspective, the latest changes are quite understandable, and the new law makes it clear, for example, that violations are meant to become significantly more costly. That said, for ordinary people the main problem is not the strictness but the large number of factors that need to be taken into account and that are easy to get confused by. Deadlines differ by country, forms change, and information on official websites is sometimes unclear. I would like to see the rules become simpler and more transparent, with more steps available online. That would reduce errors and make it easier for both migrants and host parties to do everything on time. — What are the typical mistakes migrants make when filing an arrival notification or a work permit application? — There are many mistakes, but some come up again and again. Here are the most common ones. – The registration period is counted from the day of check-in. In fact, the law requires it to be counted from the day of border crossing. The difference is only a few days, but this violation carries a fine. – People are unaware that different countries have different deadlines. For example, citizens of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan have 15 days, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan have 30, and all others have 7 working days. – People assume that the arrival notification is always filed by the migrant. In most cases it is filed by the host party — the apartment owner, hotel, or employer — although a foreigner can also do it personally through the Gosuslugi (public services) portal. – People miss the work permit deadline. Keep in mind that the application must be submitted within 30 days of entry. “ And there is one small thing that trips up many people: a last name or address on the form is written differently from how it appears in the documents. This rule must be followed strictly, with passport details double-checked. It seems like a minor issue, but then everything has to be redone, sometimes wasting precious time. — How much money does a migrant need for all mandatory payments? — I should note upfront that the amount varies by region. Let’s look at the initial costs using Moscow as an example. To obtain a work permit, you need to pay approximately the following: a state fee of 4,200 rubles ($52), an exam on the Russian language, Russian history, and the basics of legislation — 3,800 rubles ($47), and a medical examination — 6,800 rubles ($84). A voluntary health insurance policy (VHI) costs on average around 4,000 rubles ($49). Add the migration center’s own service fee — around 6,000 rubles ($74) — and a notarized passport translation, if required, at around 1,000 rubles ($12). You also need to make the first advance payment of personal income tax (PIT) right away; in Moscow in 2026 this is 10,000 rubles ($123) per month. Adding it all up, a migrant needs to have around 35,000–36,000 rubles (approximately $440) on hand at the start. And the same 10,000 rubles will need to be paid to the state every month thereafter. Fingerprinting and photos are free. But keep in mind the payment processing fee for migration center services — around 3.5% of the total amount. I will repeat that the advance payment amount differs in other regions, so before traveling it is best to check the figures for the specific oblast or city you are heading to. — What are the differences in migration rules for, say, citizens of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan compared with those from Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan? — The main difference is that citizens of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan do not need a work permit. Their countries are members of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), and their nationals may work under an employment or civil-law contract, with the length of stay in Russia determined by the duration of the relevant contract. Uzbekistan and Tajikistan are not members of the EAEU. Citizens of these countries can enter Russia without a visa, but they need a work permit (patent) to be employed. For this, they must pass an exam, undergo a medical examination, pay a state fee, and then make monthly advance payments on personal income tax. Keep in mind that an application for a work permit must be submitted within 30 days of entry. Registration deadlines also differ. Citizens of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan have 15 days to register, while citizens of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan have 30. At the same time, working citizens of EAEU member states, like everyone else, must undergo fingerprinting and a medical examination within 30 days of entry. So in practice, nationals of the economic union’s member states face fewer payments and less paperwork — but it is not zero. — Why did you create your service, when did it launch, and what are the user statistics? — The idea is simple: I saw how people were losing time and money because of mistakes on forms, while intermediaries were charging a lot for something as basic as filling them out. I wanted to build a clear and affordable tool where a person answers questions in plain Russian, gets a ready-made PDF form, prints it, signs it, and submits it to the authorities themselves. https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/04/us-s.body: Share asia+ Published 04.11.2026 15:03 The United States carried out strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on November 2, just ahead of the US midterm elections. American officials described the operation as limited and defensive, saying it was in response to Iranian forces firing on a US aircraft, the BBC reported on November 3, citing CBS News . According to US officials, the strikes targeted positions on the island after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) opened fire on an American aircraft. Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported explosions on Qeshm Island on November 2. The IRGC did not directly comment on the US strikes but claimed to have shot down two American MQM-170 drones south of the island and an MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz. The US military had not officially commented on the operation at the time of the reports. The strikes came as international mediators intensified diplomatic efforts to prevent a renewed escalation of the conflict between Washington and Tehran. Trump signals no urgency to expand military operations US President Donald Trump has faced declining poll ratings and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the conflict with Iran, which began following US and Israeli strikes in February 2026. Speaking to Axios on November 2, Trump said he was in no hurry to intensify military operations against Iran. “One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush,” he said, claiming that US actions had severely weakened Iran’s economy. In a separate interview with Fox News ahead of the midterm elections, Trump suggested that US forces could target Pickaxe Mountain, an underground facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program. He described such an operation as relatively straightforward, claiming it could be completed within an hour. Despite speculation that Washington could launch a new wave of major strikes after the midterm elections, Trump denied that such plans were in place when questioned by reporters on November 2. Meanwhile, the Associated Press reported, citing two regional officials, that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had urged Trump during a weekend phone conversation to carry out further strikes against Iran after the elections. Iran says Washington must act to prevent renewed war On November 3, Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is also Tehran’s chief negotiator with Washington, said the United States must take steps to prevent another escalation. “The ball is now in America’s court to prevent war,” Ghalibaf said in a televised address. He emphasized that Iran remained prepared for military confrontation while also being open to diplomatic efforts. It was not immediately clear what specific proposals Ghalibaf was referring to. However, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told IRNA on November 2 that intensive indirect negotiations with Washington were under way through Qatari and Pakistani mediators. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman confirmed on November 3 that both sides were reviewing proposals presented by mediators and expressed hope that an agreement could still be reached. Strait of Hormuz remains central to negotiations One of the main issues in the negotiations is the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a strategically important waterway through which approximately one-fifth of global oil and gas shipments normally pass. According to reports, Iranian negotiators recently discussed a proposal to reopen the strait within two days if Washington met seven conditions. These reportedly include lifting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and releasing frozen Iranian assets. The strait has been effectively closed to much commercial shipping since the conflict began in February, following Iranian missile and drone attacks on vessels and the imposition of a US naval blockade. Washington and Tehran reached a preliminary agreement in June to end the conflict and reopen the waterway, but the arrangement collapsed within weeks after attacks on shipping resumed and the United States reinstated its blockade. Iran has continued to insist on retaining some degree of control over shipping through the strait, including routes passing through Iranian territorial waters. According to the BBC , the US military has been providing protection for tankers transporting oil through the Strait of Hormuz to maintain exports from Gulf Arab countries. The latest strikes on Qeshm Island have added to uncertainty surrounding the negotiations, as mediators continue efforts to secure an agreement and prevent a broader resumption of hostilities. https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/04/two-.body: Share Payrav Chorshanbiev , asia+ Categories Economics Society Tajikistan Format News Published 04.11.2026 16:28 Translations Eng Рус Two new 220/110/10 kV substations are under construction in and around Dushanbe to improve the reliability of electricity supplies and reduce pressure on existing power networks. Tajikistan’s Minister of Energy and Water Resources, Daler Juma, inspected construction of the Gharbi (Western) substation in the capital on November 4 and attended a groundbreaking ceremony for another substation in Roudaki district. According to the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources, the two projects are expected to strengthen the electricity supply to Dushanbe and surrounding areas, reduce technical losses and ease the load on existing transmission lines and substations. New substation to be built near Victory Park A new 220/110/10 kV substation will be constructed near Victory Park, in Qiblai rural jamoat of Roudaki district. The facility is designed to improve the reliability of electricity supplies to Dushanbe and neighboring cities and districts. The groundbreaking ceremony was attended by Dushanbe Deputy Mayor Mehriddin Tohirzoda, Director-General of OJSC Shabakahoi Intiqoli Barq (Electricity Transmission Networks) Mirzo Mahmoudzoda, Japanese Ambassador to Tajikistan Keiko Furuta, and a representative of the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA). The project is being financed by the Tajik government and JICA, with OJSC Tajikgidroelektromontazh (TGEM – hydroelectric installation) serving as the construction contractor. The project forms part of Tajikistan’s energy sector development plan for 2022–2030. According to the ministry, the new substation will help reduce technical electricity losses and relieve pressure on existing substations and 110–220 kV transmission lines. Construction is scheduled for completion in August 2028. Gharbi substation to be completed in April 2028 On the same day, Daler Juma inspected construction of the Gharbi 220/110/10 kV substation in western Dushanbe. According to the ministry, construction is progressing according to schedule. Site preparation has been completed, and temporary administrative and production facilities have been erected. The substation will be equipped with two autotransformers, each with a capacity of 200 MVA. OJSC Shabakahoi Intiqoli Barq is the project owner, while TGEM is responsible for construction. Under the project, a double-circuit 220 kV transmission line will connect the Gharbi substation to the Regar-500 substation. Six 110 kV cable lines will also be installed to connect Gharbi with the Sanoati, Boghi Iram and Zavodi substations. These connections are expected to reduce the load on the Nav and Daryokanor substations and improve the stability of electricity supplies throughout the capital. The Gharbi substation is scheduled to be completed in April 2028. Asia-Plus previously reported on the launch of the project in April 2026. The facility is being built in the Juybodom neighborhood in western Dushanbe. In addition to its main equipment, the substation will feature voltage regulation systems, relay protection and automation equipment, technical facilities and backup power supplies. During his visits, Daler Juma instructed those responsible to ensure high construction standards and meet the established deadlines. At the Gharbi site, he also emphasized the importance of close coordination between the project owner, the contractor and local authorities to prevent delays. Join us on social media! https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/04/reco.body: Share Idibek Said , asia+ Categories Culture Governance Kazakhstan Society Tajikistan Format News Published 04.11.2026 14:36 Translations Eng Тоҷ Рус فارسی Tajik musician Nourali Shermatazoda, a member of the Daryo ensemble, and theater and film actress Mohpaykar Yorova have been awarded Kazakhstan’s Order of Dostyq (Friendship), Second Class, for their contributions to strengthening friendship and cultural cooperation between the two countries. Speaking to Asia-Plus, the two artists shared their impressions of receiving the prestigious award. The awards were presented on October 30 by Kazakh Vice President Yerlan Karin during a ceremony honoring cultural and arts figures from Central Asia in Astana. According to the Kazakh president’s press service, Karin emphasized the important role of cultural figures in strengthening friendship and mutual understanding among the peoples of Central Asia. “Art knows no borders. Through your work, you bring our peoples closer together and help the younger generation gain a deeper understanding of the culture and traditions of neighboring countries,” Karin said. “Recognition of 35 years of dedication” Honored Artist of Tajikistan Mohpaykar Yorova said the award came as an unexpected and pleasant surprise. She recalled participating in several international festivals in Kazakhstan with theatrical productions including Night Far from the Homeland and Dirafshi Koviyoni . “I received an award for Best Actress there, and cultural experts from Kazakhstan later told me they had nominated me for the Order of Dostyq,” Yorova told Asia-Plus . For the actress, the honor represents recognition not only of her personal achievements but also of the collective efforts of those with whom she has worked throughout her career. “This order is recognition of the contributions of all the creative people, cultural figures, friends and colleagues with whom we have worked over the past 35 years,” she said. “This award belongs to all of Tajikistan” People’s Artist of Tajikistan Nourali Shermatazoda, a flutist with the Daryo ensemble, also described the award as recognition of years of artistic dedication. “This award belongs to all of Tajikistan. When your work is appreciated, you feel great joy and gratitude that your efforts over many years have been recognized,” he told Asia-Plus. Shermatazoda said he and Yorova were the first Tajik cultural figures to receive the distinction. “We had the honor of becoming the first Tajik cultural figures to receive this order. It helps strengthen friendship and good-neighborly relations among the peoples of Central Asia, particularly among performers, musicians and singers,” he said. The musician has participated in numerous cultural events in Kazakhstan, including the Days of Tajik Culture, Shanghai Cooperation Organization events and other international cultural programs in Astana and Almaty. He believes his long-standing involvement in these activities contributed to his selection for the award. Shermatazoda added that he is currently on vacation but plans to resume his artistic activities and pursue new creative projects upon his return. About the Order of Dostyq The Order of Dostyq (Friendship) is a state decoration of Kazakhstan established in 1995. It is awarded to individuals who have made significant contributions to promoting peace, friendship, cooperation and mutual understanding between peoples, as well as strengthening international relations. The order has two classes. The First Class consists of a star and an insignia worn on a shoulder sash, while the Second Class is awarded as a decoration worn on the chest. Among other prominent Tajik recipients is Rustam Emomali, Speaker of Tajikistan’s Majlisi Milli (the upper house of parliament), who previously received the Order of Dostyq, Second Class, for his contribution to strengthening friendship and the strategic partnership between Tajikistan and Kazakhstan. https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/04/reti.body: Share Payrav Chorshanbiev , asia+ Categories Economics Society Tajikistan Format Details Published 04.11.2026 13:52 A new report by the Asian Development Bank (ADB) suggests considering an increase in Tajikistan’s retirement age as part of broader pension reforms. But what exactly does the bank recommend, how have the authorities responded, and would raising the retirement age address the country’s pension challenges? A new country diagnostic study by the Asian Development Bank, titled Economic Transformation for Sustainable and Inclusive Growth in Tajikistan , identifies pension system modernization as one of the reforms the country should consider. The report outlines two possible approaches to changing the retirement age. The first would gradually increase the retirement age for women from 58 to 63, bringing it into line with the current retirement age for men. The second would gradually raise the retirement age to 65 for both men and women. The ADB also recommends considering an increase in the minimum contribution period required to qualify for a pension — from 25 to 30 years for men and from 20 to 30 years for women. However, two important points should be emphasized. First, no decision has been made to increase the retirement age in Tajikistan . Second, raising the retirement age is only one of several measures examined in the report. The ADB’s recommendations go well beyond this proposal. What other reforms does the ADB recommend? The report raises a fundamental question: how can Tajikistan ensure that its pension system remains financially sustainable over the next 10, 20 or 30 years? One of the main challenges identified by the ADB is the limited coverage of the population by pension insurance. According to the report, approximately 2.1 million people were registered in the pension insurance system in 2024, representing roughly one-third of the working-age population. However, registration does not necessarily mean that a person makes regular pension contributions. The ADB attributes limited coverage partly to informal employment, irregular contributions and shortcomings in record-keeping. To address these problems, the report recommends expanding pension insurance coverage among self-employed people and informal-sector workers, improving registration procedures and strengthening information exchange between government agencies. Social pensions: who should pay? Another proposed reform concerns the financing of social pensions. Contributory pensions are based on pension entitlements accumulated through contributions during a person’s working life. Social pensions, meanwhile, provide support to certain groups of citizens who do not qualify for contributory pensions. The ADB recommends gradually transferring responsibility for financing social pensions directly to the state budget under a multi-year plan. Such a change would establish a clearer distinction between the insurance and social welfare functions of the pension system. Under this approach, contributory pensions would primarily be financed through pension contributions, while support for people without sufficient pension entitlements would come from the state budget. Pension levels remain a concern The ADB also draws attention to the relatively low level of pension payments in Tajikistan. In 2024, the average old-age pension was 475.8 somoni, compared with an average monthly wage of 2,148.9 somoni. This means the average pension amounted to approximately 22.1% of the average wage. The report recommends improving mechanisms for adjusting pensions to inflation and changes in the cost of living. It also calls for indicators to assess whether pension payments provide an adequate standard of living. Financial sustainability is important, but so is the question of whether pensioners receive enough money to meet their basic needs. Better records and more transparency Another priority identified by the ADB is improving the management of pension contributions. The report recommends strengthening individual contribution records, improving information exchange between government institutions and expanding digital services. For workers, these improvements could make it easier to check how much has been contributed on their behalf and what pension entitlements they have accumulated. For the government, more reliable information would provide a clearer picture of pension revenues and future obligations. Without accurate contribution records, it is difficult to estimate how much financing the pension system will require in the coming decades. The ADB also recommends developing voluntary pension savings schemes and introducing clearer regulations for non-state pension funds, including licensing, investment rules and supervision. What have the Tajik authorities said? Following media reports about the ADB’s recommendations, Tajikistan’s Social Insurance and Pensions Agency clarified that the proposals are advisory and do not change existing legislation. The agency stated that pension eligibility and payment conditions are regulated by national law. According to the agency, any changes to the retirement age, required contribution periods or other pension eligibility conditions must be considered and approved through the procedures established by Tajik legislation. Such changes would take effect only after the relevant legal acts entered into force. For now, Tajikistan’s retirement age remains unchanged: 58 for women and 63 for men. How many workers support each pensioner? Official statistics provide some insight into the challenges facing Tajikistan’s pension system. According to the country’s Statistics Agency, Tajikistan had 894,923 pensioners as of October 1, 2026. Meanwhile, the employed population stood at approximately 2.851 million in August. This translates into roughly 3.2 employed people for every pensioner. However, this does not mean that all 3.2 workers regularly pay pension insurance contributions. Of the 2.851 million employed people, approximately 1.307 million were registered as wage employees at enterprises of various forms of ownership in August, accounting for 45.8% of total employment. The remaining workers are not necessarily excluded from the pension system. They include entrepreneurs, members of dehqon farms and other categories of employed people who may also pay social contributions. For comparisons with neighboring countries, it is more appropriate to use statistics compiled using a consistent methodology and covering the same period. According to data from the CIS Statistical Committee , the number of pensioners per 1,000 employed people in 2024 was: Country Pensioners per 1,000 employed people Employed people per pensioner Tajikistan 318 3.1 Kazakhstan 347 2.9 Kyrgyzstan 347 2.9 Uzbekistan 347 2.9 Russia 555 1.8 The difference between Tajikistan’s more recent ratio of 3.2 and the CIS Statistical Committee’s figure of 3.1 is largely explained by the different reporting periods. Neither figure, however, is sufficient on its own to determine whether the pension system is financially sustainable. Consider two countries with three employed people for every pensioner. In one country, nearly all three workers regularly pay pension contributions. In the other, only one does. Although the ratio of workers to pensioners is identical, the amount of money flowing into the pension system would be very different. A more accurate assessment therefore requires data on the number of regular contributors, total contribution revenues and pension expenditure. Long-term projections of employment, population ageing, life expectancy and migration are also essential. Raising the retirement age is only one option The retirement age influences pension expenditure, but it is not the only factor determining the financial health of the system. When people retire later, they generally receive pensions for fewer years and may contribute to the system for longer. This can help improve its financial balan

https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/04/assi.body: Share asia+ Categories Society Tajikistan Format News Published 04.11.2026 10:36 Translations Eng Рус The Muzaffar Charitable Foundation has launched Map of Help, described as Tajikistan’s first digital charity platform, bringing together information about social institutions across the country, their specific needs and ways to provide targeted financial assistance. The platform, available on the foundation’s official website, muzaffar.tj , features an interactive map of Tajikistan, with each marker representing a social institution in need of support. The project covers all regions of the country, including the Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Region (GBAO), Sughd and Khatlon provinces, and the districts subordinate to the central government. The map includes residential care homes for elderly people and people with disabilities, boarding schools for orphans and children without parental care, and other social institutions requiring assistance. Each institution has a dedicated profile containing a description, contact information, photographs and videos highlighting its specific needs. Users can explore the map, select an institution and find out what kind of support it requires. How does the platform work? The platform is designed to make charitable donations more accessible and targeted. Each institution’s profile includes a QR code that allows donors to transfer money directly to the selected organization. To make a donation, users simply choose an institution on the map, review its needs and scan the QR code. The system allows donors to decide independently where their contributions go and which specific needs they wish to support. The platform is also intended to encourage participation by businesses, civil society organizations and other potential partners interested in supporting social initiatives. Map of Help was developed in partnership with TechnoHub Dushanbe, which provided its technical support free of charge. Educational support for disadvantaged young people The platform was unveiled at a roundtable in Dushanbe titled Strengthening Cooperation in Addressing Social Issues , organized by the Muzaffar Charitable Foundation. During the event, the foundation also presented Oyanday Nek, an educational support program for talented young people, including orphans, children who have lost one parent and those from low-income families. One of the program’s key initiatives is the creation of targeted savings to help cover tuition fees at universities in Tajikistan. The program also aims to support young people’s professional development by providing internship opportunities and assistance with future employment. Five cooperation agreements signed The roundtable brought together representatives of Tajikistan’s Ministry of Education and Science, the Ministry of Health and Social Protection of the Population, and several major companies. Participants discussed ways to strengthen cooperation between government institutions, businesses and charitable organizations, including opportunities to pool resources and expand private sector participation in social projects. The event concluded with the signing of five memoranda of understanding on cooperation between the Muzaffar Charitable Foundation and Alif Bank, Lak-Lak, Leader Consulting, Sofia Clinic and Diamed Medical Center. The agreements are intended to support future cooperation and the joint implementation of charitable and social initiatives. Join us on social media!
