https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/04/sout.body: Share Manzuma Firuz , asia+ Categories Communication Tajikistan Format News Published 04.11.2026 09:43 Translations Eng Тоҷ Рус South Korea will provide Dushanbe with a grant of up to $1.9 million to develop an intelligent transport system aimed at improving traffic management and public transportation in the Tajik capital. The agreement was formalized in a protocol signed by representatives of the Dushanbe city administration and South Korea’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport. According to the Dushanbe city administration, the agreement was reached during an official visit by a delegation from the Tajik capital to South Korea, scheduled for November 2–6. On November 2–3, the delegation held talks with Kim Seok-ji, an assistant minister at South Korea’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, and other officials. Following the talks, the two sides signed a protocol to begin implementing the Smart Transport Development in Dushanbe project. The document paves the way for South Korean grant funding to modernize the capital’s urban transport management system. ‹ › How will the funds be used? The project aims to introduce modern technologies to improve traffic management, reduce congestion and enhance the efficiency of urban transportation. Planned measures include intelligent traffic monitoring, road condition assessment, infrastructure management and improvements to public transport operations. During the visit, the Dushanbe delegation also visited the Road Traffic Research Institute, the Gyeonggi Province Transportation Information Center, KD Transportation Group and other South Korean institutions involved in transport management. Delegation members studied South Korea’s experience in applying digital technologies to traffic management, analyzing transport data and monitoring road infrastructure. The cooperation also provides for training Dushanbe’s transport specialists, introducing modern management practices and strengthening the capacity of municipal transport services. South Korea’s involvement in Tajikistan’s transport projects South Korea has also been involved in several other transport infrastructure initiatives in Tajikistan, including preparations for a proposed metro system in Dushanbe. Earlier, Tajikistan’s Minister of Transport, Azim Ibrohim, held talks with a South Korean delegation led by Yoon Hak-sun, a representative of Korea National Railway. The discussions focused on expanding railway cooperation, implementing investment projects and advancing preliminary work on the proposed Dushanbe metro. At the time, four South Korean-supported projects were being implemented in Tajikistan’s transport sector, three of which were nearing completion. In November 2025, the two cou ntries signed a memorandum covering three projects: establishing a logistics center in the Kulob Free Economic Zone, preparing a preliminary feasibility study for a metro line connecting the State Circus with Dushanbe’s eastern gates, and providing advisory assistance to the working group overseeing the metro project. In May 2026, Tajik specialists also completed a five-day training program in South Korea, where they studied tunnel construction technologies, metro station operations and transport hub management. Meanwhile, Korea National Railway has published details of a separate intelligent transport development project for Dushanbe covering 2026–2028. The project envisages developing a digital transport master plan, establishing a pilot transport corridor and preparing a concept for a centralized traffic and public transport management center. According to the published information, the contract is valued at 2.738 billion South Korean won, equivalent to approximately $1.77 million. Join us on social media! https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/04/taji.body: Share Payrav Chorshanbiev , asia+ Categories Economics Society Tajikistan Published 04.11.2026 10:13 Translations Eng فارسی Тоҷ Рус Labor migration helps Tajikistan ease unemployment and support household incomes, but maintaining migration at its current scale could become increasingly difficult in the long term, according to a new report by the Eurasian Fund for Stabilization and Development (EFSD). The report, titled Economic Growth, Demographics and the Labor Market: Realities and Challenges , was presented on October 29 at the international economic conference Toward Balanced Economic Development in Astana. According to the report, labor migration remains one of Tajikistan’s main mechanisms for easing pressure on its domestic labor market. With the national economy unable to generate enough jobs for everyone seeking employment, many citizens look for work abroad. Money sent home by migrant workers helps sustain household consumption, reduce poverty and stimulate domestic demand. The report notes that remittances have reached the equivalent of nearly half of Tajikistan’s gross domestic product (GDP) in some periods, making it one of the world’s most remittance-dependent economies. Why does dependence on migration pose risks? EFSD experts warn that changes in the migration policies of destination countries could make it increasingly difficult for Tajik citizens to find employment abroad. Russia remains the main destination for Tajik labor migrants. However, tighter migration regulations are limiting the Russian labor market’s ability to absorb foreign workers. Kazakhstan also attracts workers from neighboring countries, but its labor market remains considerably smaller than Russia’s in terms of employment opportunities for migrants. Heavy reliance on earnings from abroad also creates challenges for Tajikistan’s domestic economy. According to the researchers, while remittances boost household spending and imports, they do not necessarily lead to increased domestic production or the creation of more productive, better-paid jobs. Migration may also discourage some workers from pursuing vocational education and professional training, particularly when jobs available abroad require relatively few qualifications. Tajikistan’s working-age population to grow by 2.46 million Demographic trends are expected to put additional pressure on Tajikistan’s labor market over the coming years. According to EFSD projections, the country’s working-age population, defined as people aged 15–64, will increase from 6.34 million in 2025 to 8.8 million by 2040. This represents an increase of 2.46 million people over 15 years, potentially creating substantial additional demand for jobs. EFSD experts argue that Tajikistan cannot rely on labor migration alone to address its employment challenges. They recommend expanding domestic employment opportunities, supporting private sector development, creating more productive jobs and improving workforce skills. How dependent is Tajikistan on labor migration? World Bank data illustrate the scale of Tajikistan’s dependence on money earned abroad. In 2025, remittances were equivalent to approximately 46% of the country’s GDP, compared with 39% in 2023 and around 49% in 2024. An estimated one-quarter of Tajikistan’s workforce travels abroad in search of employment. One of the main drivers of labor migration is the substantial wage gap between Tajikistan and destination countries. According to the Agency for Statistics under the President of Tajikistan, the average monthly wage in the country stood at 3,508 somoni in July 2026. The World Bank estimates that Tajik migrants working in Russia can earn at least three times as much as they would in comparable jobs at home, even in relatively low-skilled occupations. Such dependence leaves Tajikistan vulnerable to developments in Russia’s labor market. Fewer job opportunities, stricter migration regulations or declining migrant earnings could reduce remittance inflows, putting pressure on household incomes and domestic consumption. https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/04/cent.body: Share asia+ Categories Central Asia Economics Format News Published 04.11.2026 11:07 Central Asia’s power grid could face serious pressure this winter as rising electricity demand, aging infrastructure and limited generating capacity threaten the stability of supplies across the region. Concerns are particularly acute in Kyrgyzstan, where an early cold spell has driven a sharp increase in electricity consumption. According to an October 29 report by the Kyrgyz news agency 24.kg , the region’s electricity network remains vulnerable to overloads, raising concerns about possible disruptions during the winter months. Citing a study by the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB), the agency reported that several sections of Central Asia’s power grid operated above their permitted capacity in 2024, with loads reaching 105–123% of allowable levels. Demir Kabylbayev, Senior Analyst at the Eurasian Development Bank’s Center for Industry Analysis, reportedly noted during the presentation of a new study that temporary overloads may occur under emergency operating conditions. However, as regional electricity trade expands, the limited transmission capacity of such power lines becomes a serious obstacle. Particularly vulnerable sections included cross-border transmission lines connecting Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, as well as Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. The EDB report identifies the availability of electricity during peak demand periods as one of the region’s main challenges. According to the bank, the problem is not simply a shortage of installed generating capacity. Fuel supply limitations, fluctuations in water availability, outages at thermal power plants and transmission bottlenecks mean that some generating capacity becomes unavailable precisely when electricity demand is highest. The EDB’s findings highlight the importance of strengthening electricity transmission networks and improving regional energy cooperation to reduce the risk of shortages and disruptions during periods of peak winter demand. Kyrgyzstan seeks to prevent winter power shortages Kyrgyzstan is already experiencing growing pressure on its electricity system following an unusually early onset of cold weather. 24.kg reported on October 30 that according to the National Electric Network of Kyrgyzstan (NENK), daily electricity consumption in Kyrgyzstan has increased by 29.1% compared with the same period last year. The company reported that daily electricity consumption reached 66.022 million kilowatt-hours (kWh), up from 51.132 million kWh on October 30, 2025. This reportedly represents an increase of 14.89 million kWh over the year, or 29.1%. Amid rising demand, NENK urged residents to use electricity responsibly and conserve energy resources. On October 28, Kyrgyz Energy Minister Altynbek Rysbekov met his Uzbek counterpart, Sherzod Khojayev, in Tashkent to discuss cooperation aimed at ensuring stable electricity supplies throughout the cold season. https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/03/in-s.body: Share Manzuma Firuz , asia+ Categories Governance Tajikistan Format News Photo Published 03.11.2026 17:11 Translations Eng Рус Tajik President Emomali Rahmon inaugurated a soft drink production plant in the Sughd Free Economic Zone and a riverside restaurant in Khujand on November 3. He was also presented with plans to build new bridges, hotels and other facilities in Sughd province, according to the president’s official website. New beverage plant to export 60% of its products President Rahmon inaugurated the Rayan beverage plant in the Sughd Free Economic Zone (FEZ Sughd), which will produce aloe vera drinks, iced tea and fruit juices. The plant has a production capacity of up to 65 tons per day, with approximately 60% of its output intended for export. The facility was built by entrepreneurs Sayedamon and Jahongirkhon Isomiddinzoda and has created 60 jobs. ‹ › According to the president’s official website, 29 enterprises operating in manufacturing, construction and services are currently based in the FEZ Sughd. In 2026, products manufactured there were exported to 12 countries. Industrial output in the zone reached 485 million somoni during the first nine months of 2026, an increase of 66 million somoni compared with the same period last year. Riverside fish restaurant opens in Khujand On the same day, Rahmon inaugurated the Forel Platinum restaurant on Syr-Darya Street in Khujand. The restaurant, located on the banks of the Syr Darya River, was built by Gulmohi Khujand at the initiative of entrepreneur Muhsin Shodiyev. Specializing in trout dishes, the restaurant serves smoked, fried and boiled fish, alongside traditional Tajik and European cuisine. The establishment employs both local and foreign chefs and has created around 80 jobs for local residents. It also features its own bakery and a banquet hall for weddings and other events. ‹ › According to the presidential press service, Forel Platinum is Shodiyev’s third restaurant. His other establishments include one on the banks of the Dushanbe River in the capital and another on the Syr Darya in Khujand. Visitors to the new restaurant can also enjoy boat rides along the river. During the opening ceremony, Rahmon was shown a boat built by Khujand resident Mirzorahim Qodiri over the course of a year. The president suggested launching domestic production of similar boats for use on Tajikistan’s major rivers and reservoirs. ‹ › Two new bridges planned across the Syr Darya During his visit, Rahmon also reviewed several road infrastructure projects aimed at improving transport connections in Khujand. One project involves constructing a new bridge linking Rifat Hojiyev Avenue with the turnoff to Rahmon Nabiyev Street. The proposed bridge will be 200 meters long and 25.55 meters wide, with four traffic lanes and pedestrian walkways. Its structure will include seven reinforced concrete supports and 84 beams. The second phase of the development plan provides for the reconstruction of two existing bridges and the construction of another bridge on Ismoil Somoni Avenue. ‹ › The new bridge will be 275 meters long and supported by eight reinforced concrete pillars and 140 beams. The projects also include strengthening the banks of the Syr Darya and upgrading two major roads in Khujand. On the river’s left bank, a 3.8-kilometer section of Rahmon Nabiyev Street is to be reconstructed, providing two traffic lanes in each direction. A further 3.2 kilometers of Istiqlol Avenue will also be upgraded, with the road expanded to three lanes in each direction. Additional work will include the construction of drainage systems and retaining walls, as well as the installation of street lighting. Rahmon instructed officials overseeing the projects to ensure high construction standards and the use of quality materials. The authorities have not yet announced when construction and reconstruction work will begin or when the projects are expected to be completed. Hilton hotel, new library and teahouse planned for Sughd The president also reviewed plans for several other major developments in Sughd province. These include a Center of Aryan Civilization, a regional library and a National Teahouse on the banks of the Syr Darya. ‹ › Plans also envisage the construction of a hotel under the international Hilton brand and the Istiqlol hotel complex. In the nearby city of Buston, the existing Khujand hotel is scheduled for modernization. The presidential press service did not disclose the estimated costs, funding sources or implementation timelines for these projects. In addition, Rahmon remotely inaugurated several facilities serving various purposes in Jabbor-Rasoulov district. ‹ › Join us on social media! https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/03/taji.body: Share Payrav Chorshanbiev , asia+ Categories Economics Money Tajikistan Format News Published 03.11.2026 15:08 Translations Eng Тоҷ Рус Tajikistan has received $100 million from the Eurasian Fund for Stabilization and Development (EFSD) as the first instalment of a $200 million loan aimed at supporting the state budget and economic reforms. The funds were disbursed on October 30, according to the EFSD press service. The loan has been provided for 20 years at an annual interest rate of 1%, with a 10-year grace period. The financing supports a macroeconomic stabilization and structural reform program being implemented by the Tajik government and the National Bank of Tajikistan (NBT) between 2025 and 2027. It is intended to strengthen public finances, help the government meet its budgetary obligations and support economic reforms. EFSD Managing Director Yaroslav Mandron said the financing rests on three key principles: maintaining balanced macroeconomic policies, ensuring the country’s ability to meet its financial obligations and implementing reforms to strengthen the economy. According to Mandron, these measures are expected to reduce fiscal risks, improve tax collection and strengthen the government’s financial capacity. “In the long term, this will enhance the resilience and capacity of the budget of the Republic of Tajikistan,” he said. When will Tajikistan receive the remaining $100 million? Tajikistan and the EFSD signed the $200 million loan agreement in Dushanbe on August 13, 2026. The agreement was signed by Tajik Finance Minister Fayziddin Qahhorzoda and EFSD Managing Director Yaroslav Mandron. As Asia-Plus previously reported, citing the Ministry of Finance, the financing will be disbursed in three instalments: an initial $100 million, followed by two payments of $50 million each. With the first instalment transferred, Tajikistan has now received half of the agreed loan amount. The financing is scheduled for disbursement during 2026–2027, with the release of subsequent instalments conditional on the implementation of reforms and other measures outlined in the program. The Majlisi Namoyandagon (Tajikistan’s lower house of parliament) ratified the loan agreement on October 1, and it entered into force on October 16. What will the money be used for? According to the EFSD, the loan will finance state budget expenditures, including priority social spending. The financing comes as Tajikistan faces additional pressure on its public finances from repayments of international Eurobonds. The loan is linked to a reform program. comprising 12 measures in three main areas: maintaining macroeconomic stability, improving fiscal policy and reducing financial risks, and increasing the transparency of economic policy. The measures include strengthening fiscal sustainability, improving tax administration and reducing risks arising from government liabilities and the financial obligations of state-owned enterprises. The EFSD expects these reforms to make Tajikistan’s public finances more resilient and create more stable conditions for economic growth. What is the Eurasian Fund for Stabilization and Development? The Eurasian Fund for Stabilization and Development is a regional financial mechanism established in 2009 by six countries: Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia and Tajikistan. The fund has resources totaling $9.8 billion and provides financial assistance to its member states to promote economic stability and sustainable development. It also forms part of the global financial safety net, serving as a regional mechanism for financial stability in Eurasia. Join us on social media! https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/11/03/uzbe.body: Share asia+ Categories Society Uzbekistan Format News Published 03.11.2026 10:28 Translations Eng Рус Uzbekistan plans to transfer responsibility for arranging overseas employment to approved private recruitment agencies from 2027 and establish migration centers across the country as part of a major reform of its labor migration system. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced the measures at a meeting on November 2, according to Fergana . The reforms are intended to expand access to jobs abroad, improve vocational and language training, strengthen migrant workers’ protections and support citizens returning from overseas. Officials said Uzbekistan has expanded organized labor migration partnerships from three countries to 27, while the number of major foreign employers involved has increased by nearly 400. Following simplified licensing procedures, the number of private recruitment agencies has tripled over the past two years, while the number of citizens securing jobs abroad through these agencies has increased fivefold. Under the proposed system, approved private agencies will take over overseas recruitment functions. An open ranking of agencies will also be introduced, assessing their employment results, protection of workers’ rights and provision of social guarantees. Authorities estimate that employment opportunities are available for 287,000 Uzbek citizens across 34 countries this year. However, officials acknowledged that information about vacancies remains difficult for the public to access. To address this, overseas job opportunities will be advertised through the Onlayn-mahalla digital platform at the community level. Regional governors will review the results monthly, while district officials will monitor progress twice a month. German language training and overseas jobs Improving vocational skills and foreign language proficiency will be another major focus of the reforms. Mirziyoyev cited Germany, which has requested 45,000 workers from Uzbekistan this year. However, only 2,000 Uzbek citizens have secured employment there, largely because of insufficient German language skills. The president ordered German language courses to be introduced alongside vocational training at two or three technical colleges in each region. University places allocated for training German language teachers will also be doubled. The Intil international training center, working with the language certification organization Telc, is already training 100 German language teachers. Plans also include recruiting 500 additional native speakers. Based on the center’s experience, a unified labor migration center will be established in each of Uzbekistan’s 14 regions in 2027. Each region will receive 8 billion soums (more than $660,000) to establish these centers. The government aims to train 10,000 people in vocational skills and German, helping them secure employment in Germany. Within a month, 20 technical colleges will be selected to adapt their curricula to the requirements of foreign employers. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/11/06/cott.body: Photo: Madina A'zam / Gazeta.uz Uzbekistan harvests over 5 million tonnes of cotton for first time in 35 years Uzbekistan harvested over 5 million tonnes of cotton for the first time in 35 years. The figure was achieved despite the area under cotton cultivation halving since 1990, while average yields more than doubled. Mechanized harvesting accounted for 85% of the crop this year. На русском языке Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida Yesterday, 16:19 Politics Uzbekistan harvested more than 5 million tonnes of cotton for the first time in 35 years. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, congratulating farmers, described the achievement as a “truly historic victory” and “a true miracle of New Uzbekistan in cotton farming”. The record was achieved despite the area under cotton cultivation halving since 1990, when the country harvested 5.058 million tonnes of cotton, from 1.83 million to 890,000 hectares. Since 1990, average yields have doubled, rising from 2.76 to 5.62 tonnes per hectare (compared with 4.55 tonnes per hectare in 2025). Average yields reached 7 tonnes per hectare on nearly 400,000 hectares, while yields of 10−11 tonnes per hectare were recorded on around 70,000 hectares. The average yield is expected to increase to 6.5−7 tonnes per hectare next year. Advertising on Gazeta More than 3,000 cotton-picking machines harvested 85% of this year’s crop in 30−35 days. In Jizzakh and Syrdarya regions, mechanized harvesting accounted for 100% of the crop. “We cannot help but recall the difficult times when cotton farming brought not prosperity but hardship and suffering to the country and its people, and ultimately led to unfounded slander — the so-called ‘Cotton case',” the president said. He recalled that during the Soviet era, particularly in the 1980s, around 2 million hectares in the republic were devoted to cotton cultivation, while average yields did not exceed 3 tonnes per hectare. In recent years, the area under cotton cultivation has decreased by 38%, and the cotton monopoly has been abolished. Teachers, university students, schoolchildren and public-sector employees are no longer mobilized for fieldwork and cotton harvesting. Among the factors contributing to higher yields, the president cited the adoption of new technologies, including drones, and the introduction of high-yielding cotton varieties. “It is particularly important that, thanks to the widespread adoption of water-saving technologies, water consumption has halved compared with the 1990s, while the amount of cotton produced per cubic meter of water continues to increase,” the president emphasized. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/11/06/infl.body: Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta Annual inflation in Uzbekistan accelerates to 6.5% in October Annual inflation in Uzbekistan accelerated to 6.5% in October, with consumer prices increasing by 0.6% over the month. Food accounted for nearly two-thirds of the increase. Egg prices rose by 5.2%, petrol by 1% and Tashkent bus and metro fares by 26.1%, while propane went up by 44.7% year-on-year. На русском языке Yesterday, 16:20 Economy Consumer prices in Uzbekistan rose by 0.6% in October, the National Statistics Committee said . Inflation stood at 0.7% in September and 0.6% in October last year. Annual inflation accelerated to 6.5%, up from 6.4% in September. However, it remained below the 7.8% recorded in October 2025. Since the beginning of the year, consumer prices have increased by 4.8%, compared with 5.7% in January-October last year. Food prices increased by 1% month-on-month and 6.4% year-on-year. Non-food goods became 0.2% more expensive over the month and 5.6% year-on-year. Services became 0.6% more expensive over the month and 7.3% over the year. Annual price growth for food accelerated from 6.3% in September to 6.4%, while that for services increased from 7% to 7.3%. Annual inflation for non-food goods, by contrast, slowed from 5.8% to 5.6%. Among major food products, eggs recorded the largest monthly price increase, at 5.2%. Compared with October last year, their prices were 12.7% higher. Meat prices continued to rise. Mutton prices increased by 1.4% month-on-month and 19.5% year-on-year, while beef prices rose by 0.9% and 17.1%, respectively. Poultry prices increased by 1.2% month-on-month and 2.1% year-on-year. Fish and seafood became 1.4% more expensive in October and 9% more expensive year-on-year. Milk prices increased by an average of 1% over the month and 5% over the year. Sugar prices, by contrast, fell by 2.2% over the month. However, they remained 0.6% higher than in October last year. Fruit prices fell in October, while vegetable prices increased. However, many vegetables remained cheaper than a year earlier. Petrol prices rose by an average of 1% in October and 19.5% year-on-year. Advertising on Gazeta Automotive propane became 0.4% more expensive over the month and 44.7% more expensive over the year. Methane prices remained unchanged month-on-month but increased by 10% year-on-year. In Tashkent, the introduction of new tariffs resulted in a 26.1% increase in bus and metro fares. Taxi fares increased by an average of 1.3% nationwide, including 2.5% in Tashkent. Domestic airfares, by contrast, fell by 1.4% over the month and 4.9% year-on-year. The National Statistics Committee attributed this decline to the soum’s appreciation against the euro. International airfares rose by 0.7% over the month but remained 2.5% lower year-on-year. He said this indicates that more people find employment as skilled professionals rather than unskilled workers. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 2 November 2026, 19:58 Economy Over the past 10 years, the number of citizens of Uzbekistan working abroad has halved, while the volume of remittances they send to their families has quadrupled, president Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced at a meeting on labor migration on 2 November. This indicates a change in how citizens of Uzbekistan are viewed in the international labor market, with more of them finding employment abroad as skilled professionals rather than unskilled workers, he noted. There are many citizens willing to work abroad, while other countries need workers. Bringing these two opportunities together should become one of the main tasks of the relevant government agencies and regional authorities, the head of state said. “People must become highly proficient in their profession, know their worth and be able to count on their country!” Mirziyoyev said. He noted that Uzbekistan’s approach to organized labor migration had changed significantly in recent years. Whereas the country had previously cooperated with just 3 countries in this area, that number has now reached 27. Advertising on Gazeta The number of major foreign employers cooperating with Uzbekistan has also reached nearly 400. Remittances vary significantly across regions The president pointed to significant differences in the volume of remittances across Uzbekistan’s regions. According to him, the average monthly amount sent per person working abroad is $1,850 in the Fergana region. The amounts are significantly lower in other regions: Karakalpakstan and Tashkent region — less than $400; Syrdarya region — less than $500; Jizzakh and Navoi regions — less than $600; Surkhandarya and Khorezm regions — less than $700. The president called for a review of the work of hokims (governors), ambassadors and heads of technical colleges in preparing citizens for employment in higher-paying jobs abroad. “People must know in advance where they will work, what salary they will receive and who will protect their rights!” Mirziyoyev said. Remittances continue to grow According to the Central Bank, remittances to Uzbekistan reached $18.9 billion in 2025, up 28%, or $4.1 billion, compared with 2024. The increase was driven by sustained demand for labor in destination countries, rising wages, the strengthening of certain foreign currencies and the expansion of employment opportunities for citizens of Uzbekistan abroad. In January-June 2026, remittances totaled $9.3 billion, an increase of 13%, or $1.1 billion, compared with the same period last year. The most notable growth in remittances was recorded from the United Kingdom (62%), European Union countries (27%) and the United States (19%). At the same time, Russia remains one of the main destinations for labor migrants of Uzbekistan. In April 2026, a presentation to the president said that around 1.2 million citizens of Uzbekistan were working abroad in nearly 40 countries. It was also noted that foreign employers had requested more than 100,000 qualified specialists. The coach attributed the team’s success to the athletes’ dedication, the professionalism of their coaches and strong team spirit. The latest achievement followed another successful performance by Tajik jiu-jitsu athletes in Tashkent just a week earlier. At that tournament, all nine Tajik participants won medals, securing five golds, three silvers and one bronze. Across the two tournaments, Tajik athletes collected a total of 71 medals — 40 gold, 22 silver and nine bronze . Boymurodov said the results demonstrated Tajikistan’s growing competitiveness in international jiu-jitsu, with its athletes capable of winning both individual titles and the overall national medal standings. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/11/05/nuku.body: Photo: UNICEF New health emergency operations center opens in Nukus with US support The new Public Health Emergency Operations Center has opened in Nukus with US financial support and UNICEF technical assistance. A similar center opened in Termez in April. The authorities plan to establish an interconnected system of such centers in all 14 regions of Uzbekistan. На русском языке Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida 5 November 2026, 15:28 Society The new Public Health Emergency Operations Center (PHEOC) opened on 4 November in Nukus in northwestern Uzbekistan to strengthen the country’s capacity to prepare for and respond to infectious disease outbreaks and other public health emergencies. The center was established by the Committee for Sanitary and Epidemiological Welfare and Public Health of Uzbekistan, with financial support from the US government and technical assistance from UNICEF under the Global Health Security Program. It is intended to help health authorities turn early information about emerging threats into coordinated action. Its operational functions include incident management, emergency activation procedures, situation monitoring and information sharing among the institutions responsible for public health preparedness and response, the US embassy and UNICEF in Uzbekistan said in their statements. Deputy chairman of the Sanitary and Epidemiological Welfare Committee Botirjon Qurbonov said Uzbekistan’s priority is to ensure that national and regional institutions are equipped not only with the necessary infrastructure, but also with the capacity to detect public health threats early, coordinate effectively and respond promptly to protect the health of our population. “Strong emergency preparedness is important not only for Uzbekistan, but also for the United States. Epidemics are indifferent to international borders, hence cooperating on global health protects us all,” deputy chief of mission at the US embassy Heather Byrnes noted. Advertising on Gazeta UNICEF representative in Uzbekistan Regina Maria Castillo underscored the importance of moving beyond infrastructure to readiness and coordinated action: the Nukus PHEOC “represents readiness, coordination and the ability to transform information into timely action when lives are at stake”. In April, a similar center was inaugurated in the southern city of Termez. Such centers will be launched in all 14 administrative regions of Uzbekistan to establish an interconnected system for managing public health emergencies across the country. “The long-term value of such a system will depend on more than facilities and equipment. Effective preparedness also relies heavily on community engagement, trusted information, risk communication and the ability to counter misinformation. These measures help families understand risks, take protective action and sustain confidence in public health responses during crises,” the statements said. “For children and families, effective public health preparedness means faster responses and fewer interruptions to essential health services during emergencies,” they added. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/11/03/decl.body: Photo: Shuhrat Latipov / Gazeta How much cash can foreign tourists bring into Uzbekistan? Foreign tourists can bring unlimited amounts of cash into Uzbekistan, but must declare amounts exceeding 100 million soums (currently about $8,380) and keep a copy of the declaration. International bank cards are widely accepted at major tourist destinations. 3 November 2026, 12:17 Society Uzbekistan’s Tourism Committee has reminded foreign tourists of the rules for bringing cash into the country and taking it out. Knowing these requirements in advance can help avoid problems when passing through customs, particularly when leaving the country, the committee said. Under current regulations, travelers may bring unlimited amounts of cash in foreign or national currency into Uzbekistan. However, if the total amount exceeds the equivalent of 100 million soums (around $8,380 at current exchange rate, should be checked before travel), the full sum must be declared in the passenger customs declaration and presented to a customs officer. Travelers may also voluntarily declare smaller amounts. When leaving Uzbekistan, travelers may take out up to the equivalent of 100 million soums without a declaration. If the amount exceeds this threshold, additional customs requirements apply. For foreign citizens, the amount declared upon entry is also taken into account. “A common mistake among tourists is not stating a large amount of cash in the declaration when entering the country. Part of the money may be spent during the trip, and the rest may then need to be taken out. Without a document confirming the money was brought in legally, this can cause problems,” the committee noted. The Tourism Committee gave the example of a tourist bringing $15,000 into Uzbekistan, who must declare the full amount upon arrival. Even if they spend part of the money during their stay, a copy of the declaration will serve as proof of the remaining funds, allowing them to take the remaining funds out of the country, even if they exceed the equivalent of 100 million soums. The committee also recommended that tourists: Declare the full amount if the cash they are carrying when entering Uzbekistan exceeds the equivalent of 100 million soums; Keep a copy of the customs declaration until they leave the country; Remember that the equivalent in soums is calculated using the Central Bank of Uzbekistan’s exchange rate on the day they cross the customs border; Ask a customs officer for clarification if they have any questions before going through customs control. “Following customs rules and keeping the necessary documents will help make your visit to Uzbekistan even more comfortable and stress-free”, the statement concluded. Advertising on Gazeta It is worth noting that international bank cards (like Visa and MasterCard) are widely accepted at major tourist destinations, and cash can be withdrawn (in local currency) at ATMs available in the streets, shopping centers and other places. Some banks offer withdrawal in US dollars at ATMs located inside their buildings. Subscribe to our Telegram channel Gazeta 3 287 # declaration # tourism committee

https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/11/03/oil-.body: Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta Uzbekistan seeks alternative sources of petrol and diesel amid risks of import disruptions Uzbekneftegaz is holding talks with China’s CNPC on supplies of petrol, diesel fuel, crude oil and gas condensate. The company said imports need to be diversified to ensure a stable domestic supply. Earlier, petrol imports to Uzbekistan fell sharply amid attacks on oil refineries in Russia. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 3 November 2026, 07:57 Economy Uzbekneftegaz, state-owned energy company, is negotiating with Chinese companies on supplies of AI-92 and higher-grade petrol and diesel fuel, as well as increased imports of crude oil and gas condensate for processing at the Bukhara Oil Refinery. This was announced by deputy chairman of the company’s Management Board Farid Muminov . According to him, the company is considering new sources of fuel supplies to reduce dependence on existing supply channels and ensure stable supplies to the domestic market. “Today, there are various risks associated with ensuring a stable supply of petroleum products to the population. To eliminate these risks and prevent them from arising, we are considering diversifying imports,” Muminov said. Advertising on Gazeta He added that negotiations also involve PetroChina, a subsidiary of the China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC). “We discussed supplies of petroleum products — petrol and diesel fuel — as well as increasing imports of crude oil and gas condensate for processing at our Bukhara Oil Refinery,” he said. The volumes of future supplies will depend on domestic demand. Negotiations are still ongoing. Asked whether the diversification plans were related to the situation on the Russian fuel market, the company’s representative did not directly confirm such a link, limiting his response to explaining the need to reduce the risks of disruptions to the country’s petroleum product supplies. Press conference of Uzbekneftegaz on 27 October. Between January and August, Uzbekistan imported 721.5 million liters of petrol, 41.2% more than in the same period last year. The value of imports increased by 48.6% to $437.4 million. Monthly imports fell sharply after April. While around 141.8 million liters of petrol entered the country in April, the figure dropped to 72 million liters in May, 50.7 million in June, 18.6 million in July and just 11.4 million liters in August. In August, import volumes fell by 76.8% compared with the same month last year. At the same time, the average price of imported fuel increased significantly. While it stood at around $576 per 1,000 liters in April, it reached almost $995 in August, an increase of around 73%. In August, average petrol prices in Uzbekistan rose by 20.2% year-on-year. In September, the Ministry of Energy attributed the sharp decline in imports to the shutdown of oil refineries in Russia following attacks by Ukrainian drones. Previously, Russia accounted for 85−90% of Uzbekistan’s petrol imports. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/10/28/wb/.body: Photo: World Bank World Bank allocates $100 million to modernize Uzbekistan’s electricity distribution systems The World Bank has approved a $100 million loan to modernize Uzbekistan’s electricity distribution systems. The program includes modernizing and digitizing 60 key substations and integrating at least 3.3 GW of renewable energy capacity. The ADB previously approved $200 million for the program. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 28 October 2026, 19:12 Economy The World Bank’s Board of Executive Directors approved a $100 million loan on 27 October to improve the efficiency and reliability of Uzbekistan’s electricity distribution system, the bank’s press service announced . The Modernization of Electricity Distribution Systems Program will be implemented by National Electric Grid of Uzbekistan. It includes investments in modernizing and digitizing 60 key substations across the country to reduce electricity losses and improve the reliability of power supply. The program will also help strengthen the institutional capacity of National Electric Grid of Uzbekistan and improve the company’s operational efficiency, including by upgrading financial management systems, strengthening cybersecurity, improving compliance with environmental and social standards and promoting gender equality in the company’s workforce. By 2031, the program is expected to reduce annual electricity losses at modernized substations by 20,000 megawatt-hours (MWh). It will also enable the integration of at least 3.3 GW of renewable energy capacity into the power grid. In addition, the program is expected to prevent annual greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to nearly 23,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide. The program is also expected to help create around 11,700 additional quality jobs within five years of the modernized energy infrastructure facilities becoming operational. Advertising on Gazeta The World Bank is financing the program jointly with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) under the global Full Mutual Reliance Framework (FMRF). The framework provides for a unified approach by the two financial institutions to program preparation and implementation oversight, helping reduce transaction costs and avoid duplication of procedures for the government of Uzbekistan. On 30 September, the ADB approved a $200 million loan to Uzbekistan. With the new World Bank loan and a $71 million contribution from the government budget, total program financing amounts to $371 million. “Uzbekistan aims to produce 25 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy by 2030, which will require a stronger and smarter electricity grid. Much of the electricity distribution network was built decades ago and many grid substations are overloaded, which can lead to energy losses and disruptions affecting households, businesses, schools and health clinics. With rapid economic growth increasing the demand for electricity, modernizing the network is a priority,” the World Bank said. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/10/28/dok-.body: Photo: Madina A'zam / Gazeta Uzbekistan allocates almost $5.5 million to compensate families in Doc-1 Max poisoning case Uzbekistan allocated 65.2 billion soums (over $4.47 million) from the state budget to compensate families of 90 children who died or became disabled after poisoning from cough syrups Doc-1 Max and Ambronol. The state plans to recover the funds from the convicted. На русском языке Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida 28 October 2026, 22:02 Society Nearly three years after the court ruling, families of children who died or were severely affected by the cough syrups Doc-1 Max and Ambronol have received compensation. The tragic incidents occurred in 2022. Toxic substances — diethylene glycol and ethylene glycol — were found in syrups manufactured by Indian company Marion Biotech. In February 2024, a court sentenced 23 people to prison terms of up to 20 years and ordered them to pay a total of 82 billion soums in compensation to the families of 68 deceased children and 18 children who were affected. Advertising on Gazeta In 2024, 2 billion soums was paid out, followed by 16.8 billion soums by October 2026, bringing the total to about 20% of the amount awarded by the court. The funds were recovered through the sale of property seized from those convicted. The death toll subsequently rose to 72, while 16 affected children have received or continue receiving treatment. Some children lost their sight and hearing or became unable to walk, while others suffered severe kidney and stomach damage. Throughout these years, relatives of the deceased and affected children appealed to the authorities for compensation. On 28 October, the Health Ministry announced that president Shavkat Mirziyoyev instructed to expedite the payments. The remaining 65.2 billion soums (over $4.47 million) were subsequently allocated from the state budget. According to the ministry, a total of 80 billion soums (over $6.7 million according to current Central Bank rate) has now been transferred to 88 families. Of this amount, 72.2 billion soums was paid to the families of 72 children who died, while 7.8 billion soums went to the families of 16 children who received or continue to receive treatment. A further 2 billion soums is to be paid to the families of two affected children once technical issues involving their bank cards have been resolved. The Health Ministry stressed that the 65.2 billion soums allocated by the state must subsequently be returned to the budget through proceeds from the sale of property belonging to those responsible and further recoveries from those convicted in the case. The ministry also reported that its representatives and officials from other government agencies, together with doctors from national medical centers, were visiting the families of affected children to provide additional medical and psychological assistance. The parents of the children told Gazeta that the compensation was transferred to them between 20 and 24 October. They also said that, starting on 25 October, government representatives and doctors who had arrived from Tashkent began visiting families of children who had become disabled after being poisoned by the medicines. The father of one affected child was told that treatment could be arranged in the capital, with assistance provided for travel and hospitalization. Those convicted in the case include Sardor Kariyev, former director of the Agency for the Development of the Pharmaceutical Industry, who was sentenced to 18 years in prison, and Raghvendra Pratap Singh, former head of Quramax Medical, the company that imported the medicines into Uzbekistan, who received a 20-year sentence. In October 2025, parents who had not received the full court-ordered compensation appealed to the president, asking him to intervene. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/10/27/air-.body: Morning of 27 October 2026 in Tashkent. Photo: Шоҳруҳ Ҳайдаров / Gazeta Climatologist on why air pollution increased in Central Asian cities in October The deterioration in air quality in Tashkent has become one of the most discussed topics in recent days. Erkin Abdulakhatov, head of Laboratory at the Hydrometeorological Research Institute, writes that the issue is not confined to the capital of Uzbekistan. 27 October 2026, 22:00 Society In recent days, the deterioration in ambient air quality in Tashkent has attracted considerable public attention. However, this issue is not confined to the capital of Uzbekistan. Erkin Abdulakhatov, a climatologist, PhD in Geographical Sciences and Head of Laboratory at the Hydrometeorological Research Institute under the National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, provides an explanation of the situation and its underlying causes. His article was published by the Ecology Committee. What figures show An analysis conducted by the Hydrometeorological Research Institute using international and national monitoring data has revealed a simultaneous increase in air pollution across several major cities in Central Asia. According to IQAir, on 26 October, the Air Quality Index (AQI) exceeded 100 (“healthy” level threshold — ed. ) in six of the eight major Central Asian cities covered by the monitoring. The AQI reached 160 in Bishkek, 157 in Tashkent, 149 in Shymkent, 134 in Karaganda and 134 in Dushanbe. On the same day, Bishkek ranked fourth globally among cities with the most polluted air. In Kazakhstan, the number of cities where warnings of adverse meteorological conditions were issued increased from 4 on 24 October to 10 by 27 October. These figures indicate that the deterioration in air quality is regional in nature. Simultaneous pollution episodes in cities located far apart cannot be explained solely by local emission sources. Weather conditions and the movement of air masses also play a significant role. Reasons for increased air pollution During the last 10 days, Central Asia has experienced anticyclonic conditions, weaker winds, lack of precipitation and temperature inversions. Under these conditions, air near the ground does not rise and mix sufficiently with the air in the layers above. As a result, pollutants from transport, industrial facilities, energy production and other sources, along with naturally occurring dust, accumulate in the lower atmosphere. In Tashkent, the daily average AQI rose from 93 on 21 October to 164 on 26 October, an increase of 76% in five days. Pollution tends to intensify at night. Over the past 30 days, the average AQI reached 119 at 11 PM, compared with 82 at 5 PM. This difference highlights the significant influence of air circulation and atmospheric stability on pollution levels. Contribution of natural dust Central Asia lies within an extensive dust belt encompassing the Karakum, Kyzylkum and Aralkum deserts, as well as other arid areas. Natural dust is therefore one of the key factors affecting air quality across the region. Laboratory analysis of PM2.5 samples collected between 12 and 16 October in Tashkent’s Almazar, Yunusabad and Mirzo-Ulugbek districts found that natural dust accounted for an average of 39.7% of the particulate matter, while emissions associated with fuel combustion in industry, transport and energy production accounted for 42.6%. These findings demonstrate that both natural dust and human activities make substantial contributions to fine particulate air pollution. Advertising on Gazeta During a period of intensified dust transport from 28 September to 6 October, natural dust accounted for an average of 64% of PM2.5, reaching as much as 78% in some samples. It is important to note that dust can be transported by air currents from distant areas into cities. Consequently, the problem cannot be fully addressed through measures implemented within urban boundaries alone. At the same time, reducing emissions from transport and fuel combustion remains essential. PM2.5 and PM10 in Tashkent declined over year According to the available data, between 1 January and 19 October 2026, PM2.5 concentrations in Tashkent decreased by 28% compared with the same period of the previous year, while PM10 concentrations fell by 32%. The average air quality index for October also declined from 124 to 104. Furthermore, according to IQAir’s 2025 report, the annual average PM2.5 concentration was 57.3 μg/m3 in Dushanbe, 72.6 μg/m3 in Karaganda and 39 μg/m3 in Tashkent. These figures indicate that short-term increases in air pollution in Tashkent should be assessed separately from the overall annual picture. However, a decline in certain indicators does not mean that the air pollution problem has been resolved. Effect of climate change on air quality Rising temperatures, droughts and declining soil moisture create favourable conditions for dust to become airborne. The Aralkum Desert, which has formed on the dried bed of the Aral Sea, has also become an additional source of dust in the region. Climate change can increase the risk of deteriorating air quality. However, it would be inaccurate to attribute pollution episodes on specific days solely to climate change. Each episode must be assessed by taking into account meteorological conditions, dust transport and emissions resulting from human activities. Measures required To address the problem effectively, it is essential to improve air quality monitoring and forecasting systems, provide timely public warnings and strengthen data exchange between the hydrometeorological services of neighbouring countries. Regular laboratory analysis of PM2.5 and PM10 composition is also necessary to determine more accurately the respective contributions of natural and anthropogenic pollution sources. Other priorities include reducing emissions from transport, energy production and heating systems; preventing dust generation at construction sites and on roads; and continuing systematic greening initiatives. To sum up, the increase in air pollution across Central Asian cities in October has resulted from the combined effects of adverse meteorological conditions, natural dust and emissions associated with human activities. Addressing this challenge requires not only a prompt response to episodes of deteriorating air quality, but also the identification of pollution sources, emission reductions and stronger regional cooperation. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/10/25/game.body: Photo: National Paralympic Committee Uzbekistan finishes third at 5th Asian Para Games with 145 medals, sets numerous records Uzbekistan finished third at the 5th Asian Para Games in Nagoya with 145 medals, including 45 golds, and set numerous records. The delegation received a ceremonial welcome in Tashkent, where president Shavkat Mirziyoyev congratulated the athletes. Photos from the closing ceremony and arrival. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 25 October 2026, 20:37 Sport Uzbekistan achieved a historic result at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games, which were held in Japan from 18 to 24 October and brought together 2,600 participants from 45 countries across the continent. With 145 medals (45 gold, 49 silver and 51 bronze), Uzbekistan’s para-athletes finished third in the overall medal standings for the first time, behind only China (435 medals) and Japan (186). They also set numerous records. Women won half of Uzbekistan’s gold medals. The country was represented by 149 athletes competing in 11 sports, out of the 18 included in the games program. Advertising on Gazeta Four years ago, at the Hangzhou Asian Para Games, Uzbekistan finished eighth with 79 medals (25 gold, 24 silver and 30 bronze). Eight years ago, in Incheon, it placed fifth with 31 medals (22 gold, five silver and four bronze). On Sunday, the national delegation returned to Tashkent. Officials, including the chairperson of the Senate and sports officials, as well as coaches, athletes' families and relatives, gave them a ceremonial welcome at the capital’s airport . “Our brave young men and women have, through their genuine perseverance, written another bright page in the history of our national sport, once again demonstrating the boundless potential of Uzbek para-sport,” president Shavkat Mirziyoyev said in his message of congratulations to the team. The head of state expressed confidence that the athletes' outstanding results and experience gained “will serve as a solid foundation for the 2028 Paralympic Games in Los Angeles”. Records and achievements Powerlifter Ruza Kuzieva set a world record. Asian records were set by Madina Mukhtorova and Karomat Omonova in the shot put; Shahina Yigitaliyeva in the javelin throw; Navruza Ahmadova in the discus throw; Khurshid Kodirov in the 100-meter sprint; Egor Bolotov in the 100-meter backstroke and 200-meter individual medley; and 16-year-old Lolakhon Kodirova in the 50-meter freestyle. Sixteen Uzbekistan’s athletes in para-cycling, powerlifting and para-athletics set new Asian Para Games records. Many athletes reached the top of the Asian Para Games podium more than once: Dmitry Khorlin won his fourth title, while Bobirjon Omonov, Khusniddin Norbekov, Kudratillokhon Marufkhujaev and Fakhriddin Khamraev won their third. Asila Mirzayorova, Shahina Yigitaliyeva, Guljonoy Naimova and Ruza Kuzieva each claimed their second title. Madina Mukhtorova, Navruza Ahmadova and Mubinabonu Khalilova each won two gold medals, while Khurshid Kodirov claimed three. Egor Bolotov, competing at these Games for the first time, won four gold medals and one silver in para-swimming events. Marjona Pardaboyeva, the flag-bearer for Uzbekistan’s delegation and the country’s first world champion in para-cycling, became a two-time Asian champion. Fifteen-year-old Boburbek Toshtemirov won Uzbekistan’s first gold medal in track para-cycling at the Asian Para Games, making history as the youngest champion in the event. Closing ceremony The fifth edition of Asia’s largest multi-sport competition for athletes with disabilities was held under the slogan “Imagine One Heart”. The closing ceremony at Mizuho Stadium in Nagoya began with the appearance of Uzumin, the games' mascot, who invited para-athletes and spectators to dance together. The flag-bearers then entered the stadium to ceremonial music. President of the Asian Paralympic Committee Majid Rashed declared the games closed. The Asian Paralympic Committee flag was handed over to Doha, the host city of the next Games, scheduled for 2030, and the games flame was ceremonially extinguished. Gazeta presents photographs from the closing ceremony by Husniddin Ato and Maria Malinovskaya. Subscribe to our Telegram channel Gazeta 3 889 # 5th asian para games # photo

https://kun.uz/en/news/2026/11/06/uzbeki.body: Photo: iStock The Ministry of Health has drafted amendments to the regulations governing online sales of pharmaceutical products. The draft has been submitted for public consultation. Under the proposed rules, only pharmacies holding valid licenses and their branches would be allowed to sell eligible products online. Pharmacies would also be required to have designated areas at their premises for handing over orders. To offer online sales, pharmacies would need their own digital platform, such as a website or mobile application. Alternatively, they could partner with a marketplace or order-aggregation service under a special agreement. What information must online pharmacies provide? The draft sets out requirements for information that sellers must make available on their online platforms. Customers must be able to verify the pharmacy’s legal name, taxpayer identification number, address, contact details and license information. Product listings would also have to include the international nonproprietary name of the medicine, its dosage, instructions for use, expiry date, availability and retail price. Sellers would additionally be required to disclose their trade markup and provide information about available alternatives to medicines and medical products. Before completing a purchase, customers must be able to review payment and delivery terms, including delivery charges and estimated timeframes. New requirements for delivery and packaging Orders could be delivered either by pharmacies themselves or by third-party companies contracted by them. Vehicles used for delivery would have to be equipped to maintain the storage conditions required for the products being transported, including appropriate temperature and humidity levels. Medicines would need protective packaging to shield them from external factors. Products requiring different transportation conditions could not be placed together in a single package without separation. Separate packaging would be required. Upon receiving an order, customers would be allowed to inspect the packaging and check whether the delivered products match their purchase. If the contents are incorrect or the packaging is damaged, customers could refuse the order directly through the courier. The pharmacy would automatically receive notification of the refusal.

https://kun.uz/en/news/2026/11/06/uzbeki.body: The pace of growth exceeded the average for neighboring countries and developing economies. External debt across Europe and Central Asia increased by 15.3% in 2025, while the rise among low- and middle-income countries was 5.5%. Of Uzbekistan’s total external debt, $48.46 billion consists of public and publicly guaranteed obligations. Another $32.84 billion represents private-sector external borrowing without government guarantees. Short-term external debt accounted for $6.73 billion. Who does Uzbekistan owe money to? Multilateral financial institutions are the largest category of creditors to the Uzbek government, accounting for $22.82 billion of public and publicly guaranteed debt. Of this amount, $8.36 billion is owed to the Asian Development Bank and $5.01 billion to the International Development Association (IDA), part of the World Bank Group. Other multilateral creditors account for a combined $9.45 billion. Debt owed to foreign governments stands at $10.53 billion. China is Uzbekistan’s largest bilateral creditor, with $3.85 billion, followed by Japan with $2.99 billion. Other countries collectively account for approximately $3.7 billion. Liabilities to private creditors total $15.11 billion, representing around 31% of the country's public and publicly guaranteed debt. Bond issuance becomes a major source of borrowing International bond markets have become one of Uzbekistan’s main sources of external financing. In 2025, the country issued $3.9 billion in international bonds, more than any other country eligible for concessional financing from the International Development Association. According to the report, the government issued $1.6 billion in bonds, including securities denominated in the national currency. Another $2.4 billion was raised by other public-sector entities. The two figures add up to $4 billion, exceeding the report's stated total issuance by $100 million. The World Bank also highlighted the relatively high cost of Uzbekistan’s market-based borrowing. The yield on soum-denominated bonds maturing in 2028 reached 15.5%, partly reflecting inflation risks, according to the report. Dollar-denominated bonds were issued at a yield of 7.38%.

https://kun.uz/en/news/2026/11/06/public.body: Фото: Getty Images The new procurement framework will take effect on January 1, 2027, under a presidential decree signed on November 4. Under the new rules, outsourcing contracts will generally run for up to five years, depending on the nature of the service and the investment required from the private provider. In exceptional cases, contracts may be extended to 10 years, taking into account the investment payback period and subject to an opinion from the Ministry of Health. Outsourcing projects whose existing contracts expire before the new framework takes effect will be allowed to continue until the end of 2027. The resolution also allows healthcare facilities to provide private contractors with free use of buildings, facilities, parts of premises or individual rooms under outsourcing agreements. Such arrangements must be economically justified, with the cost of using the premises factored into the price of the services. New electronic system to monitor outsourcing By April 1, 2027, the authorities will launch an electronic information system called Medical Outsourcing. It will maintain a unified digital register of services available for outsourcing, ongoing projects, service providers and signed contracts. The platform will also track the volume and quality of services delivered, key performance indicators (KPIs), service acceptance results, payments and compliance with contractual obligations. By May 1, 2027, the system is to be integrated with electronic public procurement platforms and other government information systems. New model for public-private participation From January 1, 2027, new mechanisms for public and private sector participation in healthcare development will also be introduced based on long- and short-term master plans. Facilities needed to provide state-guaranteed medical care will remain under public ownership. New healthcare facilities requiring substantial capital investment will generally be established through public-private partnerships involving private investors. By 2030, the government aims to attract reputable foreign professional management companies and teams of managers to at least five major healthcare organizations.

https://kun.uz/en/news/2026/11/06/tashke.body: According to monitoring conducted by a special commission under the National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change , the monthly average Air Quality Index (AQI) fell from 138 in October 2025 to 115 this year. The number of days classified as “good” under Uzbekistan’s national air quality index increased from three to 14. Meanwhile, the number of days with “orange” or “red” air quality levels dropped from 16 to four. The improvement was not consistent throughout the month. Air quality remained considerably better than a year earlier during the first 20 days of October, but deteriorated between October 25 and 31. The committee attributed the late-month deterioration to falling temperatures, weak winds, frequent temperature inversions and insufficient rainfall. These conditions restricted the dispersion of pollutants emitted in Tashkent and neighboring areas, allowing particulate matter to remain trapped close to the ground. What is behind Tashkent’s air pollution? The committee also examined the composition of airborne pollutants. Laboratory analysis of 60 PM2.5 samples collected in October found that components associated with fuel combustion in industry, transport and the energy sector accounted for an average of 44.4% of particulate matter. Natural dust made up another 42.6%. The proportions remained broadly unchanged even on days when air quality deteriorated toward the end of the month. The committee concluded that the worsening conditions were primarily caused by pollutants from local and neighboring areas accumulating over the city as weak winds and unfavorable weather prevented their dispersion. Air circulation patterns also play an important role in Tashkent’s pollution levels. Located in the foothills near a valley, the capital is particularly affected by winds blowing from the northeast and southwest. Wind direction and speed directly influence air exchange and the movement of pollutants. Experts say that air pollution in Tashkent is driven not only by human activity but also by natural dust, limited rainfall and unfavorable meteorological conditions. Insufficient precipitation reduces the amount of dust washed out of the atmosphere. Rainfall in the capital during October was nearly six times below the monthly average, further contributing to the accumulation of airborne particles.

https://kun.uz/en/news/2026/11/06/centra.body: Speaking at a press conference on November 3, Ochilov said the possibility of cutting the rate below 10% was outlined in the Central Bank’s monetary policy guidelines for 2027–2029. The key rate currently stands at 14%. He stressed, however, that any reduction would depend on inflation developments rather than follow a predetermined schedule. “Over the past period, we have focused more on developing the domestic money market and strengthening the channels through which we influence the cost of short-term money. Over the next three years, an important task will be to increase our influence on the cost of medium-term funds,” Ochilov said . The Central Bank also plans to improve its monetary policy operating framework, including reviewing the volume and range of instruments used in operations with maturities of up to one year. Ochilov said the regulator would reassess the current interest rate corridor, which extends two percentage points around the key rate. If inflation returns to the target and inflation expectations continue to ease, the Central Bank could consider narrowing the corridor and gradually reducing the key rate to single digits during the 2027–2029 policy horizon. Ochilov said the corridor could become relatively wide under such conditions, making it necessary to consider narrowing it alongside a gradual reduction in the key rate. He emphasized that this was a possible policy scenario, not a commitment to a specific rate trajectory. Why is the key rate still at 14%? Despite easing inflation expectations and relatively stable price growth in recent months, the Central Bank believes that strong domestic demand and external risks continue to exert upward pressure on prices. Annual inflation stood at 6.4% in September. However, the regulator said recent price movements had been driven largely by supply-side factors, and it remained uncertain whether their effects would be temporary or more persistent. The Central Bank is particularly concerned about the secondary effects of price increases – when higher costs for certain goods and services feed into broader inflation and influence public expectations about future prices. “Our main focus is on the secondary effects of price changes. The decision to maintain tight monetary conditions is intended precisely to prevent these effects from spreading and inflation expectations from strengthening,” Ochilov said.

https://www.spot.uz/en/2026/10/29/licens.body: The Central Bank of Uzbekistan has granted Open Bank the country’s first license to conduct Islamic banking activities. Spot spoke with market experts about what this means for the sector, when customers can expect the first products, and the challenges facing banks as they enter the market. Photo: Spot This week, Uzbekistan’s Central Bank issued the country’s first license for Islamic banking activities. It was granted to Open Bank , one of the country’s youngest banks. The license allows the bank to conduct Islamic financial operations and introduce new products. One example is ijara, an Islamic leasing arrangement under which an asset is leased with an option to purchase it. Islamic finance was first given a legal basis in Uzbekistan in 2022, when microfinance organizations were allowed to offer Islamic products. Banks had to wait another four years for the same opportunity: the president signed the law on Islamic banking in March 2026. An Islamic Finance Council has been established under the Central Bank. The regulator expects at least 10 Islamic banks to be operating by 2030, alongside “Islamic windows” at three state-owned banks. Between 2026 and 2030, Uzbekistan plans to attract about $1 billion in investment and deposits through Islamic banking. Advertising on Spot Spot has already explained what Islamic finance is, what myths surround the system, how Islamic banks make money , and how to keep it from becoming a mere formality . With the first license now issued, we asked market experts when customers might be able to use the first products, which banks could be next, and what risks to watch for at the outset. Khondamir Nusratkhujaev , international expert in Islamic finance, author of the Telegram channel “ Islamic Finance + ” and online courses . The first license undoubtedly marks a historic moment. We have finally moved from talk and legislative groundwork to action and implementation. A real precedent has been set. This should help other banks prepare much faster to apply for licenses to open Islamic windows or launch Islamic banks. It means people will be able to access business and consumer financing, Islamic mortgages and, importantly, Islamic deposits. International banking groups are also likely to start taking Uzbekistan seriously as a new frontier market. It is important that the Central Bank issued a license not for a single product, but for Islamic banking activities as a whole. This is a comprehensive approach that covers the regulatory framework, Shariah oversight and governance, separate accounting, methodologies and IT systems. I therefore welcome the Central Bank’s decision to make this a priority. At the same time, obtaining a license and launching products are two separate stages. The bank still has considerable work to do on individual products, particularly investment accounts. But I am confident that the first products will be announced soon. One risk at the outset is that recent events involving IMAN Invest could damage the reputation of Islamic finance. However, because the banking sector is tightly regulated, I expect public trust in Islamic windows to be high. Another risk is that individuals and businesses may misunderstand these products-or not understand them at all-because financial literacy remains very low. Loans are familiar to most people. Islamic products, by contrast, involve genuine sale-and-purchase, leasing or investment agreements with a bank, and this may put some people off. If clients do not understand the products, they may not fully understand the risks they are taking. For example, the depositor bears the investment risk on an investment deposit, which could deter some customers. That is why clear, ongoing communication in plain language is essential. There is also a risk that banks themselves will develop inappropriate products. This risk is real if they fail to establish robust Shariah oversight and promote controversial products from the outset, such as tawarruq and commodity murabaha. Nevertheless, the fact that we have begun building a genuinely new industry is a significant milestone. It is now vital to protect its reputation by maintaining effective regulation and supervision, ensuring sound risk management, raising public awareness and creating an environment that attracts international investors. Jakhongir Usmonov , expert in Islamic finance and fintech, member of the working group responsible for developing legislation on Islamic banking in Uzbekistan. The first license creates an opportunity to integrate Islamic products into a full banking infrastructure, with access to capital, payment services and a broad customer base. But the main measure of the reform’s success will not be the number of licenses issued. It will be banks' ability to offer competitive Islamic financial products to the mass market. The time between the law coming into force and the first license being issued was, in my view, reasonable. Less than four months elapsed. During that time, the regulator had to put the secondary regulatory framework in place and establish licensing and Shariah governance requirements. This is not simply a matter of licensing another banking product; it is about establishing an entirely new line of banking business. Internationally, building a full-fledged Islamic banking infrastructure often takes years. A license confirms a bank’s right to conduct Islamic banking activities, but it does not mean that its entire product range is automatically ready to launch. The main challenge lies in operational execution. A bank must ensure that its products comply with Islamic standards and adapt its IT systems, accounting practices, contractual documentation, and sales, customer service and debt collection processes. For example, murabaha requires a genuine purchase and sale of an asset, rather than simply replacing an interest rate with a trade markup. Obtaining an opinion from a Shariah board is therefore not enough: Islamic principles must be observed throughout the life cycle of a transaction, from the preparation of initial documents and invoices to electronic document management. A bank must also establish a separate framework for accounting for, reporting on and managing Islamic operations. The quality of this infrastructure-from the automated banking system to internal processes-will determine whether the bank is ready to scale up. I expect banks to enter the market gradually, starting with relatively standardized products. These are likely to include murabaha, which finances the purchase of goods through a pre-agreed markup and installment payments. This is a logical starting point. According to the Central Bank, murabaha accounts for about 63% of Islamic microfinance in Uzbekistan. Consumers in the country are also already familiar with installment payments. Over time, Islamic leasing (ijara), partnership-based financing and investment deposits may also develop. However, the scale of the rollout will depend on available capital, technology and qualified specialists-not merely on whether a license has been issued. The Central Bank says more than 10 commercial banks are preparing to introduce Islamic finance. Agrobank, Asakabank, Ipak Yuli Bank, Orient Finans Bank, Hayot Bank and Apex Bank have also spoken publicly about their plans. In June, Agrobank’s shareholders approved the introduction of Islamic banking services, while Asakabank’s shareholders approved the creation of an Islamic window. It is too early to say which banks will be next to receive a license. Timelines will depend on each bank’s readiness, its fulfillment of regulatory requirements and decisions by the Central Bank. In the initial phase, I expect Islamic windows within existing banks to be the main model. This is a more pragmatic approach: it allows banks to use existing infrastructure instead of establishing a separate bank from scratch.
