https://www.spot.uz/en/2026/10/27/sugar-.body: Domestic sugar producers will receive extended loan repayment periods, partial interest compensation and tax breaks. Photo: Sergey Pyatakov / RIA Novosti Uzbekistan plans to introduce quotas on sugar imports and provide tax incentives to local manufacturers. The measures are outlined in Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 417, dated July 30, 2026. The document is not available in the national legislation database Lex.uz but is in Spot’s possession. One informed source confirmed its authenticity to the publication. According to the document, the annual quota for white sugar imports will total 300,000 tonnes, with 100,000 tonnes allocated each to manufacturers of beverages, confectionery and other food products. The Cabinet of Ministers will approve the quota for the following year in November, based on “substantiated proposals” from the Ministry of Economy and Finance, the Competition Promotion and Consumer Protection Committee, and the National Statistics Committee. The quota may be revised every six months, taking into account domestic consumption, production capacity utilisation, and import and domestic prices. Advertising on Spot Quotas are to be allocated through electronic online auctions. The system is scheduled to launch by December 1, 2026, and will be integrated with the Customs Committee’s Single Window information system. Auction results will be published openly. Support for domestic producers The resolution provides for extending the repayment period for existing loans owed by domestic sugar producers to Uzpromstroybank by up to five years, with a grace period of up to two years. Repayment schedules and interest rates are also to be revised based on the bank’s applicable lending rates. Producers must fully repay their existing accounts receivable by the end of 2026. The document also предусматривает attracting $50 million in foreign direct investment to support the enterprises. From August 1, 2026, to August 1, 2031, the Entrepreneurship Development Company will compensate 50% of interest expenses on foreign-currency loans used to import raw materials, capped at five percentage points. The measure applies to loans taken by domestic sugar producers regardless of their sustainability rating or loan classification, including those with overdue debt. The Ministry of Economy and Finance has been instructed to prepare draft amendments to the Tax Code within one month. The proposals include exempting domestic sugar producers from corporate income tax and reducing property tax to 50% of the applicable rate until January 1, 2031. Funds saved through these tax incentives must be used exclusively to repay loans. Domestic sugar and debt controls From January 1, 2027, state organisations and enterprises must prioritise domestic producers when purchasing white sugar through public procurement. All output from domestic sugar plants will be sold through the commodity exchange, while finished products may be exported without restrictions. Domestic sugar producers will also be eligible for free certification of locally manufactured goods and inclusion in the Register of Local Products and Manufacturers. The resolution introduces additional financial oversight requirements. Producers are advised to appoint financial directors from among bank representatives. These representatives may participate in general meetings and block decisions that could worsen a borrower’s financial position. All surplus liquid funds must be used for early repayment of bank debt. Companies may not distribute profits as dividends until their loans have been fully repaid. Pledged assets may also be inventoried and transferred to the bank’s balance sheet if a company launches projects not included in its business plan, increases its debt, falls behind on loan payments, or fails to ensure that sales revenue is transferred centrally to its account at Uzpromstroybank and accumulated for loan repayment. Monitoring imports and production The Customs Committee must publish quarterly data on imports of socially important food products by the 10th day of the month following each reporting quarter. The information must include import volumes, values and average customs value per tonne, broken down by supplier country and importer. Domestic producers are also advised to hire foreign consultants to develop medium- and long-term strategies, audit their financial positions and prepare recovery measures. The resolution calls for digitising production and management processes, introducing a GMS production management system and international standards for product accounting and inventory management, and reducing production losses. The document also proposes introducing security and monitoring by the Security Department under the Ministry of Internal Affairs, along with round-the-clock online surveillance of production processes using CCTV cameras. Deputy Prime Minister Jamshid Khodjaev has been assigned responsibility for overseeing implementation of the resolution. https://www.spot.uz/en/2026/10/29/uklon/.body: The company will be required to introduce antitrust compliance measures in accordance with legislation. Photo: Yevgeniy Sorochin / Spot The Competition Committee has included Uklon UB on its list of digital platform operators with a dominant market position, the regulator’s press service reported . Uklon UB is the Uzbek legal entity of Ukrainian ride-hailing platform Uklon. Under the decision, the company is considered dominant in the market for intermediary (aggregator) services for placing passenger transport orders and providing taxi services. To prevent abuse of its dominant position, the company will be required to introduce an antitrust compliance system in accordance with competition law. Uklon’s plans to enter Uzbekistan became known in April 2023, when the company posted several vacancies in the country. The platform launched in Tashkent in June 2023 and has gradually expanded to five cities in the Fergana Valley in recent months: Fergana, Margilan, Kokand, Namangan and Andijan. Advertising on Spot In March 2025, Ukrainian mobile operator Kyivstar agreed to acquire a 97% stake in Uklon for $155.2 million. VEON, the group that includes the telecom operator, has announced plans to launch the ride-hailing platform in Kazakhstan, Pakistan and Bangladesh. In mid-October, the Competition Committee announced that it would review the ride-hailing market and pricing practices. The regulator cited fare increases during peak hours amid technical issues with Yandex Go, which sparked public criticism. What the status means Digital platforms may be classified as dominant if they benefit from network effects and meet at least one of two criteria: Annual sales revenue exceeding 100,000 basic calculation units (BCUs), equivalent to 44 billion soums; More than 50,000 monthly active end users or more than 3,000 monthly active business users. The status may also be assigned regardless of revenue or user numbers if a platform accounts for more than 40% of a particular online services market. The classification will be reviewed every three years. Digital platform operators with a dominant position or superior bargaining power are prohibited from engaging in practices that restrict competition. For example, they may not prevent businesses from dealing with users outside the platform. They are also prohibited from using data belonging to businesses competing on the platform without permission, restricting the sale or purchase of competitors' products, or promoting their own goods and services on more favourable terms than those offered by platform users or third parties. In addition, operators may not prevent users from installing third-party applications and services, unjustifiably reduce service quality, or restrict users' ability to switch to another provider. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/09/from-tank.body: World From tanks to drones: Inside Pakistan’s defense industry — and what it could mean for Uzbekistan From upgraded Soviet-era tanks to interceptor drones, electronic warfare systems and counter-drone technologies, Pakistan’s defense industry is adapting to a battlefield where traditional military hardware increasingly operates alongside cheaper, unmanned systems. A weeklong visit by a group of journalists, including a Daryo correspondent, offered a closer look at the country’s defense facilities and the capabilities Pakistan could potentially bring to its growing defense and technology cooperation with Uzbekistan. 9 October, 19:05 11 min read 1 348 views 0 comments 0 Source: AI Pakistan’s defense industry is trying to bridge two eras of warfare: modernizing tanks that have been in service for decades while developing drones, counter-drone systems, and electronic warfare technologies for a rapidly changing battlefield. That was among the key takeaways from a weeklong visit to Pakistan by a group of journalists, including a Daryo correspondent, who traveled across the country with the support of the Embassy of Pakistan in Uzbekistan. The program included visits to defense facilities involved in tank production and upgrades, drones, communications, electronic warfare, and ammunition. At Heavy Industries Taxila (HIT), the shift is visible in the equipment itself. An upgraded version of the T-59, a Chinese variant of the Soviet T-55, sits alongside newer unmanned systems designed for surveillance, strikes, and interception. The contrast reflects a broader strategy: extending the life of existing military equipment while building capabilities for a battlefield increasingly shaped by drones, electronic warfare, and lower-cost precision systems. For Uzbekistan, these developments offer a potential area of cooperation as Tashkent expands its engagement with Islamabad. Uzbek officials have already held talks with Pakistani defense and technology companies, although no major Pakistan-Uzbekistan arms deal has been publicly announced. The visits provided a closer look at what Pakistan can offer, from tank modernization and ammunition production to drones, military communications, and counter-drone technologies, as well as where those capabilities could intersect with Uzbekistan’s own defense-industrial ambitions. Giving an old tank a new lease on life At HIT in Taxila, one of the first pieces of equipment to illustrate that transformation was a tank based on a design that has been in military service for decades. A HIT representative explained that the tank on display was an upgraded version of the T-59, a Chinese version of the Soviet T-55. “ “In Russia, these are called T-55 tanks. We got the Chinese version from China,” the representative explained, adding that the tanks were inducted into the Pakistan Army around 1980. The platform has since undergone successive modifications as Pakistan has sought to keep its older armored fleet operational. “ “Over time, these tanks have gone through different modifications and updates,” the representative said. The latest configuration shown during the visit includes a 125mm gun, an upgraded engine, and improved armor and protection systems. The representative described the upgraded vehicle as “equivalent to any modern technology.” According to the representative, around 500 units had been produced or upgraded under the program. The cost of an upgrade package was roughly $2mn, depending on the requirements and production target. “ “Our main customer is the Pakistan Army,” the representative said, explaining that the army has an older fleet that it has sought to modernize into a more up-to-date configuration. The approach is significant for countries that operate large fleets of older armored vehicles. Instead of replacing every platform, modernization can extend the service life of existing equipment while introducing newer weapons, engines, and protection systems. HIT, which operates under Pakistan’s Ministry of Defence Production, was established in 1971 and initially focused on rebuilding tanks. Its Heavy Rebuild Factory for T-series tanks began production in 1980. The organization now manufactures, rebuilds, and upgrades main battle tanks, tank guns, armored personnel carriers, and other military and security vehicles. Its portfolio includes the Al-Khalid and Al-Khalid-I main battle tanks, Al-Zarrar and Haider tanks, the Talha armored personnel carrier, command and logistics vehicles, and armored recovery vehicles. HIT also works with foreign partners. The Haider, for example, was developed through cooperation involving China’s NORINCO and Pakistani industry. The organization noted that it can undertake joint ventures, commercial activities, and technology-transfer arrangements with friendly countries, giving its tank modernization experience a potential international market. The battlefield gets smaller and cheaper The same facility also offered a glimpse of a very different part of Pakistan’s defense industry. At HIT’s drone display, training, surveillance, and strike systems were shown alongside interceptor drones, loitering munitions, and counter-drone technologies. Maaz Rasool, a senior manager at HIT’s UASF, said the focus is increasingly on making unmanned systems affordable. “ “Our goal is to make drones as cheap as possible,” Rasool said, explaining that modern warfare increasingly requires large numbers of relatively inexpensive systems. He described this as part of the requirements of “fifth-generation warfare,” where the economics of deploying and countering unmanned systems can be as important as their technical capabilities. The systems displayed included an interceptor drone designed to intercept incoming aircraft and drones. A delta-wing system was shown with a payload capacity of around 50–60kg, while a smaller surveillance drone had a payload of around 30kg. A larger vertical takeoff and landing system was also on display. HIT also presented loitering munitions launched from canisters or by catapult. The range of systems reflects how quickly drones have expanded beyond their traditional role in surveillance. Unmanned platforms can now be used for reconnaissance, targeting, strikes, and interception, while counter-drone technologies are being developed to respond to them. Rasool noted that Pakistan’s military remains the priority customer, although the company also exports to different countries. The development of these systems alongside conventional armored vehicles illustrates the broader direction of Pakistan’s defense industry: maintaining the ability to produce and upgrade traditional weapons while developing technologies for a battlefield increasingly dominated by unmanned systems. The invisible side of warfare If HIT represents the physical side of Pakistan’s military industry, the National Radio & Telecommunication Corporation, or NRTC, operates in a less visible part of the battlefield. Established in 1966 under Pakistan’s Ministry of Defence Production, NRTC develops military communications equipment, electronic warfare systems, jammers, counter-drone technologies, surveillance systems, robotics, and other technology products. An NRTC representative described the organization as a federal government entity working across both military and conventional markets. “ “We develop communications, jamming, anti-drone systems, artificial intelligence, robotics, Safe City solutions, and other technologies,” the representative said. The company provides communications architecture for Pakistan’s armed forces and also works with police, highway authorities, railways, banks, and other civilian institutions. Its military portfolio includes communications systems and jammers that can be mounted on vehicles or used as portable systems, as well as technologies designed to detect and counter drones. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/09/egypt-to-.body: Uzbekistan Egypt to introduce new visa and entry requirements for Uzbekistan Egypt will introduce new entry rules for Uzbekistan citizens from November 1, requiring advance visas, authorized tour bookings, family accompaniment for travelers under 40, and minimum cash holdings of $3,000–$5,000 depending on age and travel arrangements. 9 October, 15:56 3 min read 5 341 views 0 comments 0 Source: PAC Group Egypt will introduce new entry requirements for citizens of Uzbekistan starting November 1, 2026, including mandatory advance visas, restrictions based on travelers' ages and minimum cash requirements, according to the Embassy of Uzbekistan in Cairo. The embassy announced the changes based on information received through diplomatic channels, advising Uzbekistan citizens to review the updated regulations before planning trips to Egypt. Under the new procedure, Uzbekistan citizens will be required to obtain an entry visa through Egyptian diplomatic missions before departure. Tourist visits must also be arranged through authorized tour operators. The regulations introduce additional conditions for travelers depending on their age and whether they are traveling independently or with family members. According to the embassy, Uzbekistan citizens under the age of 40 will be permitted to travel to Egypt only when accompanied by their parents, spouse or children. For travelers in this category, the accompanying family must have at least $5,000 in cash available for the duration of the visit. The requirement applies to the family traveling together rather than specifying an individual amount for each member. Separate financial conditions will apply to Uzbekistan citizens over the age of 40 who intend to travel independently. These travelers must carry at least $3,000 in cash. The announced rules do not provide further details regarding the financial requirements for travelers over 40 who are accompanied by family members. In addition to obtaining a visa before departure, Uzbekistan citizens entering Egypt will be required to provide documentation confirming their travel arrangements and financial capacity. Travelers must present proof of a hotel reservation, mobile contact information and evidence that they have sufficient financial resources for their stay. These requirements will be checked as part of the entry procedure, alongside the age-related conditions and visa documentation. The new regulations also prohibit the conversion of tourist visas into other visa categories while travelers are in Egypt. As a result, Uzbekistan citizens entering the country on tourist visas will not be able to request a change of visa category during their stay. The embassy warned that travelers who fail to meet the established conditions or cannot provide the necessary documents may be refused entry. In such cases, passengers may be returned to their point of departure by the airline that transported them to Egypt. The Embassy of Uzbekistan in Cairo has urged citizens to take the new procedures into consideration when arranging travel, including obtaining visas in advance, using authorized tour operators and preparing the required documents and cash. The announcement follows changes to entry procedures for Uzbekistan citizens traveling to Thailand. Effective September 15, 2026, Thailand abolished the 60-day visa-free entry regime previously available to Uzbekistan passport holders. Following the change, Uzbekistan citizens are required to obtain an electronic visa before traveling to Thailand. According to the Embassy of Uzbekistan in Bangkok, the officially established processing period for a Thai electronic visa is up to 10 days. However, the embassy reported that, in practice, applicants have been receiving visa confirmation notifications approximately 15 days after completing payment. The revised entry procedures for Egypt and Thailand introduce additional visa and documentation requirements for Uzbekistan citizens traveling to the two destinations, with Egypt's new rules scheduled to take effect on November 1, 2026. # Diplomatic Missions # Egyptian Visa Requirements # International Travel Regulations # Thai Visa Requirements # Travel Advisories # Uzbekistan Citizens Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/07/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan introduces new regulations for tourism services at reservoirs Uzbekistan has introduced new regulations for tourism services at reservoirs, requiring rescue services, safety measures, waste management and digital infrastructure, while planning to develop tourism facilities at 25 additional reservoirs and offering tax incentives to entrepreneurs investing in these areas. Today, 14:00 3 min read 594 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Madina Nurman Uzbekistan has approved new regulations governing the establishment of tourism and recreational services at reservoirs and their surrounding areas, according to the Ministry of Justice. The regulations were adopted under Government Resolution No. 609, dated November 5, and establish procedures for developing tourism infrastructure on vacant, non-agricultural land plots located at or near reservoirs. The document defines requirements for locating tourism and recreational facilities, organizing tourism services, ensuring visitor safety and protecting surrounding areas. The measures form part of broader government plans to develop tourism activities at reservoirs while regulating the use of adjacent land and ensuring compliance with safety requirements. Under the new regulations, businesses providing tourism services at reservoirs must ensure the availability of rescue services. Operators may establish their own on-site rescue units or conclude agreements with professional rescue organizations to provide the required coverage. The regulations also require compliance with safety standards governing the operation of small vessels and their associated docking facilities. Tourism service providers must additionally conclude agreements with specialized organizations responsible for collecting and removing household waste generated at tourism facilities. These requirements apply to the organization of tourism services at reservoirs and are intended to establish safety and operational standards for businesses operating in these areas. The regulations also provide for the introduction of digital technologies in the organization of tourism activities at reservoirs. These include digital maps, online booking platforms, QR-code-based navigation systems and other digital infrastructure intended to support tourism services. The use of these technologies will form part of the requirements for organizing tourism activities and developing recreational facilities in reservoir areas. When selecting locations for tourism and recreational facilities, operators must take into account existing environmental and geographical restrictions. In particular, the regulations require consideration of water protection zones, sanitary buffer zones and areas exposed to natural hazards, including mudflows and landslides. These factors must be assessed when determining suitable locations for tourism infrastructure and recreational activities. Land plots intended for tourism services will be allocated through electronic online auctions in accordance with procedures established by Uzbek legislation. The regulations apply specifically to vacant land plots that are not designated for agricultural use and are situated at reservoirs or in adjacent territories. The approval of the regulations follows a presentation reviewed by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on October 20 concerning the use of reservoirs and adjacent areas, as well as measures to ensure their safety. During the presentation, officials outlined plans to introduce tourism services at an additional 25 reservoirs across Uzbekistan. On October 27, the president also adopted a resolution titled "On measures to regulate the use of reservoirs and adjacent areas and to ensure their safety." The resolution provides for tax incentives for entrepreneurs establishing tourism services around reservoirs. # Environmental Standards # Government Regulations # Tourism Development # Tourism Safety # Water Reservoir Management # uzbekistan Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? Economics Uzbekistan's annual inflation rises to 6.5% in October 2026 as food and transport prices increase Uzbekistan's annual inflation rose to 6.5% in October 2026, with monthly prices increasing by 0.6%, driven by higher food, utility and transport costs, including a 26.1% rise in Tashkent metro and bus fares, while the capital recorded the country's highest annual inflation at 7.4%. Today, 11:30 4 min read 1 367 views 0 comments 0 Uzbekistan's annual inflation rate reached 6.5% in October 2026, up from 6.4% in September, while monthly inflation stood at 0.6%, according to the Statistics Committee. During the month, food prices increased by 1%, non-food products by 0.2%, and services by 0.6%. Price changes were recorded across food products, utilities, fuel, transportation and education services. Food prices increase, led by vegetables, eggs and meat Among staple food products, egg prices increased by 5.2% in October, while mutton became 1.4% more expensive. Prices for beef with bone rose by 1.2%, and minced meat increased by 1.1%. Several vegetables recorded higher monthly price increases. Cucumbers and eggplants became 9% more expensive, followed by tomatoes at 8.8% and bell peppers at 8.7%. Potato prices increased by 5.3%. Prices for fish and other seafood rose by 1.4%, while chicken drumsticks and thighs became 1.6% more expensive. Whole chicken prices increased by 1.2%. Milk prices rose by 1%, and bread made from high-grade wheat flour became 0.7% more expensive. Infographic: Statistics Committee Utility and fuel prices rise in October According to the Statistics Committee, the cost of cold water supply and sewage services increased by an average of 4.7% nationwide during October. For households, market prices for coal rose by 0.3%, while firewood became 0.5% more expensive. Gasoline prices increased by an average of 1% during the month. AI-92 gasoline became 0.5% more expensive, while AI-95 prices rose by 2.6%. Prices for AI-98 and AI-100 gasoline increased by 5.3%. In October, AI-92 gasoline prices ranged from UZS 10,500 to UZS 18,000 per liter, while AI-95 cost between UZS 13,500 and UZS 21,500 per liter. Prices for AI-98 and AI-100 ranged from UZS 16,500 to UZS 28,000 per liter. Propane prices increased by 0.4%, with the upper price limit reaching UZS 10,000 per liter. Methane prices remained unchanged. Source: “Daryo” / Farrux Aliyev Tashkent metro and bus fares increase by 26.1% Transportation services also recorded price increases in October, particularly in Tashkent. According to the Statistics Committee, the introduction of new fare structures in the capital resulted in a 26.1% increase in metro fares. Bus fares in Tashkent also rose by 26.1%, contributing to a nationwide average increase of 7.1% in urban bus passenger transportation costs. Taxi fares increased by an average of 1.3% across Uzbekistan, while the increase in Tashkent reached 2.5%. International transport fares rose by 0.7%, suburban train fares increased by 1.4%, and long-distance train tickets became 0.6% more expensive. The cost of driver training courses, driving lessons, examinations and services related to obtaining a driver's license increased by 0.8%. Source: “Daryo” / Farrux Aliyev Prices for education services also increased during October, primarily at non-state institutions. Fees at private kindergartens rose by 0.6%, while private school fees increased by 0.5%. Tuition at private higher education institutions became 0.1% more expensive. The Statistics Committee reported no changes in the cost of education services at state institutions. Meanwhile, tutoring services became 1.6% more expensive, and foreign language course fees increased by 0.8%. Despite increases across several categories, some food products and transportation services became cheaper in October. Sugar prices declined by an average of 2.2% during the month. Seasonal factors contributed to lower prices for several fruits. Lemon prices decreased by 15%, grapes became 7.5% cheaper, apple prices fell by 3%, and bananas declined by 1.3%. Domestic airfare prices also decreased by 1.4%, which the Statistics Committee attributed to the strengthening of the Uzbek soum against the euro. Source: “Daryo” / Madina Nurman Tashkent records highest annual inflation at 7.4% Annual inflation rates across Uzbekistan's regions ranged from 5.5% to 7.4% in October. Tashkent city recorded the highest annual inflation rate at 7.4%, while the lowest was registered in the Sirdaryo region at 5.5%. Samarkand region recorded annual inflation of 6.7%, followed by Fergana at 6.6%. Annual inflation stood at 6.5% in Kashkadarya, Tashkent and Khorezm regions. Andijan, Jizzakh and Navoi regions each recorded annual inflation of 6.4%, while Namangan registered 6.3%. Surkhandarya recorded inflation of 6.2%, followed by the Republic of Karakalpakstan at 6% and Bukhara region at 5.9%. Source: “Daryo” / Dilruh Isomiddinova The October inflation figures follow an upward revision of the Central Bank of Uzbekistan's inflation forecast for 2026. The regulator previously increased its annual inflation projection from 6.5% to approximately 7%. According to the Statistics Committee, annual inflation reached 6.5% in October, compared with 6.4% in September, while monthly consumer prices increased by 0.6%. # Public Transport Fares # Statistics Committee # central bank of uzbekistan # consumer prices # inflation # tashkent # uzbekistan Reporter Xadicha Abdurashidova All stories Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? Uzbekistan Uzbekistan finds missing or faulty filters at 60 greenhouses in Tashkent region Inspections of 60 greenhouses in Uzbekistan's Tashkent region found that 47 lacked filtration systems and 13 had non-functional filters, while nighttime inspections covered 15 additional facilities in the capital, where air quality measurements at 10 locations showed PM2.5 and PM10 levels remained within established standards. Today, 16:10 2 min read 748 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Madina Nurman Inspections of 60 greenhouses in Uzbekistan's Tashkent region found that 47 lacked filtration systems, while another 13 had non-functional filters, according to the Committee for Ecology. The inspections were conducted by a working group comprising specialists from the Committee for Ecology, its regional departments, the Eco-police, the National Center for Environmental Monitoring and other relevant state agencies. The inspections covered greenhouses in the Zangiota, Tashkent, Qibray, Yangiyo‘l and Yuqori Chirchiq districts. According to the committee, none of the inspected greenhouses were consuming fuel at the time of the inspections. In Zangiota district, 13 greenhouses were inspected, of which 10 lacked filtration systems and three had non-functional filters. In Tashkent district, nine greenhouses were found without filtration systems, while three had filters that were not functioning. In Qibray district, 11 greenhouses lacked filters and three had non-functional equipment. In Yangiyo‘l district, inspectors examined 10 greenhouses. Eight had no filtration systems, while two had faulty filters. In Yuqori Chirchiq district, 11 greenhouses were inspected, including nine without filtration systems and two with non-functional filters. Overall, 47 greenhouses lacked filtration systems entirely, while 13 had filters that were not functioning. Environmental authorities also conducted nighttime inspections in the Sergeli, Yangihayot, Shayxontohur, Olmazor, Yashnobod, Uchtepa and Yakkasaroy districts of Tashkent city. During these operations, 15 facilities were examined, including one greenhouse, one industrial enterprise and 13 other facilities. According to the Committee for Ecology, a total of 95 facilities were inspected across Tashkent city and the Tashkent region. These included 61 greenhouses, one industrial enterprise and 33 other facilities. Specialists from the analytical laboratory of the Tashkent City Main Department of Ecology conducted atmospheric air quality measurements at 10 monitoring points across the capital. Using a portable dust analyzer, specialists measured concentrations of fine particulate matter, including PM2.5 and PM10. According to the committee, measurements at all 10 locations remained within established standards. In addition, atmospheric air samples were collected near air quality monitoring equipment and industrial production facilities in the Yakkasaroy, Uchtepa, Olmazor, Yashnobod, Yangihayot and Sergeli districts. During talks, Tokayev described Jordan as a reliable partner in the Arab world, highlighting the momentum generated by reciprocal high-level visits last year and agreements signed between the two countries. “ “Jordan is our time-tested and reliable partner in the Arab world. Over the last years, our partnership has gained a new momentum,” Tokayev said. He added that Kazakhstan attaches importance to implementing existing agreements and identified economic cooperation as a key driver of bilateral relations. The two countries also have potential to expand academic, scientific, cultural and humanitarian ties, as well as increase tourism flows in both directions. Tokayev also highlighted similarities in Kazakhstan’s and Jordan’s approaches to international and regional issues, praising the Jordanian monarch’s role in promoting peace and stability. Source: Akorda The discussions placed particular emphasis on the Aqaba Process, an initiative launched by King Abdullah II to strengthen international cooperation against terrorism and extremism. Kazakhstan and Jordan are co-hosting the next meeting under the initiative in Astana, with a focus on security in the field of artificial intelligence. “ “In that vein, Kazakhstan highly values the Aqaba Process, launched by Your Majesty more than a decade ago. It is a great honor to co-host first-ever meeting of this format in Central Asia,” Tokayev added. King Abdullah II thanked Kazakhstan for its hospitality and highlighted that last year’s exchange of visits had given bilateral relations important momentum. “ “We look forward to building on that to advance cooperation in key sectors such as trade, investment, tourism, technology, and defense,” the King said. He also reaffirmed Jordan's commitment to working with Kazakhstan on regional security and efforts to counter terrorism and extremism. As part of the visit, Tokayev presented King Abdullah II with the Al-Farabi State Award in recognition of his contribution to strengthening relations between the two countries. The award, named after the prominent philosopher of the East, was presented to a foreign recipient for the first time. Source: Akorda Tokayev described the distinction as a symbol of Kazakhstan’s respect for the Jordanian monarch, highlighting Al-Farabi’s significance to both Central Asian and Arab cultures. “ “It is very symbolic that Your Majesty is the first person to receive this distinguished award. I believe it is a historic event,” the president said. In return, King Abdullah II awarded Tokayev Jordan’s highest state decoration, the Order of Al-Hussein bin Ali. Tokayev added that the distinction represented recognition not only of his personal contribution but also of the friendship and mutual respect between the two nations. “ “I regard this high distinction not only as recognition of my personal contribution, but above all as a testament to the strong friendship and mutual respect between our peoples,” he said. Established in 1949 by King Abdullah I, the Order of Al-Hussein bin Ali is named after Sharif Hussein bin Ali of Mecca (1853–1931), a prominent figure in the Hashemite dynasty. Its presentation is considered a mark of exceptional respect from the Jordanian monarch. # Aqaba Process # Counter-Terrorism # State Awards # State Visit # bilateral cooperation # jordan # kazakhstan Muharrir Moxinur Sultanova All stories Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/05/networks-.body: Uzbekistan “Networks are under strict control” — Uzbekistan reports no illegal sales of natural gas by producers Uzbekistan has identified no cases of illegal sales of natural gas by domestic producers, as 83 gas networks are equipped with online meters that track production, transportation and consumption, Akhadjon Isokjonov, head of Uzenergoinspection, announced at a press conference in Tashkent. 5 November, 21:30 2 min read 6 924 views 0 comments 0 Source: Akhadjon Isokjonov / Uzenergoinspection No cases of illegal sales of natural gas produced by oil and gas companies in Uzbekistan have been identified, as the country's pipeline networks and gas flows are monitored through an electronic control system, Akhadjon Isokjonov, head of the Inspectorate for Control over the Use of Electricity, Petroleum Products and Gas (Uzenergoinspection), announced at a press conference in Tashkent on November 4. According to a Daryo correspondent, Isokjonov noted that 15 oil and gas production and distribution companies operate in Uzbekistan, supplying their output through main pipelines to Uztransgaz JSC, the country's sole gas transportation operator. The country has 83 gas networks equipped with online meters that transmit data to the monitoring system. “ "There are 15 oil and gas production and distribution enterprises operating in our republic. They supply the natural gas they produce through main pipelines to the sole operator, Uztransgaz JSC. There are 83 gas networks in the country, and they are equipped with meters that transmit information online. We must state frankly that the networks do not have the capacity to transport products to neighboring countries or other regions," he said. Source: Uzenergoinspection According to the official, natural gas exports are currently handled by UzGazTrade JSC, while Uztransgaz maintains more than 13,000 kilometers of gas pipelines. Export routes include the Gazli area, while the transit pipeline passes through kilometer 287 of the Boimurod point. Another export route runs through the Muzrabot and Sherabad districts and the valley regions toward Kyrgyzstan. Isokjonov added that electronic meters installed across pipeline entry and exit points are integrated into Uzenergoinspection’s energy monitoring platform. The system records how much gas each plant produces and supplies, how much Uztransgaz receives and distributes, and the consumption volumes of individual customers. “ "Input and output networks are under strict control. Electronic meters installed on pipelines are integrated into the energy control platform of the Uzenergoinspection. Today, there is a clear calculation of how much natural gas a particular plant or enterprise produces and supplies to the network, and how much gas Uztransgaz receives and releases through each network. At the same time, the consumption volumes of each consumer are visible on the control platform," he said. The inspection agency also monitors readings at methane and gasoline filling stations. The volumes of gas or gasoline received and sold are regularly displayed in the electronic system. Earlier, UZS 900bn ($75mn) worth of gas and electricity were reported to have been illegally consumed in Uzbekistan during the first half of 2026. # Electronic Monitoring Systems # Energy Sector Oversight # Illegal Gas Sales Prevention # Natural Gas Supply # Uzbekistan Energy Sector # Uzenergoinspection Muharrir Moxinur Sultanova All stories Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/06/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan uncovers 374 cases of illegal liquefied gas sales and 16 coal violations Uzbekistan has strengthened oversight of household gas and coal supplies for the autumn-winter season after authorities uncovered 374 cases of illegal liquefied gas storage and sales and 16 coal-related violations, seizing 9,139 gas cylinders, over 92 tons of liquefied gas and 333 tons of coal, while launching a criminal investigation into alleged embezzlement by gas supply employees in the Samarkand region. Yesterday, 19:00 3 min read 3 164 views 0 comments 0 Source: Hududgaztaminot Uzbekistan's Ministry of Internal Affairs (MIA) has announced strengthened oversight of gas and coal supplies allocated to households for the autumn-winter season, following the identification of hundreds of cases involving illegal storage and sale of energy resources. According to the ministry's press service, the measures are intended to ensure the timely and complete delivery of allocated resources to consumers and prevent misappropriation during transportation and distribution. The instructions were issued during a meeting attended by Minister of Internal Affairs Aziz Toshpulatov, heads of sectoral and regional services, representatives of Hududgaztaminot JSC and its regional branches, and officials from LPG-Trade LLC. During the meeting, officials emphasized the importance of delivering liquefied gas cylinders according to established schedules, maintaining accurate records of allocated resources and ensuring transparency throughout transportation and distribution. Source: MIA Particular attention was given to preventing unjustified charges imposed on consumers and ensuring that households receive the quantities of gas and coal established under existing supply standards. According to the MIA, operations conducted over the past month identified 16 cases involving the illegal storage and sale of coal. Authorities seized 333 tons and 540 kg of coal from illegal circulation. The recovered coal was subsequently distributed to the population to meet household needs. During the same period, law enforcement agencies identified 374 cases involving the illegal storage and sale of liquefied gas. As a result, authorities seized 9,139 gas cylinders and 92 tons and 936 kg of liquefied gas from illegal circulation. Measures were taken to return the recovered resources for public consumption. The ministry reported that these violations were identified during operations aimed at preventing illegal activities involving energy resources allocated to households. The ministry also reported a case involving employees of the Pastdargomtumangaz gas supply enterprise in the Samarkand region. During operational-search activities conducted in October, authorities identified a scheme in which employees of the enterprise allegedly acted together to misappropriate household gas cylinders filled with hydrocarbon gas intended for public distribution. According to the investigation, specialized vehicles were used to transport the cylinders. Law enforcement officers seized 3 tons and 100 kg of hydrocarbon gas valued at UZS 32mn (over $2600). Following the discovery, the Investigation Department of the Samarkand Regional Internal Affairs Directorate initiated a criminal case against employees of Pastdargomtumangaz under Article 167, Part 2, Clause "v" of Uzbekistan's Criminal Code, concerning misappropriation or embezzlement. The circumstances of the case are still being established. Source: MIA Following the meeting, specific tasks were assigned to specialized internal affairs services and officials of organizations responsible for energy supplies. Regional authorities were instructed to examine problems related to the delivery of gas and coal and implement preventive measures against violations. Additional oversight will focus on monitoring the transportation of energy resources by rail, including ensuring that allocated supplies reach their intended destinations without losses or misappropriation. Officials were also instructed to ensure the safe movement of vehicles transporting energy products and strengthen security at gas-filling stations, warehouses and distribution bases. The measures additionally include monitoring the handling of material assets and preventing their illegal appropriation during storage, transportation and distribution. According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the strengthened oversight is intended to ensure that gas and coal allocated for the autumn-winter season are delivered to households in full and according to established schedules. # Criminal Investigations # Economic Crime # Ministry of Internal Affairs # Resource Misappropriation # Supply Chain Oversight # uzbekistan Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? Yesterday, 20:00 2 min read 28 255 views 0 comments 0 Illustrative image: Education Asia India has urged students planning to study medicine in Uzbekistan to ensure that their chosen universities meet the country's medical education standards, warning that graduates of non-compliant institutions could be barred from practising medicine in India. The Indian government is in constant dialogue with Uzbek authorities to ensure that Indian students receive quality education, including those enrolling in medical programmes, Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal shared at a weekly press briefing in New Delhi, as reported by India Tribune. Jaiswal was responding to questions about the recent decline in the number of Indian students travelling to Uzbekistan to pursue MBBS (Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery) degrees. “ "The government remains focused on ensuring that Indian students who are headed to Uzbekistan to pursue education, including medical education, must receive quality education, quality medical education, such that they comply with the guidelines of the National Medical Commission (NMC), which is a body here in India," he said. He also stressed the importance of protecting students from being misled or exploited by "unscrupulous elements" in both India and Uzbekistan. The Indian Embassy in Tashkent and the National Medical Commission have issued recommendations for students considering medical studies abroad, urging them to carefully verify university credentials, admission conditions and contractual terms before enrolling. “ "I urge you to look at the advisories that we've issued. You will get a clearer idea as to why things are happening the way they are happening," Jaiswal added. In April 2026, the NMC issued a separate advisory warning Indian students against enrolling in foreign medical institutions that do not meet India's regulatory requirements, including unauthorised private colleges and institutions operating under offshore programmes. The commission noted that some programmes fail to comply with India's mandatory requirements concerning the duration of medical education, language of instruction, curriculum, clinical training and internship. According to the NMC, students seeking to practise medicine in India after graduating abroad must ensure their programmes meet five key requirements: Duration of the medical education programme; Language of instruction; Curriculum and syllabus; Clinical training; Internship requirements. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/03/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan makes no gold sales in September Uzbekistan made no gold exports in September 2026, extending a trend of retaining domestically purchased precious metal in its reserves, with the Central Bank having sold gold only twice this year — in April and July — for a combined $2.8bn, compared with $9.8bn in exports during the first nine months of 2025. 3 November, 10:00 2 min read 2 623 views 0 comments 0 Source: Reuters Uzbekistan did not export gold in September 2026, marking another month without precious metal sales as the country continues to accumulate gold reserves. Since the beginning of the year, the Central Bank has sold gold only twice, generating $2.8bn in April and July combined. According to the Statistics Committee, gold exports amounted to $1.5bn in April and $1.3bn in July. In the remaining months, gold purchased from domestic producers was retained in the country's reserves. Gold exports have traditionally accounted for a substantial share of Uzbekistan's total foreign trade revenues, contributing at least one-third of exports in previous years. In the first nine months of 2025, the country exported $9.8bn worth of gold, representing 35.9% of total export revenues. During the same period in 2026, the precious metal accounted for just 10.8% of exports. Meanwhile, Uzbekistan's gold reserves have expanded considerably. As of October 1, 2026, the country's reserves held 14.3mn troy ounces (446.9 tons) of gold, compared with 12.6mn ounces (391.9 tons) at the beginning of January. This represents an increase of nearly 55 tons over nine months. Earlier, it was reported that central banks worldwide had purchased approximately 130 tons of gold since the beginning of 2026. Uzbekistan accounted for 40 tons of these purchases, ranking third globally. Gold in Uzbekistan is primarily mined by two major enterprises: Navoi Mining and Metallurgical Company (NMMC) and Almalyk Mining and Metallurgical Combine (AMMC). The Central Bank is the sole domestic buyer of gold produced by these enterprises and can sell the accumulated metal when necessary. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/06/tashkent-.body: Uzbekistan Tashkent construction company faces $103,000 compensation over air pollution violations A construction company in Tashkent’s Almazar district has been assessed more than UZS 1.23bn ($102,961) in compensation for environmental damage after inspectors identified multiple violations, including inadequate dust-control measures, mud carried onto nearby roads and the undocumented disposal of more than 87,000 cubic meters of excavated soil. Yesterday, 13:00 2 min read 2 698 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Madina Nurman A construction company operating in Tashkent’s Almazar district has been assessed more than UZS 1.23bn ($102,961) in compensation for environmental damage after an inspection found multiple violations of air pollution prevention requirements, the National Committee for Ecology and Climate Change reported . The violations at N.H.P LLC were identified by the committee’s Ecopolice officers following complaints from local residents. Inspectors found that the construction site had no wheel-washing facilities at its exit, causing trucks to carry mud and soil onto a 2–2.5 km stretch of nearby roads. The company had also failed to install water-spraying systems to prevent dust from spreading across the construction site or develop measures to protect atmospheric air. Further violations included failure to comply with requirements set out in the state ecological expertise assessment. Inspectors found that the underground parking facility under construction had not been included in the project approved by the ecological assessment. The company also failed to provide documentation showing where more than 87,000 cubic meters of excavated soil had been transported or disposed of. Under Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 202, N.H.P LLC was assessed compensation exceeding UZS 1.23bn ($102,961) for the environmental damage. The company was also instructed to address the identified violations, take measures to prevent and stop dust pollution, and plant trees. Earlier, six enterprises in the Yukori Chirchik district of Tashkent region were found to have discharged industrial wastewater into open areas without adequate treatment. Laboratory tests showed that suspended solids in the wastewater exceeded established limits several times. Authorities announced that compensation for the environmental damage would be calculated and relevant documents submitted to law enforcement agencies. # Construction Industry # Environmental Protection # Environmental Regulations # National Committee for Ecology and Climate Change # air pollution # tashkent Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/06/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan to introduce new medical outsourcing procedures from 2027 Uzbekistan will introduce new medical outsourcing procedures from January 1, 2027, allowing state healthcare institutions to contract private providers for up to ten years in exceptional cases, establish a digital monitoring system and attract foreign management companies, alongside plans for healthcare investment projects worth a combined $3.7bn. Yesterday, 18:00 3 min read 2 298 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Farrux Aliyev Uzbekistan will introduce new procedures allowing state medical institutions to procure medical and auxiliary services from private providers through outsourcing starting January 1, 2027. The changes are outlined in a presidential decree dated November 4, which also establishes new mechanisms for private investment and public-private partnerships (PPPs) in the healthcare sector. Under the new regulations, outsourcing agreements may be concluded for up to five years, depending on the type of service and the amount of investment provided by the contractor. In exceptional cases, contracts may be extended to ten years based on the investment payback period and an assessment by the Ministry of Health. Outsourcing projects whose contracts expire before the new procedure takes effect will be permitted to continue operating until the end of 2027. The decree also allows state medical institutions to provide private contractors with buildings, structures, individual sections or rooms for use free of charge under outsourcing agreements. Such arrangements must be economically justified, and their value must be taken into account when determining the cost of services. By April 1, 2027, Uzbekistan plans to introduce an electronic information system called "Medical Outsourcing" to oversee outsourcing arrangements in state healthcare institutions. The platform will maintain a unified electronic registry containing information about outsourced services, ongoing projects, service providers and concluded contracts. It will also monitor service volumes and quality, key performance indicators (KPIs), service acceptance results, payments and compliance with contractual obligations. By May 1, 2027, the platform is expected to be integrated with electronic public procurement systems and other government information systems. Starting January 1, 2027, Uzbekistan will introduce new mechanisms for state and private sector participation in healthcare development, based on long-term and short-term master plans. Under these arrangements, medical institutions required to provide state-guaranteed healthcare services will remain under state control. At the same time, new healthcare facilities requiring substantial capital investment will generally be developed through public-private partnerships involving private investors. Beginning in 2027, the Ministry of Health will also prepare an annual list of priority healthcare projects intended for implementation through private investment or PPP mechanisms. The list will be published on the ministry's official website by November 1 each year. The decree sets a target of involving established foreign professional management companies and management teams in the operation of at least five major medical organizations by 2030. As a general rule, these companies and managers will be selected through open competitive procedures. Their performance will be assessed annually against efficiency indicators established in their contracts. The results will determine whether management agreements are continued, revised or terminated. The decree also provides for the establishment of a project office under the Ministry of Health. The office will operate without separate legal entity status and will be responsible for reviewing and aligning medical facility design and construction standards with international benchmarks. In addition, the Prosecutor General's Office has been instructed to conduct a comprehensive audit of all existing agreements involving the lease of medical institution buildings, structures and land plots by April 1, 2027. The new measures follow a presentation delivered to President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on October 28 concerning investment opportunities in the healthcare sector. During the presentation, officials reported that a portfolio of 35 investment projects worth a combined $2.7bn had been formed. Proposals were also prepared for nine additional projects with a total estimated value of $1bn, bringing the combined value of existing and proposed projects to $3.7bn. The presentation additionally included a proposal to develop a long-term strategy for attracting investment into Uzbekistan's healthcare sector through 2040. # Electronic Health Systems # Healthcare Reform # Medical Services Procurement # Ministry of Health of Uzbekistan # Private Investment in Healthcare # public-private partnerships # uzbekistan Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? Uzbekistan Uzbekistan proposes electronic register of public event violators from 2027 Uzbekistan plans to introduce an electronic register of individuals banned from attending public events from 2027, alongside new security measures including drone surveillance of crowds and a proposed ban on alcohol sales within 500 metres of event venues, under a draft government resolution. Yesterday, 14:38 1 min read 1 947 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Farrux Aliyev Uzbekistan plans to introduce an electronic register of individuals who violate rules governing public events, with the system expected to come into operation in 2027, according to a draft government resolution developed by the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Under current legislation, individuals who violate the rules for holding public events may be temporarily prohibited from attending such gatherings by a criminal court. The proposed system would electronically record these individuals, allowing authorities to maintain a register of those subject to such restrictions. The draft also proposes banning the sale of alcoholic beverages within a 500-metre radius of public event venues. In addition, authorities plan to use drones to monitor security at public events. The devices would be used to track crowd movements, identify mass gatherings and concentrations of participants, and detect potential security risks. The proposed regulations would also retain a ban on attracting people to public events through the free distribution of food, goods and other products or their sale at artificially low prices for advertising, promotional or other purposes. The restriction was also included in the previous regulatory framework. The draft resolution also proposes introducing electronic ticket sales for concerts and sports competitions and prohibiting ticket sales before the relevant permits have been obtained. Uzbekistan Uzbekistan targets $2.7bn in critical metals production and 15,000 tons of uranium by 2030 Uzbekistan plans to double uranium production from 7,500 tons in 2026 to 15,000 tons by 2030 and increase the production value of 16 types of critical metals to over $2.7bn, alongside $1.1bn in planned tungsten processing investments and measures to expand mineral reserves and develop new production capacities. Yesterday, 09:00 3 min read 2 487 views 0 comments 0 Source: Presidential Press Service President Shavkat Mirziyoyev reviewed the priority tasks for 2026 and future development plans of the Uzbekistan Technological Metals Combine and Navoiyuran enterprise, according to the presidential press service. The presentation focused on increasing the production of critical minerals, developing uranium deposits, implementing investment projects and expanding the country's mineral resource base. According to the information presented, global demand for critical minerals and metals is increasing. While demand for traditional metals is growing by an average of 1% annually, the market for critical minerals is expanding at a rate of 10%. Uzbekistan is undertaking measures to utilize its mineral resources, increase the production of high-value-added goods and strengthen export potential. Source: Presidential Press Service The presentation began with a review of the Uzbekistan Technological Metals Combine's operations and development plans. Particular attention was given to establishing a complete technological chain covering geological exploration, extraction, beneficiation, deep processing and finished product manufacturing. The Combine plans to launch 12 investment projects by the end of 2026, increase the range of localized products and expand the production of high-purity selenium and tellurium. Mirziyoyev instructed officials to accelerate projects involving critical minerals. The Combine currently produces five types of metals and minerals: tungsten, molybdenum, selenium, tellurium and rhenium. Plans call for developing the production of 11 additional types, including nickel, cobalt, graphite, antimony, tin, manganese, platinum, vanadium, mercury and copper. The president also emphasized the importance of applying scientific advancements to identify additional mineral reserves. According to the plans presented, the production value of 16 types of critical metals is expected to exceed $2.7bn by 2030. Major projects involving the deep processing of tungsten have also been developed. These projects are expected to attract $1.1bn in investment and increase production value in the sector to approximately $2.2bn by 2030. Source: Presidential Press Service The presentation additionally covered proposals to develop areas containing rare and rare-earth elements, increase the Combine's resource base and accelerate the implementation of investment projects. The second part of the presentation focused on the activities of Navoiyuran and plans to develop its production operations. According to the information presented, global demand for uranium raw materials has increased by 15–20% in recent years and is projected to grow by another 28% by 2030. In response, Uzbekistan plans to increase uranium extraction, develop new deposits, improve production efficiency and ensure a stable supply of resources required by the uranium industry. Measures planned for 2026 include expanding geological exploration and technological drilling, developing production infrastructure, commissioning additional sorption units and creating 250 new jobs. The government also intends to increase uranium production from 7,500 tons in 2026 to 15,000 tons by 2030. During the same period, identified uranium reserves are expected to reach 200,000 tons. The presentation also addressed the supply of chemical reagents required for uranium production. Officials provided information on measures to strengthen cooperation among domestic industrial enterprises and increase supplies of technical-grade sulfur, sulfuric acid and nitric acid. Mirziyoyev emphasized the need to introduce alternative technologies in production and reduce reliance on sulfuric acid. Under the proposed measures, reagents that can substitute for sulfuric acid should account for 40% of the total reagents used by 2030. These measures are included in the plans to develop Navoiyuran's production capacities and increase uranium extraction volumes. At the conclusion of the presentation, the president instructed responsible officials to ensure the timely implementation of investment projects, strengthen the mineral resource bases of both enterprises and commission new technological capacities. The instructions also covered increasing the production of high-value-added goods and expanding export volumes. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/06/tashkents.body: Uzbekistan Tashkent’s air quality improves 16% in October as PM2.5 levels fall 19% Air quality in Tashkent improved by 16% in October 2026 compared with the same month last year, with average AQI falling from 138 to 115, PM2.5 concentrations declining by 19% and the number of days with good air quality rising from three to 14. Yesterday, 12:00 2 min read 2 225 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Farrux Aliyev Air quality in Tashkent improved by 16% in October 2026 compared to the same month last year, with average air pollution levels declining and the number of days with good air quality increasing, according to the National Committee for Ecology and Climate Change. Monitoring data from a special commission showed that the monthly average Air Quality Index (AQI) fell from 138 in October 2025 to 115 in October 2026. Concentrations of PM2.5 particles decreased by 19%, while PM10 levels dropped by 37%. The number of days classified as “green” under the national air quality index increased from three to 14 year on year. Meanwhile, the number of “yellow” and “red” days combined fell from 16 to four. However, air quality varied throughout the month. Conditions during the first 20 days of October were significantly better than a year earlier, but pollution levels deteriorated between October 25 and 31. The committee attributed the late-month deterioration to lower temperatures, weaker winds, frequent temperature inversions and insufficient rainfall. These conditions restricted the dispersion of pollutants from local and neighbouring areas, allowing particulate matter to remain concentrated in the air close to the ground. Source: National Committee for Ecology and Climate Change Laboratory analysis of 60 PM2.5 samples collected during October found that emissions associated with fuel combustion in the industrial, transport and energy sectors accounted for an average of 44.4% of the particles. Natural dust made up another 42.6%. The proportions remained broadly unchanged even on days when air quality worsened towards the end of the month. The committee concluded that the deterioration was primarily caused by the accumulation of pollutants from local and neighbouring regions over the city under weak winds and unfavourable meteorological conditions. What causes air pollution in Tashkent? The committee also highlighted atmospheric circulation as an important factor influencing air quality in the capital. Tashkent is located in a foothill area adjacent to a valley, where winds from the northeast and southwest play a significant role in air circulation. Wind direction and speed directly affect the exchange of air masses and the distribution of pollutants. Experts noted that air pollution is driven not only by human activity but also by natural dust, low rainfall and adverse weather conditions. Insufficient precipitation reduces the natural removal of dust particles from the atmosphere. Precipitation in the capital has been almost six times lower than the monthly norm. Earlier, forecasts indicated that Tashkent could receive 2–6 mm of precipitation overnight on November 5, potentially helping reduce concentrations of PM2.5 and PM10 particles in the air. # Meteorological Conditions # National Committee for Ecology and Climate Change # Particulate Matter # Pollution Monitoring Report # Urban Pollution # tashkent # uzbekistan Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/06/u-s-airli.body: Uzbekistan U.S. airline United Airlines eyes Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan flights U.S. carrier United Airlines is exploring the possibility of launching flights to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan after assessing opportunities in both markets, although restrictions on flying over Russian airspace remain a major obstacle, CEO Scott Kirby revealed on the Cheeky Pint podcast. Yesterday, 10:00 2 min read 2 816 views 0 comments 0 Source: Forbes / Kevin Karter U.S. airline United Airlines is exploring the possibility of launching flights to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, although restrictions on the use of Russian airspace currently prevent the carrier from operating these routes, CEO Scott Kirby shared on the Cheeky Pint podcast, as reported by Live and Let's Fly. Kirby noted that Patrick Quayle, United Airlines' head of global network planning and alliances, visited both countries this year to assess opportunities in their aviation markets. The airline is also examining destinations that other major U.S. carriers have largely overlooked when expanding their international networks. However, Kirby voiced that the inability to use Russian airspace remains a major obstacle to launching flights to Central Asia. “ "We can’t fly there today because we can’t fly over Russia," he said, while leaving open the possibility of serving the markets in the future. "This could work down the road," Kirby added. United Airlines has not announced which Uzbek or Kazakh cities it might serve, the U.S. departure airports, the aircraft it would deploy or a potential launch date. Live and Let's Fly suggests that Newark Liberty International Airport could be a possible departure point, although this has not been confirmed by the airline. Uzbekistan Airways currently operates direct flights between Tashkent and New York. However, United Airlines' exploration of the Uzbek and Kazakh markets does not indicate that the carrier has made a final decision to launch services. The developments come as other international airlines consider expanding their presence in Uzbekistan. Turkish low-cost carrier Pegasus Airlines is also negotiating to broaden its network in the country. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/05/kyrgyzsta.body: Kyrgyzstan Kyrgyzstan’s MP proposes replacing large children's care homes with smaller family support centers Kyrgyzstan’s MP Dastan Bekeshev has proposed gradually reforming children's boarding institutions and expanding Mother's House centers nationwide to support mothers in difficult circumstances and keep children with their families, as approximately 10,000 children live in 137 boarding institutions across the country, 95% of whom have living parents or legal guardians. 5 November, 22:04 2 min read 962 views 0 comments 0 Source: “24.kg” Kyrgyzstan should gradually reform its system of children's care homes and expand a network of smaller facilities where mothers facing difficult circumstances can live with their children, according to Dastan Bekeshev, a deputy of the Jogorku Kenesh (Parliament). The proposal follows his visit to a Mother's House facility in Bishkek, as reported by 24.kg. Bekeshev emphasized the importance of keeping children within their families and providing support to mothers who face difficult living conditions. He proposed expanding the existing network of facilities across Kyrgyzstan and involving businesses in their establishment. According to Bekeshev, two Mother's House facilities currently operate in Bishkek's Oktyabr district. During his visit to one of the centers, the deputy observed that eight mothers facing difficult life circumstances were living there with their young children. Bekeshev stated that such facilities allow children to remain with their mothers while receiving the necessary care. He argued that large residential institutions cannot provide the same family environment, as caregivers cannot fully replace parents. "A child should not be separated from their family. They need someone to care for them. Caregivers simply cannot fulfill this role; they cannot be a mother," the deputy said. The Ene Uyu (Mother's House) resource centers provide assistance to pregnant women and mothers with children who are experiencing difficult life circumstances. Their services include psychological, medical, social and legal support aimed at preventing infant abandonment and helping children remain with their families. The first center opened in Bishkek in May 2025, followed by a second facility in February 2026. Bekeshev proposed extending this model to other parts of Kyrgyzstan as part of broader changes to the country's child-care system. The deputy acknowledged that financing the establishment and operation of such facilities entirely through the state budget would be difficult. He therefore suggested involving the business community in creating additional centers. Bekeshev also stated that increasing social benefits alone would not be sufficient to address the challenges faced by mothers and children. According to the deputy, broader changes are needed to ensure that families receive the necessary support and feel secure. He plans to raise the issue during sessions of the Jogorku Kenesh and called on the Ministry of Labor, Social Security and Migration to take a more active role in reforming the child-care system. According to the ministry, approximately 10,000 children currently live in 137 boarding institutions across Kyrgyzstan. Of these children, 95% have living parents or legal guardians. Uzbekistan Uzbekistan does not track Coxsackie virus separately in official statistics Uzbekistan does not track Coxsackie virus infections separately in official statistics, recording them under the broader category of enteroviral infections, while health officials say the virus is not particularly widespread in the country and recommend maintaining hygiene and limiting contact with others when symptoms appear. 5 November, 21:01 2 min read 2 686 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Madina Nurman Uzbekistan does not maintain separate official statistics on Coxsackie virus infections, as cases are recorded under the broader category of enteroviral infections. This was stated by Nurmat Otabekov, First Deputy Chairman of the Committee for Sanitary-Epidemiological Well-being and Public Health, according to the Ministry of Health's press service. Otabekov explained that the Coxsackie virus belongs to the enterovirus group and is therefore not registered as a separate disease in the country's official statistics. He also noted that the risk of contracting certain infectious diseases, including Coxsackie virus infections, increases during the autumn and winter seasons. According to Otabekov, approximately 70 types of the Coxsackie virus exist, with types A and B being the most common. The infection can produce symptoms similar to those of acute intestinal infections, while some patients may experience respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms simultaneously. Type A infections may cause blisters to appear on the face, lips, nose and fingers. Type B infections are associated with gastrointestinal symptoms and may, in some cases, lead to complications affecting internal organs. Otabekov noted that most people experience mild symptoms, while some individuals may not realize they have contracted the infection. However, certain cases can result in more serious complications, including pneumonia and meningitis. When Coxsackie virus infection is suspected, patients receive symptomatic treatment, according to the official. He added that a fever lasting more than four days may also be considered a possible indication of the infection. The representative of the Sanitary-Epidemiological Committee stated that there was no reason for excessive concern over reports circulating about the Coxsackie virus. According to Otabekov, the infection is not particularly widespread in Uzbekistan, while cases associated with the virus are more frequently recorded in Europe, Latin America and other Western countries. To reduce the risk of infection, he recommended following sanitary and hygienic requirements, washing hands thoroughly and limiting contact with other people when symptoms appear. The official emphasized the importance of preventive measures, particularly during the autumn and winter seasons, when the likelihood of contracting certain infectious diseases increases. In May, the Academy of Sciences of Uzbekistan announced that the Andes strain of hantavirus, which can be transmitted from person to person, had not been detected in the country. According to the Academy, hantaviruses identified in the region are transmitted through wild rodents. Experts also emphasized the importance of following sanitary and hygienic rules to prevent infection. # Disease Prevention # Enteroviral Infections # Epidemiological Surveillance # Infectious Diseases # Public Health # Sanitary-Epidemiological Committee # uzbekistan Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? Uzbekistan Uzbekistan introduces new crime assessment model using AI and digital monitoring Uzbekistan is introducing a new crime assessment model that uses artificial intelligence, a crime stability index and regional crime maps to monitor and forecast risks, as authorities report that 701 of the 809 mahallas previously classified as having the most severe crime situations have been removed from that category. 5 November, 12:00 3 min read 1 443 views 0 comments 0 Source: Presidential Press Service Uzbekistan will introduce a new model for assessing crime, including a crime stability index, artificial intelligence technologies and regional crime maps. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev reviewed the proposed measures during a presentation on improving crime prevention on November 4, according to the presidential press service. The initiative aims to improve the analysis of crime risks by integrating information from state agencies and considering socio-economic factors. At the conclusion of the presentation, Mirziyoyev signed a decree introducing the new assessment model and instructed officials to implement digital analysis and monitoring mechanisms. Source: Presidential Press Service During the presentation, it was noted that existing crime assessment methods rely primarily on statistical data, while socio-economic factors influencing crime are not sufficiently analyzed. In addition, information systems used by different government agencies are not fully integrated, limiting the ability to assess the crime situation. To address these issues, a new assessment model was proposed, including the introduction of a crime stability index for the first time. The initiative also includes the creation of a unified crime-related data platform that will integrate information resources from various state agencies. Artificial intelligence technologies will be used to analyze and forecast crime risks, while regional crime maps will be developed to identify areas requiring preventive measures. Under the proposed system, crime conditions in individual regions and mahallas (neighborhoods) will be assessed continuously, with preventive measures determined according to identified risk levels. Source: Presidential Press Service The model will also introduce specific outcome indicators for evaluating the performance of responsible government agencies. These indicators will be used alongside digital monitoring and analysis to assess the effectiveness of crime prevention measures. The presentation also included information on the development of security infrastructure throughout the country. According to the figures presented, 263,000 identification cameras, 70,000 modern intercom systems and 22,000 panic buttons have been installed in various regions. Officials also reported the results of social preventive measures aimed at addressing factors associated with crime. Through these measures, specific problems affecting 2.1mn individuals have been addressed. Source: Presidential Press Service As a result, 701 of the 809 mahallas previously classified as having the most severe crime situations have been removed from that category. Meanwhile, approximately 4,400 mahallas remain in the green category, indicating a safe crime situation. During the presentation, Mirziyoyev emphasized that preventing offenses should not be the responsibility of law enforcement agencies alone. He stated that all relevant government authorities, mahalla committees and members of the public should participate in crime prevention efforts. At the conclusion of the meeting, the president signed a decree introducing the new crime assessment model.
