Uzbekistan Uzbekistan's cotton output reaches historic high of 5mn tons Uzbekistan has harvested more than 5mn tons of cotton for the first time in its history, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced in a congratulatory message to farmers and agricultural workers, noting that average yields reached 70 centners per hectare across around 400,000 hectares and farmers are expected to earn a combined net profit of UZS 13-14 trillion ($1.09-1.18bn). 5 November, 11:00 2 min read 4 388 views 0 comments 0 Source: Presidential Press Service Uzbekistan harvested more than 5mn tons of cotton for the first time in its history, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced on November 4, congratulating farmers and agricultural workers on the record crop. In a congratulatory message published on the presidential website, Mirziyoyev noted that the harvest had been completed before the onset of rainfall despite challenges associated with climate change. The president highlighted improvements in cotton productivity, noting that average yields had increased from 21 centners per hectare to 56 centners over the period of agricultural reforms. During the Soviet era, around 2mn hectares were allocated to cotton cultivation, while average yields remained below 30 centners per hectare. In 2000, Uzbekistan planted cotton on 1.4mn hectares and harvested approximately 3mn tons. The area under cultivation was subsequently reduced by 38%, while restrictions were introduced on involving teachers, students and employees of budget-funded organizations in fieldwork. Mirziyoyev also pointed to the expansion of water-saving technologies, which have reduced water consumption in cotton production by half compared with the 1990s. This year, average yields reached 70 centners per hectare across approximately 400,000 hectares, while nearly 70,000 hectares recorded yields of 100-110 centners. Around 1,000 farms and agricultural clusters achieved average yields of at least 100 centners per hectare. More than 4,000 farmers recorded yields of 60-70 centners per hectare, including 2,500 who reached 80 centners. Individual farms in Pakhtakor district and Zharkurgan district reported yields of 110 centners per hectare. By region, average yields exceeded 60 centners per hectare in Jizzakh, Khorezm, Bukhara, Navoi and Syrdarya. Karakalpakstan produced more than 400,000 tons, with yields increasing by 10-15 centners compared with previous years. Koson district in Kashkadarya region recorded the country's largest district-level harvest at 110,000 tons, followed by Mirishkor with 105,000 tons, Kasbi with 95,000 tons and Nishan with 90,000 tons. The president noted that 85% of the cotton crop had been harvested within 30-35 days using more than 3,000 cotton-picking machines. Mechanization reached 100% in Jizzakh and Syrdarya regions, while digitalization, drones and other technologies helped halve harvesting costs. Farmers are expected to earn a combined net profit of UZS 13-14 trillion ($1.09-1.18bn) from cotton production this year. Looking ahead, Mirziyoyev added that Uzbekistan plans to expand the use of high-yielding seed varieties, agricultural drones, water- and energy-saving technologies, and artificial intelligence in cotton farming next year. The government aims to raise average cotton yields to 65-70 centners per hectare. Mirziyoyev said the implementation of the country's agricultural development strategy would rely on more than 3.5mn people working in the sector. # Agricultural Reforms # Agricultural Technology # Cotton Production # Crop Yields # Presidential Statement # Uzbekistan Agriculture Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/05/tashkent-.body: Uzbekistan Tashkent expects air quality to improve as rain washes out fine particles Air quality in Tashkent is expected to improve overnight on November 5 as rainfall of 2–6 millimeters helps reduce concentrations of PM2.5 and PM10 particles, with readings forecast to reach moderate levels under the international Air Quality Index. 5 November, 10:00 2 min read 1 637 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Farrux Aliyev Air quality in Tashkent is expected to improve overnight on November 5 as rainfall helps reduce concentrations of fine particulate matter in the atmosphere, the National Committee for Ecology and Climate Change reported . According to forecasts, air quality in the capital during the evening, night and early morning hours may reach moderate levels under the international Air Quality Index (AQI), although it could temporarily become unhealthy for sensitive groups. Under Uzbekistan’s national air quality index, readings are expected to remain mostly in the green zone, with brief periods in the yellow zone. Global weather forecast models predict 2-6 millimeters of precipitation in Tashkent overnight. The rainfall is expected to help remove PM2.5 and PM10 particles from the atmosphere, temporarily improving air quality. By the morning of November 5, air quality is forecast to be moderate under the international AQI and predominantly green under the national index. Factors behind air pollution The committee also highlighted atmospheric circulation as one of the factors influencing air quality in the capital. Tashkent is situated in a foothill area adjacent to a valley, where winds from the northeast and southwest play an important role in air exchange and the dispersal of pollutants. Wind direction and speed directly affect how pollutants accumulate or disperse across the city. Experts attribute rising air pollution not only to human activity but also to natural dust, insufficient precipitation and unfavourable meteorological conditions. Limited rainfall reduces the natural removal of dust particles from the atmosphere. Precipitation in the capital has fallen to almost one-sixth of the monthly norm, according to the committee. Air quality in Tashkent was also forecast to deteriorate overnight from October 31 to November 1. At the time, the worsening conditions were attributed to falling temperatures, weak winds and temperature inversion. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/04/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan detects over 4,100 cases of illegal plant waste burning in 9M26 Uzbekistan recorded more than 4,100 cases of illegal leaf and plant-residue burning in January–September 2026, with repeat offenders facing fines of up to UZS 22mn ($1,845) for officials, as environmental authorities step up monitoring of open fires in residential areas and agricultural fields. 4 November, 23:01 2 min read 1 296 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Dilruh Isomiddinova Uzbekistan has recorded more than 4,100 violations involving the burning of leaves and other plant residues in the first nine months of 2026, with officials facing fines of up to UZS 22mn ($1,845) for repeat offences. According to Doston Khojanov, head of the State Environmental Control Inspectorate (Ecopolice) under the National Committee for Ecology and Climate Change, cases of open burning are commonly reported in residential areas, streets, gardens, alleys and agricultural fields during autumn. Burning leaves and other plant waste releases carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, fine particulate matter and other harmful substances into the atmosphere. The resulting smoke can spread into residential areas and deteriorate air quality. The Ecopolice has intensified monitoring to prevent such violations. In cooperation with the Uzbekcosmos agency, authorities are also using aerospace monitoring technologies to detect the burning of crop residues in fields after grain harvesting. Under the State Space Monitoring Programme, 915 cases of field residue burning were identified. Administrative fines were imposed on those responsible, while environmental damage was calculated for each hectare of agricultural land affected by fire in accordance with the law. Under Part 3 of Article 88 of Uzbekistan's Code of Administrative Responsibility, burning hay, haystacks and other plant residues in fields and settlements is prohibited. The offence carries fines ranging from UZS 1.32mn ($111) to UZS 2.2mn ($185) for individuals and from UZS 8.8mn ($738) to UZS 13.2mn ($1,107) for officials. If the violation is repeated within one year of an administrative penalty, fines increase to up to UZS 3.08mn ($258) for individuals and UZS 22mn ($1,845) for officials. A total of 711 passengers were denied entry to Georgia at its airports between January and September, including 473 Uzbek nationals. The main reasons for refusal included an inability to clearly explain the purpose of travel, a lack of hotel reservations or return flight tickets, failure to provide proof of medical insurance and insufficient financial resources. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/30/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan establishes specialized nuclear classes at two academic lyceums in Tashkent Uzbekistan's NRNU MEPhI branch in Tashkent is establishing specialized nuclear classes at two academic lyceums to prepare students for careers in the country's nuclear energy sector through advanced studies in physics, mathematics and computer science, practical exposure to nuclear technologies, career guidance and targeted preparation for university admission. 30 October, 18:00 2 min read 530 views 0 comments 0 Source: Uzatom The Tashkent branch of the National Research Nuclear University MEPhI (NRNU MEPhI) is expanding cooperation with educational institutions in the capital through the establishment of specialized nuclear classes aimed at preparing students for careers in Uzbekistan's nuclear energy sector. The initiative involves the I. M. Gubkin Academic Lyceum, affiliated with the Gubkin Russian State University of Oil and Gas, and the International House-Tashkent Academic Lyceum, affiliated with the Tashkent Institute of Irrigation and Agricultural Mechanization Engineers. Memorandums of understanding have been signed to formalize long-term cooperation on the specialized preparation of secondary school students. The educational program will include advanced studies in physics, mathematics and computer science, alongside practical exposure to modern nuclear energy technologies. Students will have access to lectures and seminars conducted by industry experts, academic Olympiads, career-oriented meetings and joint scientific and educational initiatives. The program also provides targeted preparation for admission to the Tashkent branch of NRNU MEPhI. The establishment of specialized nuclear classes is linked to the development of nuclear energy and national nuclear infrastructure in Uzbekistan. The initiative focuses on preparing future specialists with an understanding of operational safety, technological foundations and the peaceful use of atomic energy. The initiative also draws on international experience in early specialized academic preparation, including approaches to youth engagement and nuclear education associated with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). In France, preparatory classes have long been used to train engineers for the nuclear industry. In South Korea and China, technical education beginning at the school level supports the construction and operation of nuclear power plants. In the United States and other countries, secondary education focused on physics, mathematics and engineering provides a foundation for further studies in nuclear-related disciplines. According to the information provided, graduates of specialized educational programs demonstrate high academic achievement, are more likely to choose nuclear and engineering disciplines, perform well during internships and adapt more quickly to professional environments. Such specialists contribute to the workforce of nuclear power plants, design organizations and research centers, supporting both the operation of existing facilities and the development of new projects. https://daryo.uz/en/2024/11/18/from-rubl.body: Economics From Ruble zone to global fintech leader: Kazakhstan’s financial revolution in focus Discover how Kazakhstan has transformed its financial sector over three decades—from its humble beginnings to a thriving hub of fintech innovation, digitalization, and international investment. 18 November 2024, 17:01 3 min read 20 116 views 0 comments 0 Thirty-three years ago, imagining Kazakh CEOs, fintech pioneers, government officials, and banking leaders gathering in New York City to discuss Kazakhstan’s financial evolution would have seemed far-fetched. In 1991, Kazakhstan lacked its own currency, operating under monetary rules dictated by the Central Bank of Russia. The country’s banking system was rudimentary, dependent on a few traditional banks, with little diversity or competition. Economic reforms were nascent, privatization was contentious, and the creation of a Kazakh stock market faced major hurdles. Fast forward to 2024, and Kazakhstan boasts a rapidly evolving financial sector driven by digital transformation and innovation. Fintech giant Kaspi.kz made headlines with a successful Nasdaq IPO and has since expanded its reach by acquiring a majority stake in Turkey’s leading e-commerce platform, Hepsiburada. Emerging fintech leaders like S1lkPay , a certified Mastercard technology partner, further highlight the sector’s dynamism. A key player in this transformation is the Astana International Financial Center (AIFC) , an advanced financial hub that has attracted global businesses and investors. The Astana International Exchange (AIX) has seen trading volumes surpass $2 billion since its 2018 launch, with $1 billion traded this year alone. These developments showcase Kazakhstan’s integration into global financial markets and its emergence as a dynamic destination for investment and innovation. Key Developments Highlighted at Kazakhstan Finance Day Kazakhstan Finance Day , held on October 28th in New York City, brought together prominent leaders from Kazakhstan’s financial sector. High-profile attendees included Mikhail Lomtadze, CEO of Kaspi.kz, Umut Shayakhmetova of Halyk Bank, Timur Turlov of Freedom Holding, and officials from the National Bank of Kazakhstan and the Agency for Regulation and Development of Financial Markets. While the forum celebrated the sector’s achievements, it also raised questions about challenges that persist: • Small Sector Size : Despite progress, Kazakhstan’s financial sector remains modest relative to its vast size and resource wealth. • Banking Dominance : Banks represent over 60% of GDP, with non-banking institutions contributing only 4% and the insurance sector 2%. • Limited Credit Access : Bank credit accounts for just 20% of GDP—lagging behind peers, according to the World Bank . Future Financial Growth Requires Reform Under President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev , Kazakhstan aims to double GDP by 2029 and join the top 30 global economies by 2050. Achieving this ambitious goal requires substantial capital investment, efficient capital allocation, and a diverse financial system . The World Bank stresses that Kazakhstan must adopt structural reforms to support economic diversification, energy transition, and climate resilience. One initiative leading this transformation is the Baiterek National Holding Company , which is promoting over 700 investment projects valued at $28 billion. However, broader financial reforms are essential to mobilize private capital and create a resilient, growth-oriented economy. Addressing Risks and Challenges Kazakhstan faces global macroeconomic uncertainties, including inflation, oil price volatility, and geopolitical risks such as Western sanctions on Russian bank subsidiaries operating within the country. Internal challenges, like slow reforms in education and limited investor confidence, could also hinder economic growth. The proposed new banking legislation , announced by President Tokayev, aims to modernize the sector, boost competition, and create a robust environment for fintech innovation. Conclusion Kazakhstan Finance Day in New York City showcased the remarkable evolution of the country’s financial landscape while acknowledging the challenges ahead. With transformative reforms, international collaboration, and private investment, Kazakhstan is poised to unlock its immense economic potential. What will the next Kazakhstan Finance Day reveal? Only time will tell. But one thing is certain: Kazakhstan’s financial leaders are committed to driving progress and securing the nation’s place as a global financial powerhouse. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/14/cybersecu.body: Uzbekistan Cybersecurity leaders call for stronger regional cooperation at CSS2026 in Tashkent Uzbekistan’s 2026–2030 cybersecurity strategy took centre stage at the Cyber Security Summit - Central Eurasia (CSS2026), which brought together more than 600 delegates to address AI security, critical infrastructure protection and financial-sector risks, with regional and international cooperation highlighted as key to strengthening cyber resilience. 14 October, 13:59 4 min read 1 080 views 0 comments 0 Source: Daryo The summit brought together government representatives, cybersecurity experts and technology companies to discuss AI security, critical infrastructure protection and financial-sector risks as Uzbekistan implements its 2026–2030 cybersecurity strategy. The event focused on protecting critical infrastructure, securing financial services, managing risks associated with artificial intelligence (AI) and strengthening cybersecurity capabilities across Central Asia and neighbouring regions. Cyber Security Summit - Central Eurasia (CSS2026) attracted more than 600 delegates, including over 300 chief information security officers (CISOs) and more than 100 solution providers. Overall participation increase by more than 25% compared with 2025, reflecting growing interest in cybersecurity across the region. The strategy sets priorities for strengthening national cyber resilience, protecting critical digital infrastructure, combating cybercrime, developing AI-based cybersecurity capabilities and expanding international cooperation. Regional cooperation at the centre of cybersecurity Participants highlighted that cyber threats increasingly cross national borders, making cooperation between governments, businesses and international organisations essential. Marle Maigre of Estonia’s e-Governance Academy IEGA) said the summit had grown in scale and provided an important opportunity to connect regional stakeholders with international partners. She noted that the EGA and Expertise France were bringing partners involved in the EU’s financial-sector cybersecurity programme to the event, reflecting the importance of regional and international cooperation. “ “Ultimately, cybersecurity is about trust,” Maigre said, highlighting the value of meeting counterparts, building professional relationships and exchanging ideas. “We value the importance of regional and international cooperation.” She added that the summit creates opportunities for bilateral and multilateral discussions involving both governments and the private sector. According to Maigre, such platforms can help strengthen cooperation across Central Asia while connecting regional cybersecurity communities with international expertise. A similar view was expressed by H.E. Shaikh Salman bin Mohammed Al Khalifa, Chief Executive Officer of Bahrain’s National Cybersecurity Centre (NCSC). He stressed that cooperation among Central Eurasian countries could significantly strengthen the region’s collective resilience, while international engagement allows participants to learn from experiences beyond their own national systems. “ “This kind of summits are the opportunity to learn from each other, learn from successors regionally and globally,” H.E. Shaikh Salman bin Mohammed Al Khalifa added. Al Khalifa also stressed that cybersecurity requires continuous effort rather than a one-time response or the adoption of a strategy alone. Effective protection depends on the ongoing work of cybersecurity specialists, operational teams and developers. Addressing increasingly complex digital threats The summit’s agenda reflected the expanding range of cybersecurity challenges facing governments and businesses. Discussions covered AI security, critical infrastructure, information technology and operational technology (IT/OT) security, financial services and the development of a skilled cybersecurity workforce. The programme also included a dedicated discussion of Uzbekistan’s 2026–2030 cybersecurity strategy, examining its implications for the national cybersecurity ecosystem and the lessons that could be drawn from international partners. Other sessions focused on protecting banking and financial services, securing industrial facilities and networks, and developing education, training and professional certification for cybersecurity specialists. Benedicte Borel of Expertise France emphasised that cybersecurity challenges cannot be addressed effectively through isolated. She noted that the organisation was implementing a cybersecurity project in Central Asia with partners including Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. The summit, she explained, offered an opportunity to meet regional partners, exchange expertise and connect with companies developing cybersecurity solutions. Borel also pointed to the constantly changing and increasingly sophisticated nature of cyber threats, which requires technology providers to continue developing solutions and experts to maintain regular cooperation. From strategy to implementation Uzbekistan’s cybersecurity strategy provides an important policy context for the discussions. Its implementation involves strengthening institutional capacity, improving protection for critical digital infrastructure and introducing additional cybersecurity requirements for organisations covered by the strategy. For government institutions, financial organisations and technology companies, these priorities raise practical questions about compliance, investment, skills and the adoption of new security technologies. The summit provided a platform for public-sector representatives, private companies and international partners to discuss these challenges and explore areas for cooperation. The interviews also highlighted a common message: cybersecurity resilience depends not only on technology and national strategies, but also on trust, information-sharing and sustained collaboration. As digital services and AI applications become more widely used, cooperation between countries and across industries is likely to remain a key element of efforts to protect the region’s digital infrastructure. # CSS2026 # cooperation # cyber # cybersecurity # infrastructure # international cooperation # protections # ssecurity Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/12/un-womens.body: Uzbekistan UN Women’s Belén Sanz Luque on Uzbekistan’s progress and the challenges facing women Uzbekistan has introduced a series of reforms to advance gender equality over the past decade, including legal protections against domestic violence and measures to increase women’s representation in parliament. During her visit to the country, Belén Sanz Luque, UN Women’s regional director for Europe and Central Asia, sat down with Daryo to examine the impact of these changes and the challenges that remain. 12 October, 17:03 12 min read 994 views 0 comments 0 Source: Daryo Ten years of reform have brought Uzbekistan a gender equality strategy, a law addressing domestic violence and one of the region’s highest shares of women in parliament. During a recent visit to Uzbekistan, Belén Sanz Luque, UN Women’s regional director for Europe and Central Asia, sat down with Daryo to discuss the progress made and the challenges that remain. As part of her visit, Sanz Luque met with the National Statistics Committee, the EU Delegation and civil society groups, taking stock of the progress made and the gaps that remain. For her, the ultimate measure of these reforms is whether they translate into meaningful changes in the everyday lives of women and girls. “I think at this point what the real measure of success will be is whether all the changes that have been boosted over the last 10 years can result in lived experiences for women and girls,” she told Daryo. Source: Daryo Progress that is not a coincidence Sanz Luque sees Uzbekistan's progress against a global backdrop of pushback and disinformation about gender equality. She stressed that the country stands out with women holding 38% of seats in Uzbekistan's parliament, well above the Europe and Central Asia average of 26%. Sanz Luque credits policy for this trend, not chance. "It's the result of concerted efforts, including a gender quota that enabled women candidates to be part of the list," she said. She added that it is not yet parity, but "a very important progress." The legal framework has grown too, with the National Strategy for Achieving Gender Equality by 2030, a law criminalizing domestic violence and, as she learned during her visit, a new presidential decree on workplace harassment. Access to education has also expanded. Preschool coverage has risen from 27% in 2017 to about 75% in 2025, according to figures reported by the country, which gives girls an early start and frees families to take part in economic life. Source: UNDP Uzbekistan A Seat Is Not a Say Sanz Luque welcomed the 38% statistics, but claims that it hides a weaker picture closer to people's daily lives. "In Mahalla, women represent like 15% of leadership," she said. "So it's very low compared to this parliamentary representation." She wants regional and local levels to match parliament. Other figures show the same drop. Women hold 16 of 65 Senate seats, or 24.6%, and about 25% of seats in local councils. They are much rarer among governors, mayors and district heads than among councillors. These numbers measure who holds a seat, not who shapes the decision, and that is the gap between the formal figures and daily life. She did credit one institutional example, the Senate under Chair Tanzila Narbaeva, and its willingness to keep working on legislation. A crime shielded by shame Sanz Luque says violence against women was long treated as something to hide. "It has been naturalized as if it was part of the society. It was invisible, silenced. No one wants to talk about that because it generates shame. It generates fear. Not only for the women but also for the families." Source: Daryo Her answer has three steps. First, document the problem so that we are able to understand the magnitude of the problem. Second, treat it as a public matter, not a private one: "It's a public problem that has a health consequence for the woman, for the family, for society, for children of course." Third, and hardest, change the discriminatory social norms that justify violence. To persuade women to speak up, she wants them told plainly that violence against women is a human rights violation, that it is against the law, and that there are institutions that should have the capacity to respond. The aim, she said, is "no impunity." A case in Namangan this month showed how far that aim still is from reality. Police opened a criminal case on September 12 over the alleged sexual assault of a five-year-old girl at a state kindergarten in Uchkurgan district, and the suspect, the kindergarten's head of maintenance, was detained the same day. He has not been convicted. The girl's mother told a local journalist that the child had become fearful and was afraid to walk past the kindergarten. timesca gazeta The mother told local media that the kindergarten's cameras recorded nothing that day and that the suspect was reportedly responsible for them, and she said his wife offered her a bribe to close the case. The National Agency for Social Protection announced that it will arrange for the family to move to another city and receive housing, rehabilitation and social support. Source: Milliy TV The response has been swift. A bill passed its first reading in the lower house of parliament that would introduce life imprisonment for raping a child under 14, where the current penalty is 15 to 20 years, and would remove certain limitation periods. Lawmaker Gulrukh Agzamova told parliament that 445 cases of child rape under 14 were opened between 2022 and 2025. Presidential Administration head Saida Mirziyoyeva expressed that she believes the death penalty should apply to such crimes, though current law does not provide for it. The Constitution prohibits it, so restoring it would require an amendment. Critics argue the debate overlooks the failure of the systems that should have protected the girl. For Sanz Luque, the lesson is that law needs working institutions behind it. "We inform the society. We raise awareness and we ensure that the institutions are effective, so that there is no impunity." Her message was plain: "Everybody should feel safe in their own home, in their own country." When the abuse moves online Online gender-based violence is another issue that is much overlooked. According to Sanz Luque, violence on screen can sometimes reflect violence off-screen. "The violence that occurs outside of the digital world is not separated from the violence that occurs in the digital world. There is a continuum." Her concern here is survivors. She says Uzbekistan needs clear standards and mechanisms now, so that any girl who is a victim of online violence knows where to go to be protected and to report it. UN Women encourages countries to pass national laws covering technology-facilitated violence, and she named the European Union's strategy on digital violence as a model. Research by Kamola Alieva in 2025 shows why this matters in Uzbekistan. Alieva finds that online abuse targets women in public roles, including activists, journalists and public officials, through leaked intimate images, doxxing, smear campaigns and blackmail, and that it pushes women out of public life. Even in a case where Telegram channels sold intimate images and investigators identified 62 victims, prosecutors had to rely on defamation, extortion and pornography articles, because Uzbek law has no explicit offense for non-consensual intimate imagery. Stigma, limited legal aid and weak digital-evidence procedures leave many victims without recourse. A separate question, Sanz Luque said, is who shapes the technology itself. She wants women to take part in national AI strategies so that AI does not reproduce discrimination. "Globally, only 24 of 138 national strategies on AI have any mention of gender equality or women. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/11/uk-export.body: Uzbekistan UK exports to Uzbekistan could exceed £1bn within a decade, says Lord Sarwar UK exports to Uzbekistan could exceed £1bn within the next five to ten years, Trade Minister Lord Sarwar told Daryo in an exclusive interview, outlining Britain’s plans to expand economic cooperation with Central Asia’s largest economy through financial services, mining, clean energy and digital technology, while supporting investment and access to international markets. 11 October, 12:00 11 min read 1 082 views 0 comments 0 British Trade Minister identifies financial services, mining, clean energy and technology as key areas for deeper economic cooperation with Uzbekistan UK exports to Uzbekistan could exceed £1bn within the next five to ten years, Trade Minister Lord Sarwar has told Daryo in an exclusive interview, outlining Britain’s ambitions to deepen commercial ties with Central Asia’s largest economy and expand cooperation in sectors ranging from financial services and mining to clean energy and digital technology. UK exports to Uzbekistan increased from £66mn in 2016 to £592mn in 2025, reflecting the rapid expansion of bilateral economic engagement. Total trade in goods and services between the two countries reached £2.2bn in the four quarters to the end of the third quarter of 2025, according to UK government data. “ “The relationship is increasingly strong, but I believe we have only begun to realise its full potential,” Lord Sarwar said. He pointed to Uzbekistan’s sustained economic growth and reform programme as factors creating opportunities for British businesses, while highlighting the complementarity between the two countries’ economic priorities. “ “British companies can offer high-quality products, specialist expertise and innovative solutions in areas ranging from financial and professional services to advanced engineering, education, healthcare, aviation and sustainable infrastructure. The next stage should be about translating this natural complementarity into concrete commercial outcomes,” Lord Sarwar added. Source: Presidential Press Service During the visit, Lord Sarwar also met President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, describing the meeting as positive and expressing gratitude for the president’s time. “ “I also had the honour to meet His Excellency President Mirziyoyev and am immensely grateful that he found time in his tight schedule. We had a very good meeting, and it was clear that he shares with the UK Prime Minister a determination to deliver swift, tangible outcomes and drive economic growth across the region,” the minister said. Services lead bilateral trade opportunities According to Lord Sarwar, Uzbekistan offers British businesses a combination of market size, economic growth and regional connectivity. With a population of more than 38mn and foreign trade turnover approaching $50bn in January–July 2026, the country is seeking to attract investment and strengthen its participation in international supply chains. Services already account for approximately 80% of UK exports to Uzbekistan, reflecting Britain’s strengths in financial and professional business services. “ “British expertise can support companies and institutions across Uzbekistan’s economy, including by helping to raise capital, structure major projects, strengthen corporate governance and manage complex commercial risks,” the minister said. He also highlighted opportunities in mining technology and consultancy, healthcare, education, aerospace and aviation, arguing that British companies could contribute more than products and investment. “ “British companies can contribute not only products and investment, but also technical knowledge, international networks and professional standards that support Uzbekistan’s long-term development and integration into global value chains,” Lord Sarwar said. For British companies considering entry into the Uzbek market, the minister emphasised the importance of building local relationships and maintaining a long-term commitment. Source: British Embassy in Tashkent The British Embassy in Tashkent has a dedicated trade team that advises exporters, facilitates introductions to government and business contacts, and helps companies navigate the local commercial environment. Where appropriate, businesses can also explore financing options through UK Export Finance. “ “This practical, on-the-ground support is particularly valuable for companies entering Uzbekistan for the first time,” Lord Sarwar said. However, he stressed that institutional support alone would not guarantee success. British firms should take the time to understand the market, meet prospective partners and establish direct relationships with local businesses. “ “Uzbekistan is a market where trust, sustained engagement and a genuine understanding of local priorities matter enormously,” he said. “Companies should come to the country, meet prospective buyers and partners directly, and see the pace of economic change for themselves. Businesses that demonstrate a serious and long-term commitment will be best placed to succeed.” WTO accession and access to international markets The UK supports Uzbekistan’s accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO), viewing membership as an important step towards deeper integration into the global trading system and greater confidence among international investors. “ “The United Kingdom strongly supports Uzbekistan’s accession to the World Trade Organization,” Lord Sarwar said, noting that Britain completed its bilateral negotiations with Uzbekistan in 2025. Lord Sarwar noted that the UK continued to encourage the economic reforms associated with accession, which could strengthen transparency, competition and predictability for businesses operating in the country. “ “These reforms can help strengthen transparency, competition and predictability, giving domestic and international businesses greater confidence when making long-term decisions,” Lord Sarwar said. WTO membership could also support Uzbekistan’s efforts to diversify exports and participate more fully in international supply chains. “ “We look forward to Uzbekistan’s eventual entry into the WTO as a market economy,” the minister said. “Membership would open a valuable new chapter in our bilateral relationship, allowing the UK and Uzbekistan to cooperate not only on questions of market access, but also on wider global trade issues as fellow members of the organisation.” Alongside supporting Uzbekistan’s accession, Britain is seeking to expand access to its own market for Uzbek exporters. Under the UK’s Developing Countries Trading Scheme, eligible goods from developing countries can enter Britain at reduced tariff rates. Lord Sarwar encouraged Uzbek businesses to make greater use of the scheme as they seek to diversify exports and establish a stronger presence in the UK market. He also highlighted the role of the Uzbek Embassy in London in connecting exporters with British businesses and potential partners. However, he cautioned that favourable tariff arrangements alone would not guarantee commercial success. “ “Nevertheless, tariff arrangements alone cannot guarantee commercial success,” Lord Sarwar said, stressing the importance of understanding British regulatory requirements, quality standards and consumer expectations. Closer cooperation between trade institutions, business associations and private companies could help Uzbek exporters obtain the necessary guidance, identify suitable partners and position their products more effectively in Britain. “ “This will be essential if we are to create a genuinely balanced and sustainable two-way trading relationship,” he said. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/09/24/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan, Pakistan explore Babur film project as cultural and media ties deepen Babur’s legacy is moving from history books to modern cultural diplomacy as Uzbekistan and Pakistan explore ways to bring his story to the screen. During an Uzbek media delegation’s visit to Pakistan, including participation from a Daryo journalist, officials highlighted plans for a possible joint historical film project and broader cooperation in cinema, digital media and cultural exchange. 24 September, 20:00 7 min read 1 144 views 0 comments 0 The story of Zahiriddin Muhammad Babur, the ruler born in the Fergana Valley who founded the Baburid Empire (also known as the Mughal Empire) in South Asia, is emerging as a symbol of expanding cultural cooperation between Uzbekistan and Pakistan, with both countries exploring a joint historical film project and wider media collaboration. More than five centuries after Babur’s arrival in the Indian subcontinent, his legacy remains one of the most visible historical links between Central Asia and South Asia. Born in Andijan in 1483, Babur established the Baburid dynasty after his victory at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, creating a political and cultural legacy that continues to influence architecture, literature and cultural traditions across the region. Today, Uzbekistan and Pakistan are seeking to use this shared heritage as part of broader cooperation between the two countries. Relations have expanded in recent years through political exchanges, trade, transport links and cultural initiatives, with both governments describing bilateral ties as a strategic partnership. Trade turnover between Uzbekistan and Pakistan reached nearly $500mn by the end of 2025, while both sides have set a target of increasing bilateral trade to $2bn. The possible Babur film project was among the key topics discussed during a visit by an Uzbek media delegation to Pakistan’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (MoIB) in Islamabad, where officials highlighted cinema, television and digital content exchange as emerging areas of cooperation between the two countries. Photo: Asif-ur-Rehman Khan Asif-ur-Rehman Khan, Director of the External Affairs Wing of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting of Pakistan for SAARC, Central Asian Republics, West Asia, the Middle East and Africa, during the interview shared that filmmakers from both countries are working towards developing a joint production about Babur’s life, with details including locations and casting still under discussion. “The script is under consideration, and locations and casting details are yet to be finalised,” Khan told the delegation, adding that the project is expected to involve both Uzbek and Pakistani participation. The planned production is part of wider discussions between the two countries on cooperation in cinematography, documentaries and television content. Existing institutional links include cooperation between the Associated Press of Pakistan (APP) and Uzbekistan’s National News Agency (UzA), as well as between Pakistan Television Corporation (PTV) and Uzbekistan’s National Television and Radio Company (NTRC). A shared historical connection For both countries, Babur represents a bridge between Central Asia and South Asia. During the meeting, Pakistani officials highlighted the Baburid architectural legacy visible in cities such as Lahore, including landmarks influenced by the dynasty’s Central Asian roots. “When you go to Lahore, you will find the Mughal [Baburid] heritage, the Badshahi Mosque, Shalimar Gardens and various historical buildings with Central Asian motifs and designs,” Khan said. Photo: Badshahi Mosque Beyond his role as a ruler, Babur’s legacy has also endured through literature. His memoir, the Baburnama, written in Chagatai Turkic, provides first-hand observations of Central Asian and South Asian societies in the 15th and 16th centuries and remains one of the most significant historical texts of the period. The historical links between the two regions extend beyond the Baburid period. Uzbekistan and Pakistan have frequently highlighted centuries of interaction along the Silk Road, where Central Asian cities and South Asian centers were connected through trade, scholarship and cultural exchange. Scholars including Imam al-Bukhari, Imam al-Termizi, Al-Khwarizmi, Al-Biruni and Ibn Sina remain recognised across the region for their contributions to science, philosophy and Islamic scholarship. The Baburid architectural heritage highlighted during the meeting includes some of Pakistan’s most recognised historical sites. The Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens, both UNESCO World Heritage sites, reflect architectural traditions developed during the Baburid period, combining Persian, Islamic and Central Asian influences. The Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, another major Baburid-era landmark mentioned by Pakistani officials, was built between 1673 and 1674 during the reign of Emperor Aurangzeb and remains one of the largest examples of Baburid religious architecture. Modern cultural cooperation has increasingly focused on preserving and promoting these historical links. During Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s state visit to Pakistan in February 2026, the two countries signed an agreement on preserving, studying and promoting the scientific, educational, cultural and architectural heritage of the Great Baburid Dynasty. The sides also discussed Uzbekistan Culture Weeks, Uzbek Cinema Days in Pakistan and the possibility of establishing a joint cultural centre in Lahore. The symbolic importance of Babur’s legacy was also reflected in Islamabad, where Pakistani authorities named a park after Zahiriddin Muhammad Babur and named a street “Tashkent” during President Mirziyoyev’s 2026 visit. These initiatives show how historical heritage is increasingly being used as a platform for modern cultural diplomacy, including through films, documentaries and media exchanges. Media cooperation expands alongside bilateral ties The Uzbek delegation’s visit comes as media relations between the two countries continue to develop alongside political and economic cooperation. The delegation, consisting of journalists, television representatives, bloggers and digital content creators, visited Pakistan to study the country’s media landscape and explore opportunities for future collaboration. Khan noted that cooperation could include journalist exchanges, joint reporting projects, television programming, documentaries, cinema production and digital media initiatives. “Media cooperation is not just print and electronic media, but also in the digital domain,” he said. Pakistan’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting coordinates government media policy and works with institutions including Pakistan Television Corporation, Pakistan Broadcasting Corporation and the Associated Press of Pakistan Corporation. Pakistan Television Corporation, established in 1964, operates terrestrial and satellite services, while Pakistan Broadcasting Corporation manages radio services across the country through multiple broadcasting networks, according to the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. During the discussions, Pakistani officials also highlighted the rapid growth of digital platforms and the challenges created by the speed of online information distribution. Khan said social media has become an important tool for reaching audiences but has also increased the need for cooperation in addressing misinformation. “One of the challenges is to rectify fake news and baseless content,” he said. Officials noted that digital communication has become an increasingly important area of focus as audiences shift towards online platforms and social media networks. Source: Daryo Growing economic and people-to-people links The media cooperation discussions took place against the backdrop of expanding economic and social contacts between Uzbekistan and Pakistan. https://daryo.uz/en/2025/02/20/beeline-u.body: Reklama Beeline Uzbekistan started 2025 with a significant network modernization Beeline Uzbekistan upgraded over 150 base stations in January, enhancing 4G/LTE connectivity across the capital, ten regions, and Karakalpakstan, improving service quality in both urban and remote areas. 20 February 2025, 17:05 3 min read 8 847 views 0 comments 2 In January, Beeline Uzbekistan, part of the VEON Group, upgraded more than 150 previously launched base stations (BS) in the capital, ten regions, and the Republic of Karakalpakstan. The updated equipment supports high-speed 4G/LTE data transmission technology. As a result of these thorough efforts, the digital operator's service quality has significantly improved in settlements and along key highways of Uzbekistan. Photo: Beeline Uzbekistan upgraded over 150 base stations in January Source: Beeline Uzbekistan Technical upgrades were carried out in in the Andijan, Bukhara, Jizzakh, Kashkadarya, Namangan, Samarkand, Surkhandarya, Tashkent, Fergana, and Khorezm regions, as well as in the Republic of Karakalpakstan. The record holder for the number of upgraded base stations was the Fergana region, one of the most densely populated in the country. In January, the operator modernized about 90 BS there. In 2025, more than 220 stations are planned to be upgraded across the country. The applied technologies — such as Massive MIMO — significantly increase the number of simultaneously served users, which is especially relevant in densely populated urban areas and near venues with large gatherings of people, such as major shopping malls or stadiums. Thanks to more efficient frequency use, mobile device owners can enjoy higher download and upload speeds. On the base stations where the modernization took place, access speed increased by 36%, and customer traffic by 19% . Photo: Massive MIMO technology improves network capacity and speed Source: Beeline Uzbekistan The focus on developing the 4G/LTE network standard allows Beeline Uzbekistan customers not only to use mobile internet at comfortable speeds but also to make voice calls while remaining on the fourth-generation network. As a result, the Voice over LTE (VoLTE) service is becoming increasingly popular in the country — the operator's network has already recorded more than a million VoLTE users. "For our technical services, January turned out to be a busy period: in just one month, we modernized more than half of the base stations planned for the entire year. And there’s a simple reason for that. The sooner the equipment starts operating at 4G speeds, the sooner the people of Uzbekistan will be able to experience a new quality of communication and live according to VEON's AI1440 strategy, gaining access to modern digital services all 1,440 minutes a day. This is especially important for small settlements where high-speed internet is being introduced for the first time," commented Andrey Pyatakhin, CEO of Beeline Uzbekistan. *** Unitel LLC has rendered services using the Beeline Uzbekistan trademark since September 12, 2006. Beeline Uzbekistan is part of the VEON international telecommunications holding, headquartered in Dubai (UAE). Certified Top Employer 2024. VEON is a digital operator that provides converged connectivity and digital services to nearly 160mn customers. Operating across six countries that are home to more than 7% of the world’s population, VEON is transforming lives through technology-driven services that empower individuals and drive economic growth. VEON is listed on NASDAQ. Beeline Uzbekistan has about 1.9 thousand employees. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/18/british-h.body: Uzbekistan British humor in Tashkent: Inside independent theatre bringing English-language comedy to stage Script Theatre, an independent amateur theatre company in Tashkent, is attracting English-speaking audiences with sold-out performances of British comedy Out of Order, despite financial and logistical challenges, while preparing new productions and exploring plans to stage Uzbek drama in English. 18 October, 15:04 8 min read 778 views 0 comments 0 Source: Script Theatre A cast of professionals rehearsing after work, sold-out performances and a British comedy performed entirely in English. Script Theatre is creating a space for English-speaking audiences in Tashkent, despite the financial and practical challenges of running an independent production. British humor has always had a particular appeal to me. The dry wit, carefully timed misunderstandings and increasingly absurd situations are part of what makes it so entertaining. But finding that kind of comedy performed live, entirely in English, in Tashkent was something I had not expected. On October 10, I attended Script Theatre's production of Out of Order, also known as 13-raqamli xona, at Human House. What followed was a performance that kept me laughing throughout the evening. The script was well written, the humor consistently engaging and the comedic timing particularly memorable. Another aspect that stood out was that the actors were performing in English despite not being native English speakers. For English-speaking residents and visitors, it was the kind of cultural experience that could easily be overlooked when exploring Tashkent's entertainment scene. Yet behind the comedy is an independent amateur theatre project whose members have entirely different professional careers and dedicate their evenings and weekends to rehearsals. Why a British comedy from 1990 still works today According to Abdurashid Yakubov, Script Theatre’s director, one reason the company chose Out of Order was its pace. Although the play was first staged in 1990, he believes its structure is particularly suited to contemporary audiences accustomed to rapidly changing content on platforms such as TikTok and Instagram. "I think one of the biggest changes in recent years is the way we consume information," Yakubov told Daryo. Source: Script Theatre The production follows a series of misunderstandings, with each attempt to conceal a mistake creating another problem. As more characters enter the story, the circumstances become increasingly difficult for those involved to control. "Something is constantly happening: one problem creates another, one lie creates another lie, new characters keep entering, and the situation becomes more and more ridiculous," he explained. For Yakubov, this combination of traditional British farce and fast-moving storytelling made the play particularly suitable for the theatre's audience. The humor also depends on recognizable human behavior. The characters' increasingly elaborate attempts to avoid admitting their mistakes may be exaggerated, but the underlying situations are familiar. As Yakubov explained, audiences sometimes laugh not only at the characters' circumstances but also because they recognize elements of their own behavior. Lawyers by day, actors by night Script Theatre is an independent amateur project, and its cast does not consist of full-time professional theatre actors. Instead, its members include lawyers working for international companies, finance professionals, university lecturers and people from other professional backgrounds. After completing their regular working days, they come together to rehearse, study their roles and prepare for performances. The production of Out of Order required approximately six months of preparation. Source: Script Theatre Actors must learn extensive dialogue, develop stage movement and practice the timing required to make comedy work in front of a live audience. The company also studies theatrical approaches associated with Stanislavski, Chekhov, Meyerhold and Vakhtangov, applying what its members learn during rehearsals. For a cast working in a language that is not their native one, the ability to maintain the pace and rhythm of a British farce is especially noteworthy from an audience perspective. Yakubov emphasized that successful comedy requires considerably more preparation than spectators may realize. "Sometimes half a second changes a joke completely," he said. An actor must know when to speak, pause, react or wait for the audience's laughter to subside. Those decisions can also change from one performance to another. Script Theatre was not created because its founders believed Tashkent lacked theatrical traditions. Instead, Yakubov identified a more specific gap: the limited availability of regular independent theatre performances in English. "Tashkent already has a very strong theatrical tradition, so Script was never created because we thought the city lacked theatre. What we felt was missing was a consistent independent platform for theatre performed in English," he explained. The theatre aims to bring together English-speaking Uzbek residents, university students, young professionals, international specialists, foreign residents and visitors. Its performances are generally positioned for audiences aged 16 and above. During the October 10 performance, I also noticed what appeared to be a local boy, perhaps around 10 years old or slightly older, attending with an older man who seemed to be his grandfather. The boy was laughing enthusiastically throughout parts of the comedy. Yakubov said that some of the people attending Script's performances would not normally consider themselves regular theatre-goers. The company mainly promotes its productions through its website and social media. Nevertheless, every performance so far has sold out. Interestingly, Yakubov believes the project remains relatively unknown despite that demand. Source: Script Theatre Although Script Theatre has attracted audiences, financial sustainability remains one of its main challenges. "Every Script performance so far has been sold out, but even with sold-out performances we still have not reached break-even," Yakubov said. Productions require spending on costumes, decorations, props, rehearsal materials and furniture made or purchased specifically for the stage. Finding a suitable performance space is another challenge. Yakubov credited Human House and Lola Safi for providing the theatre with a location where its members can rehearse and perform. For a project without its own building, access to such a space is an important part of its ability to continue operating. Yakubov explained that Script was not established primarily as a commercial venture. Its members hope the project can eventually become financially sustainable, allowing them to stage more productions, but its current motivation is centered on artistic development and creating opportunities for English-language theatre. Can theatre compete with TikTok and Netflix? One of the questions facing theatre today is how it attracts audiences accustomed to streaming platforms, social media and short-form video. Yakubov does not believe younger generations have lost interest in live performances. Instead, he argues that young people are looking for experiences that are social, authentic and engaging. He said younger audience members frequently attend with friends, discuss scenes after performances, take photographs and share their experiences online. Digital platforms, in his view, can help people discover theatre rather than simply compete with it. The distinction between a recorded performance and live theatre is also central to Script's approach. "Even if we perform the same play with the same actors and the same script, no two performances will ever be completely identical," Yakubov said. The actors' delivery, the audience's reactions and the timing of individual moments can change from one evening

https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/26/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan wins 145 medals and finishes third at 5th Asian Para Games in Japan Uzbekistan secured a record 145 medals, including 45 gold, 49 silver and 51 bronze, at the 5th Asian Para Games in Japan, finishing third in the overall medal standings, with para-athletics contributing 64 medals and Uzbek athletes setting or breaking more than 15 international and regional records. 26 October, 13:00 3 min read 601 views 0 comments 0 Uzbekistan's national team secured 145 medals at the 5th Asian Para Games in Japan, finishing third in the overall medal standings and recording its best performance in the history of the competition. The Uzbek delegation won 45 gold, 49 silver and 51 bronze medals across 11 sports. The Games brought together athletes from 45 Asian countries competing in 18 sports. According to the competition results, athletes from 31 countries won medals, while representatives of 22 nations secured at least one gold medal. Only seven national teams surpassed the 100-medal mark. Uzbekistan was among those seven teams, with its 45 gold medals contributing to its third-place finish in the overall standings. Para-athletics accounted for a significant share of Uzbekistan's medal tally at the Games. Uzbek athletes competing in the discipline secured 64 medals, including 20 gold, 21 silver and 23 bronze. The para-athletics results represented 20 of Uzbekistan's 45 gold medals and contributed to the national team's overall performance. Athletes from Uzbekistan also established or broke more than 15 world, Asian and Asian Para Games records across various sports. In total, 81 Asian records and 27 world records were set during the competition. The 145 medals won in Japan marked Uzbekistan's highest total since its first participation in the Asian Para Games in 2010. The country's results have increased over the five editions of the competition, from six medals in Guangzhou in 2010 to 145 medals at the latest Games. Uzbekistan's medal results at previous Asian Para Games were as follows: Year Host city Gold Silver Bronze Total 2010 Guangzhou 1 2 3 6 2014 Incheon 22 5 4 31 2018 Jakarta 21 24 25 70 2022 Hangzhou 22 18 31 71 5th edition Japan 45 49 51 145 At the inaugural Asian Para Games in Guangzhou in 2010, Uzbekistan secured six medals, including one gold, two silver and three bronze. Four years later, at the 2014 Games in Incheon, the national team increased its medal tally to 31, winning 22 gold, five silver and four bronze medals. At the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, Uzbekistan collected 70 medals, comprising 21 gold, 24 silver and 25 bronze. The team subsequently won 71 medals at the 2022 Games in Hangzhou, including 22 gold, 18 silver and 31 bronze. At the 5th Asian Para Games in Japan, Uzbekistan more than doubled its previous medal total, increasing from 71 to 145 medals. The number of gold medals also rose from 22 to 45. Uzbekistan's para-athletes underwent preparation for the competition through training camps organized to meet modern standards. The training arrangements were intended to provide athletes with the conditions necessary to develop their skills and prepare for international competition. The country's approach to developing para-sports also includes support for athletes with disabilities, access to sports facilities and opportunities for regular training. Following the results of the 5th Asian Para Games, Uzbekistan's para-athletes are expected to continue preparing for upcoming international competitions. These include the 2028 Paralympic Games in Los Angeles, United States, and the 6th Asian Para Games, scheduled to take place in Doha, Qatar, in 2030. # Asian Para Games # Athletes with Disabilities # National Sports Achievements # Para-sports # japan # uzbekistan Reporter Xadicha Abdurashidova All stories Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? https://daryo.uz/en/2025/07/26/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan professor bridges cultures and fosters innovation at University of Missouri Laylo Yakhshiboeva, a professor from Uzbekistan’s Tashkent State University of Economics, completed a semester-long fellowship at the University of Missouri, where she shared her expertise in entrepreneurship, promoted cultural exchange, and launched a collaborative project empowering rural Uzbek women through sustainable design. 26 July 2025, 21:00 3 min read 6 003 views 0 comments 0 Laylo Yakhshiboeva, a professor of Management and Entrepreneurship at the Tashkent State University of Economics, recently completed a transformative semester as a visiting scholar at the University of Missouri (Mizzou), bridging cultures and fostering innovation. Source: University of Missouri Hosted by the Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation at Mizzou’s Trulaske College of Business, Yakhshiboeva spent the spring 2025 semester immersed in American academic life. She engaged in coursework, mentored students, and introduced Uzbek perspectives on entrepreneurship and sustainable development. Selected from over 700 candidates through the Faculty Enrichment Program—jointly run by the American Council and Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Higher Education—Yakhshiboeva described her stay as eye-opening. “America is a totally different culture from other places I’ve visited,” she said. “But that diversity of thought is where creativity thrives. Our values are the same because we are human.” During her time at Mizzou, which ended on May 19, she: Presented on Uzbek culture and entrepreneurship during International Week; Audited classes in design thinking, entrepreneurship, business, and strategic communication; Co-hosted a sustainability workshop using the En-roads simulator and became a certified Climate Ambassador; Shared her business idea at 1 Million Cups, a local entrepreneurial forum; Presented research on rural economic development in Uzbekistan at a major entrepreneurship conference in California. Scott Christianson, Director of the Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation, praised her contribution. “Laylo’s visit brought fresh ideas and perspectives that energized our students, faculty, and community partners,” he said. “It deepened our global engagement and helped connect us with Central Asian innovation.” One highlight of the semester was her collaboration with Mizzou Associate Professor Stacie Kane, an entrepreneur known for her line of washable, sustainable bags. Inspired by the opportunity, Yakhshiboeva contributed brightly embroidered Uzbek fabrics, merging cultural aesthetics with Kane’s sustainable designs. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/29/pegasus-a.body: Uzbekistan Pegasus Airlines to launch flights from Istanbul to Bukhara, Andijan and Termez Turkish low-cost carrier Pegasus Airlines plans to launch direct flights from Istanbul to Bukhara and Andijan in December 2026 and to Termez in March 2027, with fares starting at $99, expanding international air connectivity for three Uzbek cities without requiring passengers to travel through Tashkent. 29 October, 21:30 2 min read 4 493 views 0 comments 0 Source: Getty Images Turkish low-cost carrier Pegasus Airlines plans to launch regular flights from Istanbul to Bukhara and Andijan in December 2026, followed by flights to Termez in March 2027, expanding direct air links between Türkiye and Uzbekistan. According to the airline’s official website and mobile application, the first Istanbul–Bukhara flight is scheduled for December 14, while the Istanbul–Andijan route is due to open on December 18. Flights to Termez are scheduled to begin on March 1, 2027. Ticket sales have opened for all three routes. Fares start at $99, although the final price depends on the travel date, route and seat availability. The airline’s entry-level Light fare has separate charges for checked baggage and standard cabin baggage. Passengers travelling on this fare can bring only a small bag weighing up to 3kg into the cabin free of charge. Screenshot: Pegagus Airlines The flights are expected to operate through Istanbul’s Sabiha Gökçen International Airport, providing passengers from Bukhara, Andijan and Termez with connections to destinations across Europe, including London, Manchester, Paris and Prague, without first travelling to Tashkent. According to the Civil Aviation Agency’s registry, Pegasus Airlines received operating permit No. 58-K for passenger transportation in Uzbekistan on October 6. Pegasus Airlines’ plans to enter the Uzbek market follow several years of interest in establishing air links with the country. In 2018, Uzbekistan’s tourism authorities reported negotiations with the Turkish low-cost carrier over the possibility of establishing operations in the country. In 2021, the airline again expressed interest in launching flights to Uzbekistan, including routes aimed at supporting pilgrimage tourism. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/28/paolo-can.body: Sport Paolo Cannavaro turns down Giugliano offer, remains with Uzbekistan — media Italian coach Paolo Cannavaro has rejected an offer to become head coach of Giugliano despite reaching a verbal agreement on a contract until June 2027, choosing to remain with the Uzbekistan national team's coaching staff under his brother Fabio Cannavaro, at least until the 2027 Asian Cup. 28 October, 20:00 2 min read 7 388 views 0 comments 0 Italian coach Paolo Cannavaro, a member of the Uzbekistan national team's coaching staff, has declined an offer to become head coach of Italian club Giugliano despite reaching a verbal agreement with the club, according to TuttoMercatoWeb. The 45-year-old reportedly chose to remain with Uzbekistan’s national team rather than return to a head coaching role in Italy. According to TuttoMercatoWeb, Giugliano identified Cannavaro as its primary candidate for the head coaching position following the dismissal of Raffaele Di Napoli. The parties reached a verbal agreement on a contract running until June 2027, with an option for extension. However, Cannavaro's existing contract with the Uzbekistan national team presented an obstacle to his appointment. To take over as Giugliano's head coach, he would have needed to resolve the termination of his agreement with the Uzbek side. Cannavaro ultimately declined the offer and decided to remain with the Uzbekistan national team, at least until the 2027 Asian Cup. Paolo Cannavaro joined the Uzbekistan national team's coaching staff in early 2026. Italian media reported his involvement with the team as early as January, when Uzbekistan held a training camp in Dubai. In March, Italian journalist Nicolo Schira reported that Cannavaro had officially joined the coaching staff. Cannavaro worked with the national team during preparations for the 2026 FIFA World Cup and throughout the tournament. He continued working with the team after the tournament concluded. In September, Cannavaro was in Tashkent with the national team as it prepared for an upcoming training camp. Paolo Cannavaro has previously worked alongside his brother, Fabio Cannavaro, at several clubs. The two worked together at Chinese club Guangzhou and Italian clubs Benevento and Udinese. Fabio Cannavaro has served as head coach of the Uzbekistan national team since October 2025. https://daryo.uz/en/2024/01/01/uzbekista.body: Auto Uzbekistan contemplates stricter rules for car and electric vehicle imports The draft resolution aims to streamline processes, allowing for more efficient vehicle imports while maintaining safety standards. 1 January 2024, 01:30 2 min read 9 837 views 0 comments 0 The government of Uzbekistan is considering tightening regulations governing the importation of cars and electric vehicles, as outlined in the draft resolution regarding the measures to further improve the import of passenger cars into the country and the system for assessing their conformity. The proposal is currently undergoing interdepartmental discussions, Gazeta reports . A Mercedes car at an exhibition. Source: Daryo As per the document, the potential changes include restrictions on individuals importing cars , suggesting that they may be limited to importing no more than one vehicle for personal use in their name per calendar year. Additionally, the draft proposes a ban on individuals importing cars for commercial purposes starting from 2024. This measure appears to target those who, on customer orders, bring cars into the country, particularly from China. The draft resolution also recommends exempting state-owned enterprises , manufacturing entities, and businesses from mandatory certification for vehicles imported for internal use and not intended for sale within Uzbekistan. Furthermore, the proposal suggests allowing the issuance of vehicle type approval documents (VTA) based on valid certificates or test reports provided by accredited foreign laboratories for vehicles, electric buses, and electric vehicles manufactured in Uzbekistan through large-unit assembly and imported for commercial purposes. Cars showcased at a local exhibition. Source: Daryo The draft resolution aims to streamline processes, allowing for more efficient vehicle imports while maintaining safety standards. It proposes the recognition of small batches of vehicles, both locally produced and imported, within a calendar year. For categories M1, M2, M3, N1, N2, N3, O1 - O4, L1 - L7 , the maximum volume of a small batch would be set at 50 units . Moreover, entrepreneurs selling over 50 electric vehicles annually might be required to install charging stations to ensure their uninterrupted operation. The Customs Committee is expected to play a crucial role in implementing these proposed changes, including overseeing the release of vehicles re-imported by individuals and preventing the transfer of goods placed under the customs regime without proper documentation. The committee is also tasked with ensuring compliance with regulations related to customs warehouse procedures. Notably, these potential adjustments come after the authorization, starting January 1, 2023 , for the sale of new imported cars by entities beyond official dealers of manufacturers. https://daryo.uz/en/2025/07/28/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan, South Korea to expand academic ties with focus on engineering, green economy, and student mobility Uzbekistan and South Korea have agreed to deepen cooperation in higher education following a meeting between Minister of Higher Education, Science and Innovation Kongratbay Sharipov and Kim Tae-Gyun, First Vice Mayor for Administrative Affairs of Seoul, focusing on academic exchange, technical training, and joint innovation initiatives. 28 July 2025, 16:32 2 min read 4 818 views 0 comments 0 Uzbekistan and South Korea are set to deepen cooperation in the field of higher education following a high-level meeting between Minister of Higher Education, Science and Innovation Kongratbay Sharipov and Kim Tae-Gyun, First Vice Mayor for Administrative Affairs of Seoul. Source: Government Portal of the Republic of Uzbekistan During the meeting, both sides reviewed the current state of bilateral cooperation and discussed ways to broaden collaboration in key academic and technical fields. Minister Sharipov noted that ties between the two countries in higher education have grown steadily, citing the presence of four South Korean university branches in Uzbekistan, Korean language and literature programs, and joint academic initiatives involving more than 180 students. The discussions also touched on expanding academic mobility and strengthening joint educational programs. Particular attention was given to enhancing cooperation in emerging areas such as transport, mechanical engineering, architecture, geology, renewable energy, green economy, and vocational education. Source: Government Portal of the Republic of Uzbekistan Proposals included inviting South Korean university experts to Uzbekistan and launching joint scientific and practical centers and technoparks. Both sides also explored possibilities for engaging volunteer educators and developing collaborative projects through the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA). A key focus of the meeting was ensuring greater participation of Uzbek students in international grant programs in engineering and information technology. The parties agreed to take practical steps to promote these opportunities, including student outreach, methodological support, and better coordination of academic processes. The possibility of providing dedicated scholarships for Uzbek students in technical fields at South Korean universities was also raised. Both sides committed to turning dialogue into action by outlining specific measures to expand cooperation and build long-term academic and scientific partnerships. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/28/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan allows 2022/23 winter-intake master's students to defend theses with language certificates Uzbekistan will allow master's students admitted during the exceptional winter intake of the 2022/23 academic year who were previously unable to defend their theses to proceed with their defense upon submitting a valid, officially recognized foreign language certificate meeting C1, B2 or B1 proficiency requirements, depending on their field of study. 28 October, 16:00 2 min read 5 371 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Depositphotos” Uzbekistan will allow master's students admitted on an exceptional basis during the winter intake of the 2022/23 academic year to defend their theses if they submit a foreign language proficiency certificate meeting the requirements of Presidential Decree No. PF–81. The decision applies to students who were previously unable to defend their master's theses because they did not have the required language certificate. The Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovation announced the procedure in a letter sent to rectors of higher education institutions. According to the ministry's letter, the procedure was established based on the minutes of a commission meeting, No. 5, dated September 25, 2026. It applies to master's students who were admitted under the exceptional winter intake for the 2022/23 academic year and have not yet defended their theses. Under the procedure, these students may proceed with their thesis defense if they possess a national or international foreign language proficiency certificate that meets the requirements of Presidential Decree No. PF–81, dated May 24, 2024. The required foreign language proficiency level depends on the student's field of study. Students specializing in philology must hold a C1-level certificate. A B2-level certificate is required for students in the humanities, biological and related sciences, mathematics and statistics, business and management, law, services, social and behavioral sciences, journalism and information, and information and communication technologies. For other fields of study, as well as specializations in culture and sports, the required proficiency level is B1. To qualify for thesis defense, students must submit a foreign language certificate that has not expired. The certificate must also be included in the official list of recognized certificates registered with the Ministry of Justice under registration No. 3515, dated May 29, 2024. The Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovation has instructed the heads of higher education institutions to organize the Final State Attestation, involving the defense of master's theses, in the prescribed manner. The instruction applies to master's students admitted during the exceptional winter intake of the 2022/23 academic year who have not yet defended their theses and have submitted an appropriate foreign language proficiency certificate. # Academic Language Standards # Academic Regulations # Higher Education Policy # Master's Degree Programs # Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovation # Presidential Decree PF-81 # uzbekistan Reporter Xadicha Abdurashidova All stories Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think?
