https://daryo.uz/en/2025/04/27/saudi-ara.body: Uzbekistan Saudi Arabia suspends e-visa services for Uzbek citizens Saudi Arabia has temporarily suspended online tourist visas for Uzbek and Tajik citizens during the 2025 Hajj season, requiring travelers to apply through embassies or authorized centers from April 23 to June 9. 27 April 2025, 16:00 2 min read 10 039 views 0 comments 0 Saudi Arabia has suspended the issuance of online tourist visas for citizens of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, with the Saudi Ministry of Tourism confirming the move is a temporary measure linked to the Hajj season. Source: Daryo In a statement to Daryo, the Ministry explained that e-visa applications for Uzbek and Tajik citizens are unavailable from April 23 to June 9. During this period, travelers are required to apply for visas through Saudi embassies or authorized visa centers in their home countries. Additionally, travelers holding valid Schengen, UK, or US visas, or residents of the European Union, United Kingdom, or United States, will still be able to obtain visas upon arrival at Saudi entry points. The Saudi government has not issued a formal public announcement regarding the suspension. Citizens of Uzbekistan were first granted access to Saudi Arabia’s electronic visa system in August 2023, allowing online applications for tourist and Umrah visas at a fee of $146. The e-visa is valid for up to 90 days and permits religious and leisure travel across the country. The temporary suspension comes amid preparations for the 2025 Hajj season, for which Uzbekistan has been allocated a quota of 15,000 pilgrims. The decision follows recent incidents in Uzbekistan involving fraudulent Hajj services. In mid-April, a man in Tashkent was detained after allegedly accepting $23,600 to illegally send four people on the Hajj. Authorities have also cracked down on fake travel agencies operating in the capital. Looking ahead, Uzbekistan plans to streamline the pilgrimage process by launching a "Single Portal for Hajj and Umrah" and its corresponding mobile application by September 1, 2025. The initiative aims to simplify services and reduce bureaucratic obstacles for citizens undertaking religious journeys. He also cautioned that the recent rise in illegal activities involving Uzbek citizens abroad could potentially impact the visa-free arrangement between the two countries. Since February 16, 2024, Uzbek citizens have been able to enter the UAE without a visa for stays of up to 30 days, with Dubai among the visa-free cities included under this agreement. https://daryo.uz/en/2025/04/22/kazakhsta.body: Travel Kazakhstan to transform ski tourism with PGI Management partnership for global standards Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and PGI Management President Joan Viladomat have explored plans to elevate Kazakhstan's ski tourism by modernizing the Almaty mountain cluster, aiming to meet international standards and drive economic growth. 22 April 2025, 19:33 2 min read 3 346 views 0 comments 0 Kazakhstan is set to elevate its ski tourism sector to international standards through collaboration with one of the world’s leading ski resort developers, PGI Management. This initiative was discussed during a meeting between Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Joan Viladomat, President of PGI Management, held to explore strategic cooperation in developing ski tourism. Source: Official Information Source of the Prime minister of the Republic of Kazakhstan The meeting focused on the Almaty mountain cluster, a key hub for winter sports in Kazakhstan. Currently, the region attracts around 2mn tourists annually and supports 2,000 seasonal jobs. With 41 kilometers of pistes and 16 ski lifts, the existing infrastructure accommodates up to 6,000 visitors per day. However, growing demand from both domestic and international tourists signals the need for expansion and modernization. Plans are underway to scale the infrastructure to 227 kilometers of pistes and 58 lifts, boosting the daily capacity to 34,000 visitors — a 5.6-fold increase. By 2029, the enhanced Almaty cluster is projected to welcome up to 7.5mn tourists per year and create 10,000 direct jobs. Joan Viladomat shared insights from PGI Management’s global portfolio, which includes over 120 projects in renowned destinations such as Davos, St. Moritz (Switzerland), Courchevel (France), Ischgl and Tyrol (Austria), Vail and Aspen (USA), and Whistler-Blackcomb (Canada). The company also transformed Andorra into a thriving winter tourism hotspot, drawing 9.6mn visitors last year — a remarkable figure for a country of only 80,000 people. Source: Official Information Source of the Prime minister of the Republic of Kazakhstan Both sides emphasized the economic and social benefits of ski tourism, especially for mountainous regions. Viladomat presented examples of how tourism-focused strategies can drive structural economic change in rural and alpine areas. The parties also highlighted the importance of inclusion and year-round tourism. Modernizing infrastructure will support educational programs for children to learn winter sports and expand options for family leisure activities. Prime Minister Bektenov stressed the importance of diversifying Kazakhstan’s economy amid current global challenges. Tourism, he noted, should emerge as a key driver of growth alongside manufacturing, digitalization, and transport and logistics. At the end of the meeting, both Kazakhstan and PGI Management expressed their commitment to jointly develop ski tourism infrastructure in line with global best practices. Финляндия ушбу қайта қуролланишнинг олдини олиш имкониятига эга бўлмагани сабабли, ҳокимият органлари асосий эътиборни жиловлашга қаратмоқда. Вялимякининг айтишича, Россия ҳарбий раҳбариятини ҳар қандай ҳужум қилишга уриниш муваффақиятсизликка маҳкум эканига ишонтириш зарур. “Биз ҳозирда қилаётган барча нарсаларимиз – хоҳ умуман альянс (НАТО) ҳақида, хоҳ хусусан Финляндия ҳақида гапираётган бўлайлик, Россия янада ичкарига илгариламаслиги учун ана шундай жиловлаш чегарасини яратишга қаратилган”, дейди у. Генералнинг билдиришича, Украина кучлари ҳужум қилаётган қўшинларни жиловлаш учун кенг тармоқли мудофаа чизиқлари ва танкларга қарши ғовлардан фойдаланмоқда. Унинг сўзларига кўра, томонларнинг ҳеч бири йирик миқёсли манёврли қўшин операцияларини қайта бошлаш учун бундай мудофаани ёриб ўтишнинг ишончли усулини топа олмаган. Россиянинг Финляндия билан чегараси узунлиги 1340 км ни ташкил этади. Бу НАТОнинг Россия билан бутун қуруқликдаги чегарасининг тахминан ярми дегани. Финляндия ҳокимияти шимолнинг шафқатсиз об-ҳаво шароитида бундай истеҳкомларни жойлаштириш самарадорлигини аниқлаши керак бўлади. “Агар биз истеҳкомлар қуришни ҳамда Украинадаги каби чуқурликдаги танкларга қарши зовурлар ёки ғовлар қазишни бошласак, табиатимизнинг хусусиятлари уларни сунъий ҳовузларга айлантириши учун қанча вақт кетади?” дейди Вялимяки. Унинг сўзларига кўра, Россия аллақачон сақлаш базаларини замонавий Т-90 танклари, пиёдаларнинг жанговар машиналари ва 2С19 “Мста-С” ўзи юрарадиган гаубицалари билан тўлдиришни бошлаган. Эслатиб ўтамиз, аввалроқ Финляндия Қуролли кучлари хавфсизлик соҳасидаги вазиятнинг ёмонлашуви фонида тахминан 100 миллион евро миқдорида бир миллион дона пиёдаларга қарши мина харид қилишни режалаштираётгани ҳақида хабар берилган эди. https://qalampir.uz/news/muzokaralar-old.body: Музокаралар олдидан Россия Киевга баллистик ракеталар билан зарба берди Олам − 13:26 visibility 1293 timer 2 дақиқа Бугун, 7 ноябрга ўтар кечаси Россия қўшинлари Киев ва унинг атрофига ракеталар билан оммавий ҳужум уюштирди. Оқибатда камида беш киши жароҳатланди, турар жой бинолари, корхоналар ва энергетика инфратузилмаси объектлари шикастланди. Айрим туманларда электр энергияси, иситиш ва сув таъминотида узилишлар юзага келди. Бу ҳақда “Associated Press” хабар берди. Киев мэри Виталий Кличконинг сўзларига кўра, Россия қўшинлари баллистик ракеталарни қўллаган. Ракета парчалари пойтахтнинг ғарбий қисмидаги беш қаватли турар жой биносига, шунингдек, бошқа бир бинонинг фасадига зарар етказган. Бундан ташқари, боғча жойлашган бино шикастланган. Зарбалардан сўнг Днепр орқали ўтган кўприклардан бирида ҳаракатланиш чекланган. Россия Мудофаа вазирлиги оммавий ҳужум уюштирилганини тасдиқлаб, Украинанинг ҳарбий-саноат мажмуаси, энергетика ва транспорт инфратузилмаси объектлари нишонга олинганини маълум қилган. Россия идорасининг маълум қилишича, зарбалар, жумладан, Киевнинг Шимолий кўпригига (Москва ундан қурол-яроғ ва ҳарбий техника ташиш учун фойдаланилган деб даъво қилмоқда) ҳамда “Меридиан” корхонасига берилган. Россия томони ушбу заводда “Фламинго” қанотли ракеталари ишлаб чиқарилади, дея даъво қилмоқда. Россия Мудофаа вазирлиги томонидан билдирилган сиртқи нишонлар ва зарбалар натижаларининг барчаси бўйича мустақил тасдиқлар ҳозирча мавжуд эмас. Ҳужум Украина, Россия ва АҚШ ўртасидаги уч томонлама музокараларнинг янги раундига уч кун қолганда содир бўлди. Учрашув жорий йилнинг 10–11 ноябрь кунлари Абу-Дабида ўтказилиши режалаштирилган. АҚШ Президентининг махсус вакили Стив Уиткофф аввалроқ хабар қилганидек, томонлар урушни тўхтатиш, хавфсизлик кафолатлари, кескинликни камайтириш ва гуманитар масалаларни муҳокама қилиш ниятида. Бўлажак музокаралар февраль ойидаги учрашувлардан кейинги биринчи шундай раунд бўлади. Дипломатик ҳаракатларга қарамай, Москва ва Киев ўртасида ҳудудий масалалар ва мумкин бўлган тинчлик битими шартлари бўйича жиддий келишмовчиликлар сақланиб қолмоқда. Эслатиб ўтамиз, аввалроқ Россиянинг Ozon маркетплейси Украина дронларининг 11 та логистика марказига ҳужумлари оқибатида етказилган зарарни 30,1 миллиард рублга баҳолаганди. https://qalampir.uz/news/uzbekistonda-k-.body: Ўзбекистонда қутқарувчиларни тайёрлаш техникуми ташкил этилади Жамият − 13:33 visibility 638 timer 1 дақиқа Ўзбекистон Республикаси Фавқулодда вазиятлар вазирлиги академияси ҳузурида Қутқарувчиларни тайёрлаш техникуми ташкил этилади. Унда умумий ўрта таълим мактаблари битирувчилари давлат гранти ва тўлов-контракт асосида таҳсил олади. Техникум фаолияти 2027/2028 ўқув йилидан бошланади. Бу ҳақда Ҳукуматнинг кеча, 6 ноябрь куни қабул қилинган “Ўзбекистон Республикаси Фавқулодда вазиятлар вазирлиги академияси ҳузурида Қутқарувчиларни тайёрлаш техникумини ташкил этиш тўғрисида”ги қарорида белгиланган. Ҳукумат қарорига кўра, техникумга умумий ўрта таълим ташкилотлари битирувчилари белгиланган тартибда давлат гранти ва тўлов-контракт асосида ўқишга қабул қилинади. Таълим жараёни бошланғич, ўрта ва ўрта махсус касбий таълим дастурлари асосида ташкил этилади. 2029 йилдан бошлаб техникумнинг касбий таълим йўналишларини тамомлаган битирувчилар орасидан фавқулодда вазиятлар органлари учун кадрлар захираси шакллантирилади. Техникумнинг асосий вазифалари этиб фавқулодда вазиятлар органлари учун замонавий талабларга жавоб берадиган, назарий билим ва амалий кўникмаларга эга қутқарувчиларни тайёрлаш белгиланган. Шунингдек, ўқув жараёнида симуляция, имитация ва виртуал лабораториялар ҳамда полигонларни ташкил этиш орқали назария ва амалиёт уйғунлигини таъминлаш кўзда тутилган. Маълумот учун, 2026 йил 3 апрелдаги Президентнинг ПҚ–123-сон қарорида Фавқулодда вазиятлар вазирлиги академияси ҳузурида мазкур техникум фаолиятини йўлга қўйиш вазифаси белгиланган эди. https://qalampir.uz/news/higgsfield-asos.body: Higgsfield асосчиси Қозоғистон фуқаролигини олди Олам − 16:45 visibility 262 timer 2 дақиқа Higgsfield компанияси ҳаммуассиси ва бош директори Алекс Машрабов Қозоғистон фуқаролигига қабул қилинди. Мамлакат Президенти Қосим-Жўмарт Тўқаев жорий йилнинг 30 октябрь куни бу ҳақдаги фармонни имзолаган. Бу ҳақда Қозоғистон Сунъий интеллект ва рақамли ривожланиш вазири Жаслан Мадиев Facebook саҳифасида маълум қилди. Вазирнинг маълум қилишича, Машрабовга Қозоғистон фуқароси паспортини топшириш унинг учун мамнуният бағишлаган. Мадиев бу воқеани мамлакатда сунъий интеллектни ривожлантириш ва истеъдодли мутахассисларни қўллаб-қувватлашга қаратилаётган эътибор билан боғлаган. Унинг қайд этишича, Higgsfield жамоаси жаҳон бозорида талаб юқори бўлган ва 40 миллиондан ортиқ киши фойдаланаётган экспорт маҳсулотини яратган. Вазир компания жамоасига сунъий интеллект саноати ривожига қўшган ҳиссаси учун миннатдорлик билдирган. Машрабовнинг отаси Ўзбекистонда, унинг ўзи эса Россияда туғилиб ўсган. Кейинчалик у АҚШга кўчиб кетган. Қозоғистон Higgsfield ривожланишидаги муҳим марказлардан бирига айланган. Компания жамоаси 2023 йилдаёқ мамлакатда бизнес учун асос яратишга қарор қилган. Машрабов Қозоғистоннинг кучли муҳандислик мактаби, ижодий салоҳиятга эга мутахассислари ва Astana Hub кўмагини алоҳида эътироф этган. “Ушбу мамлакатни расман ўз уйим деб аташ ва Қозоғистоннинг бир қисми бўлиш мен учун катта ғурур”, деган у. Маълумот учун, Higgsfield AI 2023 йилда Александр Машрабов ва Ерзат Дулат томонидан ташкил этилган. Компания видео ва тасвирлар яратиш учун сунъий интеллект воситаларини ишлаб чиқади. Фойдаланувчилар тайёр шаблонлар ва турли сунъий интеллект эффектларидан фойдаланиши мумкин. Айни пайтда Higgsfield компанияси 5,4 миллиард долларга баҳоланмоқда. Машрабов маҳсулотни халқаро миқёсда ривожлантириш учун масъул ҳисобланади. https://www.cacianalyst.org/publications.body: From C5+1 to C6: Azerbaijan’s Full Participation Recasts Central Asian Regional Cooperation Monday, 02 November 2026 From C5+1 to C6: Azerbaijan’s Full Participation Recasts Central Asian Regional Cooperation Featured Published in Analytical Articles font size decrease font size increase font size Print Email By: Yunis Gurbanov The Eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State (CMHS) of Central Asia was held on October 8, 2026, in Awaza, Turkmenistan. It was the first meeting at which Azerbaijan was represented as a full-fledged member of the format. More significantly, the Awaza meeting can be regarded as an effort to provide content to the expanded format since the parties adopted a Joint Statement and decided on the regulatory documents of the Consultative Meeting, designating the format Chair in 2027 to Azerbaijan. The inclusion of Azerbaijan will not transform the Consultative Meeting into a supra-state structure or an integration association. The forum remains built on the principle of consensus and consciously maintains its flexibility. The inclusion of Azerbaijan has nevertheless shifted the geographical focus and agenda of the meeting. The Caspian Sea will connect the countries, not separate them, placing Trans-Caspian transportation and energy cooperation as well as other issues of cooperation and ecology on the agenda. BACKGROUND: CMHS is the outcome of developments in intra-regional relations due to the changing political environment in Uzbekistan from 2016 onwards. Instead of forming one more intergovernmental organization on the basis of a binding treaty, the five Central Asian countries created a leadership-oriented consultation and coordination mechanism. During the Awaza summit, Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev explicitly stated his opposition to “cumbersome structures” and advocated for a flexible format of cooperation of sovereign states based on respect and pragmatism. The importance of Azerbaijan’s involvement increased gradually. Baku was asked to participate in previous gatherings as a guest since its cooperation with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Kyrgyzstan was developing politically, economically and in transport. Azerbaijan was acknowledged by all Central Asian presidents as one of the full-fledged members of the group in November 2025. The informal consultative meeting in Cholpon-Ata in July 2026 and the adoption of the Cholpon-Ata Declaration helped establish the first CMHS involving the six presidents in Awaza. The CMHS on October 8 did more than just confirm the format’s enlargement. According to Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev, the trade volume between Azerbaijan and Central Asia increased by 50 percent in the past year, and more than 400 enterprises with capital from Central Asian countries operate in Azerbaijan. Baku also established joint investment funds with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, and cooperation in transport, energy transit, information technologies and renewable energy is growing. Azerbaijan’s involvement in the C6 format is most significant in the transport area. The Middle Corridor passes through Azerbaijan and connects Central Asia with Georgia, Türkiye, and Europe. It has become increasingly relevant for the Central Asian states seeking access to Western markets through the Caspian Sea. According to Aliyev, the volume of cargo transported via the Middle Corridor increased by more than 10 percent in 2025 and by nearly 20 percent in the first eight months of 2026. IMPLICATIONS: The inclusion of Azerbaijan expands the CMHS format while avoiding any attempts to change its geographic identity and creating a new regional concept in which connectivity becomes the main element. Another implication is the shift from trade to production. The most significant idea put forward at the Awaza summit was Mirziyoyev’s proposed new economic objective of “six economies – one product,” implying that companies in different countries that partake in the cooperation will be involved in the same value chain instead of trading. Uzbekistan also proposed to organize the “Central Asia-Azerbaijan” business forum in Khiva during 2027. This will perfectly suit Azerbaijan’s appeal to the participating states to “invest together, produce together, and enter foreign markets together,” providing for more industrial zones, factories, logistics centers and investment projects along the corridor. The meeting also addressed institutional development. The leaders adopted regulatory documents for the CMHS, while Uzbekistan proposed developing a dedicated legal framework. However, Mirziyoyev emphasized that implementation mattered more than the number of documents adopted. Greater institutionalization could improve coordination, but excessive formalization risks undermining the mechanism’s flexibility. Transport coordination is likely to remain the most practical area of cooperation. Uzbekistan proposed establishing a Council for Infrastructure Development to coordinate transport projects and integrate national infrastructure into a broader regional framework. This initiative aligns with the development of the Baku International Sea Trade Port. Cooperation also extends to energy resources. Oil from Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan is transported through Azerbaijan’s transport network, while the three countries are developing a green energy corridor to supply Western markets. These initiatives highlight the Middle Corridor’s potential for energy cooperation and digital connectivity, including the installation of fibre-optic cables beneath the Caspian Sea. Environmental challenges are equally significant. Azerbaijan has raised concerns about declining water levels in the Caspian Sea, which could influence coastal infrastructure and increase the costs and reduce the efficiency of maritime transport. Finally, Azerbaijan’s participation brings about a convergence of interests with the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), an important instrument of Baku’s foreign policy. Four of the six C6 countries are OTS members, while Turkmenistan holds observer status. Tajikistan, with its distinct linguistic and cultural identity, participates in other regional cooperation frameworks. The OTS has also gained importance in Azerbaijan’s security policy. At the October 2025 Gabala summit, President Ilham Aliyev proposed joint military exercises and subsequently emphasized defense and security cooperation in September 2026. Rather than competing with the OTS, however, the C6 format offers a broader platform for regional cooperation. However, the expanded format faces geopolitical constraints, reflecting the six states’ differing relations with Russia, China, Türkiye, the EU, and the U.S. Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan remain members of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), while Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan also belong to the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). Turkmenistan maintains its policy of permanent neutrality, while Tajikistan pursues distinct foreign policy and security priorities. CONCLUSIONS: Azerbaijan’s full inclusion in the Consultative Meeting represents not merely a symbolic expansion but a structural extension of Central Asian regional cooperation. The Awaza meeting on October 8 demonstrated that the expanded format could facilitate more practical cooperation on production chains, infrastructure, investment, energy corridors, digitalization, and environmental challenges. However, the significance of the C6 format should not be overstated. It is neither a formal organization nor an alliance, and its participants retain their sovereignty and distinct foreign policy orientations. Its potential instead lies in providing a platform for political coordination among six states connected by the Caspian Sea and increasingly integrated through transport, energy, and investment corridors, enabling them to align their interests. Azerbaijan’s first chairmanship in 2027 will provide an important test of the form

Pakistan, Central Asia, and The Transchina Trade Corridor Wednesday, 23 September 2026 Pakistan, Central Asia, and The Transchina Trade Corridor Featured Published in Analytical Articles font size decrease font size increase font size Print Email By Syed Fazl-e-Haider Tashkent and Islamabad have agreed to expand bilateral trade through routes traversing China, as Pakistan-Afghanistan tensions and the war in Iran have disrupted existing trade links. Pakistan’s conflict with Afghanistan has made the prospects for trans-Afghan corridors connecting Central Asia with Pakistan increasingly uncertain. Meanwhile, renewed U.S.-Iran fighting has made trans-Iranian routes an unreliable option for Pakistan’s trade with Central Asia. Pakistan and Central Asian states such as Kyrgyzstan are therefore promoting an overland route through China that bypasses Afghanistan. Besides providing Pakistan and Central Asia with a corridor avoiding both Afghanistan and Iran, this route creates opportunities to extend the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), a key component of China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), into Central Asia. BACKGROUND : Afghanistan has long represented the most viable transit route for trade between Pakistan and the Central Asian Republics (CARs). However, decades of conflict have prevented plans for a Trans-Afghan trade corridor connecting Central Asia with Pakistan from materialising. More recently, escalating Pakistan-Afghanistan tensions over cross-border terrorism have further undermined prospects for developing these routes. Relations deteriorated sharply in October 2025 following border clashes, prompting Islamabad to suspend truck-borne trade through the main Torkham and Chaman crossings. In February 2026, Islamabad declared an open war against Afghanistan and launched airstrikes targeting alleged terrorist sanctuaries inside the country. In April, Islamabad opened six overland transit routes for goods destined for Iran amid the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. These routes allowed goods from third countries to transit Pakistan and enter Iran by road. The designated corridors connect Pakistani seaports with two Iranian border crossings, providing a viable route towards Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. In April, Islamabad dispatched its first shipment of frozen meat to Tashkent via Iran. Pakistan activated new routes through Iran for trade with the CARs, but renewed U.S.-Iran hostilities over the Strait of Hormuz have undermined their viability. The trans-China route has consequently emerged as the most viable and secure remaining option for trade between Pakistan and Central Asia. Both sides are therefore increasingly prioritizing the development of the trans-China trade corridor. The trans-China option has long featured in discussions between Pakistani and Central Asian leaders due to security concerns in Afghanistan. In November 2025, Uzbekistan and Pakistan agreed to develop trade along two major land routes bypassing Afghanistan: the Pakistan-China-Tajikistan-Uzbekistan and Pakistan-China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan corridors. In April, Kyrgyzstan successfully tested an overland route to Pakistan via China, bypassing Afghanistan. A truck carrying Kyrgyz goods reached the Pakistani port of Karachi via China along the Karakoram Highway. Islamabad considers routes connecting Pakistan with Bishkek and Almaty more secure than the Trans-Afghan alternatives. Several Central Asian leaders have visited Pakistan over the past ten months. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov visited Islamabad in December 2025, followed by Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in February 2026. Their discussions with Pakistani leaders focused primarily on connectivity projects providing the CARs with access to Pakistan’s seaports at Karachi, Gwadar, and Bin Qasim. Uzbekistan and Pakistan have agreed to amend their transit trade agreement to formally incorporate the China corridor. This would allow goods to transit through the Sost dry port and western China before reaching Central Asia. In July, Uzbekistan’s Deputy Prime Minister was scheduled to visit Pakistan, but the visit was postponed at Tashkent’s request. During the visit, the two countries were expected to sign a protocol formally incorporating the China corridor into their transit trade agreement. Currently, routes through China have become Pakistan’s preferred option for regional connectivity and the extension of CPEC. IMPLICATIONS : Deteriorating relations with the Taliban regime, recurring border clashes, and terrorist sanctuaries in Afghanistan have prompted a major shift in Islamabad’s Afghanistan policy, accelerating its turn towards routes through China. While the activation of the China corridor could undermine planned connectivity projects between Pakistan and the CARs, it may strengthen alternative regional initiatives. The future of the Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan (UAP) railway, for instance, appears increasingly uncertain. Launched in 2021, the UAP railway aims to connect Central Asia with Pakistani seaports through Afghanistan. Conversely, completion of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway could make Pakistan’s Gwadar port one of the shortest trade routes for Central Asia. The CKU railway is a strategic connectivity project linking Kashgar in China with Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. From Kashgar, existing and planned transport links could connect the railway southwards with Gwadar through CPEC, providing Central Asia with access to the Arabian Sea. Infrastructure development could further increase trade along the China corridor. Key projects include upgrading the Karachi–Peshawar ML-1 railway, expanding the Karakoram Highway, developing Gwadar Port as a warm-water outlet for the CARs, and expanding dry ports and logistics networks. Together, these projects could improve the efficiency and capacity of the China route. Although Beijing, Islamabad, and Kabul have already agreed to extend CPEC to Afghanistan and Central Asia, the China corridor could accelerate its direct extension into Central Asia. CPEC connects China’s Xinjiang region with Pakistan’s Gwadar port in Balochistan through a network of highways, railways, and energy infrastructure. The rerouting will provide Pakistan with an alternative route to Central Asia while maintaining Uzbekistan’s access to the Pakistani ports of Gwadar and Karachi. Uzbekistan has emerged as Pakistan’s key economic partner in Central Asia. Although the China corridor bypasses instability in both Afghanistan and Iran, it is longer and more expensive than the Trans-Afghan route due to greater distances, higher handling costs, additional border procedures, and longer transit times. The China corridor could therefore serve as a strategic alternative in the short term, but is unlikely to fully replace the Afghan route commercially in the longer term. Improved infrastructure along the China route could enable Pakistan to connect with Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Tajikistan via the Khunjerab Pass. CONCLUSIONS : Geopolitics and security will ultimately determine the development of trade corridors between Pakistan and the CARs. The Pakistan-Afghanistan conflict has undermined prospects for the Trans-Afghan corridor, while the war in Iran has reduced the viability of the Trans-Iranian route. Under these conditions, the Trans-China corridor offers a comparatively secure and viable alternative for both Pakistan and the CARs. It could therefore serve as a strategic safeguard against regional instability stemming from conflicts in Afghanistan and Iran. Pakistan’s importance as a trade outlet is widely recognized in Central Asia. The landlocked CARs seek access to Pakistani seaports through Afghanistan, Iran, or China to facilitate global trade. However, growing security concerns surrounding the Afghan and Iranian routes are likely to increase Central Asian interest in accessing Pakistani ports through the comparatively secure China corr

Tajikistan Steps Out and Stands Up Monday, 26 October 2026 Tajikistan Steps Out and Stands Up Featured Published in Analytical Articles font size decrease font size increase font size Print Email By: Stephen Blank Much has been written about the decline of Russian influence in Central Asia and the rising self-assertion of local governments. Most of this commentary focuses on Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, the two richest and strongest states in Central Asia. However, the decline of Russia’s capacity for dominating Central Asia and local governments’ greater freedom of action has become equally visible to states like Tajikistan that are often overlooked. Dushanbe cannot and has not gone as far as Astana and Tashkent and frequently acts out of necessity as much as choice. Nevertheless, the signs of its growing capacity and of Russia’s parallel decline are mounting. BACKGROUND: Even though Tajikistan imported 91 percent of its petroleum products from Russia in the first half of 2026, it began importing Iranian oil in August because it cannot rely exclusively on continuing Russian supplies. Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries have forced Moscow to impose export restrictions that have rebounded on Central Asian countries like Tajikistan. Thus, while most of its energy imports originate in Russia, Tajikistan has had to risk falling afoul of U.S. sanctions on Iran to sustain its economy and other Central Asian states have also had to follow suit for the same reason. This is far from the only example of Russia’s decline. Hitherto, Russia has been virtually the sole source of Central Asian militaries’ armaments. Now, due to the pressures imposed by the demands emanating from the war in Ukraine, foreign sanctions on components, and the lackluster performance of Russian weapons, that is no longer the case for all the Central Asian states. Tajikistan and Turkmenistan have acquired India’s Akash air-defense system. Tajikistan has also purchased China’s HQ-17AE air defense systems, whereas Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan also operate Chinese systems. These purchases of diverse and heterogeneous systems from multiple suppliers generate challenges of management and integration into a functioning whole. Nonetheless, they send an unmistakable message that Russia can no longer play an exclusive role as the sole regional security manager. In many cases, Russia will not be able to maintain supply chains or provide repairs to aging equipment, thus its ability to provide for Tajikistan’s security is obviously declining. This does not imply that Tajikistan can or will go as far as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have gone in diversifying their foreign policy options to enhance their actual sovereignty and independence. For example, Tajikistan, in an apparent effort to placate Russia, has begun the procedure for withdrawing from the International Criminal Court (ICC), which has indicted President Vladimir Putin for war crimes in the war against Ukraine. Indeed, when Putin visited Dushanbe in 2025, Tajikistan refused to arrest him. This led the ICC to find Tajikistan in breach of its obligations, leaving it no choice but to initiate the withdrawal. In a contest between the ICC and Russia, Tajikistan obviously chose Russia. IMPLICATIONS: Nevertheless, Tajikistan has shown and will continue to show that it is responsive to international developments beyond Russia. Tajikistan’s Humo Bank warned its Russian clients that unless they visited one of its offices in Tajikistan and submitted to a biometric identification by September 30, their cards would be blocked starting on October 1. Although Humo Bank cited the need to protect its clients from fraud; apparently the real reason was Western pressure operating through Visa Direct to threaten sanctions unless Humo Bank stopped allowing certain clients to use it to circumvent sanctions. Although Humo Bank operates in Tajikistan under license from the government; it is owned by the Japanese Investment holding firm, Gojo & Co, and is therefore vulnerable to Western pressure. However, what is interesting in this case is that Tajikistan acceded to that pressure targeting its Russian customers. Moreover, in this context Humo Bank was not the only bank that yielded to Western pressure. For example, Revolut Bank stopped accepting top-ups from credit cards issued in Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan for EU residents, claiming that payment systems had classified those countries as high-risk. Tajikistan took advantage of foreign pressure to limit Russian influence in its banking system. And it did so despite the fact that its economy depends to a great degree on remittances from Tajik migrant workers in Russia and the ensuing unimpeded flow of capital through Russian banks. None of this suggests that Tajikistan can or will emulate the actions of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in making extensive deals with Washington, Brussels, the Gulf states, and others. Tajikistan does not have these capabilities, nor will it attain them anytime soon. Its ability to play China off against Russia, and to balance other external actors against Moscow and Beijing, is much lower than that of Astana and Tashkent. Yet the decline of Russia’s capability in the economic as well as the military sector is both creating more space for independent action on Tajikistan’s part and the necessity for it to defend its own interests. Moreover, Russia’s decline has led other foreign actors, including Western banking and financial interests as well as Chinese and Indian defense exporters, to fill the ensuing vacuum created by Russia’s increasing incapacity. In cases where the costs to Tajikistan from striking at Russian interests outweigh the benefits it might gain, as in the example of the ICC, Dushanbe has refused to antagonize Moscow. This pattern is likely to continue for some time to come, especially since the situation in and around Afghanistan, which is a vital security interest of Tajikistan that it cannot manage by itself, becomes more precarious. However, as Tajikistan continues to work more cooperatively with other Central Asian and foreign governments, its ability to stand up for itself will grow. CONCLUSIONS: Increasingly the trends towards regional self-assertion and involvement with partners beyond Russia and China are becoming more prominent in Central Asia’s politics. The fact that this is occurring not only with regard to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, but also in Tajikistan’s case suggests that these trends are putting down lasting roots. Therefore, despite the imbalance of capabilities between Moscow and Dushanbe, we should expect to see more examples Central Asian including Tajik self-assertion. Yet we should also, based on the mounting constraints upon Russia, see more examples of its growing incapacity to enforce unilateral dominance over local governments. AUTHOR’S BIO: Stephen Blank is a Senior Fellow with the Foreign Policy Research Institute, www.fpri.org . https://www.cacianalyst.org/publications.body: Central Asia’s Economic and Trade Potential via the Middle Corridor Monday, 02 November 2026 Central Asia’s Economic and Trade Potential via the Middle Corridor Featured Published in Analytical Articles font size decrease font size increase font size Print Email By: Gia Jandieri The Central Asian region possesses significant economic and trade potential, yet its realization remains constrained by traditional dependencies on Russia and China and underutilized transit pathways. Unlocking this potential through the Middle Corridor requires substantial capital investment alongside comprehensive institutional reforms and modernized trade regulations. Enhanced Western engagement, particularly from the EU and the U.S., offers a strategic framework to diversify regional trade and integrate Central Asia into global markets. Ultimately, the long-term viability of the Middle Corridor hinges on lowering transit costs, accelerating administrative procedures, and establishing a predictable, transparent economic environment. BACKGROUND: Its geographical location and available natural resources make Central Asia a top priority in contemporary global politics and economics. While the region's transit potential is high, its own economic capacity is currently underutilized; exports are dominated by energy resources, while the bulk of imports originates from China and Russia. Furthermore, certain countries within the region remain excessively reliant on remittances sent home by workers living in Russia. Significant effort is required to fully unlock the region's economic capacity and expand its trade with the West. This will require rapid infrastructure development and comprehensive institutional reforms, including the modernization of trade and border-crossing regulations. Such measures could quickly double the region's economy and lay the foundation for close coordination and strategic cooperation with Western partners. Western interest (particularly from the EU and the U.S.) in Central Asia rests on several strategic considerations: The region offers an opportunity to expand market reach and secure reliable new partners, as well as resource base. In addition, the region holds significant economic and strategic balancing importance vis-à-vis China and Russia. Consequently, numerous efforts are underway by the U.S. and EU to reconnect historical links or establish new partnerships to foster trade opportunities and build long-term strategic alliances. One major initiative currently driving international discourse is the Middle Corridor, a route designed to connect Europe and Asia through Central Asia and the South Caucasus, allowing access to energy, critical minerals, and other goods and resources from the region, as well as Central Asian markets. The People’s Republic of China (PRC) maintains strong economic interest in the region and has already invested heavily. However, its interest in using the Middle Corridor by China is limited by the capacity of the transit corridor, as well as by the availability of alternative transit routes. Although the recent surge in traffic through the corridor is notable, the route requires careful feasibility planning and substantial capital investment to fulfill its expanded role. Based on current and expected trade numbers, the Middle Corridor will be more important for trade between the Central Asian countries, Europe and Mediterranean, and less important for Chinese transit. Meanwhile, the Russian Federation (RF) maintains strong political and commercial interests in Central Asia and aims to preserve its leading role as a transit hub for goods from China. Moscow retains several political and economic leverages in the region. The Russian Federation accounts for 15 to 31 percent of imports and 11 to 42 percent of exports across the five Central Asian states. By comparison, China accounts for 1 to 40 percent of imports and 5.8 to 25 percent of exports. Intra-regional trade remains minimal, peaking at just 20 percent in lower-income nations like Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan. Interestingly, Türkiye's share of trade with Central Asia also trails behind that of both Russia and China. The Middle Corridor faces numerous economic hurdles that must be addressed, including technical and institutional reforms aimed at reducing costs, increasing throughput capacity, and shortening transit times. Estimated infrastructure investments amount to tens of billions of dollars; without a clear economic return, potential investors and traders may hesitate. IMPLICATIONS : To evaluate the prospects of the Middle Corridor, it is essential to assess the Central Asian foreign trade market, its current and potential capacity. International trade across Central Asian states, with a combined population of 83 million, averages roughly US$ 2,500 per capita. By contrast, the three Baltic states with a combined population of 6.5 million generate a foreign trade volume nearly equal to that of Central Asia (US$ 202 billion total), translating to over US$ 33,000 per capita. This gap highlights Central Asia's immense untapped potential. However, realizing this potential will require substantial capital injection and a major modernization of the institutional framework. In total, the region currently conducts around US$ 260 billion in global trade (goods and services, including intra-regional trade), with merchandise trade accounting for US$ 216 billion. One critical area for development is the removal of trade and border-crossing barriers. Harmonizing regional trade policies and regulations with EU standards represents a vital step forward, allowing greater efficiency of the trade route. However, shifting away from long-standing ties with Russia carries potential political and economic costs. Hundreds of thousands of Central Asian migrant workers currently live in Russia, sending home hundreds of millions of dollars in remittances that support local economies. Oil and natural gas represent a quarter of the region’s foreign trade. Hydrocarbon exports account for approximately 49 percent of all exports (US$ 116 billion) and are transported almost entirely via pipelines. China is the region’s largest trading partner, handling nearly half of Central Asia's total merchandise trade (US$ 106 billion). Russia remains another primary trade partner with a 20 percent share, which is nevertheless gradually declining as trade shifts toward China. Institutional environment and economic freedom remain critical concerns: Kazakhstan ranks 68th and Uzbekistan 86th (both categorized as "moderately free") on the Heritage Foundation’s Index of Economic Freedom. The remaining three states rank below 114th, categorized as either "mostly unfree" or "repressed". Upgrading institutional quality would stimulate the wider economy and attract foreign investment beyond the oil and gas sectors. Border-crossing procedures present additional challenges. Current regulatory frameworks in Central Asia are tailored primarily for trade with Russia and China. Adapting these systems to EU standards, alongside digitizing and simplifying customs procedures, will be essential to lower transit costs. Georgia’s implementation of the Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area (DCFTA) with the EU offers a proven model for regional trade regulation. Furthermore, government integrity, local corruption, bureaucratic delays, political influence, and weak rule of law present significant obstacles. Central Asian governments must actively address these issues to prevent costly delays and administrative inefficiencies. Improving governance and mitigating local corruption risks requires reducing regulatory burdens, streamlining administrative processes, and leveraging digital technologies. Accelerating these institutional reforms will give potential investors the confidence to finance regional growth, increasing the flow of goods toward the EU and justifying the substantial investments needed for the Middle Corridor. https://www.cacianalyst.org/publications.body: Central Asia's Afghan Reality: What the U.S. Might be Missing Wednesday, 23 September 2026 Central Asia's Afghan Reality: What the U.S. Might be Missing Featured Published in Analytical Articles font size decrease font size increase font size Print Email By Zabikhulla Saipov The August 31–September 1 Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek offered a revealing snapshot of Afghanistan’s changing role in the region. The massive SCO gathering brought together the leaders of China, Russia, India, Iran, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Belarus. Its expanded SCO Plus meeting added Azerbaijan, Armenia, Egypt, Laos, Mongolia, Türkiye, Togo and Vietnam, alongside the UN and other organizations. U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor was in Bishkek meeting Central Asian leaders, while former U.S. Special Envoy for Afghanistan Zalmay Khalilzad was engaging Afghanistan’s Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi in Kabul. The juxtaposition is revealing: Afghanistan may have receded from Washington’s formal strategic agenda, but it has not receded from the calculations of the states surrounding it, or from every channel of U.S.–Afghan interaction. BACKGROUND: The precipitous U.S. departure from Afghanistan in 2021 altered the form of U.S. involvement, but it did not change the geography that had made Afghanistan central to Washington’s engagement with Central Asia. Afghanistan shares approximately 2,329 kilometers of common land and water borders with Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan, while all five Central Asian states remain exposed to security, economic, and connectivity issues pertaining to Afghanistan. After 2001, Afghanistan became a central organizing factor in Washington’s engagement with Central Asia, shaping security cooperation, military access, border assistance, counterterrorism policies and regional diplomacy. The withdrawal changed that equation, but not the underlying geography. Since 2021, Uzbekistan has been particularly active in treating Afghanistan not only as a security concern but as a potential connecting link between Central and South Asia. The Termez Dialogue , launched in May 2025 as a permanent platform is perhaps the clearest example of this approach. Its second meeting in June 2026 moved toward practical mechanisms for political dialogue, connectivity, transport and logistics, climate adaptation, and cultural-humanitarian cooperation. Rather than treating Afghanistan solely as a security perimeter, Tashkent is attempting to embed the Afghan question within a broader architecture of regional connectivity. This institutionalization also began to acquire a specifically Central Asian format in August 2025, when Uzbekistan convened the first meeting of Central Asian special representatives on Afghanistan , which agreed to establish a regular Contact Group for coordinated regional dialogue on the Afghan issue. Institutionalization, however, is moving in both directions. In April 2026, Afghanistan itself initiated the first Afghanistan–Central Asia Consultative Dialogue in Kabul , bringing together all five Central Asian states and proposing regular consultations, expert cooperation and a roadmap for cooperation in trade, transit, security and connectivity. The subsequent Afghanistan–Central Asia Think Tank Forum in June 2026 extended this process into the intellectual and policy sphere, explicitly seeking research-based proposals and locally generated regional narratives. Thus, Uzbekistan is building platforms through which Afghanistan can be incorporated into wider regional cooperation, while Kabul is simultaneously seeking to engage Central Asia on its own terms. Afghanistan remains an unavoidable geographic reality, but the institutional response to that reality is increasingly being shaped within the region itself. IMPLICATIONS : Central Asian ownership, however, should not be confused with Central Asian consensus. Uzbekistan emphasizes connectivity, trade and regional integration; Tajikistan remains particularly attentive to border security, inclusive government, and militant threats; Turkmenistan prioritizes energy, transit and neutrality; Kazakhstan approaches Afghanistan through economic and diplomatic engagement; and Kyrgyzstan, although less directly exposed geographically, participates in wider regional security discussions. These differences may explain why flexible regional mechanisms are emerging alongside existing multilateral institutions. For Kabul, the emerging collaborative architecture may represent both an opportunity and a necessity. The April Consultative Dialogue was initiated by the Afghan side, but its timing is particularly significant given Afghanistan’s increasingly constrained external environment. Tensions and armed confrontation with Pakistan have disrupted one of Afghanistan’s principal trade and transit corridors, while the wider war involving Iran has created additional uncertainty around western routes and regional commerce. Against this backdrop, Kabul’s turn toward Central Asia may amount to more than diplomatic activism. It can be understood as an effort to widen Afghanistan’s room for maneuver by strengthening alternative northern connections to Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan and the wider Eurasian market. In this sense, the Afghanistan–Central Asia dialogue may function as a form of strategic insurance at a moment when some of Afghanistan’s traditional routes and external options have become more vulnerable. Kabul is therefore increasingly seeking to participate in shaping the regional architecture around it. This does not automatically imply political convergence or recognition by Central Asian governments; rather, it reflects an attempt by Afghanistan’s de facto authorities to turn geography into diplomatic and economic leverage. The Bishkek SCO summit illustrates the wider environment in which this process is unfolding. The sheer composition of the gathering demonstrated the breadth of the Eurasian strategic conversation in which Afghanistan is situated. Afghanistan remained outside the summit, yet its political future and security implications remained part of the agenda. The SCO’s call for an inclusive Afghan government showed that regional powers continue to attach political conditions to their vision of Afghan stability. Uzbekistan used the same broader setting to advance institutional mechanisms of its own. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev highlighted Uzbekistan’s initiative to establish a Universal Center for Countering Security Challenges and Threats in Tashkent under the SCO’s Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure, indicating Tashkent’s interest in strengthening the region’s permanent capacity to address emerging security challenges. Together with the Termez Dialogue, the initiative illustrates a broader Uzbek strategy: institutionalizing regional cooperation rather than relying exclusively on ad hoc responses to individual crises. Gor’s presence in Bishkek demonstrated that the U.S. remains engaged with Central Asia, but increasingly from outside the Afghan theater. His meetings with Central Asian leaders focused on strategic partnerships, economic and investment cooperation, transport, energy, critical minerals and the C5+1 framework. On September 5, Khalilzad met Afghanistan’s Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi in Kabul to discuss Afghanistan–U.S. relations and opportunities for constructive engagement. Afghanistan’s Foreign Ministry presented the meeting as part of discussions on bilateral relations, economic growth and self-reliance, while the U.S. State Department clarified that Khalilzad is no longer a government employee and was acting in a personal capacity. These engagements therefore should not be interpreted as evidence of a new official U.S. policy toward Kabul. Their significance lies elsewhere: the U.S.–Afghan relationship has not simply disappeared; rather, it now exists through channels considerably different

Several notable events have recently occurred in this area, and a collective analysis of these developments demonstrates Afghanistan’s active involvement in the expanding network of Eurasian overland routes. China is providing practical support for this within the framework of its Belt and Road Initiative. Beijing’s strategy involves diversifying east-west logistics routes via Central Asia to minimize the growing risks of uncertainty in maritime shipping. Uzbekistan is expected to benefit particularly from this progress, as it prioritizes southern transit corridors and maintains pragmatic policies towards both Afghanistan and Iran. BACKGROUND: In June 2026, an Afghan delegation led by Deputy Minister for Railways, Mawlavi Mohammad Ishaq Sahibzada, visited Iran to discuss transport logistics infrastructure projects, including the construction of the Herat–Mazar-i-Sharif railway. The parties discussed technical specifications, standards, financing mechanisms and the stages of project implementation. Prior to the meeting in Tehran, media reports had indicated that Afghan commercial banks were willing to invest in the new railway line connecting the provinces of Balkh and Herat, estimated to cost US$ 780 million. It was later revealed that Iranian companies would undertake the construction of the infrastructure facility in exchange for participating in the development of Afghanistan’s mineral resources. The Herat–Mazar-i-Sharif transport line will serve as an extension of the cross-border trade route that originates in the Iranian city of Khaf, and will be a key component of the Afghan section of the Five Nations Railway Corridor (FNRC), which is approximately 2,100 km long. The FNRC extends to Kashgar in China and utilizes a uniform 1,435 mm standard gauge, crossing the borders of two Central Asian states: Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan. In a global context, this will create a more competitive continental East-West Corridor, in which Afghanistan and its northern neighbors will play a pivotal connecting role. The strategic importance of the Herat-Mazar-i-Sharif railway project is determined by its potential to connect Iran and Türkiye with the Central Asian republics and China via Afghanistan. It is worth noting that Ankara is a third party to the agreement on the joint construction of a railway to Mazar-i-Sharif, which was signed in Istanbul during the 36th regional meeting of the International Union of Railways in October 2025. In light of the Strait of Hormuz crisis triggered by the military standoff with the U.S., it has become critical necessity for Tehran to establish additional transport routes to China, one of its largest trading partners. Beijing is interested in both the Iranian market and the Islamic Republic’s extensive transit capabilities. On May 25, 2025, the first freight train departed from Xi’an, China, bound for the Iranian dry port of Aprin, marking the official launch of direct land transport between the two countries. The Xi’an-Aprin railway route passes through Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan, making use of the Uzen (Kazakhstan)-Bereket (Turkmenistan)-Gorgan (Iran) railway line. This line was opened in 2014 and forms part of the eastern route of the International North-South Transport Corridor. Within the framework of the six-party meeting mechanism for heads of railway administrations, a China-Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan-Turkmenistan-Iran-Türkiye/EU railway corridor is being developed . This involves Uzbekistan in container transport along the southern branch of the East-West Corridor. This development forms part of the wider initiative to establish the China-Europe Railway Express Economic Corridor under the Belt and Road Initiative. The expansion of the network of freight routes connecting Chinese and Central Asian cities should also be viewed in this context. Since early 2026, several regular and test block trains have been launched from industrial and economic centers in China, such as Chongqing , Sichuan , Jiangsu , Hubei and Xining , bound for Central Asian countries, with the potential to extend into Iran and beyond. IMPLICATIONS : The practical progress being made on constructing the Herat-Mazar-i-Sharif railway line, alongside the already operational Khaf-Herat railway, reflects Iran’s desire to diversify its freight transport corridors, particularly in view of the ongoing risks of disruption to maritime shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran is therefore prioritizing the expansion of rail connections with Afghanistan and its Central Asian partners. Implementing the Herat-Mazar-i-Sharif infrastructure project is central to achieving this objective, as announced by the Iranian government in August 2026. In light of the escalation of the Afghan-Pakistani conflict, the rail link between Iran and Afghanistan has given Kabul a significant opportunity to access the markets of the Persian Gulf states, Türkiye and the EU, offsetting the costs resulting from the temporary lack of access to the seaports of neighboring Pakistan. This has also boosted Iranian-Afghan trade, with an annual volume reaching US$ 3.6 billion. Similarly, bilateral freight traffic has sharply increased. From March 2025 to March 2026, over 640,000 tons of cargo were transported via the Khaf-Herat railway, compared to fewer than 15,000 tons during the previous period. Monthly volumes have already approached 130,000 tons, and projections indicate growth to 160,000 tons per month, or 1.5 million tons per year. It is estimated that, once the Khaf-Herat railway line is fully operational, the annual volume of interstate freight traffic could increase to 3 million tons, and transit freight to 1.7 million tons. These figures are in line with Tehran’s ambitious plan to increase the volume of cargo transported by rail to 60 million tons per year. This goal will be achieved by developing North-South and East-West international transport corridors, which will require close cooperation with neighboring countries, including those in Central Asia. Tehran has already announced plans to increase rail freight traffic with Kazakhstan to 5 million tons per year, with Turkmenistan to 4 million tons , and with Uzbekistan to 2 million tons . In order to speed up the transportation process and remove the physical barriers hindering the movement of cargo, Iran has reached agreements with Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan regarding the passage of its wagons, which should ensure their free movement throughout the CIS. However, these agreements have not yet been implemented. CONCLUSIONS: A review of Afghanistan’s foreign policy activities over the past few months reveals a noticeable synchronization of efforts between Kabul and Tehran in promoting the construction of a railway line to Mazar-i-Sharif. This project would establish an additional transport link to Central Asia via the Uzbek border. In this context, the visit of an Afghan technical delegation to Tashkent on July 22, 2026, is noteworthy. https://www.azernews.az/nation/266968.ht.body: Azerbaijan’s victory is a legacy for generations to come [OPINION] 7 November 2026 14:00 (UTC+04:00) By Mazahir Afandiyev In the “Year of Urban Planning and Architecture” declaring in accordance with the Order of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan our wise people mark November 8 – Victory Day with great enthusiasm, as it has for the past six years. The entire Azerbaijani people began November 8, 2020, with a new tremendous victory. Azerbaijan has experienced the power and pride of the victorious Azerbaijani Army throughout its existence as a state, and this has once again been shown to the world. That day, our heroic soldiers and officers pushed the enemy out of Shusha, the beating heart of Karabakh, by traversing deep ravines, steep cliffs, and great distances in difficult terrain. Naturally, the state and people of Azerbaijan have faced many challenges during the past 30 years in order to accomplish their objectives. In accordance with international legal standards and principles, and guided by four well-known United Nations Security Council resolutions that had existed on paper for 27 years, Azerbaijan carried out military operations on its sovereign territories on September 27, 2020, to put an end to the occupation of its territories that had been ongoing for more than 30 years. Following Armenia's formal request to the Russian Federation on November 10 of that year, Russia directly intervened in the conflict, and the heads of all three governments agreed to end it. Armenia signed an act of capitulation after a nine-point declaration between Azerbaijan and Armenia was approved. According to Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, Armenia was forced to concede defeat in front of our Glorious Army. As a result, the occupying side accepted defeat, and the conflict was formally declared over. Thus, our long-awaited efforts to liberate our native Karabakh resulted in victory in the 44-day Second Karabakh-Patriotic War and the raising of our cherished three-colored flag above our liberated city. This amazing victory, which became a triumph of our people's force and national pride, was memorialized by a decree issued by Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev. Considering the historical significance of Shusha's liberation from occupation, November 8 was designated as Victory Day. The Patriotic War's magnificent triumph of our brave army, led by Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev, which has been recorded as the "Iron Fist" operation in Azerbaijan's new history, serves as unambiguous evidence of the modern Azerbaijani state's military might and the Azerbaijani people's desire for victory. As was appropriately stressed in the address of the chairman of the Milli Majlis and the statement adopted at the Milli Majlis of the Republic of Azerbaijan's plenary session on November 3 in observance of Victory Day, the significance of the historic victory led by the triumphant Supreme Commander-In-Chief Ilham Aliyev is becoming more obvious. The core of success in the 44-day Patriotic War is built on four fundamental concepts: justice, statehood, law, and construction. Our territories were freed from 30 years of occupation as a result. The victory on November 8 paved the path for the total restoration of our state's territorial integrity and sovereignty. And the local anti-terrorist operation, which lasted one day in September 2023, put an end to the junta regime, which was functioning unlawfully in the nation. It also reinstated historical justice, creating a new, glorious chapter in our military history. The principles of states' territorial integrity and international law's supremacy were founded. Azerbaijan has frequently emphasized its position at every bilateral, multilateral, and international conference during the past six years thanks to its successful foreign policy. According to this position, it is now time to sign a Comprehensive Peace Agreement and usher in a period of reconstruction based on the region's new realities. The Washington Declaration was signed by the President of Azerbaijan, the Prime Minister of Armenia, and the President of the United States on August 8 of last year, marking a significant milestone. The prompt reconstruction and building work being done today in the Karabakh and East Zangezur Economic regions, as well as the successful implementation of the "Great Return" State program, demonstrate to the entire globe that the Azerbaijani state and its people are messengers of peace, tranquility, and sustainable development, especially in the South Caucasus. This is clearly shown by President Ilham Aliyev's routine travels to the newly liberated areas. At the same time, this triumph was the consequence of President Ilham Aliyev's effective continuation of the powerful state-building started by great leader Heydar Aliyev. The National Leader's persistent efforts led to the establishment of Azerbaijan as an independent, democratic republic in the modern era and the adoption of the State Flag and the Constitution, which served as symbols of our independence. The date of November 08 becomes the ultimate manifestation of the people, the army, and the state's unity. It's not a coincidence that November is among the months that are especially significant to us. This month, the grateful Azerbaijani people celebrate National Flag Day and Constitution Day with immense pride. As always, the Azerbaijani people express their sincere gratitude to the triumphant Supreme Commander-in-Chief, President Ilham Aliyev, as well as our heroic martyrs and veterans, and commemorate Victory Day with tremendous pleasure, pride, and glory. Under the leadership of President Ilham Aliyev, our courageous people continue to write history. Future generations, as well as ourselves, will continue to be proud of this illustrious past. As the head of State noted, “The people of Azerbaijan are united like this fist today! This will always be the case! This unity will last forever! This unity will help us to accomplish all our goals in the future.” ------- Mazahir Afandiyev is an author and a member of the Azerbaijani Parliament Tags: Victory Day 44-day Patriotic War

https://www.cacianalyst.org/publications.body: Turkmenistan Moves Toward Active Neutrality Wednesday, 07 October 2026 Turkmenistan Moves Toward Active Neutrality Featured Published in Analytical Articles font size decrease font size increase font size Print Email By Erlan Benedis-Grab On May 20, 2026 the UN General Assembly unanimously adopted a Turkmenistan-initiated resolution recasting neutrality as active stabilization rather than withdrawal from the global stage. Although it was ratified domestically in 2025, in July 2026 Turkmenistan became the last of the five Central Asian states to sign the Treaty on Friendship, Good-Neighborliness, and Cooperation for the Development of Central Asia in the 21st Century, nearly four years after it was opened for signature in 2022. On October 8, Ashgabat hosted the region’s newly consequential gathering, the Consultative Meeting of Central Asian and Azerbaijani heads of state (CMHS) in Avaza. Turkmenistan's recent actions suggest that a country once largely absent from multilateral institutions, is now an active participant in Greater Central Asian initiatives. BACKGROUND: Turkmenistan has, in the name of neutrality, pursued one of the most isolationist foreign policy orientations in Central Asia, if not the world. Unlike Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan is not a member of the Eurasian Economic Union; unlike Tajikistan, it is not a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization; and unlike Uzbekistan, it holds only associate status in the Commonwealth of Independent States. Saparmyrat Niyazov, or Turkmenbashi, intended to build neutrality into a sovereignty-as-state ideology , reinforcing his legitimacy, while also giving Turkmenistan a role as a neutral-venue country where opposing parties could meet. With almost 35 years having passed since independence, though, neutrality in Turkmenistan has yielded mixed results. Its benefit stems mainly from its energy policy. Turkmenistan’s ability to reach various markets has depended mainly on relations with transit countries, where its neutral posture serves as a positive factor. Yet, Turkmenistan’s economy remains in a precarious position , with persistent food, budget, and gas shortages. And, while it was able to serve as a host between warring parties during the Tajik and Afghan civil wars, it has not convened a major mediation since, while its neighbors have. Astana hosted the years-long talks on the Syrian conflict, one of the most violent in the contemporary period. Perhaps out of recognition of these shortcomings, Turkmenistan, while maintaining its policy of neutrality, is starting to emerge from its longstanding isolation. Most notably, it has begun to participate more substantially in regional cooperation projects. The Consultative Meetings of the Heads of State of Central Asia (CMHS), the region’s standing summit format convening the five presidents, launched in 2018. It was at the CMHS's 2022 summit that Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan signed the Treaty on Friendship, Good-Neighborliness, and Cooperation for the Development of Central Asia in the 21st Century. The treaty outlines cooperation agreements , including in critical areas like defense, law enforcement, water, energy, and a mutual-assistance clause. Tajikistan and Turkmenistan were both initially hesitant to sign on, citing the need to “complete all domestic procedures.” However, in August 2025 Tajikistan acceded , following a breakthrough in delimiting the borders of the Fergana Valley. Turkmenistan formally signed in July 2026. Turkmenistan previously hosted the CMHS at Avaza in 2021, its only turn as host to date. Since then, the format has grown more consequential, admitting Azerbaijan as a full member in 2025. Turkmenistan’s return as host in 2026 therefore fits its broader pattern of renewed regional engagement. Turkmenistan is also pursuing a renewed effort to participate more seriously in international intergovernmental organizations like the United Nations. In May 2026, Turkmenistan introduced the UN resolution “The Role and Importance of a Policy of Neutrality in Maintaining and Strengthening International Peace, Security and Sustainable Development” which the General Assembly adopted. The same language Turkmenistan once used to keep the world at a distance now draws it closer. IMPLICATIONS: Signing onto a regional cooperation treaty, hosting the CMHS, and making diplomatic pushes at the UN mark a Turkmen shift from isolation. Turkmenistan’s recent actions suggest a country poised to try to take on a bigger role in world affairs, motivated by a fear of being left behind, the changing external environment, the need for economic diversification, and regime legitimacy. Serdar Berdimuhamedov, who became president in 2022, has continued a doctrinal shift, begun under his father, away from Turkmenbashi’s “ permanent neutrality ” towards what might be called “active neutrality.” This policy seeks to utilize Turkmenistan’s non-aligned status as a platform for diplomacy. aPreviously, Turkmenbashi’s “permanent neutrality” was essentially a shield for disengagement, codified within the constitution. The changing nature of Russia's role in Central Asia partly explains this shift as well. That shield was primarily aimed at one country: Russia. Non-alignment justified staying out of Russian-led integration projects; however, Moscow's leverage has since thinned. China is moving in, and Russia's attention is fixed west, on Ukraine, so Turkmenistan has had to update its strategy to this new environment. Turkmenistan is pursuing renewed engagement with its neighbors. Turkmenistan’s signing of the Treaty on Friendship, Good-Neighborliness, and Cooperation for the Development of Central Asia in the 21st Century is the clearest marker of this. Although formally binding, the treaty is noncommittal, with no automatic trigger or enforcement mechanism. This is a significant factor in Turkmenistan’s accession, even though it was delayed. If a security threat arises, the response is “determined through bilateral consultations and within the framework of Consultative Meetings.” That falls well short of the CSTO treaty , which requires members to “immediately provide ... the necessary help, including military one,” or the CIS treaty, which permits “the use of the Armed Forces” in individual or collective self-defense. Regionalism is advancing regardless of Turkmenistan, and Ashgabat appears unwilling to be the one state left out of it. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have driven the push for deeper integration—and they have been largely successful in this. Intra-regional trade nearly doubled from 2020 to 2025, while the Fergana Valley states settled their long-running border dispute. Staying outside would have left Turkmenistan negotiating from outside a structure its neighbors had already built without it. Thus, by hosting the Avaza summit on October 8, Turkmenistan has a chance to set an important agenda. Ahead of the summit, Ashgabat circulated a draft agenda to its partners spanning security, diplomacy, trade and logistics, climate and water, and humanitarian cooperation. As Kazakhstan pointed out in July, the next steps should be to develop a concrete action plan as the CMHS format moves along. Economic diversification is an important focus for Turkmenistan. It remains constrained by near-total reliance on natural gas exports, the overwhelming majority bound for China. While mutual-assistance commitments are a tougher sell, proposals like Tajikistan’s prospective joint oil refinery are the kinds of economic initiatives that appeal to Ashgabat. International validation of Turkmenistan’s neutrality reinforces the legitimacy of the ruling family, making prestige a significant motivator for Ashgabat. The May 2026 UN resolution gave neutrality a standalone General Assembly agenda item , strengthening Turkmenistan’s diplomatic profile. This momentum also supports its bid for a 2031–2032 UN Security Council seat, which would provide another significant

https://www.azernews.az/karabakh/266982..body: Azerbaijan, Armenia and US launch trilateral working groups to advance TRIPP corridor 7 November 2026 15:12 (UTC+04:00) Akbar Novruz Read more Azerbaijan, Armenia and the United States have launched trilateral technical planning groups to accelerate implementation of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), marking a new stage in efforts to develop regional transport and energy connectivity. According to a joint statement released by the governments of the three countries, the initiative was launched by US Assistant Secretary of State for European and Eurasian Affairs Brendan Hanrahan, Armenian Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Trade Vahan Kostanyan, and Azerbaijani Deputy Foreign Minister Elnur Mammadov. The newly established mechanism will bring together policymakers and technical experts from Azerbaijan, Armenia and the United States to address practical aspects of implementing TRIPP, a multimodal transit route intended to strengthen regional connectivity and economic cooperation. The initiative follows the August 8, 2025, Washington Peace Summit Declaration, brokered by US President Donald Trump, which established a framework for advancing peace and regional cooperation between Azerbaijan and Armenia. As an initial step, the three countries agreed to establish two technical planning groups focusing on transportation infrastructure and electricity transmission. The transportation group will address technical issues related to the development of the transit route, while the electricity transmission group will examine the energy infrastructure required to support regional connectivity. According to the joint statement, these mechanisms are intended to help resolve complex technical challenges and facilitate progress towards subsequent stages of implementation, including connections with existing regional infrastructure networks. The three governments emphasised that the initiative reflects their shared commitment to translating the agreements reached in Washington into practical results. They also highlighted the potential contribution of TRIPP to long-term regional stability, economic development, commercial opportunities and stronger connections between neighbouring countries. The sides reaffirmed their commitment to accelerating the operationalisation of all elements of TRIPP. https://www.azernews.az/oil_and_gas/2669.body: Azerbaijan's Chirag platform produces nearly 108 million tonnes of oil over 29 years 7 November 2026 10:54 (UTC+04:00) Akbar Novruz Read more Azerbaijan's Chirag offshore platform has produced 107.8 million tonnes of oil and 25 billion cubic metres of natural gas since operations began in 1997, according to the Ministry of Energy. The figures, recorded as of November 1, 2026, mark 29 years since the launch of production at Chirag, one of the landmark facilities in Azerbaijan's offshore oil industry. The platform played a pivotal role in the development of the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli (ACG) field, with the commencement of production in 1997 marking the beginning of Azerbaijan's so-called Early Oil programme. Located approximately 120 kilometres east of Baku in the Caspian Sea, Chirag operates in waters around 120 metres deep. The offshore facility is designed to support oil and gas production, drilling operations and accommodation for personnel. Its infrastructure includes a platform with 24 well slots and water-injection facilities, alongside an extensive network of subsea pipelines connecting the field to Azerbaijan's energy infrastructure. These include a 176-kilometre, 24-inch oil pipeline transporting crude to the Sangachal Terminal, a 48-kilometre, 16-inch gas pipeline connecting the platform to Oil Rocks (Neft Dashlari), and a 12-kilometre, 18-inch gas pipeline linking Chirag to the Central Azeri Compression and Water Injection Platform. According to operational figures, production from the Chirag platform averaged approximately 19,300 barrels of oil per day during the first half of 2026. Tags: Oil Rocks field Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli (ACG)
