https://www.azernews.az/analysis/266948..body: Azerbaijan’s Karabakh victory offers lessons in the future of warfare 7 November 2026 07:00 (UTC+04:00) Ulviyya Poladova Read more 10 November 2020 was a date that would be written in golden letters in Azerbaijan's history. It marked the day when territories forcibly separated from Azerbaijan in the 1990s and kept under occupation for more than three decades were finally restored to its control. Yet the significance of that day extended beyond a military victory. It also demonstrated how advanced technology, military preparedness and evolving battlefield tactics could determine the outcome of a conflict. Over the course of 44 days, Azerbaijani forces advanced through challenging terrain, covering kilometres of winding roads, steep slopes and mountainous landscapes. Their campaign culminated in the liberation of Jabrayil, Fuzuli, Zangilan, Gubadli and, finally, Shusha – a city whose return had become a long-awaited national aspiration. The operation, codenamed Iron Fist, demonstrated the tactical capabilities, discipline and combat readiness of the Azerbaijani armed forces. On 10 November 2020, Armenia signed a trilateral statement bringing the fighting to an end and accepting the new military realities on the ground. When hostilities erupted in September 2020, Azerbaijan's objective was clear: to restore control over territories lost during the First Karabakh War. Forty-four days later, Azerbaijani forces had fundamentally altered the territorial map and military balance of the South Caucasus. Several factors contributed to Azerbaijan's success. Its armed forces made effective use of drones and other precision-guided weapons, weakening Armenia's military positions and exposing the limitations of conventional military tactics. The coordination of air power with ground operations, alongside the maintenance of reliable supply lines, also proved crucial. Equally important were years of investment in military modernisation, advanced weaponry and the development of the country's defence capabilities. Much can be said about the course of the 44-day war, its military strategy and its wider consequences. But one point stands out: the conflict did not simply transform the geopolitical balance of the South Caucasus; it also resonated far beyond the region, attracting international attention and prompting wider discussion about sovereignty, territorial integrity and the changing nature of warfare. It is no coincidence that Azerbaijan's experience has acquired particular relevance in the context of Ukraine's ongoing struggle to regain control over its territories. As the Ukrainian people continue their fight, Azerbaijan's historic victory in Karabakh has also served as an example and a source of motivation, reinforcing the belief that the restoration of territorial integrity remains an achievable objective, even after decades of conflict and difficult political circumstances. In a comment for AzerNEWS, Ukrainian military expert Oleg Zhdanov noted that Azerbaijan’s military success in restoring control over its internationally recognised territories was the result of long-term strategic planning, patience and the gradual strengthening of its armed forces. Assessing Azerbaijan’s military strategy, Zhdanov said one of the most important decisions made by the country’s political and military leadership was to avoid rushing into action before the armed forces were sufficiently prepared. "The most important decision taken by Azerbaijan’s leadership, first and foremost at the political level, was patience - patience in assessing the adversary and in evaluating the country’s own capabilities to achieve victory on the battlefield," he said. According to the expert, Azerbaijan’s leadership recognised that a significant difference in military capabilities would be essential to securing success. This required a comprehensive process of modernisation, rearmament and investment in the armed forces, which could not be achieved overnight. Zhdanov stressed that strengthening military capabilities also depended on economic development, as a strong financial foundation was necessary to purchase modern weapons and equip the army with advanced systems. Commenting on the relevance of Azerbaijan’s military experience in the context of the ongoing war in Ukraine, Zhdanov said the conflict had marked an important turning point in the evolution of warfare. Zhdanov suggested that Azerbaijan’s experience could be viewed as a historical milestone in the transition towards a new model of warfare. In his opinion, the conflict may go down in history as one of the last wars fought predominantly according to the conventional military model of the 20th century. According to him, the broader significance of Azerbaijan’s experience is for countries seeking to restore their territorial integrity. He said Azerbaijan’s example demonstrates that the passage of time and the complexity of political and military circumstances do not diminish the importance of sovereignty and internationally recognised borders. "I believe this will serve as an example, including for our country. Regardless of how much time has passed and how difficult the decision to begin military operations may be, sovereignty and territorial integrity remain the most important principles for any state," he emphasised. The expert described Azerbaijan’s achievement as a positive example for other countries, emphasising that the country had ultimately restored control over territories that had remained under occupation for nearly three decades. ------ Photo credit: Forbes Tags: Azerbaijan Karabakh Armenia Ukraine Garabagh Patriotic War drones

https://www.azernews.az/oil_and_gas/2669.body: China tightens control over fuel exports amid market pressures 6 November 2026 18:29 (UTC+04:00) Ulviyya Poladova Read more China’s state-owned oil refineries are expected to reduce diesel exports this month due to limited stockpiles. According to consulting firm Energy Aspects, the restrictions could be eased only if domestic demand weakens. In its latest report, the company cut its forecast for China’s diesel exports this month by 400,000 tonnes to 580,000 tonnes. However, Energy Aspects noted that refineries are seeking to maintain high export levels and expect domestic demand to weaken from mid-November. The company therefore does not rule out the possibility of revising its forecast upwards. Last month, China allocated additional fuel export quotas to refineries, bringing the total volume of export quotas issued since the beginning of the year to its highest level since 2021. However, following the outbreak of the US-Iran conflict, authorities tightened controls over monthly fuel exports. In August and September, Chinese refineries increased exports, playing a stabilizing role in the global market, which had been disrupted by the conflict in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war. Energy Aspects also attributed the downward revision in its diesel export forecast to weaker export margins. Meanwhile, the consulting firm left its forecasts for gasoline and jet fuel exports unchanged. China’s gasoline exports are expected to reach 780,000 tonnes in November, while jet fuel exports are projected at 2.21 million tonnes. Tags: Middle East Russia China Ukraine export diesel

https://www.azernews.az/region/266961.ht.body: Iran: We won't be satisfied with US paper commitments 6 November 2026 22:00 (UTC+04:00) Akbar Novruz Read more Iranian Supreme National Security Council Deputy Secretary Ali Bagheri stated on Friday that Tehran will no longer be satisfied with Washington's "paper commitments," claiming that the United States "disrupted" peace talks several times this year by "breaking their promises." "It is the right of the Islamic Republic of Iran not to be satisfied with the Americans' paper commitments before entering a new arena of diplomacy," Bagheri said. "Iran must see with its own eyes the practical actions of the United States, and once these actions are observed, the ground will be open for opening a new chapter," he added. https://www.azernews.az/culture/266951.h.body: Azerbaijan Dance Festival brings together more than 1,000 participants from 20 countries [PHOTOS/VIDEO] 6 November 2026 17:37 (UTC+04:00) Qabil Ashirov Read more The fifth Azerbaijan Dance Festival was held in Baku, bringing together more than 1,000 participants from over 20 countries during a four-day international event. She is the granddaughter of Tarana Muradova, Azerbaijan's People's Artist and a renowned dancer, teacher and choreographer, Trend reports. Despite her young age, Zahra has already developed a strong interest in various forms of art. She is talented in drawing, studies music, and this year fulfilled one of her biggest childhood dreams by gaining admission to the Baku Choreography Academy. Ballroom dancing has now become another passion in her artistic journey. It also gave her a chance to gain her first stage experience in a new dance discipline. Her performance could mark the beginning of her own journey in the world of dance. Notably, Zahra had been studying ballroom dancing for just one month before taking part in the festival, yet she had already demonstrated promising progress. "She has a strong passion for art, but I have given her the freedom to choose her own creative path. I have always believed that children should decide for themselves which artistic direction to pursue and what profession they want to follow in the future. Zahra was actually the one who persuaded us to enroll her in the academy. Her greatest New Year's wish was to gain admission to the Baku Choreography Academy. She is very determined and likes to achieve things independently," the People's Artist said. Zahra's story is particularly noteworthy given the important role art plays in her family. Her grandmother has devoted her life to dance, the stage and training new generations of performers. However, as Tarana Muradova emphasizes, what matters most is not simply carrying on a family tradition, but a child's genuine passion for creativity, willingness to develop, explore new horizons and achieve personal goals through independent effort. The festival was organized by Smooth & Rhythm Dance Style (SRDS), led by its founder and president, Olga Krasnyanskaya, together with the Azerbaijan Dance Council (AzDC), headed by Azerbaijan's People's Artist Tarana Muradova. https://www.azernews.az/culture/266932.h.body: Azerbaijan National Library opens Victory Hall ahead of November 8 Victory Day [PHOTOS] 6 November 2026 16:50 (UTC+04:00) By Alimat Aliyeva The Azerbaijan National Library inaugurated a new “Victory Hall” and presented a digital information database entitled “November 8 – Victory Day” on November 6. The event was jointly organized by the Ministry of Culture and the Azerbaijan National Library. The ceremony opened with the national anthem, followed by a minute of silence in memory of Azerbaijani martyrs who sacrificed their lives for their homeland. Speakers at the opening ceremony included Karim Tahirov, Director of the Azerbaijan National Library and professor; Polad Bulbuloglu, Member of Parliament and Chairman of the Parliamentary Committee on Culture; Farid Jafarov, Deputy Minister of Culture; MP Aydin Mirzazade; academician Nizami Jafarov; Teymur Karimli, Director of the Institute of Manuscripts of the Azerbaijan National Academy of Sciences and academician; Rashad Majid, Deputy Chairman of the Azerbaijan Writers' Union; and Ibrahim Aliyev, Head of the Baku City Main Department of Culture. In their remarks, the speakers emphasized that the historic victory achieved during the 44-day Patriotic War represented a triumph of the Azerbaijani people's national unity, the strength of the state and the heroism of the Armed Forces. They noted that the victory, achieved under the leadership of Victorious Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev, marked the beginning of a new chapter in Azerbaijan's history and would remain forever etched in the nation's collective memory. The speakers also stressed that preserving the historical record of the Victory, passing the realities of the Patriotic War on to future generations and keeping alive the memory of the fallen heroes constitute an important moral and public responsibility. In this regard, the establishment of the Victory Hall at the National Library was described as particularly significant. The new space is designed to present Azerbaijan's Victory history through documents, books, photographs and other informational materials. It will also bring together relevant publications and historical records in one location, making them accessible to readers and researchers. The speakers highlighted the important role of libraries as cultural institutions responsible for safeguarding national memory and transmitting historical truths to future generations. The Victory Hall is expected to contribute to fulfilling this mission. The event continued with the presentation of the electronic information database entitled “November 8 – Victory Day.” It was noted that the digital resource provides a unified platform for collecting and organizing information related to Azerbaijan's Victory, making relevant materials more accessible to users. Following the presentation, participants toured the newly established Victory Hall. The exhibition features books, publications and other materials dedicated to the Patriotic War, the restoration of Azerbaijan's territorial integrity, the historic Victory and the memory of the country's fallen heroes. The establishment of the Victory Hall and the launch of the digital database at the National Library represent an important contribution to documenting, researching and promoting Azerbaijan's Victory history, preserving national and spiritual values, and educating future generations about the historical significance of the Patriotic War. Tags: Culture Azerbaijan National Library Patriotic War

https://www.azernews.az/business/266917..body: Azerbaijan's non-oil tax revenues rise 13.1% to nearly $7 billion 6 November 2026 12:29 (UTC+04:00) Akbar Novruz Read more Azerbaijan's tax revenues from the non-oil and gas sector increased by 13.1% year on year to AZN 11.78 billion ($6.93 billion) in January–October 2026, according to the State Tax Service under the Ministry of Economy. The figure represents an increase of AZN 1.36 billion ($802.7 million) compared with the corresponding period of 2025 and exceeds the budget forecast by AZN 297.4 million ($174.9 million). Overall, tax revenues collected for the state budget through the State Tax Service reached AZN 16.07 billion ($9.45 billion) during the first ten months of 2026. This was AZN 1.27 billion ($749.5 million) above the forecast, while year-on-year collections increased by AZN 1.69 billion ($992.2 million), or 11.7%. The figures indicate that non-oil and gas activities accounted for approximately 73.3% of total tax revenues collected through the State Tax Service during the reporting period. Tax revenues from the oil and gas sector, calculated as the difference between total collections and non-oil revenues, amounted to approximately AZN 4.29 billion ($2.52 billion). Social insurance contributions also exceed forecasts Alongside the increase in tax revenues, Azerbaijan recorded higher-than-expected receipts from mandatory social insurance contributions. Between January and October 2026, mandatory state social insurance contributions totalled AZN 5.67 billion ($3.34 billion), exceeding the forecast by AZN 297.1 million ($174.8 million). Of this amount, more than AZN 3.84 billion ($2.26 billion) was collected from non-budgetary organisations. Meanwhile, unemployment insurance contributions reached approximately AZN 201.5 million ($118.5 million), surpassing the forecast by AZN 8.3 million ($4.9 million). Non-budgetary organisations accounted for AZN 156.5 million ($92.1 million) of unemployment insurance receipts. Mandatory health insurance contributions also exceeded projections, reaching more than AZN 849.3 million ($499.6 million) during the reporting period. This represented an additional AZN 20.4 million ($12 million) above the forecast, while receipts from non-budgetary organisations amounted to approximately AZN 570.9 million ($335.8 million). https://www.azernews.az/business/266913..body: Azerbaijan recovers 107 million manats as financial oversight tightens 6 November 2026 12:04 (UTC+04:00) Qabil Ashirov Read more Azerbaijan recovered 106.9 million manats in public funds and prevented unjustified expenditures totalling 100.9 million manats through financial oversight measures conducted during January-September 2026. The Ministry of Finance disclosed the figures in its report covering the first nine months of 2026. The State Financial Control Service completed oversight activities covering 84 organizations during the reporting period. Of these, 52 inspections were conducted based on decisions received from law enforcement agencies, while the remaining 32 were carried out as unscheduled inspections. The oversight measures resulted in the recovery of 106.9 million manats in public funds from the organizations examined. Furthermore, the authorities prevented unjustified or legally non-compliant expenditures amounting to 100.9 million manats. The Ministry of Finance also continued its financial expertise activities during the reporting period, with particular attention to improving the efficiency of state investment projects in territories liberated from occupation. The measures were designed to ensure the efficient implementation of public investment and infrastructure projects, promote the economical use of state budget resources, optimize project costs and strengthen preventive financial oversight. A total of 91 projects underwent financial expertise during January-September. Of these, 59 had been completed, while implementation of the remaining 32 projects was ongoing. The combined value of the 59 completed projects amounted to 1.038 billion manats. Financial expertise covered assessments of both project costs and the scope of planned works. During cost assessments, specialists evaluated whether expenditures on goods, materials, equipment and labor, as well as the use of machinery and mechanisms, corresponded to applicable standards and prevailing market prices. The assessment process also examined the consistency of work quantities and calculations presented in project drawings and cost-estimate documentation. In addition, specialists reviewed project documentation to identify discrepancies between approved designs and estimated costs, helping detect potential deviations during implementation. These measures form part of the government's efforts to improve the management of public investment, strengthen financial discipline and ensure the efficient allocation of budgetary resources, particularly in reconstruction and infrastructure development across liberated territories. Tags: Manat finance Ministry of Finance

https://www.azernews.az/events/266936.ht.body: Georgia deports 143 Azerbaijani nationals in first nine months of 2026 6 November 2026 14:39 (UTC+04:00) Ulviyya Poladova Read more A total of 3,170 foreign nationals were deported from Georgia between January and September this year. During the reporting period, 143 Azerbaijani citizens were deported from Georgia. This was reported by Georgia’s Ministry of Internal Affairs. Amendments to the law have strengthened procedures for deporting foreign nationals who overstay their permitted period of stay, lack the required visa or residence permit, or work without the necessary authorization. India ranked second with 306 deportations, followed by Turkmenistan (274), Russia (254) and Iran (180). The list also includes citizens of China, Pakistan, Egypt and Uzbekistan. https://www.azernews.az/analysis/266838..body: SOCAR’s US gas deal advances Azerbaijan’s ambitions as global energy investor 6 November 2026 08:30 (UTC+04:00) Qabil Ashirov Read more SOCAR’s $1.65 billion agreement with Comstock Resources reshapes the geography of Azerbaijan’s energy investments. By acquiring interests in the Legacy Haynesville and Western Haynesville upstream assets and a share of Pinnacle Gas Services, Azerbaijan’s state oil company is purchasing exposure to the United States’ natural gas economy. The central question is how effectively it converts national capital into durable foreign earnings and a stronger international position. The transaction gives SOCAR a 20% interest in Comstock’s Legacy Haynesville upstream assets, a 15% interest in its Western Haynesville assets and 15% of Comstock’s 73% stake in Pinnacle Gas Services, equivalent to 10.95% of the company. The $1.65 billion cash price is subject to customary adjustments, with an effective date of July 1, 2026. Comstock retains operatorship, while SOCAR participates through its ownership interests. Comstock’s operating figures show the scale. In the third quarter of 2026, the company produced 122.4 billion cubic feet equivalent, up 9% year on year and 8% quarter on quarter. It reported $359.3 million in natural gas and oil sales, including realized hedging gains, and $180.2 million in operating cash flow. Its realized price reached $2.94 per thousand cubic feet equivalent after hedging, while average production costs stood at $0.80 per Mcfe. These figures cover Comstock’s entire operation, rather than SOCAR-attributable output or income. The deal also has a corporate-finance dimension. Comstock said the proceeds would reduce its net debt from approximately $3.1 billion, measured at June 30, 2026, to around $1.5 billion. That is a reduction of roughly 52%. SOCAR’s capital helps the US producer strengthen its balance sheet and fund acreage development, while Azerbaijan gains exposure to a growing production platform. Western Haynesville adds another strategic layer. The implied debt reduction also matters for project execution: lower leverage can improve access to credit, support drilling schedules and strengthen the producer’s capacity to connect new wells to gathering infrastructure. For SOCAR, this financial reset may improve the operating environment surrounding the assets it has acquired. Comstock has identified 545,000 net acres in the area as a major development resource. During the third quarter, six Western Haynesville wells were brought online, each with an average initial production rate of 33 million cubic feet per day. Sixteen Legacy Haynesville wells also entered sales, with average initial production of 25 MMcf per day. These initial rates indicate development potential, while sustained output and cash generation remain the decisive measures. A key potential benefit for Azerbaijan is geographic diversification of SOCAR’s earnings. Domestic hydrocarbon production remains central to exports, public revenues and the country’s external balance. Overseas assets add income tied to another market, regulatory system and customer base. If SOCAR receives distributions in dollars and channels part of the proceeds to Azerbaijan, the investment could support foreign-currency inflows, domestic capital expenditure and, ultimately, state dividends. That contribution depends on financing, taxes, operating costs, gas prices and distribution timing. The 15% return mechanism deserves attention. SOCAR’s Western Haynesville interest is scheduled to fall from 15% to 7.5% after five years and once a 15% return on investment has been achieved. This structure sets a return threshold while allowing Comstock a larger share of future upside. The precise definition of the return measure, including whether it is calculated as an annualized internal rate of return or another metric, will be central to assessing the deal’s value over time. The investment also links Azerbaijan commercially with the US gas industry. Comstock’s September announcement said the partners would explore international marketing opportunities for gas attributable to Comstock’s interest, including potential LNG sales outside the United States. That possibility could connect SOCAR’s global gas-trading capabilities with Haynesville production and international buyers. Such exports depend on liquefaction capacity, shipping costs, approvals and contract prices. The $1.65 billion price should be assessed against attributable production, free cash flow, capital expenditure, financing costs, realized prices and internal rate of return. Comstock’s quarterly operating cash flow of $180.2 million offers context, although it represents the entire company. The deal converts Azerbaijani energy capital into an overseas producing asset. Its national value rests on cash generation, expertise and future dividends to Azerbaijan. That strengthens the long-term value of SOCAR’s entry. For Azerbaijan, disciplined execution will ultimately determine the investment’s long-term national value. https://ashgabat.osce.org/news/centre-as.body: News News Item OSCE promotes exchange of experiences in penitentiary reform between law-enforcement agencies of Moldova and Turkmenistan Issued on: 6 November 2026 Issued by: OSCE Centre in Ashgabat Fields of work: Human rights Representatives of law-enforcement bodies and the Office of the Ombudsperson of Turkmenistan discussed best practices in reducing prison populations during an OSCE-organized study visit to Chisinau, Moldova, held from 4 to 6 November 2026. The delegation visited the Head Office of Moldova’s Probation Service, where they were briefed on its legal framework, institutional structure, mandate and functions. The Turkmen delegation discussed with their Moldovan counterparts community-based (non-custodial) sanctions, supervision of probationers, community service and social reintegration programmes. A visit to the Electronic Monitoring Centre provided the delegation with an opportunity to learn about the electronic monitoring system, its software platform and related procedures. “This visit is part of the Centre’s efforts to support Turkmenistan in advancing its penitentiary system in line with international standards and OSCE commitments,” said William Leaf, Head of the OSCE Centre in Ashgabat. “The visit provided an excellent platform for discussing Moldova’s good practices in reducing prison populations, including the use of non-custodial sentences as an alternative to incarceration and expanding opportunities for rehabilitation,” added Leaf. During a visit to the territorial office of the Probation Service in Ceadir-Lunga, Gagauzia, the delegation learnt about Moldova’s social reintegration programmes for probationers, post-detention support, and co-operation with civil society and social partners. They also met with representatives of the National Legal Aid Council (NLAC) to discuss the state-guaranteed legal aid system. A meeting with representatives of Moldova’s Office of the People’s Advocate focused on the National Preventive Mechanism against Torture, complaint-handling procedures and co-operation between the Ombudsperson’s Office, the Probation Service and the NLAC. https://hcnm.osce.org/news/hcnm/669507.body: News News Item OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities convenes roundtable on multilingual education with education ministers from Central Asia and Mongolia Issued on: 5 November 2026 Issued by: OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Fields of work: Conflict prevention and resolution , Human rights , National minority issues , Tolerance and non-discrimination , Education , Youth OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Christophe Kamp and Turkmenistan’s Education Ministry hosted a ministerial roundtable on multilingual education in Ashgabat on 22 October 2026. The roundtable was attended by education ministers and ministerial representatives from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, together with representatives of international organizations and academia. Speaking on behalf of the High Commissioner,* Eleonora Lotti, HCNM Senior Adviser and Head of Section, drew attention to the particular character of the region, where the languages are spoken across state borders in every direction. “Almost every state language represented at this table is also a mother-tongue spoken by communities across a border,” she said. “A child who cannot follow the language of the classroom is not only shut out of one part of school, they are shut out of all of it, no matter how well the school is resourced,” Lotti said. She also stressed the value of language-in-education policy for society as a whole. “Education systems that give children a secure footing in their first language as well as a genuine command of the state language instil a strong sense of belonging, which leads to trust, stability and a more cohesive society, which can prevent tensions from taking root,” she said. The delegations discussed how they can address common challenges together. They identified the availability and training of teachers able to teach through more than one language, the development and sharing of teaching materials and subject terminology, and educational data and assessment as areas that could benefit from more co-operation. The delegations reached a tentative agreement on a joint communiqué on fostering regional co-operation through multilingual education in Central Asia and Mongolia. The event builds on the HCNM’s long-term inter-state dialogue on social integration and the education of national minorities, which began 20 years ago. This initiative also included the Central Asia Education Programme, which was implemented by the office of the HCNM and UNICEF between 2012 and 2021. The roundtable also marked the 30th anniversary of The Hague Recommendations Regarding the Education Rights of National Minorities . * Due to unforeseen circumstances, the High Commissioner was unable to travel to Ashgabat. https://rfom.osce.org/representative-fre.body: Press release OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media warns of growing pressure on journalists in bi-annual report Date: 5 November 2026 Place: VIENNA Source: OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media VIENNA, 5 November – The OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media (RFoM), Ambassador Jan Braathu, highlighted the crucial importance of media freedom to strengthen security and democratic resilience in his fourth bi-annual report to the OSCE Permanent Council. “Citizens need to be able to question decisions that affect their lives, hear competing perspectives, and make their own judgements. Independent and pluralistic media help make this possible. Democracy depends on these freedoms every day,” the Representative said. Legal harassment, hostile rhetoric and the safety of journalists In his report, the RFoM examines the gap between OSCE participating States’ commitments and the realities observed within the OSCE region, highlighting growing hostility against journalists and efforts by some participating States to control the media narrative. Legal harassment can lead to heavy sentences against journalists and media organizations, lengthy imprisonments and the criminalization of legitimate, public interest journalism. At the same time, so-called strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPP) impose financial and psychological pressure on journalists, and discourage critical and investigative reporting, the Representative noted in the report, calling on participating States to enact anti-SLAPP legislation covering both domestic and cross-border cases. Hostile rhetoric by public officials and political figures further deepens an already difficult working environment, particularly when it is followed or amplified by online harassment, threats, or attacks on journalists’ families. Media professionals continue to face harassment and violence while carrying out their work. Excessive force and obstruction when covering demonstrations and public events, including by law enforcement officials, as well as attacks and intimidation typically targeting investigative journalists, prevent reporting on issues of particular public interest. The role of technological development Alongside physical dangers, cyberattacks targeting media outlets and online harassment of journalists — in particular women and members of minorities — hinder journalistic reporting, encourage self-censorship, and, as a result, deprive audiences of important information. Emerging technologies pose additional threats as digital platforms increasingly determine what people encounter through ubiquitous algorithmic systems that lack transparency and accountability. Artificial intelligence is changing how information is produced, selected, and presented. These technologies offer opportunities, but also concentrate influence over the visibility and financial viability of journalism, Braathu noted in his report. “When reliable reporting disappears, it leaves information vacuums. Rumour, propaganda, and manipulation will fill the void. Our response must strengthen the conditions that allow trustworthy information to be produced and shared,” the Representative added. Independent public service media are essential infrastructure to ensure a diverse media environment and informed public debate. “While trust in media in general is declining across the region, trust in public service media remains generally high. This is important to sustain, especially as public service media contribute as a societal bulwark against disinformation,” the Representative noted. The RFoM report also pointed to important progress, including recent releases of journalists from detention, and legislative advances against abusive lawsuits and in other areas in a number of participating States. However, further efforts are needed to build on these developments and ensure their effective implementation. “Can a journalist investigate without fear? Can a source speak in confidence? Can a newsroom withstand political pressure? These are the questions by which implementation should be judged. The commitments are already ours. So is the responsibility to give them effect,” Braathu concluded. Full report by the Representative on Freedom of the Media Annex to the RFoM's Permanent Council Report The OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media observes media developments in all 57 OSCE participating States. He provides early warning on violations of freedom of expression and media freedom and promotes full compliance with OSCE media freedom commitments. https://www.osce.org/chairpersonship/669.body: Press release OSCE Chairman-in-Office Cassis visits OSCE Missions in Belgrade, Pristina and Skopje Date: 6 November 2026 Source: OSCE Chairpersonship BERN, 6 November 2026 – OSCE Chairman-in-Office and Swiss Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis visited OSCE Missions in Belgrade, Pristina and Skopje, meeting with Mission heads and staff to acknowledge their work on the ground and reaffirm the OSCE’s commitment to the region. In Belgrade, Cassis met with Ambassador Marcel Peško, Head of the OSCE Mission to Serbia, and Mission staff. During his visit, the Transparency and Accountability for Serbia: Key Reforms project, to which Switzerland financially contributes, was signed. The Chairman-in-Office highlighted the Mission’s work with Serbian institutions and partners to support reforms in areas including democratization, the rule of law, media freedom, security co-operation, and human and minority rights. In Pristina, Cassis met with Ambassador Gerard McGurk, Head of the OSCE Mission in Kosovo, and Mission staff. He commended their commitment to strengthening democratic governance, supporting a transparent judiciary and security sector, and protecting and promoting human and community rights. For more than 25 years, the Mission has worked with institutions and communities to foster trust and dialogue. In Skopje, Cassis met with Ambassador Kilian Wahl, Head of the OSCE Mission to Skopje, and Mission staff. He recognized the Mission’s continued work with national institutions and local communities to strengthen the rule of law, improve criminal justice, combat corruption, promote gender equality and support young people. He also highlighted the importance of the OSCE’s longstanding partnership with North Macedonia, built over 30 years, and the Mission’s concrete achievements. Looking back on his trip, the Chairman-in-Office said that “OSCE field operations are one of the Organization’s greatest strengths. Through their long-term presence, local knowledge and trusted partnerships, the Missions help translate OSCE commitments into practical support, facilitates dialogue and contributes to lasting reforms. Dialogue and co-operation are at the heart of the OSCE and will remain central to Switzerland’s Chairpersonship.” Contacts Press Office Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, Bern Email: kommunikation@eda.admin.ch Elisa Raggi Head of Communications, Permanent Mission of Switzerland to the OSCE Email: elisa.raggi@eda.admin.ch Communication and Media Relations Section OSCE Secretariat Email: press@osce.org About us Chairpersonship Chairpersonship The country chairing the OSCE for one year
